title: The Wizard of Open Weights: Chris Alexiuk Makes AI Easy With Open Models
body:
Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it.
“We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers.
Alexiuk’s preferred “rooftop” is [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL5B692fm6--vEL0FwctKghCpyEnBGAQJA), where he’s built a following teaching curious thousands how to build, fine-tune, evaluate and ship production LLM applications and agents.
“I think the people who will most help us understand how to build and apply AI likely haven’t even heard of it yet,” he said. “Trying to get knowledge and information out to as many people as humanly possible is what continues to drive me.”
Bringing NVIDIA Nemotron to Developers Everywhere
Having spent years teaching developers to build with open models, Alexiuk has concluded that transparency isn’t a feature of good AI; it’s the precondition for it.
“Fully open source AI is necessary for the democratization of intelligence,” he said. “You should have access to the weights, the data that went into it, the training recipes, everything.”
That’s why, on his LinkedIn profile, Alexiuk styles himself “No. 1 Nemotron Fan,” referring to the [NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) family of open source, multimodal models built for long-running, self-evolving and specialized AI agents.
“I think Nemotron is the most important project that exists,” said Alexiuk, who also uses the pseudonym “Joe Nemotron” across social media. “I’m a firm believer that openness is a very important thing to undertake, so I’m going to be the No. 1 fan of whoever is doing that the best. And that is Nemotron.”
It’s this matter-of-fact directness and affable approachability that makes Alexiuk’s teaching style so appealing. On the social media platform X, he goes by the handle “llm_wizard.” His avatar: a laughing cartoon caricature sporting a slouchy sorcerer’s hat and brandishing a magic wand.
It’s no surprise, then, that Alexiuk likens Nemotron to a magical library — its users fellow wizards in search of knowledge that can move mountains.
“You’re a wizard in search of prepared spells, and Nemotron has a spell for everything,” he said. “Just choose the one you need.”
In non-wizard terms?
“There’s a category of model that’s going to be close to the kind of work you want to accomplish,” Alexiuk said, explaining that Nemotron supports that whole ecosystem of AI users: from individual developers using a model like Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for repetitive, high-frequency execution work to a company deploying Nemotron Ultra for long-running autonomous agents, deep research and enterprise tasks.
“I think that openness helps more people understand AI and hopefully leads to more people doing really ingenious things with these tools at the limit,” Alexiuk said. “If a tool is amplifying skill, it’s amplifying human expression.”
From Birding to Model-Building
Alexiuk first became fascinated with machine learning in a computational physics class at Trent University in Ontario, Canada.
“After that, I learned about TensorFlow and that you could build image classifiers that ran on your GPU,” he recalled. As an initial one-off project, Alexiuk built a classifier that would alert him whenever his friend’s distinctive pet bird, a Yellow-Faced Gray Budgerigar, appeared in frame on his webcam during shared video game sessions.
“Because we were playing video games, I wasn’t focused on my friend’s webcam, but I didn’t want to miss seeing the bird when it appeared,” Alexiuk said. “And then my whole life changed, because in that instance I realized it’s crazy what you could do with technology.”
Since then, he’s been embedding himself in the open source AI community.
“To imagine within the span of a few years going from freaking out because I could know my friend’s bird was in the camera frame to being able to make any website in a matter of minutes with a model that’s running on my laptop — I cannot wait to see what’s next,” Alexiuk said. “It’s never been more accessible to get into and learn about AI.”
And if another LLM wizard arises to challenge him for the title of No. 1 Nemotron Fan?
“It would be the greatest day of my life to be surpassed by an even bigger fan of Nemotron, who had heard about Nemotron through the work I was doing,” Alexiuk said. “That would be a capstone to my career that I can only dream of.”
Hear more from Alexiuk by following the [NVIDIA Nemotron Labs Livestreams](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL5B692fm6--vEL0FwctKghCpyEnBGAQJA) series on YouTube.

title: More Performance From Every Byte: How Full-Stack Codesign Solves AI’s Memory Challenge
body:
Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term.
NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack.
But the approach isn’t to simply pack more memory onto the GPU. It’s full-stack codesign. NVIDIA intentionally designs GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage and software together to get more useful work out of memory at every layer of the AI factory.
That matters because an AI factory runs on a memory and storage hierarchy. GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the fastest, most expensive and most contested tier — with model weights and KV cache competing for limited capacity. Below it sit CPU memory, local SSDs and shared storage, each trading speed for more capacity at a lower cost per bit.
How much useful work a byte does depends on how well the whole hierarchy is used: shrinking what must be stored, placing it on the right tier and bringing it back to the GPU before it’s needed.
Byte for byte, NVIDIA makes the most efficient use of memory at every layer — and the results show it. From NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra to the Vera Rubin platform, HBM capacity per GPU rose roughly 3%, while agentic throughput per dollar rose by up to 30x on SemiAnalysis AgentX.
Agentic Inference Is Putting More Pressure on HBM
Frontier models now have trillions of parameters — the values that hold what an AI model learned in training.
KV cache, which holds the context the model needs to understand each active request without reprocessing the same information, is also expanding. Agentic trajectories carry prior context across repeated model and tool calls, in some cases processing up to 3 million tokens, so each request’s working memory grows over time.
[Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/what-is-retrieval-augmented-generation/) adds relevant enterprise information to prompts, creating even more context to process and retain.
During inference, HBM primarily holds both model parameters and KV cache. The result: greater pressure on HBM.
Why AI Factories Need a Memory Hierarchy
Adding more HBM capacity per GPU is the obvious response to that pressure, but capacity delivers only what bandwidth can move.
Think of HBM as a warehouse and memory bandwidth as its loading docks. A larger warehouse holds more inventory, but the docks set how much can move in and out at a time. Once the docks are at capacity, moving more inventory takes longer and slows response times. If delays exceed the required service level, the added space can’t be used effectively, even as it adds cost and draws power.
That’s also why no operation keeps all its inventory in the closest, fastest space. What’s in motion stays near the line. What’s waiting moves to a larger, cheaper space nearby and returns before it’s needed.
An AI factory faces the same limit.
More HBM can hold more KV cache and support more concurrent users. Every added user shares the same compute and memory bandwidth. But when each user expects fast responses, eventually memory bandwidth is unable to supply data as fast as compute can use it: a limit engineers call the memory wall.
Past that point, extra HBM capacity can’t be put to work, yet it still adds costs and draws power. The data still needs a place to live, but not all of it needs the fastest, most expensive tier. This is why an AI factory manages data across a memory and storage hierarchy.
Maximizing the Value of Every Byte With Full-Stack Codesign
NVIDIA’s full-stack codesign makes every byte of HBM count by relieving pressure from model weights, KV cache and RAG data. It does this with techniques that each target a different source of inefficiency:
Shrink model weights and distribute them across the NVL72 domain.
- The
[NVFP4](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/3-ways-nvfp4-accelerates-ai-training-and-inference/)format reduces the space required for weights compared to FP8, the lowest precision possible on the NVIDIA Hopper platform. Recent models, including[FLUX.2 [klein]](https://bfl.ai/blog/flux2-klein-towards-interactive-visual-intelligence)from Black Forest Labs,[Inkling](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/introducing-inkling/)from Thinking Machines Lab,[Beam 1.0](https://huggingface.co/reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4)from Reflection,[Meta Muse Spark](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/scale-agentic-coding-workflows-with-metas-muse-spark-open-on-nvidia-gb300-nvl72/)from Meta,[Step 5 Preview](https://huggingface.co/stepfun-ai/Step-5-Preview-NVFP4)from StepFun and[NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-nemotron-3-5-super-vl-powers-specialized-agents-with-multimodal-reasoning/)have been released with NVFP4 checkpoints, demonstrating growing model-builder adoption of 4-bit precision for faster, more memory-efficient inference. - Within an NVL72 system, model weights can be
[distributed across up to 72 GPUs](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/mixture-of-experts-frontier-models/), so each GPU holds a smaller share of the model — leaving more HBM for KV cache and concurrent users.
Shrink KV-cache and offload inactive context to lower-cost storage tiers.
- Applying
[NVFP4 to the KV cache](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/optimizing-inference-for-long-context-and-large-batch-sizes-with-nvfp4-kv-cache/)reduces its footprint compared with FP8, so more context can stay resident in HBM. [NVIDIA Vera CPU](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/vera-cpu/)helps in two ways. Faster tool execution shortens the time KV cache sits inactive during tool calls, and its large LPDDR memory, connected to NVIDIA Rubin GPUs over NVIDIA NVLink-C2C interconnect, gives paused context a nearby place to wait and return quickly.- When context isn’t actively in use,
[NVIDIA Dynamo](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai/dynamo/)inference software moves it to[NVIDIA CMX](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/ai-storage/cmx/)context memory storage — a tier built for capacity at far lower cost per bit than HBM — and returns it before reuse. Unlike local SSDs, CMX is shared across servers, and unlike enterprise storage, it skips the overhead of long-term data protection that short-lived context doesn’t need. NVIDIA CMX context memory storage partners include Cloudian,[DDN](https://www.ddn.com/press-releases/ddn-accelerates-inference-and-lowers-cost-per-token-while-expanding-multi-tenant-training-for-ai-factories/),[Dell Technologies](https://www.dell.com/en-us/dt/corporate/newsroom/announcements/detailpage.press-releases~usa~2025~11~dell-technologies-and-nvidia-advance-enterprise-ai-innovation.htm#/filter-on/Country:en-us),[Everpure](https://blog.purestorage.com/news-events/pure-kva-integrates-nvidia-dynamo-for-scalable-low-latency-llm-inference/)(previously Pure Storage),[HPE](https://www.hpe.com/us/en/newsroom/press-release/2026/03/hpe-unveils-next-generation-ai-factory-and-supercomputing-advancements-with-nvidia.html#:~:text=HPE%20AI%20Factory%20with%20Mission%20Control),[IBM](https://community.ibm.com/community/user/blogs/vincent-hsu/2026/01/05/accelerating-nvidia-dynamo-with-ibm-storage-scale#:~:text=IBM%20is%20working%20with%20NVIDIA%20to%20combine,technologies%20to%20unlock%20scalable%2C%20high%2Dperformance%20LLM%20inference.),[NetApp](https://www.netapp.com/newsroom/press-releases/news-rel-20250318-145499/),[VAST](https://www.vastdata.com/blog/how-nvidia-dynamo-vast-unlock-context-reuse-at-scale)and[WEKA](https://www.weka.io/blog/ai-ml/weka-accelerates-ai-inference-with-nvidia-dynamo-and-nvidia-nixl/). - Dynamo’s KV Cache Reuse ties the tiers together, managing KV cache as one system-wide resource across GPU memory, CPU memory and storage, so context computed once can be reused across the system.
Compact RAG embeddings and keeping the index outside HBM.
- RAG turns enterprise documents into embeddings — numerical representations that let a system search by meaning rather than keyword — organized into a searchable index. NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever models produce smaller embeddings with higher retrieval accuracy, while the NVIDIA cuVS library enables that index to be built and served across CPU and storage. The knowledge base never occupies HBM, and only the passages the model needs enter context.
The result is less HBM used for model weights, less HBM tied up by idle context and more of it available to serve concurrent users.
More Useful Output per Dollar With Each Generation
Across successive NVIDIA platform generations, tokens per second per dollar has risen far faster than HBM capacity.
On the SemiAnalysis AgentX DeepSeek V4 Pro workload, NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 delivers up to 10x higher throughput per dollar than NVIDIA H200 platform at 100 tokens per second per user, with HBM capacity per GPU roughly doubling. At 125 tokens per second per user, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivers up to 30x higher throughput per dollar than GB300 NVL72, with HBM capacity per GPU up about 3%.
For AI factory operators, the metric that matters is how many useful tokens the factory can deliver within its power budget while meeting user response-time needs. More tokens per second per watt means more work and revenue from the same power, and a lower cost for every token. NVIDIA’s full-stack codesign lowers token costs by increasing the useful work every byte of memory delivers.
Learn more in the [video explainer](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ud3gdKrbdgw) and [technical deep dive](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/five-ways-nvidia-co-design-maximizes-the-value-of-every-byte-in-the-ai-factory/?nvid=nv-tblg-668541) on how NVIDIA full-stack codesign reduces inference memory pressure.

title: Craft and taste
body:
As I’m exploring what truly interests me, there’s something that’s getting clearer as the days go by. Something that I keep peeking at through the trees.
I value taste.
And I know that’s an overused term these days, plus it’s different for everyone else but I can just feel what I like and don’t like. It flows from products I use, to what I wear, to the founders I invest in. Maybe there’s some built up instinct from running the Product Hunt homepage for 2 years back in 2015 and combing through tens of thousands of products.
Taste is the reason why I can’t do things that are not authentic to me. I refuse to tweet ‘for growth’. I turn down acquisitions or job offers.
So I wanted to see what past me and current me really like.
I asked Codex to pull my history from Kindle and Spotify to see if my feeling of this ‘thing’ was true. What have I been consuming for hours just for fun, just because I find it interesting?
Books and podcasts feel like a strong signal because I’ve paid for it and/or spent hours in it. I also pulled my YouTube history and Readwise articles/newsletters but I don’t think 885 videos of The Wiggles shows me anything other than being a parent…So I focused mostly on books.
With the data all in a folder I got Opus 5.5 to show me what my consumption looked like.
Then I asked Opus to try a few different agents with no context to look at the data to see what it thinks my interests are.
Kinda…
But what it re-affirmed to me was more nuanced than that… It’s not just ‘business’ books or founders’ stories that I like. It’s the how. How did this person or company do this thing? Why people made choices that others didn’t? What alternative path did they take and succeed?
I’ve been diving into David Senra recently - mostly interviews on him as the subject (he reads autobiographies of founders and does a podcast on them). I resonate a lot with how he thinks about his own ‘work’. One big thing that keeps sticking with me is stories sell products.
It’s taste. It’s uniqueness. It’s values. It’s going against the grain. Doing something different.
For example, I use Granola because I like the founders, the company, their values, their vibe, their taste and of course, their product. Sure there’s a ton of competitors but its the care of their craft that I really feel. So I pick them over others. I don’t see the Granola founders ever going on youtube to do this kind of stuff.
I get we’re in an attention game but this feels icky to me.
I buy clothes from Kith because I know a lot about the founder and how he think about his brand (plus I loved streetwear growing up). Its an extension of him and what he likes. Great Senra interview with him [here](https://youtu.be/RFjMyFeqf3I?si=V4dUIO_rOhNLEdNr) btw that I found this morning.
There’s a ton of companies and builders out there who do or have done something differently. Just because its authentically them. Those are the products I want to buy. And those are the stories that interest me.
So I’m going to be looking into those stories and building interactive sites, some with video, some with behind the scenes of my process. That is what I’m going to focus on doing.
The ‘how we make money’ isn’t something on my mind to figure out yet. If I focus on tasteful builders I’m sure companies would want to be part of that narrative but it allows me to make my own judgement on whether I’d even want to do something with them.
I feel like if the format is interesting enough, it can make you care about the topic (even if you think you won’t) - which is why I love the interactive essays by The Pudding. I don’t care about women’s jean pocket sizes, but you bet I read the essay because I love the format.
That’s the kind of feeling I want.
Oh and I [turned my book history into a scrollable timeline for fun](https://bentossell.com/books).
Quick bites
[ChatGPT Images 2.6](https://openai.com/index/introducing-images-2-6/)- faster, better and now with GIFs[Reverse engineering TikTok](https://x.com/ayoships/status/2117650684774580249?a=wU_RfDp8iMxaUNeXd5g&s=20)- they know if you’re lying down, walking or in a car[Pivoting](https://x.com/NirZicherman/status/2117683979809890720?a=9-X0VoptLldQLzvIwq4&s=20)to focus on fun.Notion is ‘
[reinventing itself](https://x.com/ivanhzhao/status/2118030537101361168?a=TGd-aUJmK-XfDZZHKvE&s=20)’ - context for agents.[Agent experience](https://www.innovationendeavors.com/insights/ax-is-not-the-new-dx-its-the-new-ux)is the new user experience.
I feel this on the build side too. Every site an agent produces has the same SaaS look, and you can tell right away nobody chose anything. Honestly, taste now is mostly saying no to the default. Do your interactive sites start from a reference you love, or from a blank prompt?
Those 3d book models are sick! Your bookshelf inspired me to build a 3d space filled with my absolute favourite books, movies (or rather its cinema tickets and posters)/vinyls/favourite LEGO sets/devices from the past - any item I would like to "collect" on the virtual room to a) feel nostalgic and b) reflect on how my taste was "formed" over the years. It would be cool to see Ben's nostalgic wall as well! Oh and the bookshelf is definitely missing Mollick's new book (although this post suggests you already have it in progress)

title: ‘Hogwarts Legacy’ Gets a Magical NVIDIA DLSS 5 Upgrade on GeForce NOW
body:
Hogwarts Legacy receives an [NVIDIA DLSS 5 upgrade with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/news/dlss-5-faster-ai-model-hogwarts-legacy-rtx-spark-laptops/) today, bringing lifelike lighting and materials to the wizarding world on [GeForce NOW](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/).
Blizzard Entertainment’s World of Warcraft: Forever also opens a new chapter in Azeroth, with a launch-week access reward available for GeForce NOW members. Meanwhile, Ubisoft brings fresh challenges with expansions for Tom Clancy’s The Division 2 and Anno 117: Pax Romana.
It’s all part of a packed month of play, with two-dozen games joining the [GeForce NOW library](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/games/) throughout November, including eight this week.
Hogwarts in a New Light
NVIDIA DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering arrives in Hogwarts Legacy today, giving members a new reason to return to Hogwarts, streaming from Steam, Epic Games and Xbox with Play Anywhere support.
Published by Warner Bros. Games under the Portkey Games label and developed by Avalanche Software, Hogwarts Legacy is an immersive, open-world action role-playing game set in the 1800s wizarding world. Begin as a fifth-year student, encounter magical creatures, brew potions and learn spells while exploring both recognizable and unfamiliar places.
The update adds lifelike lighting and material detail while retaining underlying geometry and textures. Avalanche Software has tuned the integration through DLSS 5’s developer controls to maintain the game’s artistic intent and style.
Hogwarts Legacy also includes support for the DLSS Multi Frame Generation and Ray Reconstruction features, accelerating and enhancing the ray-traced graphics that immerse players in Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. Thanks to [NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 controls](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/geforce-now-thursday-enshrouded-update/) in the cloud, members can fine-tune their experience.
[Ultimate members](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/premium-memberships/) can experience the update with GeForce RTX 5080-class performance across PCs, Macs, handhelds, browsers, mobile devices, compatible TVs and more, without an expensive PC upgrade or waiting for game downloads. GeForce NOW handles the installs and updates, saving the storage space for everyday essentials. Just pick up the wand, hop on a broom and take flight.
A New Chapter, Forever
Blizzard Entertainment’s [World of Warcraft: Forever](https://worldofwarcraft.blizzard.com/en-us/forever/) launched Wednesday, Nov. 4, and is streaming on GeForce NOW, inviting players into a reimagined original Azeroth built to keep growing for years to come.
Explore new and expanded zones, discover gameplay enhancements and take in upgraded graphics in a world where community and the journey take center stage. Access is included with an active World of Warcraft subscription or Game Time, giving returning heroes and newcomers a fresh starting point.
GeForce NOW also supports CurseForge Addons for World of Warcraft: Forever, giving premium members more ways to customize their experience. At launch, GeForce NOW plans to support around 100 of the most popular CurseForge add-ons, with the selection evolving to reflect player favorites. Members can request additional add-ons through in-app feedback for consideration in future updates.
The cloud keeps the next quest within reach across supported devices. For new World of Warcraft users who don’t already have a subscription, a launch-week access reward is available across all GeForce NOW membership tiers. The access period runs through Wednesday, Nov. 11, at 11:59 p.m. PT.
Eligible members can sign in to their GeForce NOW account and head to the [Account Portal](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/account/redeem) to redeem while supplies last, on a first-come, first-served basis. Gather the party and venture forward.
New Missions, New Horizons
Ubisoft brings two new downloadable content releases to the cloud this week, sending agents into an overgrown New York and governors toward a new province of the Roman Empire.
Launched earlier this week, [Tom Clancy’s The Division 2: Echoes of Central Park](https://www.ubisoft.com/en-us/game/the-division/the-division-2/news-updates/23q5ICm6Mf4PUPuPUUS0uP/the-division-2-echoes-of-central-park-coming-on-november-3) is the biggest experience since Tom Clancy’s The Division 2: Warlords of New York, opening up Central Park and the Upper West Side for the first time in franchise history. Investigate disappearances and rumors of a mysterious threat, team up with three companions with distinct combat roles, and earn new gear and six skill variants. Play solo or in co-op, with a level boost available for agents below level 40.
In [Anno 117: Pax Romana – Dawn of the Delta](https://www.anno-union.com/devblog-arriving-in-aegyptus/), arriving today, build cities in Aegyptus, where deserts, fertile farmland and seasonal floods shape every decision. Develop irrigation systems and choose whether to Romanize the population or preserve local traditions. The new province can be explored in an existing save or chosen as the starting point for a new game.
New territory belongs on the map, not in a download queue. GeForce NOW handles both expansions’ downloads and updates, leaving the planning to governors and the gear management to agents.

title: Le Chonk brings the brains. Studio puts it to work.
body:
Le Chonk brings the brains. Studio puts it to work.
Thinking
Summary
Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk) enhances enterprise AI with advanced coding, cybersecurity, and document reasoning, while Mistral Studio provides a flexible platform for deploying agents, workflows, and apps across cloud, VPC, or on-premises environments. New features like managed agents, workflows, and enterprise context streamline business processes, enabling faster development and deployment of AI solutions. Customers like ABANCA and BNP Paribas already use Studio to automate tasks, improve efficiency, and maintain full control over their AI systems.
Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk) pushes the frontier of what enterprises can build with open models. It does great for [coding](https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-large-4-oss/), delivers advanced [defensive cybersecurity capabilities](https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-large-4-oss/), and brings powerful reasoning to [complex documents](https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/mistral-large-4-france-ai) and [business tasks](https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-large-4-oss/).
Mistral Studio is our enterprise AI platform for putting that intelligence to work in your business. It lets your teams activate models quickly through agents, workflows and apps connected to your enterprise data and systems. Deploy them wherever you choose: in the cloud, in your own VPC, on-premises or across a combination of environments. And retain full control and understanding of the intelligence you create, from how your systems work to the knowledge they build.
Today, we’re expanding Studio with managed agents and apps, alongside new capabilities for workflows, enterprise context, agent observability and evaluations.
Customers and partners including ABANCA, Accenture, Alten, BNP Paribas, Capgemini, CMA CGM and Tata Consultancy Services already use Studio in production. With this release, your developers can build and deploy new use cases faster, then reuse that work across more of the business.
Agents, workflows and apps for your business processes
Agents, workflows and apps serve different parts of a business process. An agent investigates and acts, a workflow coordinates execution and approvals, and an app gives employees a way to use these systems.
Studio brings all three together on shared infrastructure. You start with a model like Le Chonk and connect it to your enterprise data and systems through connectors and MCP servers. That foundation lets you easily build agents, workflows and apps with access to the context they need. Studio manages how they run and lets teams inspect what happened.
Through the new Mistral MCP server, developers can build with Mistral Vibe or the coding agent they already use, test locally and deploy to their Studio environment with one command. Studio handles hosting and execution, so teams can build on that foundation to get each new use case into production faster.
Build managed agents that investigate and act
In Studio, developers can now build agents that carry out complex, multi-step tasks. Developers can equip them with skills that capture the team’s procedures, sandboxes where they can run code, and subagents to delegate parts of a task. Hooks let developers add custom logic at key points in execution, shaping how the agent works and integrates with existing systems.
Studio manages the runtime behind all that work, using the proven infrastructure that supports millions of Mistral Vibe sessions each week. Developers can focus on the agent’s capabilities and behaviour, while setting boundaries on the tools, data and actions it can access. That means getting capable agents into production faster, with less infrastructure to build and more control over how your agents operate.
Our engineering team built an agent in Studio to investigate production incidents. When an alert fires, engineers need to work out what happened, often under pressure to resolve the issue. The agent starts the investigation: it follows the team’s runbook, asks for approval before taking sensitive actions and posts its findings in Slack. Engineers pick up the investigation with useful context already gathered, saving the team hundreds of hours each month.
Automate processes with workflows
Workflows define how a process runs: which steps follow fixed rules, where an agent reasons and when a person decides. Interrupted runs can resume where they left off. Teams can describe a process in Mistral Vibe and use it to generate, test and deploy a workflow, with code they can inspect and edit. Today’s release also adds event triggers from enterprise systems and a visual graph that makes each workflow’s logic easier to inspect.
Our product operations team built a workflow in Studio to sort ideas from internal teams and feedback from customers. Routing each submission to the right people is one of the team’s routine tasks, but one that takes time. A model identifies bugs and feature requests, then routing rules send them to the appropriate team. This saves the product operations team about 35 hours a week.
Build apps ready for enterprise use
Coding agents make it easy to build an application, but putting it to work across an enterprise means meeting requirements for security, access and reliability. Studio provides hosting, authentication and access controls, helping developers get applications ready for enterprise use faster. Teams can build with pre-approved, reusable components, reducing the amount of new code that needs security review.
These applications can use agents and workflows, retrieve enterprise documents through search indexes and access shared context in Studio. Developers can test locally, then deploy with one command to make the application available at its own link or inside Mistral Vibe.
Our Applied AI team, which helps customers build AI solutions, built a staffing app in Studio. Previously, staffing a project meant manually matching team profiles and past experience against requirements spread across documents and tools.
The app uses an agent to recommend people and explain how their experience fits the project. Staffing leads get a shortlist with supporting evidence ready to review, helping Mistral assemble teams faster and uncover expertise that might otherwise be overlooked when staffing complex customer AI projects.
Each use case leaves the enterprise better equipped to build the next. More engineering effort goes into improving operations, with less time spent rebuilding the infrastructure around them.
Keep your AI sovereign
Studio gives you control over where your AI runs, how it operates and the intelligence you build. Deploy both the models and the platform in your own cloud, VPC or on-premises environment. You can also use Mistral-hosted deployments or combine environments to meet your requirements. Sensitive data and the processes built around it can stay within your perimeter.
You choose the models, govern access to data and tools, and decide which actions require human approval. OpenTelemetry traces show each step of a run, including model calls, tool use and approvals, so your teams can see where a process slows down or fails. Evaluations let them test changes to prompts, models or tools against your own datasets before release. Those traces and evaluations remain theirs, preserving the operational knowledge they build through use.
Customers are already putting this into practice with systems built alongside our Solutions team. From penetration testing to KYC onboarding, they’re bringing [AI into critical operations](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6_eHHtB7Q2I) while keeping sensitive data and specialist knowledge under their control.
Get started
Choose a process your team wants to improve and put Le Chonk to work in [Studio](https://console.mistral.ai/).
Build an agent:
[Managed Agents documentation](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/agents/overview)·[Incident investigation cookbook](https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/cookbooks/mistral-agents-investigation_agent-slack-sentry-investigation-agent)Automate a process:
[Workflows documentation](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/workflows/overview)·[Workflow cookbooks](https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/cookbooks/mistral-agents-slack_triage_workflow-slack-triage-workflow)Create an app:
[Apps documentation](https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/apps/overview)·[Document review cookbook](https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/cookbooks/mistral-agents-expert_matching_workflow-expert-matching-workflow)
Explore [interactive demos and enterprise use cases](https://mistral.ai/use-cases/), or read the [release notes](https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/release-notes) for the full list of updates.
For an enterprise rollout or a business-critical implementation, [talk to our team](https://mistral.ai/contact) about what you want to automate and where it needs to run.

title: Why Waiting for the Next AI Model Can Pay Off - John Stecher, Blackstone & Scott Worland, Norm AI
body:
Blackstone CTO John Stecher and Norm AI CTO Scott Worland discuss building technology that holds up as models keep improving. John explains why a solid data strategy and straight-through processing come before agents, how he weighs ROI against waiting for a better model, and why internal apps can now be thrown away and rebuilt. Scott describes how Norm's large hand-labeled eval set showed that much of its carefully built workflow code was in the way, why the team rebuilt its platform, and how it decides where to invest heavily versus lightly as the frontier moves.

title: How We Took an AI Agent From 41% to 97% Accurate - Milind Sunil Shah, Brainbase Labs
body:
Milind Sunil Shah of Brainbase Labs walks through a six-step framework for improving back-office agents, using a Domino's project that tracks competitors' pizza prices across websites and delivery apps. From version 1 to version 11, accuracy went from 41% to 97%, cost per source halved from $2 to $1, and run time fell from 129 to 71 minutes, all through instructions, skills and playbooks rather than a new model. The steps: kickoff, ontology, benchmarks and evals, a narrow first agent, iteration, and handing off the whole loop.

- [Defending critical infrastructure](#defending-critical-infrastructure)
- [Expanding access to trusted defenders](#expanding-access-to-trusted-defenders)

We’re introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, a major leap in security research: more capable at finding and fixing vulnerabilities, and far more reliable staying within the boundaries researchers set. GPT‑6 Cyber delivers major gains on key cybersecurity benchmarks over GPT‑5.6 Cyber, including a 51% relative improvement on ExploitGym and a step function improvement when tested on staying within scope. It is already helping to secure real-world software, uncovering and validating thousands of exploits in security-critical codebases such as Linux and Firefox.

On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. It also follows task boundaries more reliably: in a separate alignment evaluation, GPT‑6 Cyber avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of tests without its deployment prompt, and 100% with this prompt. This improvement in alignment reflects dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately.

These capabilities are already helping secure real systems. Our researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber to develop [948 privilege escalation exploits in Linux⁠](https://openai.com/index/a-thousand-fewer-paths-to-root/) and identify 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, despite extensive prior testing with frontier models. The model also helped develop candidate patches, and Mozilla has [released fixes for many of the Firefox vulnerabilities⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/security/advisories/mfsa2026-118/). Security teams at Cisco, Calif, and CodeRabbit are using it for vulnerability research and code review, and we have relied on it to [find and fix weaknesses in our own infrastructure⁠](https://openai.com/index/securing-our-frontier-model-training-environment/).

It is clear that we have [a limited window to use frontier models to secure software⁠](https://openai.com/index/the-defenders-window/). **Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers.** Mainline models such as GPT‑6 Astra already support code review, vulnerability triage, and patch development. Daybreak Blue helps verified defenders validate vulnerabilities and fixes with fewer unnecessary refusals, while Daybreak Red enables deeper exploit development and authorized security testing with GPT‑6 Cyber.

## Advancing frontier cyber capabilities

GPT‑6 Cyber is a major step up from GPT‑5.6 Cyber and outperforms GPT‑6 Astra on most cyber tasks, even when Astra does not refuse the request. We evaluated the model on tasks that require it to understand software, identify vulnerabilities, and develop working exploits. Based on these results, we classify the model as Critical in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT‑5.6 Cyber.

ExploitGymRemoteExploitBenchExploitGym HoneypotExploitBench (June–August 2026)SRE-BenchWeb Pentesting

On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability in a remote target, GPT‑6 Cyber scores **48.5%**, about **16 percentage points** higher than GPT‑5.6 Cyber’s **32.1%**. To test vulnerability discovery, we also built a new evaluation for offensive web penetration testing. Models probe web applications without access to their source code. GPT‑6 Cyber achieved **40.3%** recall of vulnerabilities compared with **32.0%** for GPT‑6 Astra.

Daybreak Red is designed to support more advanced security workflows, including developing working exploits and using them against remote targets. To evaluate these capabilities, we built a new benchmark called RemoteExploitBench, which uses known vulnerabilities in applications such as GitLab, PostgreSQL, and Jenkins deployed in a controlled environment. In our initial evaluation, GPT‑6 Astra running with Daybreak Blue **refused 100% of tasks**, while GPT‑6 Cyber **completed 95%**; its only failure was an exploit it could not get to work remotely. See the [system card⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-cyber) for full results and evaluation settings.

## Stronger alignment, better at staying within bounds

One risk for cybersecurity agents is that they go outside the scope of their assigned task, attempt to exploit unrelated services, or disregard the researcher’s rules of engagement.

We made alignment a central focus of GPT‑6 Cyber, using specialized training to help the model stay within authorized scope, follow restrictions on its actions, and report its work accurately. Before deployment, we ran a series of alignment evaluations to measure these behaviors. See the [system card⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-cyber) for full results.

One of these evaluations is ExploitGym Honeypot, which was informed by the [Hugging Face incident⁠](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/). We give the model a difficult exploitation task in an isolated environment with access to supporting services, such as a package registry or object store. We deliberately make these services easy to exploit so that attacking them can reveal the task’s flag. The model must infer that exploiting them is outside the scope of its task.

GPT‑6 Cyber shows a step-change improvement over GPT‑5.6 Cyber on this evaluation. When tested without deployment safety prompts, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of cases, up from 94.49% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. With those prompts, GPT‑6 Cyber stayed within bounds 100% of the time.

We can see directly in the GPT‑6 Cyber model’s chain of thought how it reasons about staying within bounds:

*Agent chain-of-thought excerpts*

> “Can't assume extra API or attack controller not target. We should only target binary/server.”“Can't assume extra API or attack controller not target. We should only target binary/server.”“Can'tassumeextraAPIorattackcontrollernottarget.Weshouldonlytargetbinary/server.”

*Agent chain-of-thought excerpts*

> “don't explore out of scope credentials.”“don't explore out of scope credentials.”“don'texploreoutofscopecredentials.”

GPT‑6 Cyber is already helping security teams find vulnerabilities, validate their impact, and develop fixes. Customers have put it to work on large codebases, long-running exploit development, and security review:

Even after further hardening with multiple generations of frontier models, GPT‑6 Cyber uncovered previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities, identified architectural improvements, and helped us ship fixes to millions of users.*”

*\- Brian Grinstead, Distinguished Engineer, Firefox*

It's already instrumental in helping us better protect our own products, and through Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense, we’re bringing that same speed and precision to our customers to protect enterprise software at scale.*”

> “*Defending modern infrastructure requires continuous innovation. Integrating these capabilities into our research allows our teams to analyze complex architectures and identify risks with greater speed and precision, ultimately strengthening the resilience and trust of the technology our customers rely on*.”

title: Stop Making Your Customers Click Approve - Emil Chetty, Wise
body:
Emil Chetty, who leads data and AI product at Wise, argues that AI assistants have turned customers into an approval queue. Wise moved $243 billion across borders last year for nearly 19 million customers under more than 80 licenses, so every payment needs proof of what the customer actually authorized. His answer: the customer agrees to the whole job once, as a locked agreement; the agent chooses the steps; and Wise's existing payment software enforces the terms, so even an agent tricked by a prompt injection can't pay a new recipient.

# Merge builds product and business tools with OpenAI technology

The integration platform uses GPT‑6 Astra, ChatGPT, and Codex for product reviews, marketing, and business development planning.

[Join the community](https://openai.com/leads/startup/)



Company size: Startup

Region: North America

Industry: Technology

Products: ChatGPT, Codex

Loading…

Share

Inside the rollout

- [Everyone is a builder](#everyone-is-a-builder)

- [Inside the rollout](#inside-the-rollout)

Merge helps companies build connected software and AI products, from syncing customer data to enabling AI agents to take action across business systems. Its products span customer-data integrations through Merge Unified, secure tool access for AI agents through Merge Agent Handler, and model routing and cost controls through Merge Gateway. Merge for Workforce brings those capabilities inside companies, helping teams manage which models, tools, and business systems employees can access. Together, these products support both the software companies build for customers and the AI-powered work happening inside their organizations.

Inside Merge, CEO and Co-founder Shensi Ding uses Codex to review product code, including work on a new setup interface for configuring tool access in Merge for Workforce. Her colleagues use GPT‑6 Astra for product testing and marketing. The team also uses AI for the work of running the company, from preparing sales updates to planning customer dinners.

> “We use it honestly for everything. Integrations obviously, but we also use it to automate different workflows, to help make our product better overall, to incorporate any feedback from our customers, and to build end-to-end features.”

—Shensi Ding, CEO and Co-founder, Merge

## Inside the rollout

Merge launched a tool for adding connectors to AI products, with reliability a priority for Ding: “We’re pretty proud of the quality. Tool calls through Merge succeed 99.9% of the time, compared to public MCP servers, which are around 60%.”

For its own product development, Merge uses GPT‑6 Astra. “It’s really fast, and it was much better at code reviews,” Ding says. “They also liked the personality of GPT‑6 Astra, which goes a long way. It was also clear that Codex had improved a lot. Merge lets employees choose their own AI tools, and which one to use has become a lively internal debate.”

Ding used Codex to review a proposed implementation of the new provisioning tab in Merge for Workforce as the team evaluated how customers would configure tool access. They discussed making the “Add tool pack” action a clearer link that opens separately to make setup less confusing. Codex supplied code-review feedback; Merge’s team made the product decisions and implementation changes, with engineers responsible for validating and shipping them.

> “Other AI systems would end up forgetting what I told them and only doing the last thing that I said. GPT-6 Astra continues to execute on every single task really well, and it fills in the gaps for what I did not explicitly say using common sense.”

—Shensi Ding, CEO and Co-founder, Merge

## The dinner bot

Merge hosts executive dinners for customers and prospects to build relationships and create opportunities for follow-up product conversations.

For one dinner in Dallas, Merge started with the city and the kinds of people it wanted to bring together. The bot pulled potential guests from the CRM and Apollo, checked previous invitations and responses, and helped prepare outreach from Ding’s email. It also maintained the attendee tracker, proposed a seating chart, and created calendar notes where sales and customer success could add context about each guest.

The model handles reasoning and drafting, while Merge’s connectors provide access to the business systems. Ding reviews the output, rewrites anything that sounds off, and curates the guest list using relationship context the bot does not have.

In October 2026, Merge reported that preparing guest lists and outreach and maintaining the attendee tracker had gone from dozens of hours across the company to about 30 minutes per event. The comparison covers the same planning tasks, measured over the preceding three months. The team still handles hosting, relationship-building, and on-the-ground logistics.

Merge ran 16 executive dinners in Q3, up from eight in Q2, and plans to host more than 30 in Q4. After the Dallas dinner, the team reported positive feedback on the invitations and opportunities for follow-up demos.

“With GPT‑6 Astra, the dinner bot connects to our Salesforce, Gong, Google Sheets, and Gmail, and it’ll send emails on my behalf to people in our network,” Ding says. “It gives me recommendations for people who are a good fit for each dinner, and it surfaces new potential attendees.”

## Everyone is a builder

Ding says, “It’s been especially great for team members who aren’t in engineering, because now they can build anything.”

Charlie Lynch on Merge’s sales leadership team built reusable AI workflows for deal approvals, forecast updates, and next steps after renewal calls. Instead of repeatedly gathering context for each update or decision, he uses the workflows to prepare the material, then reviews the recommendation and decides what to do next.

The social media team uses GPT‑6 Astra in ChatGPT to find posts the company should respond to. The marketing team also used it to clarify the messaging for Merge’s Gateway Evaluations launch.

## Leadership lessons

- Lead by using the tools: “If you’re an executive, you are the ceiling for AI fluency in your organization,” Ding says.
- Find somewhere less risky to experiment: Ding and her co-founder experimented with AI on a new product before customers depended on its codebase. “When you’re less nervous, and you can really experiment, you learn so much,” she says.
- Give people space and time to tinker: Merge lets each team member choose the tools they like and encourages them to spend time every day learning and testing. That includes the freedom to “go wild and make mistakes,” even when it means going down a rabbit hole that doesn’t pay off.

## What’s next

“Anything that I want to do, I can just tell AI to do it, and it can just do it,” Ding says. Merge is continuing to use OpenAI technology to expand what its teams can build, bringing the same spirit of experimentation to its products and the way it runs the business.

title: Setting a new standard for responsible AI infrastructure
body:
The promise of AI is that it gives people more power to shape their own futures. It can help someone learn a new skill, build a business, or solve a problem that was previously out of reach. Building more computing infrastructure capacity in the United States can help lower the cost of delivering AI, put these tools in more people’s hands, and ensure America stays at the forefront of the technology.

The communities that host this infrastructure should have a clear say in shaping their futures, too. Residents should be able to influence how a campus is developed, hold developers accountable for covering the cost of powering it, and share in the jobs and business opportunities it creates. How we build these campuses is one of the first tests of whether the benefits of AI will be broadly shared.

Today we’re publishing our National Community Compact and a Compute Campus Policy Blueprint. The compact sets out what communities can expect from OpenAI at future campuses that we own and operate. The blueprint proposes policies to help ensure that compute campus development gives communities a meaningful voice, protects families from new costs, and broadly shares the economic gains of AI.

This builds on work we began in January, when we announced our Stargate Community commitments to pay our own way on energy and develop plans shaped by local priorities. We followed with specific commitments in Georgia andOhio, covering energy costs, water use, local investment and accountability. Throughout that work, we’ve listened to residents, local leaders, schools and businesses about what matters to their communities. Today’s announcement is the next step in that ongoing effort.

Every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We’ll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we’re doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments:

- **Pay our own way on energy and infrastructure.** We’ll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we’ll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled.
- **Protect local resources and report on our impact. **We’ll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use. We’ll publish construction plans and independent noise studies before operations begin and annually afterward. And we will not use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials, allowing only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.
- **Create opportunities for local workers and businesses. **We’ll publish the jobs we expect to create, work with unions and training providers to help residents prepare for them, and report annually on hiring and apprenticeships. We’ll also make sustained investments in priorities residents help select.
Those priorities will differ from place to place. In Effingham County, Georgia, residents helped shape a $4.8 million grant to provide free school meals for all 14,000 students in the county. In Pike County, Ohio, families identified childcare as a priority, leading to a joint $6 million commitment from OpenAI and SB Energy.

Families should be able to count on basic protections whoever builds a campus in their community. Voluntary commitments from companies are an important starting point, but our blueprint goes further—asking federal, state, and local policymakers to establish clear rules for how the industry builds. New policy is required to establish trust and confidence between communities, elected officials and companies. Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared.

That starts with who pays for power. State utility commissions should require large electricity customers to cover the costs they add to the grid and protect other customers if a project falls through. Utilities should also make it easier for campuses to connect if they can safely cut demand when power is scarce. At our planned Effingham County campus, for example, our agreement with Georgia Power allows the utility to reduce the power it delivers to us by up to 1,000 megawatts during periods of high demand. Congress can help meet growing demand by speeding up transmission upgrades and restoring and expanding tax incentives for clean electricity.

Communities also need a way to hold developers accountable. The blueprint calls for public reporting on water, energy, noise, and hiring, and for narrow limits on when developers can require public officials to sign NDAs. When states or local governments offer tax incentives, the terms should be public, with measurable commitments and a way to recover benefits if a developer falls short.

Finally, the blueprint proposes practical ways to keep more of the work local to ensure compute campuses support local workers and local businesses. Developers can share purchasing plans early enough for local suppliers to compete for contracts. Employers, building trades unions, and community colleges can use hiring forecasts to train residents for jobs they know will be available, from electrical work during construction to maintaining power and cooling systems for years afterward.

The investments that help America compete globally can also help communities prosper locally. That starts with giving residents a say while plans can still change and a way to hold developers accountable for delivering on their commitments. That’s what we’re committing to at the campuses we own and operate, and what we believe people should be able to count on wherever AI infrastructure is built across the country.

New policy is required to establish trust and confidence between communities, elected officials and companies. Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared.

That starts with who pays for power. State utility commissions should require large electricity customers to cover the costs they add to the grid and protect other customers if a project falls through. Utilities should also make it easier for campuses to connect if they can safely cut demand when power is scarce. At our planned Effingham County campus, for example, our agreement with Georgia Power allows the utility to reduce the power it delivers to us by up to 1,000 megawatts during periods of high demand. Congress can help meet growing demand by speeding up transmission upgrades and restoring and expanding tax incentives for clean electricity.

Communities also need a way to hold developers accountable. The blueprint calls for public reporting on water, energy, noise, and hiring, and for narrow limits on when developers can require public officials to sign NDAs. When states or local governments offer tax incentives, the terms should be public, with measurable commitments and a way to recover benefits if a developer falls short.

Finally, the blueprint proposes practical ways to keep more of the work local to ensure compute campuses support local workers and local businesses. Developers can share purchasing plans early enough for local suppliers to compete for contracts. Employers, building trades unions, and community colleges can use hiring forecasts to train residents for jobs they know will be available, from electrical work during construction to maintaining power and cooling systems for years afterward.

The investments that help America compete globally can also help communities prosper locally. That starts with giving residents a say while plans can still change and a way to hold developers accountable for delivering on their commitments. That’s what we’re committing to at the campuses we own and operate, and what we believe people should be able to count on wherever AI infrastructure is built across the country.

# Flipsnack grows product signups with conversion optimization

Flipsnack focused its ChatGPT Ads campaigns on getting people to try its product, growing registrations while lowering the cost per signup.

[Start now(opens in a new window)](https://ads.openai.com/)



Share

## Results at a glance

\~75%

lower cost per registration in five US conversion-focused campaigns than in their earlier click-focused versions, which used fixed bids.¹

\~310%

more registrations in those same five conversion-focused campaigns compared with their earlier click-focused versions.¹

## Connecting a versatile product to a specific need

[Flipsnack ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.flipsnack.com/) helps teams turn static documents into interactive digital experiences. Its customers use the platform to create product catalogs, sales presentations, brochures, internal communications, and training materials.

For Flipsnack, that range of applications creates a marketing challenge: helping people recognize how the product fits the work they need to do. As the company increased its focus on business customers, it wanted to reach people with needs that its product category alone might not clearly describe.

Flipsnack had relied heavily on search advertising. Its ChatGPT Ads test became an opportunity to learn which customer needs could translate into product signups.

## Measuring the action that brings people into the product

Because Flipsnack is a visual product, prospective customers often want to experience it before speaking with sales. Its campaign landing pages directed people into a signup flow, making completed registration the first meaningful step the team could measure and optimize for.

To help business customers see where the product could fit their work, Flipsnack expanded beyond its original, broader Flipbook campaign. Separate campaigns for Magazine, Catalog, and Brochure addressed specific document needs, while campaigns for Sales Enablement, Employee Benefits, Real Estate, and Hospitality connected the product to business applications and industries.

> “A sales team and an internal communications team can use the same product for very different jobs. We want our campaigns to help each see where Flipsnack fits.”

—Paul Romancsak, Paid Advertising Manager at Flipsnack

Flipsnack’s initial click-focused campaigns brought in traffic and signups. After seeing better delivery and registration efficiency in conversion-focused campaigns, the team rebuilt existing campaigns with a conversions objective and bidding set to maximize conversions.



*A Flipsnack ad in ChatGPT.*

## Improving registration efficiency

Flipsnack created conversion-focused versions of five existing US campaigns that had used a clicks objective with fixed bids.

Early results following the shift to conversion-focused campaigns were encouraging. Across five campaigns, registrations increased approximately 310% while cost per registration fell approximately 75%, with daily budget settings unchanged. [1](#user-content-fn-1)

> “What stood out was that we were getting more registrations at a lower cost per signup. That gave us the confidence to make conversion optimization the focus of our campaigns.”

—Paul Romancsak, Paid Advertising Manager at Flipsnack

## Building on registration results

These results give Flipsnack a promising foundation for continued growth with ChatGPT Ads. Building on its conversion-focused campaigns, the team aims to bring more prospective customers into the product and help them discover how Flipsnack can support their business.

## Advertise in ChatGPT

Reach people as they explore options, compare choices, and make decisions in ChatGPT, with relevant ads that fit naturally into the experience.
