title: AI for scientific discovery: How researchers use Claude
body:
Johannes Hermle*, Ben Jones*, Lukas Althoff*, Ryan Heller, Thomas Lyttelton, Carolyn Stein, Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory
*Lead authors of the report
Summary
- What we measure. AI could speed up scientific discovery, but by how much depends on what AI can do and how scientists use it. Using privacy-preserving methods, we study 207,000 Claude and Claude Code research sessions to understand how Claude is used across scientific fields and research tasks. We are conducting this research to help the public better understand the state of AI for science today and assess the impact that AI may have on scientific discovery in the future.
- Where scientists use Claude. Relative to the number of researchers in each field, Claude is used more in the formal sciences, such as computer science, mathematics, and statistics, and less in health and lab-based physical sciences. Scientists primarily use Claude to analyze data and to write. Data analysis alone accounts for about one-third of sessions on Claude and nearly half of sessions on Claude Code. Scientists use it less for idea generation and data gathering, even though, in an accompanying survey, they rank those tasks as the most important for scientific discovery. That said, specialized AI tools designed for scientific work could narrow the gap between the research tasks scientists use AI for and the ones they consider most important. On Claude Science, for instance, idea generation makes up about twice the share of use that it does on Claude.
- How Claude use tracks AI capability. We create a measure of how well AI can, in theory, perform each research task. The tasks AI is best suited to (the top 20% on this measure) get two to four times as much Claude use as the time researchers spend on them would predict. The tasks AI is least suited to (the bottom 20%), which include most physical work, get very little. We observe the same pattern across fields: fields where AI can perform many tasks well, such as computer science and statistics, use Claude more.
- What this could mean for the speed of scientific discovery. Using a simple model, we explore scenarios for how much AI could speed up research. If existing AI capabilities are widely adopted, they could double research output in some fields. If AI could carry out all non-physical research work, output in fields such as computer science and statistics could rise as much as 15-fold, while output in bench sciences such as chemistry and biology, which are held back by physical bottlenecks, would rise three- or fourfold. In our survey of researchers who actively use AI, about 40% expect AI models to carry out full research projects on their own by 2030.
Introduction
Science has been described as an “endless frontier” (Bush 1945). But how fast we explore that frontier has historically been limited by a scarce resource: the time and talent of human researchers. Artificial intelligence could ease that limit by amplifying what researchers can do, transforming both the process of discovery and the pace of exploration (Wang et al. 2023; Amodei 2024). Few applications of AI could matter more for human welfare. Given the highly cognitive nature of research compared with most sectors of the economy, AI’s effects may be particularly large and early in this domain.
Recent examples show AI playing a growing role in scientific discovery. In structural biology, AlphaFold predicted the three-dimensional shapes of over 200 million proteins (Jumper et al. 2021; Varadi et al. 2024), and its creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In materials science, GNoME predicted 380,000 stable new crystals (Merchant et al. 2023). In mathematics, researchers have used AI systems to help resolve decades-old Erdős problems, produce a potential proof for a Millennium Prize problem, and make progress on other major problems, from open conjectures to verifying landmark proofs (Anthropic 2026a, 2026b; OpenAI 2026a, 2026b; Tsoukalas et al. 2026).
Beyond these developments, most scientific progress involves many specialized, interlinked research tasks, which can vary substantially across fields. How much AI accelerates scientific discovery depends not only on AI’s capabilities, but also on how it is adopted across these tasks. In this report, we use privacy-preserving infrastructure to study the scientific use of Claude, Claude Code, and Claude Science. We document how usage varies across fields and tasks, identify what explains these usage patterns, and outline scenarios for how AI could accelerate research.
Claude use in science varies by field. Relative to their number of researchers, formal sciences such as computer science, mathematics, and statistics use Claude more heavily, while health and lab-based physical sciences use it less. Across research tasks, scientists use Claude more for analyzing data and writing, and less for gathering data or generating ideas and hypotheses. This is consistent with self-reported AI use from an accompanying survey of scientists.
To understand these differences, we develop a measure of theoretical AI capability. Claude use is higher in tasks and fields that score higher on this measure. These also tend to be more cognitive in nature and better suited to reinforcement learning, in which AI learns from feedback on repeated attempts. In short, scientists appear to use AI where it works best.
Based on these findings, we outline scenarios for how AI could accelerate scientific progress. With current capabilities, research output in some fields could as much as double, primarily from task-level augmentation. Researchers in our survey expect much greater capabilities to come. In a hypothetical scenario where AI fully automates all non-physical work, highly cognitive fields such as computer science or statistics could see up to a 15-fold increase in output. Because the fields with the largest potential for acceleration include those that produce AI itself, these gains could create an additional feedback loop, in which faster AI research produces more capable AI, which in turn could further accelerate research.
While faster scientific discovery could bring substantial benefits to humanity, AI-driven research also carries risks and uncertainties. Less human oversight could lead to the pursuit of dangerous or unethical research. AI could also reshape researchers’ careers, making research work more or less rewarding, and alter the sense of purpose associated with the human pursuit of knowledge.
How we conducted this research
Our goal with this research is to measure the different ways scientists use Claude while protecting the details of their work. To do this, we use privacy-preserving infrastructure to analyze the scientific use of Claude on consumer plans. A language model, used here as a “classifier,” reads each session transcript and labels it with a fixed set of categories, such as the field and the research task it involves, according to a predefined taxonomy (SciNet taxonomy by Alamos and Althoff 2026). The resulting labels, such as “chemistry” or “data cleaning,” are the only information from these conversations retained and analyzed by the research team for this report. No classifier employed in this study extracts and stores open-ended information or details on research content, such as research datasets, hypotheses, experimental methods, early findings, or unpublished papers. Results are reported only in aggregate and only for cells that meet a minimum number of distinct accounts. All classifiers introduced in this study are listed in the [Appendix](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/files/4zrzovbb/website/fafb3d4237f9b53fe114fef4fb5109b9cf5b5e60.pdf).
Our measurement involves two steps. A first classifier identifies whether a session transcript involves scientific work. A second classifier then assigns each of these transcripts to a field, subfield, and task in the SciNet taxonomy. SciNet contains 7,262 tasks, spanning 34 fields and 318 subfields. Some tasks in the taxonomy, such as drafting manuscripts, are universal to all fields. Others are specific to individual fields or subfields. For instance, in the taxonomy, the task of predicting optical absorption and emission spectra is specific to materials science. Together, the tasks cover the full process of producing a new research finding.
Our main sample consists of 207,049 sessions on consumer plans from August 2 to September 30, 2026, which were assigned a scientific field and a research task: 128,914 from Chat and Cowork, two general-purpose interfaces for conversation and knowledge work, hereafter referred to as “Claude,” and 78,135 from Claude Code, an agentic coding tool that works directly with a user’s files, writing and running code. We also study a supplemental sample of Claude Science sessions. For details on sample construction, see the [Appendix](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/files/4zrzovbb/website/fafb3d4237f9b53fe114fef4fb5109b9cf5b5e60.pdf).
Combining usage data and a structured taxonomy of research tasks allows us to study which fields adopt Claude and for which parts of the research process. This research contributes to a growing body of work attempting to measure the adoption of AI technology for scientific discovery (Kobak et al. 2025; Liang et al. 2025; Hao et al. 2026; Codreanu et al. 2026).
How Claude use varies across scientific fields
We begin by describing how Claude use varies across scientific fields. Figure 1 compares a field’s share of sessions against the share of global researchers in that field, giving us a sense of relative use per scientific field.[1](#footnote-1) On Claude, the three largest fields by session share are computer science (11.9%), engineering (8.4%), and medicine (7.7%), which are also among the largest fields by global researcher counts.[2](#footnote-2) Overall, fields with a larger share of researchers also tend to account for a larger share of Claude sessions (log-log correlation of 0.79).
However, Claude use per field cannot be explained by the number of researchers alone. In Figure 1, fields above the 45-degree line show higher usage relative to their size, while fields below the line show lower usage. Relative usage is especially high for the formal sciences, including computer science, mathematics, and statistics. Usage is also high for the social sciences. By contrast, physical sciences such as chemistry, where work often happens in a lab, tend to show lower relative usage. So does medicine, the third-largest field by session volume, where researchers spend much of their time with patients.
On Claude Code, usage is less strongly related to field size (log-log correlation with researcher counts of 0.62) and concentrates in more quantitative fields. Despite making up only 4.3% of the world’s researchers, computer science alone accounts for 32.7% of Claude Code sessions.[3](#footnote-3) Other formal sciences, such as mathematics and statistics, also show high relative usage. Relative usage is low in the arts and humanities and in the social sciences, with the exception of economics, a comparatively quantitative field.
We observe similar patterns when comparing usage across 318 subfields within those 34 fields (Figure 2).[4](#footnote-4) This more granular subfield view reveals that artificial intelligence and machine learning stands out, with session shares of 5.0% for Claude and 15.2% for Claude Code, despite making up only 1.2% of the world’s researchers. More generally, regardless of the broad scientific domain, computational subfields are among the strongest adopters. These subfields include computational biology, computational linguistics, and computational neuroscience. Robotics also shows high relative usage, likely because it builds heavily on computational methods despite its focus on physical systems.
How Claude use varies across research tasks
Beyond understanding which fields use Claude, we also want to understand what scientists use it for. Re

title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
body:
[content type highlight](/highlights)published November 5, 2026
Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
Maximum inner product search (MIPS) sits at the core of recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Given a query vector, MIPS systems search within a database of millions of candidate key vectors for the one that best matches the query. The original data point associated with that best-matching key is then used to handle the query: in RAG, the document that is best suited to answer the question is typically prefixed to the query.
As the number of keys grows to millions and vector dimensions reach thousands, the computational cost of running an exhaustive comparison of the query to all keys grows dramatically. Numerous approximate methods have been proposed to trade off accuracy for speed using clustering and quantization. While these baseline methods focus on the properties of the set of keys to build up clever indexing structures, their geometric arguments loosely assume that the set of queries itself will resemble that found in keys, or bypass any considerations about what the queries will look like. This can be problematic on two fronts: In the crucial RAG case, queries arise from short user-generated questions, whereas keys represent long, informative, and curated pieces of text, making keys and queries substantially different. Additionally, most MIPS use cases deployed in production target an existing base of users with a stable, well-characterized query distribution â a signal that generic, query-agnostic methods leave untapped. Crafting methods that work best for a likely source of inputs â rather than aiming for good performance on all possible inputs â is a central tenet of modern machine learning that helps redirect compute resources more efficiently.
In [Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions](/research/amortizing-inner-product-search), a paper presented at ICML 2026, researchers from Apple train small neural networks (NNs) â once, offline, for a fixed database of keys â that learn how to route queries toward their best match faster. Their approach trades off an upfront amortization cost to understand how typical queries tend to be matched in exchange for faster, more accurate retrieval at inference time through these small NNs.
A fundamental principle in MIPS is to leverage the geometry of the set of keys to speed up search: Typical MIPS systems split the set of keys into k clusters â k is typically much smaller than the total number of keys n â keeping track of a representative centroid for each cluster. When receiving a new query, the system compares it with these k centroids. The query is then routed toward the cluster of the representative centroid it is closest to, and subsequently compared exhaustively with all keys stored in that cluster. If the database has n keys and k evenly distributed clusters, the effective number of keys that will be considered in that second step is on the order of n/k â a factor-of- k speedup when compared to the n comparisons done in the naive exhaustive approach. Unfortunately, this routing mechanism can result in errors, since centroid routing is not an exact approach, as illustrated in [Figure 1](#figure1) below.
What makes MIPS interesting from a machine learning perspective is that it is built on a mathematical structure that had been largely overlooked before this work: The function that maps a query to the largest inner product with any key in a set is the [support function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Support_function) of that set, a well-studied object in convex analysis. This function has two important properties: First, it is convex, so it can be approximated by a class of neural networks specifically designed for convex functions, [input convex neural networks (ICNNs)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/amos17b.html). Second, the gradient of that support function at any query returns the best-matching key itself.
The broad idea behind this work is to learn a neural network that can mimic the ground-truth support function (or its gradient directly) for a much lower computational cost. This can be achieved through a classical ML technique known as regression: one simply needs to precompute a large number of training examples formed by sampling input vectors (user queries) and pair them with the relevant output signal produced by MIPS (either the optimal score or the optimal key vector itself). All that is then needed is to train a suitably parameterized neural network to replicate the output given the input.
If the regression problem were to be solved perfectly, according to the mathematical approach outlined above, the same neural network that is trained to mimic the support function could also output the optimal key by evaluating its gradient (through automatic differentiation). In practice, we observe that training separate, specialized networks for each of these two tasks works best:
The SupportNet neural network architecture can learn the support function directly, using a (loosely constrained) ICNN. The approach is mathematically principled and aligns with the convex structure of the problem. We find that this approach can shine when used to compute one support function per data cluster to improve routing quality.
KeyNet models learn to directly output the best-matching key vector when fed a query. A consistency loss derived from Eulerâs theorem for homogeneous functions keeps their predictions geometrically grounded in the underlying support function, even though no convexity is explicitly enforced.
Both models are trained on examples drawn from the relevant query distribution: for each sampled query, the ground-truth best match is computed once via exhaustive search and stored, creating a supervised dataset that captures the MIPS solution landscape for the distribution of queries that actually matter.
As shown in [Figure 1](#figure1), the simplest way to handle larger scales is to split the keys into clusters, compare the query to each clusterâs centroid, and route the query to the most promising clusters based on these k scores. This provides a cheap yet coarse rule that can be prone to mistakes because a centroid alone cannot account for the spread of its cluster. Indeed, a cluster can hold a key that sits far from its own centroid yet close to the query, and when the query is near such an outlier, centroid routing scores the cluster low and skips it, missing the true best match.
If one were given access to the support function of each cluster, then one would instead be able to do exact routing, since each support function quantifies exactly to what extent any key within each cluster can match the query with a large score. This is illustrated in [Figure 2](#figure2), in which the support function of each of the four clusters is plotted for a query that varies in the space of embeddings.
Leaning on this theoretical insight, we propose to learn these k support functions jointly with a trained SupportNet that can output k scores at once. We can then use the largest of these k scores to route any new query instead. The SupportNet model can answer a more useful question than a simple comparison to the centroid can: âHow good is the best key inside this cluster for this query?â SupportNets are trained in a classic machine learning fashion, also known as regression: we generate sample queries that are drawn from the distribution (typically embeddings for text queries), compute the ground-truth support functions at those queries, and train a neural network to replicate these values.
We trained SupportNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L â 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) on [Natural Questions](https://huggingface.co/datasets/BeIR/nq-generated-queries) partitioned into 128 clusters. Natural Questions is a retrieval benchmark that pairs general-knowledge questions with passages from a large document database, roughly 2.6M unique passages in our setup.
[Figure 4](#figure4) below shows the retrieval performance in terms of recall as a function of different notions of cost. Routing recall is the fraction of queries whose true partition, the one holding the exact best key, lands among those the router chooses to probe. For both plots, an exhaustive search is carried out in the top-s clusters matched with the query, where s grows as powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8, â¦, 128). Naturally, all methods reach a recall of 1 when they survey all 128 clusters.
The first tab shows that for a fixed retrieval performance the learned routers reach it at lower latency than centroid routing. The small SupportNet model hits 95% routing recall about 1.9Ã faster than centroid routing (1.74 ms vs 3.36 ms), and gains are even greater with the large model, which hits 97% in 1.74 ms. This plot explicitly factors in the additional compute incurred by running our small NNs rather than simply comparing to centroids.
The plot on the second tab looks exclusively at routing quality, neglecting the overhead incurred by running NNs. At a fixed budget of explored clusters, they find the right partition more often: scanning just 5% of the database, the learned routers recover the true partition ~90â93% of the time â up to 92.6% for the mid-size (M) â versus 87.5% for the centroid baseline.
SupportNet routing replaces the simple centroid-based routing found in existing inverted file index (IVF) systems. With KeyNet, we can also keep the IVF system as is and just feed it a modified version of the query. In that scenario, KeyNet works naturally as a âquery rewriterâ in front of a standard approximate search index: predict where the best match is likely to be in embedding space, then ask your favorite IVF system to look there instead of starting from the original query. Because the IVF index is highly optimized, it can find the result faster when assisted by KeyNet. We also rely on regression to train KeyNets, as summarized in [Figure 5](#figure5): sample queries are matched with their ground-truth, best-matching key, and the KeyNet neural network is trained to reproduce that association.
We evaluated KeyNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L â 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) and in [Figure 6](#figure6) below, we show recallâcost tradeoffs for these different sizes. On the first tab, the search budget is wall-clock latency: reaching 99% recall takes up to ~8Ã less time with the largest model (0.23 ms vs 1.8 ms for the raw query). As before, the second tab focuses exclusively on the boost in âqualityâ provided by replacing the original query with its KeyNet transformation. The x-axis is the fraction of the database the index actually scans: scanning just 0.001% of the database, KeyNet-mapped queries retrieve the true key 89â97% of the time â up to 96.7% for the largest model (L) â versus 86% for the raw query, and reaching 99% recall takes up to ~11Ã fewer keys (0.009% vs 0.10% raw). Better recall for the same cost, or the same recall for a fraction of it.
We show examples obtained from the same [Natural Questions](https://huggingface.co/datasets/BeIR/nq-generated-queries) dataset discussed previously, served through a [FAISS IVF](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss) index. It is one of several datasets we studied, and the trend is consistent across them. Querying the index with KeyNetâs predicted key consistently beats querying with the raw question, across the full search-budget sweep.
Namely, [Figure 7](#figure7) below shows five Natural Questions examples: top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query.
The choice between the two ends up being a practical one. Use KeyNet when inference speed is the bottleneck and you just need to approximate the best key. Use SupportNet when you also want a calibrated score (for re-ranking, thresholding, or downstream use), or when compute is tight at small

title: More visibility and control over Claude Enterprise for security teams
body:
More visibility and control over Claude Enterprise for security teams
Claude Enterprise has new security and admin features, including a security center, generally available inference hooks, centralized management, and additional access controls.
To see how Claude is set up, the security center shows how your organization’s Claude settings compare with Anthropic’s recommended configuration. To apply your policies, inference hooks send prompts and tool calls to your data security tools for a check. To manage access, centralized management gives your company one admin console for company-wide settings, and new access controls let you sign members out through the Admin API, manage your IP allowlist yourself, and help prevent shadow IT by blocking personal and other outside Claude accounts in Claude Desktop on managed computers.
We also recently announced an Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) integration, which runs your organization's sensor inside the [unified Claude](https://claude.com/resources/articles/unified-claude-enterprise) and Cowork virtual machine on the user's computer.
Security teams need to see how Claude is configured, what it does on company devices, and how data is handled as people work. These features give them that visibility and control.
Security center: review your Claude security settings in one place
Security teams can review Claude's security settings for chat, Cowork, and Claude Code on one page, instead of setting by setting. The security center is a new page in Organization settings that compares settings with Anthropic's recommended configuration, so your team can see what to change and where to change it.
For each control, the security center shows the current value, the recommended value where there is one, and a link to the setting where you can change it. It also shows which settings are new or recently changed. The security center checks your configuration each time the page loads, so automatically checked controls reflect your current settings. Organizations with the Compliance API can read the same results through it.
Attestations give your admins a shared workspace for security reviews. They can work through the process together once, recording the current state of each control, accepting risks, and flagging issues in one place.
You can download the security center page as a report to share with auditors and relevant stakeholders. The report marks which controls the page checked automatically and which an Owner confirmed. The security center is guidance based on Anthropic's recommendations, not a certification or a guarantee of compliance with any law or standard.
Inference hooks
Inference hooks connect Claude to the data security tools your organization already uses, so your data loss prevention (DLP) and security policies can apply to prompts and tool calls as people work.
There are two kinds of hooks, both now generally available:
- Prompt hooks send prompts from supported Claude products to your security tool for a check.
- Pre-tool-call hooks check tool calls in supported Claude products before they run.
Hooks work with security vendors. Your team keeps the policies it has already written and applies them to Claude.
Centralized management: one console for identity and access across your organization
Centralized management gives your parent organization, which represents your company across its Claude Enterprise and Claude Platform organizations, its own admin console at admin.claude.com. Admins manage company-wide settings there once for the organizations under your parent, instead of from individual organization settings. These settings include single sign-on, directory sync (SCIM), domain verification, groups, and Compliance API keys.
The console shows every organization under the parent in one place and adds two roles. Parent organization owners can manage everything at the parent level, including who holds the owner and admin roles. Parent organization admins can manage everything except those role assignments.
Companies can also connect more than one identity provider, each with its own single sign-on and SCIM configuration. An acquired company can keep its existing provider, or your team can move to a new provider one domain at a time.
Each organization keeps its own members, roles, settings, and organization-level security controls, such as IP allowlisting, tenant restrictions, and session duration. A parent role doesn't grant access inside an organization by default, but Compliance API keys created at the parent can read data across organizations.
Access controls: member sign-out and shadow IT prevention
Security teams can now sign a member out of Claude with a single Admin API call, without removing them from the organization. The call ends that member's sign-in sessions on every browser and device, and apps like Claude Code have to sign in again. It doesn't end API keys, cloud sessions already running, or scheduled routines, and the member can sign in again afterwards.
Enterprise admins can now set up and manage their IP allowlist themselves, without going through Anthropic. An IP allowlist limits access to most Claude products to the IP addresses your organization approves.
Admins can now set the most-used Claude Desktop settings, with no device management push. To help prevent shadow IT, admins can also block personal and other outside Claude accounts in Claude Desktop on managed computers. Owners can also limit which workspace folders people can use with Claude.
Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) in Cowork and unified Claude
When Cowork and unified Claude work locally, they run shell commands and code in an isolated virtual machine on the user's computer for additional protection. That isolation helps protect the device, and security teams have asked for the same visibility into the virtual machine that they have everywhere else on the endpoint.
Admins can now run their organization's EDR sensor inside the Cowork virtual machine. The sensor reports activity there to the same console your security team already monitors. This covers the virtual machine on the user's computer, not Cowork sessions in the cloud.
Admins set up the integration through device management on macOS and Windows. Each time the virtual machine starts, Claude verifies the sensor package's signature from your EDR vendor before installing it. Sensors run in detection mode: they report activity to your security team and don't block it. The integration works with supported EDR vendors, which are listed in the [Help Center](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/17828685-run-your-endpoint-detection-and-response-edr-sensor-in-claude-cowork-on-claude-desktop).
Getting started
These features are available for Claude Enterprise, with some exceptions during beta listed in the [Help Center](https://support.claude.com/en).
The [security center](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/18246629-review-your-organization-s-security-posture-with-the-security-center) is in beta. [Inference hooks](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/16059458-inference-hooks-overview), including prompt hooks and pre-tool-call hooks, are generally available. Admins can manage both inference hooks and the security center in Organization settings.
[Centralized management](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/18232924) is also in beta. To start setup, an admin of any organization under your parent goes to admin.claude.com and proposes the parent organization admins. Admins of the other organizations review and approve, and the last approval completes setup. Setup can't be undone, so identify your parent organization admins before you start.
[Signing members out](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13133750-manage-members-on-team-and-enterprise-plans#h_3cba7d14e5) through the Admin API and the [self-serve IP allowlist](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13200993-restrict-access-to-claude-with-ip-allowlisting) are in beta. Owners can manage [Claude Desktop settings](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/12622667-enterprise-configuration-for-claude-desktop#h_21135034c8) in Organization settings, also in beta.
[Endpoint detection and response](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/17828685-run-your-endpoint-detection-and-response-edr-sensor-in-claude-cowork-on-claude-desktop) in Cowork is in beta on macOS and Windows for Claude Team and Enterprise, and for the Claude desktop app on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry, deployed through MDM for supported vendors.

title: Introducing Personal Finance in Claude
body:
Introducing Personal Finance in Claude
Ask Claude about your money and get straight answers from the accounts you connect.
Getting answers about your money no longer means opening every banking app and doing the math yourself. With Personal Finance in Claude, you can securely connect your bank and card accounts and ask in your own words. Access is read-only, and Personal Finance can’t move, manage, or invest your money.
Claude gives you answers in everyday language, from your balances and transactions, and explains any term that's new to you. Like [the rest of Claude](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-is-a-space-to-think), Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it doesn’t offer credit cards, loans, or savings accounts of its own, so your money questions get a straight answer.
Personal Finance starts rolling out in beta this week, on the Pro, Max, and Ultra plans in the US.
What it looks like
Say it's late in the month and payday is still 10 days away. When you ask Claude, "Where did my money go this month?" it adds up your spending across the accounts you connected and sorts it by category. In this example, that comes to $4,309.37, with more than half going to rent and utilities and $1,024.51 to food and drink.
From there, you can dig deeper: "Is that more than usual?" "Anything else I'm missing?" "So what's left before payday?" Claude checks the previous months and points to a membership renewal. Then Claude tells you about four payments that will come out of your checking account before payday, and what you’ll have left: $1,393.22.
If you ask whether anything looks off, Claude reads across every account you've connected and can point to what's easy to miss, like charges that hit twice, unexpected fees, or a bill that’s crept up all year. You can also ask bigger questions, like "Am I spending more than I make?" or "What's an APR, and what has mine cost me this year?" Claude explains the term, then adds up the interest you've been charged.
Ask for a weekly spending chart, a calendar of what's due, or a dashboard of the numbers you choose, and Claude builds one you can keep adjusting.
Security and privacy
Claude's access is read-only. Personal Finance helps you understand your money, and it isn't designed to give investment advice. Claude can make mistakes in its answers, so ask which transactions are behind a number, and check important figures with your bank.
Your accounts are only connected once you sign in to your bank yourself through [Plaid](https://plaid.com/), a service that connects apps to banks. That's where you agree to its terms and approve Claude's read-only access, so Claude doesn't ask for or see your bank password.
For the accounts you choose to connect (and only those), Claude sees the bank's name, each account's name, type, and last four digits, balances and credit limits, and up to two years of transactions. When you chat with Claude in the Personal Finance hub, those conversations aren't used to train our models. For anything you share with Claude outside the hub, your [privacy settings ](https://claude.ai/settings/privacy)apply. You can unlink an account anytime, and then Claude can no longer see its data. More details can be found in our [Privacy Center.](https://privacy.claude.com/en/collections/10663362-consumers)
Getting started
When you see Personal Finance in Claude's sidebar, open it, connect one account, and ask a single question, like "Can I afford a trip this spring?" or "How much could I save each month?" You'll find the setup steps, and how your data is used and kept, in the [Help Center. (opens in new tab)](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/18185620-use-personal-finance-with-claude)
What’s next
Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust. We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it.

title: Build Live Apps in Cursor
body:
Build Live Apps in Cursor
Agents have lowered the cost of writing code, but most apps and tools that users build never make it off of localhost.
Now, you can build live apps directly in Cursor and share them with a link. Describe what you want to create and Cursor will handle the rest: build the app, set up a database, configure auth, and deploy it.
With this release, anyone in your org can now build useful tools for their work and share them with teammates. Update Cursor to try it out.
How it works
To get started, kick off a [cloud agent](https://cursor.com/docs/cloud-agent) and tell it explicitly that you want to build an app.
Cursor will scaffold the web app, spin up a Postgres database if needed, set up authentication behind Cursor SSO, and provision hosting. If the app needs to connect to your systems, like a data warehouse, Cursor will ask for the secrets it needs.
When you go to publish your app, you pick a unique domain and Cursor gets you back a live link.
At Cursor, users across sales, operations, legal, finance, and engineering are building internal apps. Some of the most useful ones are:
- Internal ops tools for event registration, account assignments, and desk seating
- Multimedia presentations for customers that combine slides, videos, and interactive demos
- Training, enablement, and onboarding experiences for new hires
- Live dashboards and tools for sales teams to understand their pipeline and opportunities
- Portals to manage engineering services
Cursor can deploy apps from new or existing repos across Cursor Origin and GitHub. Support for other git providers like GitLab is coming soon.
Controls and guardrails
When you publish an app, Cursor will run deterministic and agentic security checks to catch common issues, like secrets written in app files or exposed credentials. If a check fails, the agent tells you what it needs to fix. Nothing goes live until the checks pass and you explicitly publish the app.
Team admins can see every app and secret on the team. They can also add their own rules to the security review, approve publishes the review blocked, and unpublish any app.
Share with your team
Once the checks pass, Cursor deploys the app to the URL you chose. You can then share your app with specific people, groups, or your entire team, all behind Cursor sign-in. On individual plans, you can also share apps publicly.
You can also provision a Cursor API key if you want a script or Grok Bot to use your app.
Get started
This capability is now available on all paid plans with cloud agents enabled. Learn more by reading our [docs](https://cursor.com/docs/cloud-agent/apps).

title: A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.
body:
Text-to-Speech • Updated • 54
[
](#a-closer-look-at-phonon-tts-launching-high-quality-on-device-speech-that-tops-the-benchmarks)
A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.
[Update on GitHub](https://github.com/huggingface/blog/blob/main/phonon-tts.md)
Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.
We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.
[
](#why-a-voice-should-live-on-your-device)
Why a voice should live on your device
Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.
Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.
We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.
Phonon is based on the [Pocket TTS](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/pocket-tts) lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.
[
](#what-we-released)
What we released
Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in [Gradium Studio](https://studio.gradium.ai/). Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.
It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can [hear it right now](https://huggingface.co/spaces/gradium/phonon). Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.
[
](#demos-and-first-projects)
Demos and first projects
[The launch](https://gradium.ai/blog/release-phonon-open-weight) came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.
The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.
Developers have started building on it too. An [ExecuTorch conversion](https://huggingface.co/executorch-community/Phonon-31M-EN-ExecuTorch-WebGPU) runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, [Micdrop](https://micdrop.dev/docs/ai-integration/provided-integrations/phonon.md) brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like [smallest-s2s](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Steveeeeeeen/smallest-s2s) build on it.
Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.
[
](#how-phonon-did-on-the-hugging-face-open-tts-leaderboard)
How Phonon did on the Hugging Face Open TTS Leaderboard
The [Open TTS Leaderboard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/hf-audio/open_tts_leaderboard) is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the [Hugging Face Hub](https://huggingface.co/models?pipeline_tag=text-to-speech), the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.
On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in [German](https://huggingface.co/spaces/hf-audio/open_tts_leaderboard?languages=de) and [Spanish](https://huggingface.co/spaces/hf-audio/open_tts_leaderboard?languages=es), and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.
Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the [CPU streaming benchmark](https://huggingface.co/spaces/hf-audio/open_tts_leaderboard?streaming-cpu) on time-to-first audio.
[
](#inference)
Inference
We built a new inference framework, [ptts](https://github.com/gradium-ai/xn-ptts), specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).
Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts
runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile
, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.
It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a [modular](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/modular_transformers) model: about [200 lines](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/src/transformers/models/gradium_phonon_tts/modular_gradium_phonon_tts.py) describing only what differs.
Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an [audio tokenizer](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/model_doc/pocket_tts_audio_tokenizer), held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:
from transformers import AutoProcessor, GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration
model_id = "gradium/phonon-31m-en"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto")
model = GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto")
print(f"{model.num_parameters():,}") # 30,788,354
print(f"{processor.audio_tokenizer.num_parameters():,}") # 10,305,313
A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: [gradium/phonon-voices](https://huggingface.co/gradium/phonon-voices).
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from safetensors.torch import load_file
path = hf_hub_download("gradium/phonon-voices", "voices/LMDIYE0Oa377Qh6Z.safetensors")
voice = load_file(path)["speaker_wavs"][0].T # (num_frames, 512)
The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio
item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:
conversation = [
{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "audio"}, {"type": "text", "text": "Hello from Phonon."}]}
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
conversation,
tokenize=True,
return_dict=True,
add_generation_prompt=True,
processor_kwargs={"audio_prompt_latents": [voice]},
).to(model.device)
# prompt: <|audio_prompt|> × num_frames, "Hello from Phonon.", <|audio_bos|>
generate
returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:
outputs = model.generate(**inputs) # audio_latents: (batch_size, num_frames, 32)
audio = processor.decode(outputs.audio_latents, outputs.audio_latents_mask)
processor.save_audio(audio, "phonon.wav")
See the [docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/model_doc/gradium_phonon_tts) 🤗 for more!
[
](#whats-next)
What's next
Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in [Gradium Studio](https://studio.gradium.ai/). Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.
We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. [Get in touch](https://gradium.ai/contact?subject=Sales) and tell us what you need.
Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.
Phonon is our first open release. [Try it out](https://huggingface.co/spaces/gradium/phonon) and tell us what you build.

# Franklin Templeton uses OpenAI to support investment research

Starting with equity research, Franklin Templeton is developing AI workflows to help portfolio managers compare views and examine risks.

[Contact sales](https://openai.com/contact-sales/)



Company size: Enterprise

Region: North America

Industry: Finance

Products: Codex

Loading…

Share

Creating connected, continuous intelligence

- [Creating connected, continuous intelligence](#creating-connected-continuous-intelligence)
- [Creating workflows specific to each role](#creating-workflows-specific-to-each-role)
- [Building AI around how investing works](#building-ai-around-how-investing-works)

- [Creating connected, continuous intelligence](#creating-connected-continuous-intelligence)
- [Creating workflows specific to each role](#creating-workflows-specific-to-each-role)
- [Building AI around how investing works](#building-ai-around-how-investing-works)

Franklin Templeton wants AI to help portfolio managers examine different research views and the risks behind an investment idea. Codex is one of several tools our investment teams are using to develop workflows for investment research.

> “The biggest unlock from using OpenAI’s tools is the ability to merge continuous intelligence with human judgment. It has really transitioned because, beforehand, AI was automating our human-led process. Now AI is actually automating the ability to surface intelligent insights, and that intelligence layer plus human judgment is just a fantastic unlock.”

—Katrina Dudley, Senior Vice President, Public Market Investments, Franklin Templeton

## Creating connected, continuous intelligence

When Franklin Templeton first tried using AI, the team put data in a database and connected the models to it. But it didn’t produce the answers the teams needed because the models didn’t understand how the data fit together. When the team added agents and a semantic layer, a structured model of what the firm’s data means and how it’s connected, the results changed. The team is using Codex and other tools to develop this connected intelligence layer. "We've been able to build what we think of as a connected intelligence layer," Dudley says. "We're bringing the data into the tools, and we're surfacing insights that make a difference."

Research, risk, compliance, and trading offer different perspectives on an investment. Franklin Templeton’s ambition is to bring those inputs together for portfolio managers. “We're able to bring that all in and then use that to surface insights to the people who are making decisions, which are our portfolio managers,” Dudley says.

Dudley describes the earlier equity-research workflow as human-led and sequential: an analyst performs first-pass stock analysis, reviews earnings calls, and studies competitors in each business line. The goal is to surface useful information as analysts prepare new ideas to be pitched to portfolio managers or provide updates on existing positions in the portfolio. As she puts it, “It's just continuous intelligence combined with that human judgment.”

In the workflow Franklin Templeton envisions, its investment teams will have access to a governed, reusable intelligence foundation that brings together trusted connectors, portfolio and workflow context, and agentic capabilities that surface actionable insights for its analysts and portfolio managers.

## Creating workflows specific to each role

Franklin Templeton has used Codex in hackathons, bringing experts alongside investment practitioners as they develop their own tools. Its Investment AI champions are working to turn experiments into production-ready workflows, with security review, expert support, and data controls as part of that process.

Dudley says, “We have moved from augmenting our research process to reimagining the investment research workflow.”

## Building AI around how investing works

Some of what makes AI helpful in other settings doesn't work in asset management. Many tools learn a user's preferences and show them more of the same, so if someone favors one research provider, the tool surfaces more of that provider's reports. For an investment team, that narrowing potentially brings a biased perspective into the investment process. Franklin Templeton wants the opposite. "We want to make sure that they're accessing that diversity of research and diversity of opinion," Dudley says.

Franklin Templeton wants its AI systems to emphasize investment risks. “We need AI to understand that a great investment idea is one that is well reasoned, but it also has analyzed the risks and makes our portfolio managers aware of the risk,” Dudley says. “If you’re looking at a research note, focusing on the fact someone has identified the investment risks is not a bad thing from our perspective. It makes for a more informed investment decision.”

Franklin Templeton's experience points to some investment management best practices:

- “Our message from leadership is consistent: we encourage innovation and experimentation with AI within clearly defined risk guardrails. Not every initiative will succeed, but each should generate insights that strengthen our capabilities, inform future decisions, and drive continuous improvement,” Dudley says.
- Get new tools into people's hands: Dudley says Franklin Templeton has brought practical labs to teams quickly after new technology launches, so they can test how it fits their work.
- Help teams learn the tools: Dudley says, "The goal is getting them to actually understand the power of the technology."
- Build with appropriate controls: Security review, expert support, and data agreements are part of Franklin Templeton’s path from experimentation toward production-grade tools.

> “With OpenAI, our teams feel like they’re at the forefront of technology.”

—Katrina Dudley, Senior Vice President, Public Market Investments, Franklin Templeton

title: Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out
body:
Image-Text-to-Text • 4B • Updated • 544 • 23
[
](#dharma-field-extractor-any-document-in-structured-fields-in-json-out)
Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out
[Team Article](/blog)
A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.
[
In April, we released ](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/6a725daa5ca641a21ab61956/JIRHcND5LFS_JhgAe-ObV.png)[DharmaOCR-LITE](https://huggingface.co/Dharma-AI/Dharma-OCR-LITE), a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14314) behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.
OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.
However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.
Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.
A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.
So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.
You can try it yourself [here](https://ocr-portal.prd-us-east-2.dharma-ai.com/login).
[
](#what-the-model-does)
What the Model Does
Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:
- Open: no schema supplied. The model reads the page and works out which parts of it are structured fields (a label followed by a value, a table with a header row over its columns) from context and layout, not from a fixed list of field names, and returns everything it finds as key-value pairs.
- Schema-directed: you specify the exact shape wanted, field by field, with a type for each one (string, number, or boolean), under the key names your system already uses. Ask for "service_provider" and "client_company", and those are the exact keys that come back. Ask for a table and it fills it row by row, column by column, matching each cell to the key it belongs under. Ask for a field that isn't on the document, and it returns null instead of inventing a value.
The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.
Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null
where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.
[
](#how-it-was-trained)
How It Was Trained
The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.
The data is organized into three streams:
- English multi-domain data: diverse documents collected from the public web, spanning many document types.
- Brazilian domain data: real Brazilian documents sourced internally, in Portuguese.
- Multilingual data: a smaller share covering other European and Asian languages, for broader generalization beyond English and Portuguese.
All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.
[
](#where-the-benchmark-draws-the-line)
Where the Benchmark Draws the Line
The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.
We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.
Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).
Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.
This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.
[
](#a-test-of-generalization)
A Test of Generalization
SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.
On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.
On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.
[
](#quality-and-cost-at-the-same-time)
Quality and Cost, at the Same Time
A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.
This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.
Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.
Try it on your own documents [here](https://ocr-portal.prd-us-east-2.dharma-ai.com/login). To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit [dharma-ai.com](https://dharma-ai.com).
[
](#sources)
Sources
- BID. Brazilian Identity Document Dataset. Soares, Neves Jr., Bezerra (2020), "BID Dataset: a challenge dataset for document processing tasks," Anais Estendidos XXXIII SIBGRAPI.
[github.com/ricardobnjunior/Brazilian-Identity-Document-Dataset](https://github.com/ricardobnjunior/Brazilian-Identity-Document-Dataset) - CORD. Park et al., NAVER CLOVA (2019).
[huggingface.co/datasets/naver-clova-ix/cord-v2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/naver-clova-ix/cord-v2) - DocVQA. Mathew et al., WACV 2021 (ICDAR 2019).
[huggingface.co/datasets/lmms-lab/DocVQA](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lmms-lab/DocVQA) - WildReceipt. Sun et al., IJCAI 2021.
[huggingface.co/datasets/Theivaprakasham/wildreceipt](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Theivaprakasham/wildreceipt) - SROIE (ICDAR 2019). Held out from training, evaluation only.

- [Bringing the work together in Codex](#bringing-the-work-together-in-codex)

Today we're announcing that OpenAI will acquire [Pierre Computer Company, Inc⁠(opens in a new window)](https://pierre.computer/). (“Pierre”), the company behind [Code Storage⁠(opens in a new window)](https://code.storage/) and a family of standout open-source developer tools. If you’ve browsed files or reviewed a change in the Codex app, you’ve already used Pierre’s Trees and Diffs libraries. We’re excited to work with the Pierre team to build on the Git workflows that developers already rely on and adapt them to how teams work with coding agents.

We’ve seen in our own engineering work how the systems around Git need to evolve as more of that work happens in parallel. Earlier this week, we shared how we’re [scaling Git at OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/scaling-git-at-openai/) with Pando, our in-house source control backend for engineers and agents. With the Pierre team, we wish to set the standard for modern software development: from the first branch an agent creates to that magic moment when code is deployed to the world. We want to make Codex the place where developers and agents take on their most ambitious projects.

## Craftsmanship meets scale for the agentic era 

We’ve long appreciated the care Pierre brings to another part of working with Git: how developers review code. You can see that care in the libraries we use in Codex today. Trees lets developers quickly navigate a project’s files, and Diffs makes it easy to see what changed. Both of these tools make it easy to review and navigate large volumes of code with uncompromising performance. 

That same attention to detail runs through Pierre’s other work. Diffs’ *Edit* mode lets a reviewer fix a line of code right where they spot the problem. Pierre recently released *Highlights*, an extremely fast syntax highlighter that updates as a developer types or an agent streams code. The same small team that put an editor inside a diff also designed the API for Code Storage, a service that lets apps store code and track its history using Git.

## Bringing the work together in Codex

Pierre has built tools that developers love, and together, we will ship new products and platforms that benefit all. Once the acquisition closes, our ambition is to advance the future of source control across the industry. We want Codex to connect the code a company ships with the decisions its people make, at the scale the future demands.

Pierre’s open-source projects will remain open-source, and we’ll continue to contribute to them. Customers can continue using Code Storage after the acquisition closes while we work to bring its features and functionality into Codex.

*The closing of the acquisition is subject to customary closing conditions, including receipt of regulatory approvals. Until closing, OpenAI and Pierre will remain separate and independent companies. *

title: Don't Approve the AI Model. Approve the App - Doneyli De Jesus, Langfuse
body:
Doneyli De Jesus, who leads AI engineering solutions at Langfuse by ClickHouse, shares how his team helped a top-five bank put deployment gates on AI agents. Banks don't certify models, they certify applications, and they need setups that are on-premises, gated and air-gapped. He walks through building a golden data set, scoring traces across several dimensions, and how a small model that was 97% grounded but only 60% accurate on numbers cleared the bank's 85% gate once it got a calculator tool. Domain experts set the thresholds and review failures, taking evaluation from weeks to minutes.

title: Building the AI Agent Is Easy. Proving It's Safe Isn't - Jonathan Osborne, NatWest
body:
NatWest lead AI engineer Jonathan Osborne shares how the UK's second-largest retail bank, with 19 million customers and about 100,000 assistant conversations a day, is moving its digital assistant Cora from scripted answers to AI agents. Building the agent was the easy part; proving it was safe was the hard part. He covers the routing funnel that limits what ever reaches a model, why quality is several scores instead of one, human reviews where an 83% pass rate hid a 54-point gap, an LLM judge that scored far higher than humans with almost no correlation, and shadow deployments with feature flags for a safe rollout.

# A thousand fewer paths to root

We've developed an autonomous vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and patching pipeline. In one run with our cyber model, it validated and generated patches for 948 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Linux at an API cost of $1.2 million.

Security research that once required a separate, sustained investigation for each finding can increasingly be run as a systematic process. This document explores one of our efforts in this area.

Vulnerability discovery is becoming easier to scale, but prioritization and validation remain operational bottlenecks. We built a prototype to look for security flaws in the Linux kernel inside a controlled research environment. Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access.

We used this evidence to prioritize vulnerabilities for reporting and developed candidate patches for maintainer review. Following guidance from the Linux kernel community, we began with critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners on further reports and patches.

In June, as part of our [Patch the Planet initiative](https://openai.com/index/patch-the-planet/), we shared that GPT‑5.5 Cyber had identified Linux kernel vulnerabilities and developed 24 local privilege escalation exploits to validate and report them. We expanded that work into a pipeline, powered by an upcoming cyber model, covering vulnerability discovery, dynamic validation, exploitability assessment, and patch generation. When it finished, human researchers reviewed the outputs and reported found vulnerabilities alongside patches.

## Summary

**Methodology**

- At a high level, our pipeline works as follows: first it identifies security-relevant parts of the Linux kernel, statically scans those audit targets for candidate findings, dynamically reproduces those findings in an isolated environment, creates a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit to demonstrate exploitability, generates patches, and finally a human security researcher reviews the results.
- The output of the pipeline includes a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes.

**Findings**

- In a run in mid-October 2026, our pipeline using an upcoming cyber model dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and generated PoCs for **291 information leak** vulnerabilities and **948 working local privilege escalation** (LPE) exploits for a commonly used Linux distribution. The total run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or **$1,279 per LPE exploit.**
- The target virtual machines ran a stock desktop operating system, not a weakened target, under the same threat model used by cybersecurity competitions (e.g. [Pwn2Own ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.zerodayinitiative.com/blog/2026/3/11/announcing-pwn2own-berlin-for-2026), [TyphoonPWN ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://typhooncon.com/typhoonpwn-2026/)). Historically, Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN offered a $20,000 and $70,000 bug bounty for Linux kernel LPE exploits. Applying those historical bounty amounts to the 948 exploits produces a hypothetical valuation of **$18.9M—$66.3M**, approximately **16x to 55x** our pipeline’s cost.
- On an adapted [kernelCTF ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://google.github.io/security-research/kernelctf/rules.html) environment, which is a version of the Linux kernel with reduced attack surface, our pipeline obtained **25 information leak PoCs** and **21 LPE exploits**. For comparison, 26 confirmed 0-day LPE exploits have been accepted by kernelCTF in 2026 at the time of writing.
  - The campaign cost roughly $32,936 in API credits. If the 21 vulnerabilities were accepted by the program, it would lead to around a **$1.5M bounty award**, **\~45x** the scanning cost.
- To the best of our knowledge, the agents in this pipeline discovered and used at least 10 novel Linux exploitation techniques.

**Reflections**

- The Linux maintainers and security community are working hard to rapidly discover and fix vulnerabilities. Within 10 days while the scan was running, we observed over 100 Linux LPEs had been patched or had staging patches from other contributors, with \~300 more being publicly discussed.
- Given the rate of vulnerability discovery by frontier models, we believe automated patch generation is essential to secure software at the pace required, and to limit the exploitation window. With human expert-guided iteration, we believe AI-generated patches can be functionally correct, aligned with existing coding styles, and robust to attack variants. This is an important area for further research.
- More capable models are able to discover new vulnerabilities in existing code, often including ones that have been around longer and are more complex to identify. Our analysis pipeline using the newer cyber model in mid-October discovered >5x more novel LPEs than a GPT‑5.6 Sol run in July, despite three months of hardening between the scans.
- Large, complex software projects likely require multiple rounds of scanning and fixing vulnerabilities to “bottom out” latent bugs. Ideally this process is repeated with each subsequent generation of frontier models. This applies to both proprietary and open source software.
- For the near and medium term, having access to a low-privileged account on an operating system, that isn’t up-to-date on its latest available patches should be considered functionally equivalent to root access for a well-resourced threat actor. Defense in depth, using sandboxes and isolation approaches like Firecracker and gVisor are important for limiting the blast radius of exploited vulnerabilities.
- Within the next few years, we believe that if there are vulnerabilities in a given software project, frontier models will likely be able to discover them and even less capable models may be able to develop exploits once disclosed. In a world of no unknown vulnerabilities, it will be critical to build and maintain high assurance software, especially core software such as operating systems, browsers, image parsing libraries, the TCP/IP stack, and more. Investing in training models to write secure code by default, minimizing attack surface by removing unnecessary features, and formal verification are promising areas of future research to effectively scale software security, in addition to finding and fixing existing vulnerabilities.



## Why the Linux kernel

The Linux kernel underpins Android devices, cloud infrastructure, supercomputers, and other systems used by billions of people. With more than 40 million lines of code, the kernel exposes a broad attack surface through system calls, networking, filesystems, and device drivers. We chose Linux to study how effectively frontier models could find vulnerabilities and demonstrate their security impact in a codebase of this scale and importance.

The initial vulnerability discovery stage produced thousands of candidate findings, too many for security researchers to manually review and triage. The operational challenge of our vulnerability discovery pipeline was not discovery, but determining which findings could be reproduced, what security boundary they crossed, and which warranted the earliest maintainer attention.

## Cost analysis

The mission of OpenAI’s Cyber team is to help secure the software the world relies on. We report API costs for each stage to help researchers assess the resources needed to reproduce and extend this work. These costs reflect the models, target configurations, and workflow used in this evaluation. Our broader goal is to help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities, reducing the opportunities available to attackers and raising the cost for them to exploit software.

Finally, note that we focused on methodology and measuring model capability in this research, not cost. We expect that sufficient harness engineering could meaningfully reduce the cost at each stage; thus, the costs we report are more an upper bound.

## The vulnerability research pipeline

Our vulnerability research prototype is a pipeline of five stages, which uses an upcoming cyber model at its core:

- **Vulnerability discovery:** Agents identify security-relevant parts of the codebase and scan them for candidate findings.
- **Dynamic validation:** Agents attempt to reproduce each candidate in an isolated environment and preserve runtime evidence. This step outputs the reproduced and validated vulnerabilities.
- **Exploitability assessment:** Agents test whether validated vulnerabilities could ena
