Building on the availability of Daybreak models on Amazon Bedrock, GPT‑5.6 Cyber is now available to approved customers [in AWS GovCloud (US-East)⁠(opens in a new window)](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/10/openai-daybreak-red-govcloud-east/) through Daybreak Red. This expansion gives government security teams a new way to apply advanced cybersecurity capabilities within the AWS environments they use to support critical missions.

Daybreak Red provides access to OpenAI’s purpose-trained cybersecurity models for authorized vulnerability research, exploit validation, and security testing. GPT‑5.6 Cyber can help defenders investigate complex software weaknesses, reproduce vulnerabilities in controlled settings, and develop mitigations. Qualified security practitioners should review findings and proposed fixes before implementation.

## Bringing frontier cybersecurity capabilities to government teams

For government organizations, adopting advanced cybersecurity capabilities requires more than model performance. Teams also need to work within established security, governance, and operational requirements.

Availability in AWS GovCloud (US-East) gives eligible teams a path to incorporate GPT‑5.6 Cyber into those workflows through Amazon Bedrock. Defenders can use it to reason through security findings, assess their impact, and evaluate fixes, helping connect vulnerability research to practical improvements in defense.

Daybreak Red gives verified defenders greater latitude for authorized cybersecurity work, with fewer refusals for these tasks alongside stronger identity verification, monitoring, and access controls.

For Daybreak Red on Amazon Bedrock, inference data is not used to train models, and customers do not need to share their Daybreak Red data with OpenAI.

## Get started

Access requires OpenAI Daybreak Red approval and AWS provisioning. To get started, complete the [Daybreak application](https://openai.com/form/enterprise-trusted-access-for-cyber/) or contact your OpenAI or AWS account team about eligibility. Once approved, work with your AWS account team to enable access. Daybreak Red approval does not automatically enable model access on AWS.

Learn more about [Daybreak models on AWS](https://openai.com/index/daybreak-models-are-now-available-on-aws/).

title: Why AI Makes You 100x Faster but Not Your Company - Mitchell Troyanovsky, Basis
body:
Individual engineers have seen huge productivity gains from AI, but most companies haven't. Mitchell Troyanovsky, co-founder of Basis, argues that agents need to be simple and reliable to spread through a company, and the way to get there is to make them opinionated. He covers behavior specs, why outcome evals don't generalize to production, and two tools for finding out why an agent made a bad call: forking and sub-agent simulations.

title: Investigating vault particles with Claude
body:
We’re sharing another finding from[Anthropic’s biology research lab]: the first 3D structure of a vault particle found in prokaryotic cells. Vaults are large, hollow barrels of protein found in cells across the tree of life, and their function is still unknown. Below, we describe how Claude helped at each step of this research: searching across sequence literature, optimizing a method of isolating particles, and mapping the vault’s structure. More information is[in our preprint], which we’ve submitted to bioRxiv; we’ll update the link as soon as it goes live.
Biological cells were first detected in 1665, but more than three and a half centuries later, much of how they work remains unknown. Until relatively recently, [the existence of some crucial components](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12360195/), let alone [their function](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3184113/), was controversial. Even today, more than a third of the roughly 4,400 genes in one of the most comprehensively studied cells, the bacterium E. coli, [remain poorly understood](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6412132/). Another such enigma is the vault particle.
A vault particle is a large, hollow protein shell found in nearly all the cells in our body. [It was discovered in 1986](https://rupress.org/jcb/article-abstract/103/3/699/13490/Isolation-and-characterization-of-a-novel?redirectedFrom=fulltext) by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha, but its function remains elusive. At roughly three times the mass of a ribosome, it’s one of the largest known molecular complexes in eukaryotes—organisms with complex cells, such as mammals (as opposed to simple, usually single-celled “prokaryotes,” such as bacteria). Vaults take their name from their shape. When observed under an electron microscope, the ribbed shell reminded Dr. Rome and Dr. Kedersha of the vaulted ceiling of a cathedral. In mammals, the shell is made of 78 copies of the major vault protein, arranged as two identical halves joined at the middle.
Vaults are [found across most of the eukaryotic tree](https://doi.org/10.1093/gbe/evt113), from slime molds to humans, so scientists believe that they must do something useful. Researchers have proposed various functions, including [transporting molecules between the nucleus and cytoplasm](https://doi.org/10.1242/jcs.106.1.23), [protecting cells from toxic compounds such as cancer drugs](https://doi.org/10.1038/nm0695-578), and [supporting innate immunity](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1142311), but none of these proposals have been conclusively confirmed. Other studies have shown that [mice lacking vaults still survive](https://doi.org/10.1128/MCB.24.12.5314-5323.2004), which suggests that vaults may be necessary only under specific environmental conditions. Still, the question remains: why would evolution retain something so large if it didn’t have an important function?
Interested in whether Claude could help make progress on this long-standing open problem, our biology research team has been investigating vaults. We haven’t yet determined their biological function, but we did find that many more vault proteins across the tree of life, including those in prokaryotes and the bacteriophages that infect them, can assemble into complete vault-like particles. Related proteins had [already been found](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2023.11.10.566534v1.abstract) in the genomes of both prokaryotes and phages, but to our knowledge no one had shown that they assemble into vaults.
A vault in a prokaryotic cell gives researchers a simpler system to study. Compared with mammalian cells, bacteria are quick to grow, which makes it easier to investigate where vaults came from, what their basic structure looks like, and what, if anything, they contain. Studying the bacterial relatives of human proteins has been informative before. Bacterial versions of [cGAS–STING signaling](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1605-5), [gasdermins](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abj8432), and [viperins](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2762-2) revealed the microbial origins of these human immune defenses. In those cases, their function in humans was already known. For vaults it is not, and their prokaryotic relatives may help reveal it.
Here, we describe how we uncovered the molecular structure of a vault from a bacteriophage. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria. Like all viruses, they hijack their host cells to make their proteins, so this vault would be built inside a bacterium, a prokaryotic cell. The vault is built from 96 copies of a single protein, compared with 78 in human vaults. By duplicating part of the protein, we engineered the vault to be even larger. Together, these results shed light on how such complexes assemble and suggest how they could be adapted for [biotechnology](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adz9353)—for example, as [nanocapsules for delivering enzymes](https://www.pnas.org/doi/abs/10.1073/pnas.0500929102).
This work also demonstrates our team’s wider aim: to speed up research in fundamental biology by building Claude into every step of the process. Under our direction, Claude searched protein databases, designed the DNA constructs, optimized the isolation method, and processed the microscopy data. As a result, a vault purification that conventionally takes three days took us about 90 minutes, and a first structural model was ready 34 hours later, which we estimate would normally have taken us weeks.
Despite this progress, there is still much to be learned about these perplexing structures. When we shared the structure with Dr. Rome, whom we brought on to advise us on this research, he said:
Figuring out the function of vaults is still enormously challenging. I am pleased that Anthropic has so much good data. Now, other people will be working on this problem … The broadness of Anthropic’s finding[s] suggests that it is going to be a complicated function and an interesting ride.
Our lab is releasing these findings early to continue to show the scientific community how Claude can be used for discovery. You can read more about our results and methods [in our preprint](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/76e55fbe85697afbaae16b839498dc00797dec30.pdf), and we will be releasing the structures and additional data soon.
A vault-like structure in prokaryotes
We uncovered the vault structure using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), in which many copies of a particle are flash-frozen and imaged with an electron beam, before being combined into a single 3D model. The vault is built from 96 copies (48 copies per half) of a single phage protein, which we call L05, with a combined mass of about 9.5 [megadaltons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalton_(unit)). By contrast, the mammalian version has 39 copies per half. The phage-derived vault is also shorter and wider: roughly 54 nanometers long and 45 wide, compared with 67 by 40 in mammals. Despite being shorter, it encloses about 25% more volume because it is more spherical. The protein chain that makes up its wall is built from seven repeating segments stacked end to end, rather than the nine in mammalian vaults, and its end caps are flatter. It’s among the largest protein shells ever identified in prokaryotes.
One notable feature of its structure is how the caps close. A wall 48 copies around must narrow toward the pole, and it does so in three steps, like a tiered dome. In every group of three neighboring copies, one ends at the first step, one at the second, and one continues to the tip. The three copies are identical along the wall, but take different shapes (conformations) in the cap.
Given that we can make this vault in the lab and isolate it quickly, we also experimented with altering its structure to learn more about how these proteins assemble. Working with Claude, we made 15 altered versions of the protein, most with changes at the points where neighboring copies touch. Some single changes near the cap were enough to prevent the shell from closing: in place of sealed vaults we saw open, rosette-like particles, which shows that this region is needed to seal the shell.
We also tried making the vault even bigger. Ordinarily, the wall is built from seven repeating segments. When we copied two of them, giving the protein nine—the same number as in the human vault—it assembled into even larger vault particles, increasing the enclosed volume by approximately 20%. These experiments demonstrate how vaults could have changed size over their evolutionary history by duplicating pieces of their own wall without disrupting how they assemble.
Finding, isolating, and mapping a new vault with Claude
Part of the reason vaults have remained unexplained for 40 years is that they are [missing from the organisms biologists rely on most](https://doi.org/10.1093/gbe/evt113) for genetic experiments, including baker’s yeast, fruit flies, and nematode worms. In mice, which do have vaults, animals that are bred without [a vault partner protein](https://doi.org/10.1128/MCB.24.12.5314-5323.2004) or [the vault RNA](https://doi.org/10.1261/rna.080161.124) develop normally, leaving no obvious defect to follow up. In recent years, bioinformaticians [identified distant relatives](https://doi.org/10.1101/872010) of the vault protein in prokaryotes, but it wasn’t clear whether these proteins formed vaults.
Our team set out to answer that question. The research required several steps: surveying genetic sequences to find where vault proteins occur across the tree of life, producing and isolating the most promising candidates to test whether they actually assemble into vault-like particles, and determining the structure of one of the particles to see how its chains fit together.
We began by using [Claude Science](https://claude.com/product/claude-science) to search for the vault protein’s relatives across a database of about 15 billion predicted proteins. They turned out to be rare but widely distributed, present in 29 major groups (phyla) of bacteria and four of archaea (the other main group of prokaryotes) but in less than 1% of species with a sequenced genome. We then chose 44 of these proteins and tested each in [a cell-free system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell-free_system) to see which genes yielded full-length protein and how much. We chose the proteins, and Claude turned each protein sequence into DNA tailored to the host cell, added the control sequences that switch a gene on, and prepared the designs for ordering. We moved the best performers into living E. coli bacteria, where 15 of 24 produced soluble protein.
Next, we needed to isolate the particles. The conventional method, developed for eukaryotic vaults, spins the sample through a tube of increasingly dense sugar and takes approximately three days. To speed this up, we decided to try size-exclusion chromatography. In this process, the sample flows through a column of porous beads. In a process called fractionation, small molecules get stuck in the pores, while the vaults, which are too big to enter, come out first, in what’s known as the void volume.
Claude first argued against taking the chromatography approach, because clumps of misfolded protein come out in that same void volume. We went ahead anyway, and Claude helped make it work by recommending a specific column as well as methods to track the vault protein and check whether particles had formed. Claude then proposed loading the contents of ruptured cells straight onto the column with no purification beforehand. We were reluctant at first because these columns are expensive, and the raw contents of ruptured E. coli cells can clog them or cause contamination. But we were willing to test an unconventional idea, and it worked.
We are not [the first group to isolate vaults on sizing columns](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30036602/), but our optimized method takes about 90 minutes from cells to microscopy grid instead of days. Under an e

title: New agents and products for security, productivity, and creative work on Claude Marketplace
body:
New agents and products for security, productivity, and creative work on Claude Marketplace
We’ve added new agents and products to [Claude Marketplace](https://claude.com/marketplace), where teams find partner tools and services to help them get more from Claude. The additions cover security, developer infrastructure, creative, and productivity.
Eligible enterprise customers can apply a portion of their committed Anthropic spend toward these solutions. This lets them use one commitment across Claude and partner products, whether they’re buying something new or expanding with a platform they already use.
There are now over 25 partner agents and products on the marketplace. Here are the latest additions and what teams can do with them.
Products and agents for securing code and systems
[Chainguard](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products/chainguard): Chainguard Harness builds applications from source in an isolated microVM and probes the live app for exploitable vulnerabilities. It helps teams fix what Claude finds, with custom remediation recommendations for reproducible vulnerabilities.
[Checkmarx](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products/checkmarx): Checkmarx One pairs rules-based analysis with AI reasoning to find vulnerabilities in code. It helps teams prioritize findings and fix them before code ships.
[Cyera](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products/cyera): Cyera Agent Guardian inventories Claude deployments, governs permissions before Claude runs, and enforces policy on prompts, files, and tool calls. It helps teams test those controls through red teaming.
[Rubrik](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products/rubrik): Rubrik Code Guardian uses frontier AI models from Anthropic to review a secure copy of GitHub or Azure DevOps repositories for multi-step attack paths. It helps security and engineering teams rank issues by severity and turn confirmed critical ones into tracked tickets.
[Tanium](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products/tanium): Tanium Cloud gives teams real-time visibility and control across their endpoints. It helps IT and security teams find and fix vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and missing patches.
Development infrastructure for engineering teams
[Datadog](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products/datadog-agent-observability): Datadog Agent Observability traces agent execution through tools and services. It helps teams improve agent quality, performance, and cost efficiency by surfacing production patterns and recommending fixes.
[Netlify](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products/netlify): Netlify Enterprise deploys apps, sites, and agents to a global edge network, with preview URLs on every change. It helps teams take what they build with Claude from prototype to production with no infrastructure to configure, and includes SSO, role-based access, and audit logs.
Tools for marketing and creative work
[AirOps](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products/airops): AirOps provides an agentic platform for AI search strategy, content, and multichannel execution. It helps marketing teams analyze brand performance in AI search and tie results to pipeline and revenue.
[Runway](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products/runway): Runway generates and edits video, images, and audio. It helps creative and marketing teams turn a brief into finished assets and edit footage with natural language.
[Webflow](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products/webflow): Webflow provides built-in tools to build, manage, and optimize websites. It helps marketers, designers, developers, and agents make changes, with controls and governance built in.
Productivity apps for every team
[Asana](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products/asana): Asana AI Teammates are prebuilt agents that use context from the Asana Work Graph, each with its own identity, scoped permissions, and audit trail. They help teams handle multi-step work, routing decisions that need judgment to the owner.
[Glean](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products/glean): Glean connects company knowledge and workflows across systems. It helps employees find answers and complete multi-step tasks across connected apps.
[monday](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products/monday): monday agents work inside projects, boards, docs, and meetings, using their owners and deadlines as context. They help PMO, IT, marketing, finance, and operations teams control what AI can access, approve, and spend.
[Zoom:](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products/zoom) Zoom Agentic Search answers questions inside Claude using the latest meeting summaries, work conversations, documents, and connected third-party sources. Teams get permission-aware results without analyzing raw transcripts or chaining tools together.
Get started
You can browse all agents and products on [Claude Marketplace](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products) and request to buy from any listing. If you’re building on Claude and want to join the marketplace, see the [ways to join](https://claude.com/marketplace#join).

title: Embed 5 and Rerank 5 now on OpenRouter
body:
[Embed 5](https://openrouter.ai/cohere/embed-5-pro) and [Rerank 5](https://openrouter.ai/cohere/rerank-5-pro) are now live on OpenRouter. Here’s how to turn them into a working RAG pipeline in a few dozen lines of Python code through a [single API](https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/rag).
There are Cohere’s most powerful retrieval models yet, delivering leading performance on enterprise documents and complex retrieval tasks. If you’re already using OpenRouter, you can get started immediately - using the same API key and credits as your existing models, with no additional setup.
RAG grounds an LLM's answer in your own data by fetching relevant chunks before it writes. Embedding search provides a fast and effective first-stage approximation. A reranker then reads the query and each candidate together, adding precision to what’s been retrieved.
Two features of the Cohere models shape this design:
- Embed 5 Pro and Fast share one embedding space. Index with
embed-5-pro
for quality, then query withembed-5-fast
for latency. - Rerank 5 scores are calibrated. A score means the same thing across queries and domains, so one relevance threshold can filter out weak context before it reaches the LLM.
By the end you'll have a short Python script that answers questions over your docs with scored citations. This same approach can be applied to virtually any retrieval use case, from enterprise search and customer support to knowledge management and document discovery.
Setup
You’ll need Python 3.10 or newer, an [OpenRouter API key](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api/api-reference/api-keys/create-a-new-api-key), the [OpenRouter Python SDK](https://openrouter.ai/docs/client-sdks/overview), and NumPy for an in-memory vector store.
Embed 5 returns Matryoshka vectors at six sizes, 2048 by default. We [suggest](https://cohere.com/blog/embed-5) 1,024-dim int8 vectors as the best quality-to-cost point; OpenRouter's [embeddings API](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api/api-reference/embeddings/submit-an-embedding-request) returns floats, so this post uses 1,024-dim floats.
The NumPy store keeps this demo simple. For production, replace it with your preferred vector database, such as pgvector, Qdrant, Pinecone, or Weaviate.
Indexing
Indexing turns each chunk of text into a vector, a list of numbers where similar meanings sit close together. It runs once per corpus, so it's the step where the highest-quality model pays off.
Split each document into chunks, embed them with Embed 5 Pro as search_document
, and normalize the vectors so a dot product equals cosine similarity.
The sample corpus is a fictional API's docs, with a few near-misses on purpose:
Three key details to point out:
input_type:
tells Embed 5 which side of the search a text is on. OpenRouter passes it through to Cohere.- Batching: sends many chunks per request, which cuts round trips and speeds up indexing. It doesn't change the cost, since embeddings are priced per token.
- Chunk size: packing whole paragraphs follows the by-paragraph strategy in
[OpenRouter's guide](https://openrouter.ai/docs/cookbook/evaluate-and-optimize/rag), and 1,500 characters is roughly 300–400 tokens of English. Embed 5 accepts up to 128k tokens, but every chunk also goes through Rerank 5, which reads up to 32k tokens of query and chunk combined and splits anything longer into several passes.
Retrieval
Retrieval finds the chunks whose vectors sit closest to the question's vector. This acts as a representation of semantic similarity between the two pieces of content.
Embed the question with Embed 5 Fast as search_query
, then pull a wide candidate set of 20 chunks by cosine similarity.
Querying a Pro-built index with Fast works because the two models [share an embedding space](http://www.cohere.com/blog/embed-5), as long as both sides use the same dimensions
. It's the split we recommend: in [Cohere's tests](https://cohere.com/blog/embed-5) across 40 datasets, Fast queries on a Pro index kept 98.4% of all-Pro retrieval quality, against 96.6% for Fast on both sides. With any other model family, you’d have to use the same model on both sides.
Let’s cast a wide net at this stage: recall is the retriever's job, precision is Rerank’s. OpenRouter's guide suggests 10–20 candidates feeding a top 3–5 rerank.
Reranking
Reranking re-scores the shortlist by reading the question and each chunk together. That's too slow to run over a whole index but more accurate than vector similarity, so it runs only on the top candidates. Rerank doesn’t require Embed - or any embedding model. It works as a simple second stage with your existing semantic, keyword, or hybrid search system.
Send the query and the 20 candidates to Rerank 5, keep the top 5, and drop anything under a relevance threshold.
Each result carries the candidate's position in your list (index
) and a relevance_score
, per the [rerank response schema](https://openrouter.ai/docs/sdks/typescript/api-reference/operations/creatererankresponsebody).
What [Rerank 5](https://docs.cohere.com/changelog/rerank-v5) adds at this step:
- Calibrated scores. Scores stay consistent across queries and domains, so a single
MIN_SCORE
decides what reaches the LLM. - 32k-token context. Long chunks are scored whole.
- Semi-structured data. JSON records and tables rerank well when formatted as YAML strings.
- No re-indexing to upgrade. Rerank reads raw text at query time, so switching models is a one-line change.
Use rerank-5-pro
for reasoning-heavy queries and long or domain-specific documents. Use rerank-5-fast
for high-volume search and agents that search many times per task. One thing to note: [Rerank 5](https://docs.cohere.com/docs/rerank) is text-only, but will work for parsed pdfs.
Generation
Generation hands the best chunks to an LLM as numbered sources and asks it to answer from those alone. That keeps answers grounded in your docs and gives readers citations they can check. If nothing clears the threshold, skip the LLM call entirely.
Sending each chunk's title with its text lets the model cite something readable; add URLs too if your docs have them. OpenRouter's guide uses the Responses API for this step instead. To follow it, call client.responses.send
with the system prompt as instructions
and the sources and question as input
, then read the answer from the message item in res.output
rather than from choices
.
Results
Here we’ll validate whether the steps we implemented improved our responses.
Reranking earns its extra call when it confidently picks the right chunk and drops near-misses that embedding search ranks just below it.
| Rank | Embed 5 only | Embed 5 + Rerank 5 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rotating API keys · 0.522 | Rotating API keys · 0.808 |
| 2 | Webhook signing secrets · 0.337 | below 0.3 cutoff |
| 3 | Creating API keys · 0.316 | below 0.3 cutoff |
Wrap-up
Everything in this pipeline ran through one API key and one client. Embed 5 Pro built the index, Embed 5 Fast and Rerank 5 handled each question, and a chat model wrote the answer, with no separate SDKs, accounts or bills to juggle.
That single surface is also what makes the pipeline easy to evolve. Every model is just a string, so trying rerank-5-fast
instead of rerank-5-pro
, or a different chat model, is a one-line change.
Start with the sample corpus, swap in your own docs, and see what Rerank 5 moves to the top.
Where to take it next:
- Hybrid search. Add keyword (BM25) hits beside the vector hits. Rerank reads raw text, so it scores both lists in one call.
- A smaller index. Drop to 512 or 256 dimensions, or use int8 or binary vectors through Cohere's own API.
- Images and PDFs. Embed 5 embeds images and mixed text-and-image inputs such as PDF pages, and OpenRouter's embeddings API accepts
image_url
content parts. Rerank 5 is text-only, so rerank those results on their text, such as parsed page text or captions, or skip reranking for them. - Evaluation. Label a small set of real queries, compare hit rate at 5 with and without rerank, and tune
MIN_SCORE
on the same set. - Explore
[Compass](http://www.cohere.com/compass). Cohere’s enterprise search and retrieval platform brings Embed and Rerank together in a single solution, making it easier to build powerful search and AI applications across enterprise data. Now available to[cloud customers](http://www.cohere.com/blog/compass-cloud-beta).

[DevRev⁠(opens in a new window)](https://devrev.ai/) built Computer and Operator to help service and operations teams carry even the hardest customer and employee requests through to completion. Computer and Operator are designed to reason across live data. Actions are reversible, and answers point back to their sources, explains Ahmed Bashir, DevRev’s chief technology officer.

DevRev combines OpenAI models, including GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol, with its harness for connecting company knowledge and giving teams control over the actions an agent can take. DevRev sees OpenAI models as providing reasoning and reliability with the speed and cost of serving customers and employees.

> *“It’s a combination of being able to have the right reasoning capabilities, being able to be trusted, highly aligned, and most importantly, it has to work from a latency perspective.”*

—Ahmed Bashir, Chief Technology Officer, DevRev

## Making AI work with company context

OpenAI models power the reasoning, planning, and tool selection behind both Computer and Operator. In DevRev’s Agent Studio, users can describe how they want a tool to behave in a conversation with AI and define parts of its behavior with fixed rules.

DevRev tests the models together with the software that supplies company context, enforces permissions, and controls actions. Its Enterprise-Bench benchmark evaluates how well they work when data has multiple versions, information sits in different systems, and access depends on a person’s role.

Ahmed says GPT‑6.1 Sol performs well in those evaluations. When a customer or employee is interacting with an AI agent, the model needs to understand the nuances of the request and respond quickly, at a cost the business can sustain. “I think it strikes the balance perfectly,” Ahmed says.

## Building software and sales demos with Codex

Inside DevRev, engineers have made a clear choice about the best way to build. “Our entire team uses Codex,” Ahmed says. The adoption grew organically after engineers explored multiple coding tools. By the time of the interview, DevRev had moved fully to Codex and dropped its Cursor licenses.

For Ahmed, this reflects what developers value: “Developers are really just looking for the best tool, and you can’t fool them.” His engineers were unequivocal about wanting to continue with Codex.

> *“We think that Codex is far and away the best experience.”*

—Ahmed Bashir, Chief Technology Officer, DevRev

DevRev’s sales engineers also use GPT‑6 Astra to create demos for the company’s booths at international conferences.

## Responding faster to customers and employees

When a customer or employee asks for help, the request may require Operator to understand the issue, take approved action, or route to Computer to prepare the right person to act. Ahmed sees opportunities for the Decisions API and Ultrafast to help those workflows finish quickly, without requiring deep reasoning at every step.

Some of those decisions are difficult and expensive to define with fixed rules, especially when the information they depend on keeps changing. Ahmed wants builders to be able to describe more of that logic conversationally and choose the right kind of intelligence for each task. “These things have to be able to run and complete themselves in seconds, not minutes,” he says.

## Realizing the promise of self-service

DevRev’s next ambition is for Operator to take on longer, more demanding customer and employee requests while keeping actions traceable, permissioned, and reversible.

Ahmed sees familiar support tasks, such as finding a knowledge-base answer, upgrading a plan, or getting a refund, as only the beginning. “We want to really realize that promise of self-service,” he says.

With OpenAI’s frontier intelligence, DevRev is building toward Computer and Operator carrying more complex requests through to resolution, with the company knowledge and controls to act on a person’s behalf.

Faster iteration and more professional visuals

We’re introducing Images 2.6 in ChatGPT, Codex, and the API, bringing your ideas to life faster. With this, you can bring motion to your images with GIFs — from animating a brand mascot or character to turning a product shot into an eye-catching loop. You can also create polished visuals faster and refine them with greater precision — keeping characters, products, and brand details consistent as you edit.

People around the world now create 4 billion images per week across ChatGPT, Codex, and the API. On average, that’s more than half a billion images created per day.

## Faster iteration and more professional visuals

Images 2.6 generates images 50% faster than before. In the API, we offer GPT‑Image‑2.6 Flare and Sunburst for developers to choose from. When quality is set to low, Flare can generate images in as little as six seconds. For work that calls for greater detail and precision, GPT‑Image‑2.6 Sunburst brings higher-quality image generation and even greater image consistency across edits when quality is set to medium or high. Flare also improves layout quality for posters, product imagery, and other professional visuals.

## Animate your ideas with GIFs

For moments that call for motion, GIFs bring another dimension to your ideas. Marketers and creators can animate a brand mascot for a campaign, create reactions and memes for social media, or use animated storyboards to explore character movement before video production.

*Created by OpenArt*

**Prompt 1****:** Create a single animation sprite sheet for a seamless looping GIF. A super-cute chibi adult office worker sits at a desk watching a computer monitor with a clearly plunging stock-market line chart. The sequence: hopeful expression, notices the chart falling, eyes widen, face crumples, large cartoon tears stream down both cheeks, then quietly wipes tears while still staring at the falling chart. Oversized round head, tiny body, big expressive eyes, soft rounded features, messy fluffy hair, white shirt and loosened tie. Exactly 6 sequential frames arranged in a precise 3-column by 2-row grid, read left-to-right then top-to-bottom. Every panel has identical dimensions. Fixed front three-quarter camera, same character, same desk, monitor, outfit, and cozy miniature office background. Clear incremental facial and tear motion; sixth frame transitions smoothly toward the first. Polished kawaii chibi 3D toy-like style, warm pastel lighting, funny and sympathetic mood. No captions, no words, no numbers, no logos, no speech bubbles, no panel labels, no borders, no gutters.

*Created by OpenArt*

**Prompt 2:** Create a single animation sprite sheet for a seamless looping GIF. A super-cute chibi adult office worker sits at a desk watching a computer monitor with a clearly soaring stock-market line chart and a large upward arrow. The sequence: notices the chart rising, eyes widen with delight, jumps up cheering, grabs a handful of generic paper banknotes with no readable currency markings, then happily tosses the banknotes into the air like confetti while laughing. Oversized round head, tiny body, big sparkling expressive eyes, soft rounded features, messy fluffy hair, white shirt and loosened tie. Exactly 6 sequential frames arranged in a precise 3-column by 2-row grid, read left-to-right then top-to-bottom. Every panel has identical dimensions. Fixed front three-quarter camera, same character, desk, monitor, outfit, and cozy miniature office background. Clear incremental body, arm, and flying-paper motion; sixth frame transitions smoothly toward the first. Polished kawaii chibi 3D toy-like style, bright celebratory pastel lighting, funny joyful mood. No captions, no words, no numbers, no logos, no real currency symbols, no speech bubbles, no panel labels, no borders, no gutters.

> “GIFs are the native language of social media, and GPT‑Image‑2.6 lets every OpenArt creator speak it fluently from a single prompt.”

*—Coco Mao, CEO & Co-founder at OpenArt*

And you don’t need a polished design to get started — even a simple sketch can become an expressive, animated character for videos, games, and more.



From personal reactions to brand mascots and product visuals, GIFs give people and businesses a playful way to communicate. Town, a startup building an AI work assistant, used Images 2.6 in the API to explore how animated characters could bring more personality to everyday interactions at work.

## More ways to create and edit in the API

With Images 2.6, developers get more control over how images are created, edited, and carried into the next stage of a project. Image markup, already available in ChatGPT, comes to the API so teams can pinpoint exactly where to make specific changes. SVG exports make designs ready to use across websites, apps, and print.

A new complexity parameter lets developers adjust how much planning the model does to meet a request, with lower settings suited to quick edits. Image quality controls visual detail and fidelity, while complexity guides how much goes into the scene.

> “GPT‑Image‑2.6 brings speed and creative control together, helping you generate and edit images while preserving the details that define a character, product, or brand. We’re excited to add it to Figma Weave, giving teams another powerful model for creative production, all within a reusable workflow.”

*—Itay Schiff, Creative Director at Figma Weave*

For most editing tasks, we recommend low complexity for faster edits, paired with the image quality your workflow requires. For scenes with many elements or constraints, try medium or high complexity effort.

See what early access customers generated using Images 2.6:

PicsartfalSableHiggsfield

## Pricing and availability

Images 2.6 is available globally today in ChatGPT and Codex across all subscription tiers on desktop, mobile, and web.

GPT‑Image‑2.6 Sunburst and GPT‑Image‑2.6 Flare are available in the API. See [pricing details here.⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing#image-generation)

Learn more about our safety evaluations and safeguards for Images 2.6 in the [system card⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/chatgpt-images-2-6).

title: Polymorphic Inference: self-tuning inference for open models
body:
At Together AI, we focus on making AI abundantly available to every individual user and organization. Our research team – the researchers behind FlashAttention, ThunderKittens, ThunderAgent, and more – has been a key driver behind our inference excellence. As the inference market grows exponentially, we’ve been focusing on how to scale our research capacity to enable abundant intelligence for all.
This has required a shift in our thinking from Static Inference to Polymorphic Inference – which is our response to the velocity of new model releases, diversity of model architectures, fast-changing workloads, and fast-changing hardware platforms. In this blog, we’ll highlight our research agenda for the Polymorphic Inference era – and how we are continuously using AI agents to optimize their own inference with Continuous Compilation.
What is Polymorphic Inference?
Over the past year, there has been a marked step change in the diversity of open-source models and the ways that these models are deployed in production environments. We see this step change as requiring a new approach that we call Polymorphic Inference.
Polymorphic Inference (inference in “many shapes” from Greek) is a response to a number of changes we are seeing across the industry, for us primarily defined by the convergence of a few trends:
- Increasing velocity of model releases. Open-source models are coming out at a faster clip – and are far more diverse – than ever before. 80% of traffic on OpenRouter goes to models released in the last three months.
- Increasing diversity of model architectures. All of the top-ten most popular OSS models in use today use different architectures (not to mention the many closed-source architectures served by our partners).
- Traffic shapes that continuously evolve. We serve new users, organizations, and geographies every day across a broad range of workload shapes and SLAs. Product or algorithmic changes in harnesses, post-training of open-source models can all lead to changes to traffic shapes (e.g., a new post-train that increases the amount of tokens that a model spends thinking in exchange for higher quality).
- Hardware that is changing faster and more frequently. We have seen major changes in inference serving capabilities from B200 to GB300, and are on the cusp of seeing the first Vera Rubin deployments (not to mention CPU-level optimizations, advanced storage systems, and alternative inference chips).
Polymorphic Inference is our response to these changes – inference that changes and adapts to these rapidly-changing environments.
We contrast this against the state of the world before the explosion of OSS inference – which we retroactively call the era of “Static Inference.” Whereas modern Polymorphic Inference takes on infinite different shapes, Static Inference is defined by closed models, traditional Transformer architectures, single-user, and single-hardware-platform inference.
From Static to Polymorphic Inference
One of our motivations behind writing this blog post is that a lot of the discourse around inference systems remains quite focused on the legacy Static Inference paradigm.
- For example, the typical vLLM, SGLang, or InferenceX / AgentX recipe online is launched with a static hyperparameter-tuned inference engine configuration. A config optimized for one setting is not necessarily the best one for another setting.
- Open-source kernels are frequently released assuming some static traffic shapes and design decisions that can be miscalibrated against real production traffic. A classic example is MoE kernels; an MoE kernel that works well against random tokens may not transfer to real production settings.
We take some of the blame here! For a long time, it has been possible to write kernels that are optimal for a variety of settings. FlashAttention, near and dear to our hearts, is still one of the best ways to run training workloads and many prefill workloads.
And nearly two years ago we wrote about megakernels for AI inference, a single kernel painstakingly designed around a single static shape (e.g., batch size one Llama 1B). But through the experience of putting some of the first megakernels into production for our customers last year, we learned an interesting lesson: megakernel fusion is actually not the right design goal for modern Polymorphic Inference! In the era of Polymorphic Inference, every variation – from model architecture (e.g. MoE), to workload (dynamic workloads larger than batch size 1) – requires different technical approaches.
Optimizing Polymorphic Inference for diverse, rapidly-changing conditions
At Together, we are systems and AI researchers at heart – so we view this as an incredibly exciting time to be rethinking our research agenda for this bright new future.
So, what’s the solution when your production traffic becomes ever more diverse? Get the AI agents to optimize themselves. This is the RSI moment for OSS models!
Achieving Polymorphic Inference requires solving a number of technical challenges in how we serve models. An ideal Polymorphic Inference experience is one that responds to the rapidly changing landscape of model architectures and workloads.
For example:
- If your traffic shape changes – either through a product change or a change in user behavior – you should expect your inference system to adapt quickly.
- If you are deploying workloads on a new model – you should expect your inference provider to approach ideal hand-tuned baselines as soon as possible.
- If you have an existing product with stable user traffic, and you deploy it on a new hardware platform – you should expect performance to approach hardware bounds as quickly as possible.
These are lofty goals, but we believe that they are worth striving for. For us, one of the keys to achieving these goals is getting AI agents to help optimize themselves. The RSI loop is here for OSS models!
Continuous Compilation with Together Compiler
One of the projects that we’re announcing today as a first step towards achieving our goals for Polymorphic Inference is [Together Compiler](https://www.together.ai/blog/together-compiler-continuous-compilation-for-ai-inference), a rapid AI-powered performance optimization RSI loop. Today, Together Compiler powers Continuous Compilation optimization loops across many of our top production inference workloads.
Together Compiler takes the classic challenge of optimizing inference workloads and recasts it from a traditional compiler translation problem to an agentic search problem. Together Compiler identifies a core set of key optimization patterns and pairs a swarm of agents with a high-fidelity persistent engine for fast iterations. This work was the result of many months of work by Together’s Frontier Performance team, notably from Reyna Abhyankar and Dylan Lim!
Together Compiler is running in production today on some of our most popular serverless endpoints, where it has found further gains on top of already highly optimized code.
Excitingly, Together Compiler gives us the ability to quickly adapt to rapidly changing model architectures and traffic workloads. We call this capability Continuous Compilation. Whereas previously new workloads would require new sets of hand-written kernels and optimizations, Continuous Compilation driven by Together Compiler means that we can automatically adapt to new traffic shapes and workloads.
What’s coming next from Together AI’s Research team
We’ve learned a ton scaling Together AI to serve trillions of tokens per day (and for the first time even serving more tokens than closed-source model labs on OpenRouter earlier in October!). This has informed our vision and research agenda for the Polymorphic Inference era. Here’s a little preview of some of the things coming up on our research agenda:
Self-serve Continuous Compilation with Together Compiler
Performance optimization needs to be a function of the workload deployment: the model, engine, traffic shape, and customer use case. Soon, our customers will be able to use Together Compiler to optimize their dedicated endpoints for their unique workloads at the click of a button.
Together Compiler is available to end customers in limited beta today – [reach out](https://www.together.ai/contact-sales) if you want early access!
Shape-shifting speculative decoding
Inference engine configurations proposed in open-source repositories, VLLM, InferenceX, AgentX launch the engine with a fixed speculative decoding draft model and lookahead parameter. Speculative decoding needs to adapt per-domain, per-request, per-token and as a function of the traffic load.
ThunderAgent Router: Routing across heterogeneous deployments
Serverless inference endpoints serve an enormous number of users, each bringing their own traffic shapes and SLAs. This heterogeneity requires us to dynamically route requests across workers and deployment configurations across our clusters. We released ThunderAgent as an ICML 2026 Spotlight paper to share some early insights and have expanded on these foundations in production.
Together Post-Training
Several customers now want to incorporate open-source model backends into their AI applications. This requires choosing an open-source model, selecting and customizing the harness to the customer’s specific tool calls and use cases, and post-training the model to interact well with this harness. Our close partnerships with model labs including Moonshot, Minimax, and others allows us to help our customers customize open-source models for their own use cases and really own their intelligence stack.
TogetherLink: Workload-aware model routing
As OSS models improve, a key piece is getting them into everyone’s hands. The common perception is that a closed source model like Opus 5.5 is always best. But, as the history of AI has repeatedly shown us, ensembling a few pretty good models can definitely outperform using a singular great model, if combined in the right way. This builds on our roots in weak supervision at Stanford’s Hazy Research Lab ([Ask Me Anything](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02441)) and on our own work on combining models ([Mixture-of-Agents](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/5434be94e82c54327bb9dcaf7fca52b6-Paper-Conference.pdf), ICLR 2025).
Abundant intelligence for all
Inference is one of the most fascinating problems in AI Systems and we’ve unlocked a whole host of new insights through the scale at which we serve. To achieve our goal of making AI abundant for everyone we need our inference systems to continuously customize to each user and each workload in the Polymorphic Inference era. We’re excited to help close the loop and play a small role in making AI systems truly recursively self-improving.
If the ideas behind Polymorphic Inference ring true to your organization or your use case, [please reach out for early access](https://www.together.ai/contact-sales) – we’d love to help you navigate these new complexities.
And lastly – if you want to help us tackle the challenge of Polymorphic Inference together, please take a look at our [careers page](https://www.together.ai/careers) – we’re hiring!

title: Together Compiler: Continuous Compilation for AI inference
body:
AI inference workloads are dynamic. There are thousands of regimes spanning new models, hardware platforms, customers, use cases, and traffic shapes. It’s no longer scalable to optimize each of these regimes by hand.
- Architectures are highly variable: it’s been ~11 years since the Transformer. We might have thought there would be more consolidation, but none of the top-10 open-source LLMs on OpenRouter use the same architecture!
- Workloads are highly variable: Together serves many trillions of tokens per day across thousands of customers, each with a different traffic shape (batch size, sequence length, MoE expert imbalance, attention sparsity, session duration, domain).
- Hardware is highly variable: H100s, B200s, B300s, NVL72, VR, Groq, and more each require distinct strategies.
Agents are a great fit for this problem, in theory. They can adapt to new workloads and search over the space of possible optimizations without relying on fixed rules or heuristics that plague human experts and traditional machine learning compilers. However, today’s agentic systems are bottlenecked by the speed of experimentation.
We introduce Together Compiler (TKCC), the first truly continual optimization loop that leverages high-throughput agents to optimize to diverse inference workloads
In less than 24 hours, TKCC achieves up to 2.6x higher TPS across frontier open source models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1-Flash, DeepSeek v4.1-Flash), sets the state-of-the-art on SemiAnalysis’ InferenceX benchmark for low-latency with 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1-Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1-Flash, and outperforms available open-source megakernels by 1.7x on their workhorse Llama 1B batch size 1 setting. Furthermore, TKCC generalizes to domains beyond language model inference (weather modeling, PDE, time-series, and biology). This performance boost is enabled by TKCC’s 252x higher experiment throughput compared to baseline agentic performance optimization systems. Together Compiler is serving trillions of tokens today.
Traffic is continually changing
As an inference provider, we see a variety of user behaviors based on regional patterns, new model releases, and burstiness.
- Regional patterns: Users across the world may have different model preferences. We’ve observed traffic for one country’s working hours to have 1.4x longer prompts than another country (97k vs 70k).
- Model releases: Users take time to figure out how to integrate new model releases into their workflows. First, they tend to opt for chat-based interaction and evaluation. This is swiftly followed by an 80% increase in prompt length just two weeks after the release as users shift towards agentic workloads.
- Burstiness: Customers may send bursts of requests at random times throughout the day. Prompt lengths can suddenly double and cache hit rates can fall if not handled carefully.
It’s clear that we must adapt to ever-changing user behavior with specialized optimizations for each new deployment.
Overview of Together Compiler
TKCC takes as input the traffic shape, model, and hardware. TKCC uses agents to generate a series of optimizations for an inference engine.
The core insights in TKCC are as follows:
1. TKCC maximizes experimentation throughput and minimizes GPU idle time during agent optimization
Most existing agentic inference optimization systems require agents to launch and teardown engines like VLLM, SGLang, or TRT-LLM to test each new experiment. However, engine start times are tens of minutes, significantly impeding experimentation throughput (see table below). Instead, TKCC proposes a new paradigm of “persistent engines” where the engine starts up once and can hot-reload any candidate forward pass, without any restarts. To ensure that the persistent engines constantly have new optimizations to test, TKCC spawns multiple agents that continually generate ideas and communicate via a message board to parallelize their efforts.
2. TKCC balances the tradeoff between measurement throughput and measurement fidelity
Existing agent optimization systems either iteratively relaunch the inference engine, suffering from low experiment throughput, or optimize standalone kernels in isolation, outside of the inference engine, suffering from poor measurement fidelity. Systems that optimize standalone kernels often evaluate them using random input data. However, with modern architectures using data-dependent primitives like MoE and sparse-k attention, input data distributions have a direct effect on which optimization strategies may win (see figure below). High-fidelity inputs are important for effective optimization. TKCC uses a tier of persistent engines to balance the throughput-fidelity tradeoff: “fast engines” load a few layers and are ideal for rapid iteration and low-variance timings, while “slower engines” load many layers and are ideal for testing whether optimizations hold-up on real data distributions.
3. TKCC utilizes a custom cost model to select parallelism strategies (e.g., TP, EP, DCP, etc.) for agents to achieve the highest performance
Existing systems have sophisticated methods for selecting inference configurations under SLA requirements. However, selecting the ideal configuration faces the same throughput-fidelity tradeoff: it is intractable to measure each parallelism configuration, especially because software implementations are immature. A naive approach is to select a parallelism strategy based on raw hardware specs or micro-benchmarks. However, this insufficiently captures data dependent traffic properties like MoE expert imbalance or uneven prompt length distributions. We designed a cost model that uses a tiered measurement strategy involving hardware specs, microbenchmarks, and measured forward passes to construct a high-fidelity representation while rapidly pruning the configuration search space to support continual traffic drift.
Results
We evaluate TKCC against three different types of baselines: Hand-tuned megakernels, InferenceX engine configurations, and popular AI codebases from diverse domains like weather modeling, PDE, time series and biology models.
MegaKernel workloads
We start by evaluating the canonical MegaKernel workload: Llama 1B at batch size 1. This model architecture has been well-optimized by both human experts and traditional machine learning compilers. TKCC generates 1.7x higher TPS and continues to perform as sequence length increases.
InferenceX AgentX workloads
We evaluate TKCC on the AgentX benchmark from SemiAnalysis. We start from the best-reported open source engine configurations for frontier models across inference engines and hardware platforms. TKCC consistently sets the performance frontier across all settings, outperforming highly-optimized baselines by up to 2.6x higher TPS.1
We also evaluate specifically on the low-latency use case at batch size 1 and set the state-of-the-art performance with 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1-Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1-Flash. For these results, we use our cost model to select the parallelism configuration instead of using the InferenceX configuration. We observe speedups with this approach.
Across AI workloads
We select popular open-source code bases across weather modeling, PDE, time-series, and biology. We show the geometric mean speedups of TKCC over simply using Claude Code with the /goal command, illustrating that the principles of TKCC generalize across domains. We have been using TKCC as a general purpose AI compiler beyond LLM inference.
Polymorphic AI systems is the next frontier
For Together AI, the most exciting systems challenge has been [Polymorphic Inference](https://www.together.ai/blog/polymorphic-inference). Inference is no longer about optimizing for a single traffic shape for a single hardware platform and model, traffic is constantly and dynamically evolving, much like financial markets, and that dynamism has opened up a whole host of new research questions.
Check out our [paper to learn more](http://www.together.ai/together-compiler-paper).
And if these frontiers of AI systems excite you, feel free to [reach out to us](https://www.together.ai/contact-sales)!
1 Trainium2 was run on a synthetic multi-turn dataset (70k ISL, 3.5k new ISL 95% cached, 700 OSL) instead of AgentX since our implementation does not yet support higher concurrencies on the limited HBM capacity.
