title: StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents
body:
Viewer • Updated • 68k • 381 • 3
[
](#statebench-testing-how-language-models-track-state-changes-over-long-documents)
StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
📄 [Tech Report](https://allenai.org/papers/statebench) | 🤗 [Data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/state-bench) | 💻 [Code](https://github.com/allenai/state-bench)
We’re introducing [StateBench](https://github.com/allenai/state-bench), a benchmark for long-context state tracking—how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve.
State tracking underlies tasks from reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, to following a story as characters physically move around and objects change hands. For example, if a mystery novel states that “John gave Mary the knife” right before a murder occurs, it’s important to know that the state of each character has changed. However, not all state-tracking problems are created equal: some require only finding the latest update; harder ones require following a chain of changes, where one missed step can throw off the final answer. For example, a harder variant of our mystery state tracking would be if John gave Mary the item in his backpack, with it previously known that Edward put a knife in John’s backpack.
Transformers have well-documented theoretical limits on hard variants of state tracking with long dependency chains, helping motivate recurrent and hybrid architectures such as Gated DeltaNet that carry a running memory forward. Existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, but as these designs become more common, researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle. We would like to understand the differences between architectures not just on the hardest kinds of state tracking, but also on the simpler, potentially more common kinds.
To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer.
[
](#four-levels-of-state-tracking)
Four levels of state tracking
StateBench consists of four difficulty levels that permit increasingly complex state update operations. For programmers, these levels of state tracking complexity can be understood as allowing different types of variable assignment operations:
- R-trivial problems use immutable assignment. A variable’s value never changes, so the model only needs to recover what it was first set to. In code, this looks like let x = 4; in everyday life, it’s like a birth date—it stays fixed.
- Aperiodic problems allow reassignment by value. The model needs to find the most recent value and can ignore earlier ones. In code, this looks like x = 4 followed later by x = 2; in everyday life, it’s like a thermostat, where the latest setting determines the current temperature.
- Soluble problems add self-referential updates. Each update builds on the current value, so the model has to carry changes forward rather than simply find the latest assignment. In code, this looks like x = x + 5; in everyday life, it’s like a game score, where each point adds to the running total.
- General finite problems add assignment by reference. One variable can take on another variable’s current value, creating dependencies across updates. In code, this looks like x = y or swapping two variables. Imagine a magician hiding a ball under one of five cups, then repeatedly swapping their positions. Finding the ball means keeping track of how those swaps change its location. This illustrates the S₅ state-tracking problem: following how successive swaps rearrange five objects. It belongs to the hardest of our four levels and is discussed in
[previous work on the limits of state tracking](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.08819v2#S3.SS1).
These levels can be intuitively understood in terms of variable assignments, but they also represent theoretically motivated distinctions in state tracking rooted in Krohn–Rhodes theory, a branch of algebra that describes how state-tracking problems – which can be viewed as word problems over finite monoids – can be decomposed into atomic primitives. Each level in our hierarchy corresponds to a class of state-tracking problems that can be built out of a different set of primitives.
To compare the four levels fairly, we start with a general finite sequence of variable assignments and derive three easier versions from it, producing four comparable StateBench problems—one at each difficulty level. All four use the same number of variables and distinct values, with assignments appearing at the same points in the sequence; only the type of assignment changes.
[
](#what-we-found)
What we found
[
](#pretrained-models)
Pretrained models
We tested a range of open pretrained models on the r-trivial, aperiodic, and general finite levels of StateBench to see where their state tracking breaks down, and whether different architectures fail where theory predicts. Under standard theoretical assumptions, transformers can handle r-trivial robustly (and soluble and aperiodic to some degree) but are predicted to fail on general problems. In contrast, Gated DeltaNet with a more flexible memory update can, in principle, handle all four levels.
We started with open pretrained models, where the training data and context lengths are fully documented. These included two 7-billion-parameter models, Olmo 3 (a transformer) and Olmo Hybrid (which adds Gated DeltaNet layers), along with smaller models with 275 million and 2.7 billion parameters. All of these models were pretrained on the same data; none had seen contexts longer than 64,000 tokens during training, and we tested most of them on inputs well beyond that length.
When we scored each model, almost all performed well on r-trivial problems, lost accuracy on aperiodic ones as inputs grew, and stayed at chance on general finite problems. Problem format mattered here—the 275-million-parameter hybrid and Gated DeltaNet models scored near the ceiling on RULER-style r-trivial problems but were near chance on the same problems framed as spreadsheet edits. That gap is one reason StateBench tests the same underlying problem in several formats.
[
](#frontier-models)
Frontier models
We then tested four frontier models – Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna – asking them to read each sequence of variable assignments and generate the final value of every variable.
All four performed well on r-trivial and aperiodic problems. But on soluble and general finite problems, accuracy fell sharply as inputs grew longer, dropping to 13% or lower on the longest general finite problems. One likely factor is sensitivity; at these harder levels, many more steps can affect the final answer, leaving less room for a model to miss an update without getting the result wrong.
[
](#models-trained-directly-on-the-task)
Models trained directly on the task
Next, we investigated whether models’ difficulty with the harder levels reflects limits of the architectures themselves, or whether pretraining simply doesn’t teach models to solve them. Targeted direct training is a more favorable setting that reveals to what degree state-tracking issues come from the underlying architecture and optimizer rather than the data used to pretrain a model.
We trained several 275-million-parameter models from scratch on StateBench: two transformer variants, two hybrids, and two Gated DeltaNet variants with different memory-update constraints. The models trained on sequences of up to 256 assignments and were tested on sequences as long as 64,000 assignments, or 250 times the maximum training length.
The architectures began to diverge as sequences grew longer. Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models generalized almost perfectly on r-trivial, aperiodic, and soluble problems out to the longest sequences we tested, tens of thousands of assignments. Transformers learned the easier levels but degraded on longer sequences, and they never learned general finite problems. On the hardest level, the Gated DeltaNet variant with a more flexible memory update generalized the farthest, staying near perfect out to roughly 10 times the length of the longest sequences it saw during training.
For Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models, the gap points to training rather than architecture; trained directly, they learned to handle state-tracking levels their pretrained counterparts couldn’t. Transformers were different—even trained directly, they could never learn the hardest level.
[
](#open-questions-and-the-release)
Open questions and the release
Some questions remain open. Our new proof shows that Gated DeltaNet with a more limited memory update (non-negative eigenvalues) can solve all aperiodic tasks and certain periodic tasks, such as tracking whether a repeated input has occurred an even or odd number of times, under the paper’s fixed-precision arithmetic with rounding. Its exact placement in the hierarchy remains open, including whether it can solve all soluble tasks and how numerical precision or combining it with attention layers affects its capabilities. StateBench also assumes a fixed number of variables, while real tasks often introduce new entities over time. In a long conversation, for example, new people and objects can appear as it unfolds, and the model has to begin tracking them too. The current framework doesn’t yet cover that setting.
As new flavors of recurrent and hybrid architectures emerge, understanding which kinds of state tracking each can handle could help guide how future systems are developed and trained. We hope StateBench gives researchers a finer-grained way to find where models break down—and to build training and evaluation data for the capabilities that still fall short. More fundamentally, we hope it serves as a North Star for researchers to develop new architectures with more robust state-tracking abilities compared to current models.

title: Agentic cheminformatics with Google Antigravity
body:
Agentic cheminformatics with Google Antigravity
Designing new medicines requires curating complex data from charts, figures and literature, training predictive models, and proposing candidate molecules to synthesize â a workflow that typically takes multiple days for a single iteration.
Here we show how [Google Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/use-cases/science), equipped with our new Cheminformatics Skills, accelerates drug discovery workflows. Using real-world lung cancer treatments, an agent searches through thousands of compounds, performs matched molecular pair analysis, and proposes novel rigidified macrocycles with synthetic routes in just an hour.
Chemistry is one of scienceâs richest public records â spanning millions of structures across journal articles and vendor catalogs. It provides a common representation that links physics and mathematics to the life and environmental sciences. Molecules and their transformations are ubiquitous and shape the everyday world.
Despite decades of progress in cheminformatics, chemists still spend too much time wrangling data, a process complicated by the fact that molecules can be represented in many ways: from text descriptions to images or data structures. The same molecule can appear as an [IUPAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUPAC_nomenclature_of_organic_chemistry) name in a paper, a [Markush structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markush_structure) in a patent, or a structure-data file (SDF) in a catalog. Advanced cheminformatics systems must be able to unify these sources and deal with the many ways errors can arise in them. This task has no margin for error â alter a single atom or bond and you have described a different compound altogether, rendering a promising inhibitor or catalyst inert.
To let scientists focus on hypotheses rather than data wrangling, we built a suite of Cheminformatics Skills for[ Google Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/use-cases/science), turning the surface into a collaborative science workbench with full access to local tooling for both computational chemists and experimental bench chemists.
The skills also create a division of labour where the underlying language model handles workflow orchestration, database navigation and scientific reasoning, while deterministic chemistry tools execute molecular calculations. Grounded in [RDKit](https://www.rdkit.org/), the foundational open source cheminformatics toolkit developed over two decades by a global community of contributors, alongside connectors to curated resources from [ChEMBL](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/) and [PubChem](https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/), the skills encode domain best practices directly into the agentâs workflow.
Rigidifying a floppy molecule
In this technical walkthrough, we highlight a classic medicinal chemistry technique to improve drug potency: rigidification.
Drug molecules can be complex, often linking multiple substructures through rotatable bonds. Those bonds let the molecule twist into many 3D shapes (conformations), making it âfloppyâ in solution. To bind its target, however, a floppy molecule must lock into a single active shape. Losing that freedom of motion carries an entropic penalty, which weakens binding affinity and lowers potency.
To solve this problem, medicinal chemists often rigidify molecules by adding new bonds. Two substructures linked by a single rotatable bond can twist into many conformations, but adding a second bond to tie them together sharply limits how they can move in three dimensional space. By placing that bond in the right spot, chemists can lock the molecule into the exact shape needed to bind its target. This strategy, often called âpaying the entropic cost in advanceâ, can dramatically boost potency.
Here, we will focus on a well-known case of successful rigidification. The drug crizotinib is a first-generation, small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) used to treat certain forms of non-small cell lung carcinoma. In crizotinib, there are five major rotatable bonds. Lorlatinib is a third-generation, small-molecule TKI that resembles crizotinib, but has been cyclized at its end to reduce the effective number of rotatable bonds to zero, leading to higher potency among other effects.
Collaborative Intelligence
We will ask the agent to search through literature for these drugs and their analogues. With the Cheminformatics skills in Antigravity, the agent is able to extract molecules from these documents, associate them with the data reported, and prepare the compounds for downstream analysis.
For deeper exploration, the agent launches an interactive viewer displaying the curated compounds, their associated data, and customizable scatter plots. For example, plotting potency against rotatable bonds, colored by macrocycle status, immediately reveals that macrocycles like lorlatinib tend to have fewer rotatable bonds and higher potency. Ultimately, we designed these skills to not only expand the agentâs chemistry capabilities, but also to make user-agent collaboration seamless.
After downloading and curating all the data, the agent is able to perform more advanced analysis to support the work of a computational chemist. As a next step, we will perform matched molecular pair analysis, a technique used in medicinal chemistry to isolate the effects of small, discrete changes to a molecule, by comparing pairs of molecules that only differ by that change. The agent had also independently suggested this analysis, as we expect the dataset to include many informative pairs. We will also ask the agent to build a predictive model using its molecular machine learning capabilities.
The matched molecular pair analysis (MMPA) compared many pairs of molecules that differ by whether or not they are cyclized. The results of the analysis show that cyclization reduces the number of rotatable bonds while generally increasing potency, as expected. The agent also built a large number of potency models using varying feature sets and model architectures, and validated them on a held-out set. The skills provide the agent with guidance on how to best build molecular machine learning models - for example, the agent will often use chronological splits, training on older compounds to predict newer ones, when this information is available, but can fall back to scaffold splits to better estimate generalizability.
Finally, we ask the agent to design new, improved macrocycles based on its learnings and it recommends multiple reactions and synthesis routes involving different compounds. The agent can prepare these compounds for further analysis with AlphaFold or physics-based techniques like molecular dynamics simulation.
Once we are done with our analysis, the results can be exported in various formats, ready to be loaded into many industry standard chemistry software packages.
At the same time, it is also important to know what these tools cannot do. Sparse data, inter-lab assay noise, and narrow dynamic ranges limit the predictive precision of even the most powerful models; computational designs are testable hypotheses, not finished drugs. With the Cheminformatics Skills in Antigravity, a drug discovery scientist can generate more strongly-supported design hypotheses faster, but every proposed design must be synthesized and validated experimentally.
The speed at which researchers can make meaningful scientific decisions is accelerating. Not long ago, the workflow demonstrated here would have taken multiple days and required significant computational expertise. Using Antigravity as a science workbench allows both computational and experimental chemists to accelerate their workflows and focus on the questions that really matter.
Acknowledgements
The cheminformatics skills are available on Google Antigravity today. Download the Antigravity App and install the Science plugin to start using these skills. Explore Science use cases [here](https://antigravity.google/use-cases/science).
You can also get started with cheminformatics on Antigravity today as an Enterprise user, by choosing âUse Business Accountâ and logging into the app with your Google Cloud credentials.
To further advance the pace of research, weâre offering 10,000 scientists the highest usage tier in Google Antigravity free of charge for 6 months (onboarded on a rolling basis), subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection. Applications are [now open](http://forms.gle/WvmBbPvRbpKG1BPn9).
We would like to acknowledge the contributions of the following team members: Filip Radlinski, Artem Sobolev, Victoria Johnston, Hannah Kiely-Collins, Zachary Wu, Jue Wang, Jack Dunger, Adriana Fernandez Lara, NgÃ¢n VÅ©, Doug Fritz, Yunhan Xu, Sebastian Nowozin, Pushmeet Kohli.

title: Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language
body:
Viewer • Updated • 238 • 60.4k • 13
[
](#palette-teaching-a-small-model-to-build-decks-in-your-design-language)
Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.
Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.
Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the [IBM Design Language](https://www.ibm.com/design/language/resources/), and on [PresentBench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/PresentBench/PresentBench) it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.
[
](#why-decks-are-hard-for-small-models)
Why decks are hard for small models
A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.
It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.
It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.
There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.
[
](#build-it-like-a-human-a-designer-and-a-coder)
Build it like a human: a designer and a coder
Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:
- The designer reads the plan and writes a structured JSON brief: the palette, the type system, and for each slide its layout, its exact content and a short design rationale.
- The coder takes one slide's spec from the brief and writes the
[pptxgenjs](https://gitbrent.github.io/PptxGenJS/)JavaScript that draws it, preceded by its reasoning.
Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.
We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.
[
](#synthesizing-decks-and-their-reasoning)
Synthesizing decks and their reasoning
There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.
Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:
"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."
The coder reasons about geometry:
"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."
The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.
The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.
What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.
[
](#steering-a-deck-in-plain-english)
Steering a deck in plain English
Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]
:
## Rollout plan
- March: pilot with two teams
- May: security review complete
- July: rollout to all of engineering
- September: company-wide launch
- November: first adoption review
[[make this a timeline]]
The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.
The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.
| Category | Example directive |
|---|---|
| Layout | [[make this a timeline]] |
| Tone | [[be candid, no spin]] |
| Audience | [[this is for the board]] |
| Order | [[lead with the ask]] |
| Leaving out | [[no pricing]] |
| Emphasis | [[highlight the headline number]] |
[
Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the ](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/63890e3843d8b0797a0ad606/YTsME8ZIwzzxmo-QmpTQq.png)[[make this a timeline]]
directive.
[
](#building-a-check-and-repair-harness)
Building a check-and-repair harness
Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.
[
Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/63890e3843d8b0797a0ad606/PZoiyAFg_nrWRryQhjGN_.png)
First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.
The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.
[
Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/63890e3843d8b0797a0ad606/iZzBRJXOUxncecFIEgw-B.png)
To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.
[
](#evaluation)
Evaluation
We evaluate on [PresentBench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/PresentBench/PresentBench), which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.
[
Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/63890e3843d8b0797a0ad606/QiWVeHtadoTFYsfdPjkDr.png)
Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.
PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.
[
](#whats-next)
What's next
The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.
We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with [Docling](https://github.com/docling-project/docling)) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx
files, without retraining.
[
](#what-we-learned)
What we learned
Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:
- Put the reasoning in the data. Training on why a choice was made, including what was rejected, teaches more than the choice alone.
- Fix the examples before adding a rule. When

title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
body:
Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
3rd November 2026
Yesterday’s hot paper was [Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights](https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/) by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!
Weight-Space Programming
Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:
Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.
Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own
[model card]warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.
The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.
spaCy author Matthew Honnibal [called the paper misleading](https://honnibal.dev/blog/astra-read-write-misleading) for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke [deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example](https://www.seangoedecke.com/llms-are-not-superhuman-at-reading-and-writing-neural-network-weights/) as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.
I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.
The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had [to look that one up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeway_(video_game)), it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question:
The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response.
The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is [RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs](https://github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs). The [exp1_which_game](https://github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/tree/main/exp1_which_game) folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games:
I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others.
Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models
The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My [LLM](https://llm.datasette.io/) tool has a -f/--fragment
option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this:
llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \
-m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro
This example requires the [llm-openrouter plugin](https://github.com/simonw/llm-openrouter) installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s [what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro](https://gist.github.com/simonw/9f18d2945a105c04734ef7e5cd95717c), which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens.
But how about [Qwen 3.8 27B](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Aug/16/qwen-38-27b/)? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use [this version](https://huggingface.co/lmstudio-community/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF/blob/main/Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf)) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025.
I fired up [LM Studio](https://lmstudio.ai), ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the [llm-lmstudio](https://github.com/llm-lmstudio/llm-lmstudio) plugin and ran this command:
LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \
llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \
-m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b
(I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see [this issue](https://github.com/llm-lmstudio/llm-lmstudio/issues/16).)
After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop [returned a response](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F387d3a7927f165b1986bb6c2099d0f53#response-1) that ended like this (here’s [the reasoning trace](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F387d3a7927f165b1986bb6c2099d0f53#reasoning-1)):
Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets.
Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards.
Confidence: 72%
This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It [identified Pong](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F387d3a7927f165b1986bb6c2099d0f53#response-2) ([reasoning](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F387d3a7927f165b1986bb6c2099d0f53#reasoning-2)) in 1h 4m 54s:
Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object.
Description:
The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized.
Confidence:
75%
And [Breakout](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F387d3a7927f165b1986bb6c2099d0f53#response) ([reasoning](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F387d3a7927f165b1986bb6c2099d0f53#reasoning)) in 52m 25s:
Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game.
Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty.
Confidence: 88%
Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn’t surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here’s [that transcript](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F6ed68f659e26a32e7d9096391d92f326)—Qwen thought it was “A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally”.
The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here’s a sample:
What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let’s list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right?
That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort.
It’s a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I’ve seen around it does not feel justified. I’m not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways.

title: AI Is Changing How Semiconductor Fabs Work — and Engineers Are Moving Faster Because of It
body:
Demand for advanced chips is rising. The processes to build them are getting more complex. And the margin for error is shrinking.
For engineers, understanding how a process change will behave, how a material will interact with a new step, how a defect maps back to a root cause are critical, challenging steps in semiconductor manufacturing — and these analyses can take days. Physical experiments on a fab line are slow and expensive. A wrong call on yield or process quality has real consequences.
AI is transforming semiconductor manufacturing, impacting what engineers can do — and how fast.
Accelerated computing shortens simulation time, allowing engineers to evaluate more alternatives before committing to physical trials.
Physics-based AI helps engineers predict process behavior without running a full simulation every time.
AI agents handle sequences of engineering tasks that once consumed hours.
And [digital twins](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/digital-twin/) let teams test changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials.
Together, these capabilities describe an AI-defined fab: a [semiconductor](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/industries/semiconductor/) manufacturing factory where AI helps engineers optimize processes, catch problems earlier and make better decisions across the full manufacturing chip lifecycle. Engineers direct the work and make decisions based on their expertise while spending less time waiting for answers.
Shorter Simulation Cycles Change What Engineers Can Explore
Accelerated computing doesn’t just speed up individual calculations — it changes how many alternatives engineers can test before committing.
Multiphysics simulations model interactions among physical effects, such as heat transfer, electrical behavior and mechanical stress.
Using the [NVIDIA cuDSS](https://developer.nvidia.com/cudss) library, multiphysics software provider [COMSOL](https://www.comsol.com/blogs/accelerating-semiconductor-manufacturing-simulation-with-nvidia-cudss) is accelerating such simulations for semiconductor manufacturing by up to 10x. This helps engineers optimize equipment and processes, compare alternatives and decide which changes to test physically.
Applied Materials and NVIDIA are collaborating to accelerate atomic-scale materials discovery and process development. By integrating NVIDIA cuDSS, Applied’s Ginestra simulation platform runs up to 10x faster than CPU-only approaches. And with NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo, Applied’s ACE+ multiphysics platform delivers topography simulations up to 35x faster.
In some cases, acceleration doesn’t just shorten the calculation — it enables it altogether. Computational lithography — which defines how circuit patterns are printed onto silicon — involves calculations too intensive to complete on CPU at production scale. Siemens is integrating [NVIDIA cuLitho](https://developer.nvidia.com/culitho) into its Calibre lithography software, delivering up to 17x acceleration on key simulation workloads. That expands what engineers can verify before a wafer goes to print.
As such, faster calculations can help researchers explore material behavior and reaction pathways that influence next-generation semiconductor processes.
Predicting Process Behavior Without Running Every Simulation
In addition to accelerating simulations, AI trained on physics can predict how materials and processes will behave — without running a full simulation each time.
The payoff is most visible in complex calculations that are expensive even on accelerated hardware.
Plasma — the electrically charged gas used in semiconductor etch processes — is one example. Modeling plasma behavior requires solving equations that capture how electrical, chemical and thermal processes interact, making repeated simulation costly. Lam Research demonstrated that the [NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo](https://developer.nvidia.com/physicsnemo) framework can predict plasma behavior in milliseconds, compared with days for a full simulation — giving engineers a faster way to explore process conditions without rerunning the full model each time.
Agents Handle the Steps Between Decisions
Engineers turn analyses into decisions — revising a design, investigating a test failure, adjusting a production process and more.
AI agents can help carry out the steps between those decisions.
Evaluating which AI model to apply to a given task is one example: a sequential, manual process that can consume hours on the test floor.
Advantest is using [NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/route-ai-agent-workloads-across-models-with-nvidia-nemo-switchyard/) AI agents to automate that selection, reducing response times from hours to minutes.
Testing Factory Changes Before They Reach the Line
Digital twins let teams simulate equipment configurations, layouts and process changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials. This reduces experimentation costs, especially as fabs become more complex and the stakes of a wrong change get higher.
[Applied Materials](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/advancing-semiconductor-innovation-across-materials-engineering-and-manufacturing/) uses [NVIDIA Omniverse libraries](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/omniverse/) to build physically accurate digital twins of entire fabs. Teams can simulate material movement, identify bottlenecks and evaluate layouts and operating strategies — extending virtual experimentation beyond individual processes to how the factory works as a whole.
The Connected Loop
The future of semiconductor manufacturing lies in connecting these capabilities: using production data to inform models and models to evaluate changes, then bringing those findings back to the engineers making production decisions.
That’s the promise of the AI-defined fab: where AI helps people learn from each production cycle and act on that knowledge sooner.
Explore how [NVIDIA is working with semiconductor leaders](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/industries/semiconductor/) across the chip lifecycle.

title: Finding my thing
body:
How do I follow up my last post…I’ve never had such a response before, I’m still working my way through every reply.
And I wasn’t actually going to post today.
Since last week I’ve been having great conversations and spent a lot of time thinking, without my agent. I’m back to actually jotting stuff down in my notes rather than agents.
Inertia is my problem. Just because this newsletter is sent tues/thurs in a specific format, it’s easier to keep that going. I feel obliged.
But really I’m trying to find something. My thing. And if I do what I’ve done, I won’t find it. I need to change it up. So from now until the end of the year, the formats will vary, the content, even the days + frequency of when I post. I’m in experimental mode. The digital equivalent of going to Thailand, slinging on those awful trousers and finding myself.
I need to post what I’m interested in. For me to continue doing this for a long time, I have to make these for me. So what am I interested in?
I’m following my nose. It’s already led me to have convos with Stripe, Granola, Zed and Raycast about how they’re building in this new world, while staying sane and nurturing a considered culture. I think there’s a ton of interesting stuff here I’ll write and build on top of. Coming soon-ish.
I said I wasn’t going to post today, but you’re reading this…so, what gives? Well in my deliberation of to post or not to post, I felt like I wanted to bring you along in my thinking. I want to bare all whilst we see where we end up.
I’ve stopped using Grok Bot for everything, except to ping me when Carlos Alcaraz is playing. I’m reading more long-form. I’m consuming less slop (and spending a little less time on X). I’m recording a voice-note every morning for a minimum of 10 minutes, and not doing anything with the transcript. I’m letting things percolate, noticing what I come back to.
Agents give you answers to everything. But if we’re ‘soul-searching’ or trying to connect the dots, an answer presented to us may not be the right path. Even if it’s a reasonable one. All I’m ‘optimising’ for here is - what do I really want to do? And noticing what I keep coming back to when I take the time to think on it.
This is not an ‘anti-ai’ stance at all. I love AI. I can do so much more than I ever could. It’s a tool though, not a person, and I use it as such. You probably need a grand total of one tool (an agent). Instead of looking at everything as an opportunity to optimise, I want to use AI for fun.
Quick bites
[Try](https://fandf.co/4jP1ZH2)[doubleAI’s](https://fandf.co/4jP1ZH2)[Maxwell](https://fandf.co/4jP1ZH2), a code execution model that speeds up software as it runs. Results: 38x faster data pipelines with no code changes.*Patrick Collison posted about
[adding a feedback box](https://x.com/patrickc/status/2116636967517798672)to what you build as a quick way to keep iterating.A few links to get your agents to make good UI:
[Stageshow](https://github.com/benjitaylor/skills)for making product demos,[BoardUI](https://www.boardui.com/)for great-looking components and[Looseleaf](https://kevintngo.github.io/looseleaf/)for a hand-drawn feel.I enjoyed this post on how Jakub built a
[personal health app](https://jakub.kr/writing/the-era-of-personal-software)for just himself. He puts out a lot of great visual work.[Nobody knows anything](https://burcs.dev/notes/nobody-knows-anything/)- ‘if you feel behind right now don’t worry you aren’t.’ Fun site, but if it’s hard to read, hit the grid icon in the top right.[Kino](https://kino.ai/)- edit video with your agents.[Hex](https://anoma.ly/hex/)- A free voice dictation app for Mac, Windows and Linux. The landing page is pretty good!I like this… a
[Chrome extension](https://github.com/851-labs/honest-thumbnails)that swaps clickbait thumbnails for real stills from the video.
Its interesting hearing you say you are looking for your "thing" (you are one of my favorite susbtack / x follows, and have always admired how clear your angle was!).
Also, this helped me, just go sit down quietly for 10 minutes / day (don't even call it meditation) and train attention. The more I've done it the clearer the signal to follow fun / curiosity gets.
Trite but really useful as a tool, go read "the power of now".
A few posts back, you'd had this section in the newsletter, 'Try this', where you posted a sample prompt for us to try. It was cool cause it was something that I hadn't seen before. The one you posted turned out to be really useful. Wondering if you can keep that going for future posts?
Thanks, Terry

Today, we’re sharing advances in how OpenAI models help engineers design, simulate, and build physical products. These capabilities span mechanical and electrical engineering and end-to-end system design, and are already helping our internal teams test ideas and iterate faster.

Across these projects, engineers need to bring together mechanical designs, electronics, software, and manufacturing requirements using specialized tools. We’re teaching models to support that work, from preparing drawings and setting up simulations to coordinating changes across disciplines. Our goal is to give engineers more time to explore ideas and improve designs.

Over the past year, improved frontier model capabilities have helped our internal teams test new ideas and iterate faster, and we are seeing early evidence of these capabilities improving professional workflows in industry as well. We’re working with collaborators to understand where these capabilities can make the biggest difference and what needs to improve. If you’re an engineer, engineering firm, or software vendor involved in the design, simulation, manufacturing, or production of complex physical products, we’d love to [work with you](https://openai.com/form/computer-use-research-collaboration/) to shape this effort around the tools you use and the problems you need to solve.

## Designing a device with Astra

We tested [Astra’s state-of-the-art performance⁠](https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/) in multimodal and computer use workflows by seeing if we can create a device without any direct human edits. To do this, we used GPT‑6 to define the functional requirements and design the enclosure, printed circuit board (PCB), and software integrations needed to create a device users can use to talk to Codex.

- **Aesthetics and design:** Astra developed the look of the device, drawing on our recent [Work Louder⁠(opens in a new window)](https://worklouder.cc/codex-micro) collaboration and references from games and toys.
- **Mechanical design:** Astra designed the [enclosure⁠(opens in a new window)](https://images.ctfassets.net/kftzwdyauwt9/5aP4AhwHhDUmDxisSLcb2X/12114476f73d643b73dffe90b819cc0c/prototype-device-enclosure-diagram.png) and the internal structures that hold the components in place.
- **Electrical design:** Astra selected the electrical components and designed the printed circuit board (PCB), including component placement and connections, to fit within the enclosure.
- **UI/UX and software:** Astra designed the user interface and generated the firmware and software integrations needed to connect the device to Codex.

Two team members designed this test device with Astra in under a week while working on it as a side project. A contract manufacturer built a small batch of prototypes in under a month.

Getting the device ready for manufacturing still required several rounds of review and iteration. Astra did not consistently account for the manufacturer’s production limits, tolerances, or details required for assembly. These gaps are helping us identify what future models need to do better.

## Accelerating OpenAI hardware teams

OpenAI’s hardware and infrastructure teams use Codex and ChatGPT to create and revise computer-aided design (CAD) models, prepare manufacturing drawings, set up simulations, and review designs. This work spans robotics and compute infrastructure. Since February, model usage across our hardware teams, measured in tokens, has grown 23-fold.

1 of 3

> *“Codex has dramatically accelerated how we move from an idea to an engineered part. We’re iterating faster across CAD, converting 3D designs into production-ready 2D drawings, and setting up simulations and FEA with far less manual work.”*

*— Grace Lam, Forward Deployed Engineer at OpenAI*

> *“As system hardware designers, we use Codex and ChatGPT to organize cross-functional design constraints, explore system architectures, execute across ECAD environments, and conduct thorough design reviews. Today, Codex and ChatGPT are dependable, around-the-clock partners in engineering and project management, with the potential to grow into teams of hardware specialists that can take a board from concept to Gerber out.”*

*— Qiong Wang, Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI*

> *“In AEC and BIM, a lot of time goes into repetitive modeling, checking information across drawings and specifications, and coordinating changes between disciplines. We're starting to use Codex to automate routine tasks, flag inconsistencies, and turn coordination findings into clear, actionable issues. This frees up time for teams to evaluate design options and constructability, with architects, engineers, and BIM professionals reviewing and validating the results.”*

*— Jackie Lee, Member of Infrastructure Staff at OpenAI*

## Measuring progress on engineering tasks

We’re also measuring progress in newer models on tasks that combine coding with engineering knowledge. BenchCAD 2.0 tests whether models can reconstruct 3D parts and assemblies and identify connections in circuit boards. A newer internal model achieved an average score of 0.875, compared with 0.594 for GPT‑6 Astra at its highest reasoning setting. While the engineering lifecycle includes many other elements beyond design, we view improvements in capability here as early evidence of the ability of AI models to positively impact iteration speed for professional workflows.

## Safely deploying with industry collaborators

We’re working with a small group of industry collaborators to test these capabilities on real engineering problems. Their engineers review model outputs for accuracy and practical use, helping us understand which tasks models can support today and what needs to be improved for safe and reliable use.

We’re expanding our collaboration with [Chip Ganassi Racing](https://openai.com/index/chip-ganassi-racing/) (CGR) to explore how OpenAI models can accelerate engineering and prototyping. Working with its R&D team, we’re testing workflows that turn 3D scans of existing parts into editable CAD models and 2D manufacturing drawings. This is particularly useful when the original design files are unavailable.

CGR engineers review the models and drawings for accuracy and manufacturability. Their feedback helps us identify where models can reduce manual work and where further improvements are needed.

> “*The model has been useful for going from raw scan data to a solid body. I have been working with Codex directly in CAD. The feedback I give the model is directly applied, the manual tweaks can be made directly, and this has become a faster, more hands-off process for me**.*”

*— Matthew Ortman, R&D Engineer at Chip Ganassi Racing*

We’re also announcing a new research collaboration with Mazda. Our research and Forward Deployed Engineering teams are working with Mazda’s aerodynamics and crash-safety engineers to explore how OpenAI models can help develop and evaluate new vehicle designs.

The work uses simulations of airflow and structural behavior to explore improvements in performance while accounting for styling and cost. We’ll share more progress and results in the coming months.

*GPT‑6 Astra helps Mazda’s aerodynamics engineers explore ways to reduce vehicle drag by modeling new nose shapes, simulating airflow, and refining the most promising designs. Agreement for use has been obtained from Mazda Motor Corporation. Any republication or reuse elsewhere is strictly prohibited.*

> *“**Does it have to look like that?” Our designers often ask us when we find a shape that improves airflow. By exploring and simulating dozens of variations, Astra in Codex helps us understand which features matter for aerodynamics and where designers have room to explore. That’s why the value of Astra and collaborating with OpenAI goes beyond task automation and shortening development cycles: it is helping us bring together Mazda’s distinctive design and aerodynamic performance without treating either as a compromise.”*

*— Akihiro Nakata, Principal Engineer at Mazda*

## Help shape AI for engineering and manufacturing

We have been working closely with industry partners and early adopters to push the bounds of what we can do with AI agents in hardware and manufacturing. These early results have shown exciting promise, and we’re now looking for collaborators to accelerate these capability improvements and ensure we deploy these safely into industry.

If you are interested in working with us to shape the training and development of our frontier models by identifying high-value use cases, software tooling, or future opportunities in mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, electromechanical design, mechatronics, or a related field, please fill out [this form](https://openai.com/form/computer-use-research-collaboration/) and we'll be in touch.

Cisco combines network intelligence and OpenAI models to build more adaptive defenses.

Cisco builds the networking and security infrastructure that organizations rely on to connect and protect their systems. As adversaries leverage AI to scale automated attacks and craft exploits at machine-speed, defending enterprise infrastructure must evolve. Pairing Cisco’s vast network telemetry with frontier AI reasoning gives defenders the toolkit necessary to outpace emerging threats. OpenAI’s rigorous approach to enterprise data privacy—centered on zero data retention, strict customer data boundaries, and verifiable isolation—means Cisco could confidently deploy frontier intelligence across mission-critical systems without compromising customer priorities or sensitive telemetry.

## Connecting network intelligence for stronger defense

Cisco’s defense starts where threats move: the network. Patel describes a shift from a single security perimeter to controls distributed across microservices, containers, and clusters. “We can put a mini security stack in front of every microservice, every Kubernetes container, and every Kubernetes cluster, and fuse security into the fabric of the network,” he says.

Controls at the application level can restrict communication to the connections each service needs, reducing the paths an attacker can use to spread. Security teams can also isolate affected systems more selectively, allowing unaffected services to keep running while they investigate and respond.

Combining that network intelligence with OpenAI’s models allows Cisco to correlate signals at machine scale, Patel says. “Two signals might seem benign in isolation, but together they can reveal a meaningful pattern. Network intelligence allows us to correlate data across the network and derive insights to inform secure operations.”

## From investigation to remediation

Patel points to a pressing challenge for defenders: the gap between how quickly attackers can exploit a vulnerability and how long organizations take to patch it. He sees AI as a way to help narrow that gap, giving defenders the capacity to investigate more threats and respond faster. “AI hands attackers speed and scale. Using AI for defense is a prerequisite for staying safe,” he says.

He describes initiatives like Daybreak and GPT‑6 Astra as advances that strengthen security for both Cisco and its customers. “We’re able to find and patch vulnerabilities more efficiently, while shortening the time needed for investigation, response, and remediation,” Patel says.

> “Daybreak and GPT-6 Astra have been step function improvements, not just for our security posture, but for our customers’ security posture.”

—Jeetu Patel, President and Chief Product Officer at Cisco

Patel sees a path to adoption that builds on the processes teams already use to find and address vulnerabilities. “These capabilities can fit into your existing scanning workflows, so you don’t have to fundamentally change how your team works.”

## Rethinking security for an agentic world

As agents become more autonomous, security teams also need to distinguish malicious interference from an agent pursuing a legitimate goal in an unintended way. Patel says that requires security telemetry alongside observability data, so teams can assess both threats and agent behavior.

He outlines three priorities: protect agents from malicious attacks, detect and intercept unintended behavior, and operate in near real time. These priorities are guiding the shift towards policies and controls that can adapt as agents act.

Through the Daybreak Defense Network, Cisco and OpenAI are exploring how to help security teams triage exposure faster and enforce the right controls in Cisco Cloud Control. For Patel, that can help shift the advantage back to defenders.

> “OpenAI is shifting the advantage to defenders by allowing us to operate at machine speed and scale.”

—Jeetu Patel, President and Chief Product Officer at Cisco

## The buildings haven’t changed. Everything around them has.

A hundred years ago, managing a residential building meant finding tenants, collecting rent and keeping properties in good condition. Today, these fundamentals remain remarkably similar. What is changing is *how* that work gets done.

For European residential real estate operator [**Heimstaden**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://heimstaden.com/), this presents an opportunity: what if AI could fundamentally change how thousands of homes are managed?

In June 2025, Heimstaden’s leadership decided to accelerate its bet on AI. After evaluating several platforms, the company chose OpenAI. The goal was twofold; empower employees and rethink the processes at the heart of its business.

The ambition is to move towards increasingly self-operating buildings, where AI can help anticipate needs, coordinate work and support decisions across the property lifecycle. “The purpose of our buildings hasn’t changed.” says Helge Krogsbøl, Co-CEO at Heimstaden. “We provide homes for people. But the way we operate them continues to change as we challenge conventions and adopt new technology.”

> ***“We see AI as one of the biggest opportunities to accelerate that transformation.”***

—Helge Krogsbøl, Co-CEO, Heimstaden

## Reimagining the business of letting homes

Consider what happens when a property becomes vacant.

Traditionally, getting it back onto the market involves assessing rental value, arranging photography, producing advertisements and responding to market demand. Each stage requires time, coordination and specialist input. And it is an information challenge; understanding what you own, what the competition has, and what the customer wants.

AI is now supporting all the key steps in this process:

- **Pricing:** Intelligence and recommendations based on tools built in ChatGPT Sites
- **Advertising:** Image styling and apartment descriptions done by AI
- **Review listings:** Agent reviews all live ads against Heimstaden’s quality standards
- **Feedback:** AIgenerated market feedback helps letting teams take corrective action which makes prices increasingly dynamic

Employees remain responsible for reviewing and approving decisions. But the work surrounding those decisions is changing.

In the Netherlands, the cost of producing a virtually staged property image has fallen from approximately €50 to less than €0.10 which is a reduction of more than 99%. Heimstaden estimates annual savings potential of €130,000 in that market alone.

The significance extends beyond cheaper advertisements. By applying AI across the letting process, Heimstaden is building a more responsive way to bring homes to market.

“Our AI strategy is based on three pillars.” saysNikolaj Brammer, Heimstaden’s Chief Digital Officer, “First, we empower employees through training and access to the right tools. Second, we have a central transformation office and a network of AI champions to drive larger AI initiatives. Third, we strengthen the foundations by making our property management systems and data models ready for AI.”

Letting puts all three pillars into practice: tools and training enable colleagues to create virtually staged images and listings; our central team coordinates improvements across pricing, advertising, ad review and market feedback; and we are making property data accessible to the AI tools that support pricing and listing creation.

> ***“We started by breaking down our most important business processes and asking where AI could create value. Letting is a good example: it’s not about automating one task, but improving how the whole process works.”***

—Nikolaj Brammer, Chief Digital Officer, Heimstaden

## When domain experts become builders

Some of the most significant changes are happening far from traditional software engineering teams.

Heimstaden needed to assess environmental risks across its portfolio. The information existed, but was scattered across public sources, formats and datasets. Turning it into a usable assessment would have required substantial manual work and technical resources.

Heimstaden’s Julia Erlandsen, an environmental sustainability analyst without a software development background, used Codex to help build a different approach.

Codex supported the discovery, cleaning and standardisation of data, quality checking and the development of repeatable processing pipelines. Julia retained control over the methodology and validation.

The result: 20,112 assets assessed, more than six million rows of useful data generated, and an estimated delivery requirement reduced from five people working for a year to two people working for two months.

Heimstaden also avoided engaging external consultants which would otherwise have been needed to solve the problem.

What began as a complex analytical project is becoming a repeatable capability, supporting climate-risk assessments, reporting requirements and investor decision-making.

> ***“Codex helped us build a solution that would previously have required substantial technical support. We now own the methodology and can continue developing it ourselves.”***

—Julia Erlandsen, Environmental Sustainability Analyst, Heimstaden

## Responsible AI adoption

Heimstaden’s AI adoption focuses on tasks employees need help with. After ChatGPT Enterprise launched in September 2025, half of employees were using it within two to three months. A central AI transformation office maintains a library of use cases so colleagues can learn from examples across the business.

Employees use approved tools within rules for data security. They remain responsible for reviewing AI-generated content before sending it and for approving decisions.

Adoption extends to real estate caretakers, including some who were initially sceptical. In Norway, one caretaker used ChatGPT to assess a neglected apartment and draft a prioritised refurbishment plan, turning observations into a structured plan they could review and refine.

> ***“People across the business are finding practical ways to use AI in their daily work. Our job is to scale what works while keeping data secure, responsibilities clear and people in control.”***

—Andreas Kalmar Lindquist, Manager AI First Team Heimstaden

## The next frontier: From answering questions to taking action

Heimstaden is already preparing for the next stage: AI that can work across systems and coordinate multi-step processes.

Its Procurement Intelligence Platform, currently being rolled out, combines workflow automation with OpenAI models accessed through APIs. Designed to operate across Outlook, SharePoint and Teams, it supports contract analysis, negotiation preparation and contract lifecycle management, with employees retaining responsibility for commercial decisions and approvals.

The longer-term ambition is more fundamental.

Heimstaden is co-developing Amplio Estate, a modern property management system designed to support AI-powered workflows through MCP. The goal is to enable employees to use AI, such as ChatGPT, to retrieve property information and take action in core business systems, with appropriate human oversight.

This is how Heimstaden begins turning the idea of self-operating buildings into a practical technology roadmap.

## Results at a glance

- **More than 99% lower image production costs** in the Netherlands.
- **20,112 property assets assessed with Codex**, reducing the estimated delivery requirement from five people over one year to two people over two months.
- **50% employee adoption within 2–3 months** of rollout.

## Leadership lessons:

- **Focus on people:** Adoption and imagination are the bottlenecks (not tech)
- **Find your champions:** The biggest returns come from colleagues driving change locally
- **Get the process right:** AI will not fix a broken process, but it can dramatically scale a good one.

## What’s next

Heimstaden’s vision is not of buildings without people, but of properties supported by increasingly intelligent systems which will improve decision making for employees and increase ability to resolve matters for customers.

The buildings will remain much as they have always been—homes and roofs over people’s heads. The way they’re operated has forever changed.

title: Cities Worldwide Build and Scale AI Services With NVIDIA Physical and Agentic AI
body:
Cities generate enormous amounts of data from cameras, sensors and operational systems, but turning it into useful action — for planning, maintenance and public services — remains a challenge.
Physical and agentic AI offer new ways to close that gap, from digital twins for infrastructure planning to vision and service agents, while keeping local governments in control of how sensitive data is processed and used.
Building on [initiatives announced at GTC Berlin](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/european-cities-agents-urban-operations/), NVIDIA and its partners are expanding physical AI and AI agents to cities worldwide. Shared computing infrastructure gives city departments, neighboring municipalities and local developers a common foundation to build on — extending services without each organization having to acquire and manage resources of their own.
Agentic AI for Cities
From resident services to vision agents, cities are adopting NVIDIA agentic AI to deliver faster, more responsive public services. City teams don’t need a massive infrastructure investment to get started building these AI services: depending on the workload, NVIDIA RTX workstations or a small GPU system may be enough.
In Spain, 1MillionBot combines open source ALIA models trained at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center with [NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) and other models in resident-service agents for Madrid Digital (Comunidad de Madrid), Administració Oberta de Catalunya and 150+ deployments across Spain, handling municipal procedures, appointment requests, urban-planning incidents and service inquiries.
In the San Francisco Bay Area, [LiveX](https://livex.ai/insights/livex-unveils-ai-city-bringing-physical-ai-to-everyday-spaces-with-nvidia) is bringing its AI City vision to life with NVIDIA [Cosmos](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai/cosmos/) world models and Nemotron open models, and [Omniverse](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/omniverse/) and [Metropolis](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/autonomous-machines/intelligent-video-analytics-platform/) libraries on NVIDIA RTX PRO GPUs. The interactive, conversational AI hosts understand people’s needs, provide answers and take action, and can be tailored to local languages and service needs in airports, hospitals, local events and other public spaces.
Vision AI agents can turn existing city camera feeds into operational insights, helping teams identify mobility and safety issues and coordinate emergency responses across city services.
In Wrocław, Poland, K2K is building shared AI infrastructure using NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA Cosmos world reasoning models, and NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) to transform existing camera streams into actionable intelligence for mobility, safety and event response — using the same infrastructure across several city functions.
In Malaysia, [ITMAX](http://www.itmax.com.my/newsroom/itmax-and-nvidia-use-ai-to-give-kuala-lumpur-commuters-time-back) bundles infrastructure and agentic AI applications into long-term managed services for cities, including for traffic management. Built with reference to Cosmos, Nemotron and the Metropolis VSS blueprint, ITMAX’s SamurAI V2 vision agents are scaling on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs to support 17,000+ cameras by 2027. ITMAX integrates TeraSim, an open source traffic simulation platform from Laplace Intelligence, to test signal timing, reducing peak-hour corridor travel times by up to 26%.
Plan and Operate Critical Infrastructure With Digital Twins
Beyond public-facing services, digital twins can help cities expedite infrastructure planning, minimizing disruption to local communities. City digital twins can also serve as a real-time operational simulation to facilitate faster decision-making.
At Dangote’s Lekki refinery in Nigeria, Honeywell Technologies’ Forge Plant Cognition uses Nemotron-powered AI agents to understand operational data. A digital twin of the plant and its processes, built using Omniverse libraries, is also planned to support simulation and training. The platform, built on Dell PowerEdge servers with NVIDIA RTX PRO accelerators, helps operators identify bottlenecks, anticipate equipment and process issues, and optimize plant performance.
In Taiwan, [Linker Vision](https://www.linkervision.com/post/linker-vision-unveils-linker-ai-nexa-to-bring-physical-ai-to-city-governance) and Dutch architecture firm MVRDV are using NVIDIA Omniverse and Nemotron to build environmental, social and governance agents that can assess the environmental impact of various urban planning scenarios, simulating 15-year outcomes of an urban forest canopy in 10 minutes — increasing design iteration speed from two weeks per iteration to less than an hour.
Build a Broader Local AI Ecosystem
Cities can extend AI to more services by building on infrastructure already in place and adding capacity. Shared resources and managed services can help extend those capabilities across departments and municipalities.
At Morocco’s Tanger Med port, Cires Technologies is expanding a sovereign AI factory for planned applications in worker safety, congestion analysis, cargo routing and port operations. Cires Technologies is also building an ecosystem of application providers to develop local models and applications for ports and cities.
Beyond city services, Barcelona Supercomputing Center’s [AI Factory Accelerator Programme](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/spain-startups-barcelona-supercomputing-center/) gives startups access to sovereign computing, technical support and training. BSC AI Factory also supports research and innovation for startups — spanning agriculture, medical imaging, knowledge access and speech services.
Learn how NVIDIA and its ecosystem are bringing physical AI, agentic AI and local AI factories to cities worldwide at Smart City Expo World Congress, running Nov. 3-5 in Barcelona, where NVIDIA Vice President of EMEA Paolo Guglielmini will deliver a [keynote address](https://www.smartcityexpo.com/agenda/from-ai-factories-to-intelligent-cities/) followed by a [panel](https://www.smartcityexpo.com/agenda/by-the-city-for-the-city-making-ai-work/) moderated by Charbel Aoun, director of smart city and spaces for EMEA at NVIDIA.

Runway's first AI film in 2019 was 128x128 pixels. Today, people can't tell generated video from real footage.
