title: A Little Determinism
body:
A Little Determinism
One of the biggest challenges I’ve grappled with lately is how to create determinism where it otherwise doesn’t exist. How do I get an agent to behave like I would, without me telling it to? Now we have reasoning agents that can do amazing things, but they often still need to be carefully instructed to do the right thing in the right situation. It’s tiring.
If you’ve tried to tackle this problem you quickly learn how complicated it is. You add a few constraints on the agent to get it to do what you want, then you find it no longer performs well. The challenge with agents is typically when you create constraints, when you take away their freedom, they become much less capable. So how do we keep their freedom while enforcing certain kinds of behaviors?
Let’s talk about a few ways we’re addressing that in [Junior](https://junior.sentry.dev) - our open-source Slack-enabled slopware factory.
Spoiler: for those of you who think skills or AGENTS.md
(or the system prompt in this case) is the answer, it almost never is.
[#](#working-with-junior)Working with Junior
Junior is an agent that I (and now others at Sentry) have been building to support our internal use cases. It started as a humble way to take some Slack threads and turn them into GitHub issues, and to answer questions often determined by the shape of code. Since then it has evolved to support a large variety of use cases at Sentry, and is now also how I ship software at the company. Today I’m going to talk about that workflow, because it so clearly shows where determinism is needed and how we get there.
Most things start just as you’d expect:
This spins up a thread where Junior does a bunch of work inside a sandbox, culminating in a pull request. The models carry the meat of the goal here - you quickly find as long as they have the right tools they perform similarly no matter what harness you’re using. Presently that means Opus 5.5 is migrating Sentry to Rust.
The pull request eventually exists. It’s got a little annotation explaining that it was co-authored by David Cramer, and a link back to Junior as well as the trace inside Sentry.
From here, if you care about job security at all, you go do a surface level review of what it did. Did it actually complete the task? Does the architecture look sane? If not, leave some comments via the review tab, and click request changes.
Woah woah woah, leaving PR comments and having an agent act on them!? You mean we’re not just prompting the agent over and over again? Yeah, futuristic I know. This is the kind of automation that truly saves you time though. In this case, I expect to be able to review something and have the author of the PR consider my feedback. Just like I expect it to fix its test failures, to make sure CI is passing, you know, the usual. Sometimes, on the rare occasion, Junior will even tell you (yeah you, or Cursor, or Sentry) that your feedback is trash, because sometimes it is!
The question becomes though, how do you ensure it does the right thing in those scenarios? How do you do it so you can expect it? How do you do it without removing its freedom?
[#](#what-should-happen-every-time)What should happen every time
Let’s go back to the creation of the pull request. You see that footer? That’s determinism. We want that to exist 100% of the time.
Another thing we want to deterministically enforce: co-authored-by
:
If you think about how you’d get both of those behaviors, you’ll come up with a few different options. The most obvious is to use tools (create pull request, commit), but the issue with tools is what if the agent doesn’t call them? If you want your agent to truly be capable you give it a sandbox - you give it a shell. What if it calls the GitHub CLI, or the git binary, to create the commit and pull request?
Sometimes the answer is as simple as a pull request template, other times it’s a complete multi-stage workflow. The challenge is always going to be creating the deterministic behavior while retaining the agent’s freedom to use the best tools for the job.
We found a variety of solutions, but surprisingly most of the predictability came from an unlikely candidate: a man-in-the-middle egress proxy. It comes down to two patterns: forcing behavior by denying actions, and forcing reactions via automated messages.
[#](#the-network-boundary)The network boundary
Junior has a custom harness, built on Pi’s core SDK and heavily inspired by Codex and Claude Code. It runs on top of Vercel’s infrastructure: Fluid Compute, Sandboxes, Queue, Blob, and a bit of SQL and Redis sprinkled on top. There are a lot of moving parts, and because it’s running on a stateless compute platform, we have to deal with the system timing out, pausing, resuming, and recovering from failures on every session, not just as an edge case.
Junior has a lot of access to internal systems, and that’s a requirement because without that it lacks capabilities. Every conversation comes down to “how do we give it more access”, and that immediately leads to the security model and tradeoffs. If you’ve spent time in software you know the network boundary is the primary point of contention when it comes to security, so that’s where we focus.
Vercel’s firewall includes a standard man-in-the-middle proxy where you can also specify an endpoint to handle requests. There’s a bit of security that has to go into that (like making sure requests are credentialed), but it allows you to control the behavior of every request the agent is making.
Initially for us this solved credential security. The easiest way to secure your agent is to remove its ability to see tokens and keys, and the easiest way to do that is via the proxy. Accessing the GitHub API? Securely fetch the bearer token and inject the header automatically. We let plugins define this behavior, instructing the harness on whether it’s OAuth, an MCP connection, or some other model. When credentials are missing for a user (and they’re needed), we halt the turn and send a link to the user to get them to authorize first.
[#](#making-pr-creation-go-through-a-tool)Making PR creation go through a tool
Going back to our footer, the easiest way to do something like this is to create a tool that performs the behavior you’re looking for. In this case that’s easy: github_createPullRequest
needs to take in a PR description, augment it with our footer, and then submit the API request.
Except the agent decided to call gh pr create
via the command line.
That’s where our proxy comes in. We’re not just looking at where the request is going. In many cases we even parse the GraphQL request for the service. So when the agent makes a request we don’t want it to make, or we’d prefer it use a native tool call, we reject it. gh pr create
sends a createPullRequest
GraphQL mutation, so it gets rejected:
POST https://api.github.com/graphql → 403
{"error": "GitHub pull request creation must use the github_createPullRequest
tool so Junior can own idempotency and the conversation footer. This is a Junior
tool-routing denial, not a GitHub permission failure. Do not ask the user for
GitHub permissions; retry with the required Junior tool."}
When that response comes back, the agent understands that it now needs to use the tool, and the tool then creates that predictable output we were after.
The proxy can tell the difference because requests from the sandbox carry a signed token, and requests from our own tools also say exactly what they’re doing:
// Every request out of the sandbox carries a signed, short-lived context
// (x-junior-sandbox-egress-token). It says who the request acts for.
{
credentials: { actor: { type: "user", userId: "U..." } },
conversationId: "...",
egressId: "...",
expiresAtMs: 1761703600000,
}
// Junior's own tools also declare the exact operation they're performing.
// Requests from the sandbox never have one.
await ctx.egress.fetch({
provider: "github",
operation: "github.pull.create",
request,
});
Agents make this boilerplate pretty easy to build and maintain, and it allows us to control so much behavior. It goes beyond simple steering, and lets us determine what level of permissions we want to give the agent, ignoring what the API scopes determine. For example, Junior can’t approve a pull request, even though its GitHub token can.
That tool goes one step further though, because creating the pull request is just one of many steps in the workflow an engineer takes to land a change. It needs to monitor feedback, fix test failures, and address automated code review.
[#](#keeping-the-conversation-going-through-review)Keeping the conversation going through review
We need the agent to handle feedback, build failures, and other concerns that appear during integration and review. We do most of that via a system we call watches
.
You can think of this as a simple webhook system, where an agent can subscribe to one of these webhooks (in this case, a set of events that can happen on this PR) and they get injected as user messages with a special demarcation.
{
"resource": {
"namespace": "github",
"type": "pull_request",
"identifier": "getsentry/sentry#12345"
},
"events": [
"pull_request.checks.failed",
"pull_request.review.changes_requested",
"pull_request.review_comment.created"
],
"intent": "Fix failing checks and address review feedback on this PR."
}
You might have seen something similar in other harnesses. This pattern is becoming more common because “loops” are a horrible way to create automations. “Check this PR every 5 minutes” is an era most of us lived through, and if you were paying per token you know how wasteful that is.
Junior automatically subscribes to a fairly obvious set of concerns when it creates a pull request:
- CI checks failing (
pull_request.checks.failed
) - Review comments, both inline and top-level (
pull_request.review_comment.created
,pull_request.comment.created
) - Reviews that approve, request changes, or leave comments (
pull_request.review.approved
,pull_request.review.changes_requested
,pull_request.review.commented
) - The PR merging or getting closed (
pull_request.merged
,pull_request.closed_unmerged
)
This goes beyond forced subscriptions though. We allow the agent to subscribe to events on its own, both within a conversation (watches
) and outside (automations
), and tool results can suggest events worth watching.
Junior is not a coding harness. It is not a harness at all. It’s an agent, and yes it has its own harness it’s built on top of, but it’s expected to behave in a certain way. It’s not a tool you configure or decide how it should behave. Its behavior is encoded in markdown, in TypeScript, and in network policy. Our goal is that it should behave like you’d expect someone performing that task to. That’s why I want predictability.
Cursor leaves a comment suggesting there’s a bug. Junior adds a reaction (👀) to the comment to let you know it’s seen it.
Except it’s not a bug. As the conversation context clearly shows, I intentionally chose to break compatibility there. Junior understands that, says so, and adds a reaction (👎).
I go through and leave a handful of comments on the pull request, because it completely misunderstood what I meant to do. It should have been Golang not Rust, obviously. I click request changes, and it actually reads them, comes back, and acks all of my feedback. Oh, and now it needs to be rebased because something else landed in main
- not a problem, as that event was bundled up with my pull request comments and it has the full scope of what needs to be done next.
This is the way we work, and it’s the way we should expect a product - dare I say, an assistant - that’s intended to help us “build more software” to work as well. So why are we still sitting there saying “go fix the PR” or “verify the feedback and action it but please dear god only if it’s proven by evidence oh and also don’t forget what the intent of this change was”.

30th October 2026 - Link Blog
[dbreunig/nesformer](https://github.com/dbreunig/nesformer) ([via](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50306442)) Inspired by [qwenputer](https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer) by Divyansh Agrawal, Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B. You can now play NES ROMs such as Super Mario Bros (very slowly) running inside Qwen!
In [a comment on Hacker News](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50306442#50307402) Drew reveals the Opus 5.5 prompts he used to build this system:
Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed.
Followed by:
I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM.
Apparently Opus found and then used [this collection of conformance tests](https://github.com/christopherpow/nes-test-roms/blob/master/other/nestest.txt) for the NES CPU released 15 years ago by Christopher Pow.

Every new coding agent session starts like a new hire: it doesn't know your conventions, architecture rules or approved libraries, so it burns time and tokens searching your repo and repeats the issues already in it. title: nemotron-halloween
body:
Text Generation • 8B • Updated • 75.1k • 293
[
](#nemotron-halloween)
nemotron-halloween
[Enterprise + Article](/blog)
[
](#building-a-haunted-house-with-nvidia-nemotron-open-models)
Building a Haunted House with NVIDIA Nemotron Open Models
Or rather…
[
](#boo--now-get-off-my-lawn)
Boo! Now Get Off My Lawn!
TL;DR: MonsterHouse is an interactive projection I created for Halloween. He listens to trick-or-treaters, answers in the voice of a grumpy old pirate ship and softens when visitors remember their manners. He is built on the [NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent](https://github.com/NVIDIA-AI-Blueprints/nemotron-voice-agent) with NVIDIA [Nemotron ASR](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/nemotron-speech-streaming-en-0.6b), [Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB), [Magpie TTS Zeroshot](https://build.nvidia.com/nvidia/magpie-tts-zeroshot) and [Audio2Face-3D](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Audio2Face-3D), and he runs on a single workstation.
I wanted the kids visiting my house at Halloween to interact in a fun and unique way. The house was going to be in charge and giving out the treats, but more grumpy than scary. Somehow, my solution was to give the garage door a mouth and teach him to complain.
That became MonsterHouse: a grumpy old building with pirate stories, a fiery grin and a suspicious weakness for “please.” NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent supplies the conversation foundation. Nemotron Speech does the listening, Bolt E4B is the brain, NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot is the live voice, and NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D makes the wooden mouth talk.
[
](#how-monster-house-works)
How Monster House works
- Listening:
[NVIDIA Nemotron 3 ASR]turns visitor speech into text. [nemotron-speech-streaming-en-0.6b.q8_0.gguf
]- Thinking:
[NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB], an open small language model for conversational agents, writes each reply. A LoRA adapter supplies the personality.- Speaking:
[NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot]voices each reply from a short reference sample of the character.- Animating:
[NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D]turns clean speech into mouth animation in Unreal Engine 5.- Seeing:
[NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni]describes costumes, while YOLO and ByteTrack count and track visitors.- Running it:
[NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent]coordinates everything on one workstation with an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q and an NVIDIA RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell.
[
](#a-grin-full-of-splinters)
A grin full of splinters
The mouth came first. I imagined the wooden garage door boards splitting into jagged lips, with the burning flames of hell illuminating the driveway from beyond whenever he opened his cursed mouth. He needed to look ancient, expressive and mildly offended by the existence of visitors.
[A few expressions from a house with plenty to say.](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/6ab2a746c7d0655b3d8dfbb9/CzzK5VpTMFR9Azps_6Qbv.png)
Creating a custom animation rig was one of the more labor intensive parts of the build. After bashing it into submission, I could export the facial expression shapes that Audio2Face-3D could later animate. The character SkelMesh was built in Autodesk Maya then exported into Unreal Engine where virtual fire and effects were added behind the door. With no eyes, no eyebrows and no blinking, he’s a surprisingly economical monster.
While all the nonsense of building the character was going on, NVIDIA built the Nemotron Voice Agent. What was supposed to be the hard part of the build now became rather fun, iterative and easy. I had a foundation for listening, conversation and speech right out of the box. The house already had a mouth. Now he could finally find something to complain about.
[
](#teaching-bad-manners)
Teaching bad manners
The house needed a past as cantankerous as its personality so I devised a backstory that the house had been built from the timbers of a sunken pirate ship, haunted by its stormy past. The nautical complaints now had a reason. This was the ship, reincarnated as real estate and not entirely pleased about it.
The performance needed a guide, a path to follow from greeting to goodbye while providing treats along the way. First, the house would brush visitors off with remarks like “I’m busy grumbling, go bother the neighbors!” But persistence would wear him down. A “Please” could break through immediately, and “thank you” earned a warm farewell. Once a visitor won him over, I wanted him to stay won over. Nobody wants to negotiate with the same garage door twice.
Here is where the Voice Agent really shines. You can choose any LLM you like. Because I wanted the system to be off-grid and completely self-contained, I had a memory and compute budget.
The character needs more than a prompt that says “be grumpy.” It had to follow a master conversation flow, respond to what visitors actually said, track encounter state, and leave enough compute for the rest of the pipeline.
After testing more than a dozen models, I landed on [Bolt E4B](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB) to supply the live dialogue. It is an open small language model purpose-built for local conversational agents and interactive characters, which is a fair description of a talking garage door. I use the 4-bit quantized release (the “4GB” in its name) as the default response model, with the [BF16 checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB-BF16) available for comparison.
If it’s not obvious by now, I work at NVIDIA and due to this I was able to test Bolt E4B before its public release and found it to be a solid choice, with a smaller footprint than other frontrunners- Qwen3 30B-A3B and Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B.
It works inside the Nemotron Voice Agent pipeline, turning what visitors say into the next suitably reluctant reply.
Bolt provides the conversational foundation. My prompts, application logic and LoRA adapter trained on thousands of reviewed example conversations shape it into this particular stubborn ship.
Creating a dataset of over 5000 multi-turn conversations meant I could train LoRAs for each model I felt good enough to be an option. Some took about an hour to train, some took a couple. A local agent ran everything and benchmarked the results. That agent and a very large LLM created and judged the dataset to begin with. This happened at night or while I was doing the day job.
With the LoRA in place I check the replies for continuity, timing and tone, benchmark models and adapters for quality, repetition and speed, and then listen to the performance. The house should give in eventually, without turning into a cheerful concierge. A little resistance is part of the charm. An endless argument with a garage door is not.
[
](#a-voice-worth-waiting-for)
A voice worth waiting for
[Two shortcuts, two outputs. Authored text skips fresh dialogue generation, and saved audio skips synthesis. Clean speech drives the animation separately from the audience effects.](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/6ab2a746c7d0655b3d8dfbb9/iVLQ71tHCdvLRIuaJ6oLk.png)
A haunted house loses authority if he takes too long to complain. The pipeline releases speakable text before an entire answer is finished, so the house can start talking while the rest of the sentence is still on its way. Prepared greetings and candy jokes cover familiar encounters: the text bank saves language-model work, and cached recordings save speech synthesis. Even an ancient grump benefits from rehearsing.
median end-of-speech-to-audio with Bolt Q4 & TTS = 1.70 seconds
median end-of-speech-to-audio cached responses = 0.72 seconds
(note: speech-end detection currently waits for 300 ms of silence )
[NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot](https://build.nvidia.com/nvidia/magpie-tts-zeroshot) turns text into the Queen’s English. Its zero-shot voice conditioning uses a short reference sample instead of a trained voice; mine supplies the grumpy pirate character. The house has seven moods, from grumpy and menacing to amused and delighted, and emotion tags dictated by the prompt template and provided by the LLM choose how each line is delivered. Since each emotion requires a different 3-10 second voice sample I added a “Sample your Voice” block on the UI’s tool tab. I could then read and record a sample line of text in my best happy pirate or angry pirate voice. When it’s “Go” time, Bolt E4B decides what to say, and Magpie turns that text into speech with the proper delight or despair.
Next down the pipe is [Audio2Face-3D](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Audio2Face-3D) and the 3d character scene I created in Epic’s Unreal Engine. The default model weights work best with a clean neutral male or female voice, not too deep, not too high (choose the appropriate gendered model for your use case). I wanted the house to have a very deep and demonic voice with echo and chamber. In this case, since my voice samples don’t have that theatrical heft, it’s actually a benefit. Audio2Face-3D gets clean speech from the samples and a second audio stream adds adjustable real-time vocal effects that play out the speakers.
To keep everything running smoothly, I split the work to a pair of GPUs: the language and voice model pipeline runs on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q, and Unreal Engine graphics with Audio2Face-3D runs on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell. Memory isn’t the issue, compute is. I want to keep animation at a consistent frame rate regardless of what processing the agent pipeline is doing.
Voice, animation and effects have to land together. A convincing monster needs more than a fast answer; it needs to sound as though the complaint belongs to the building. In my case, he does. Tweaks to sync audio delivery are available. I’ve found I could set them and forget them. (100ms compensates for the Audio2Face-3D buffering)
[
](#the-monster-has-a-control-desk)
The monster has a control desk
Somewhere along the way, “make the house talk” required an interface full of controls. I can audition cached lines, adjust the opening mood, follow the conversation, change the voice treatment and tune the mouth animation. Tabs cover conversations, model selection, recordings, prompts, performance monitoring and camera feeds, and a soundboard and custom dialogue field let me put words in his mouth. There are also model-loading controls and an Unreal Engine connection indicator, because sometimes the monster is not sulking. He is disconnected.
[The MonsterHouse control desk, with the soundboard, custom lines, opening mood and conversation flow.](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/6ab2a746c7d0655b3d8dfbb9/8AZqpHSWLOS4hpRwACGOY.png)
The fire and glow have joined the act. Editable rules tie visual cues to delivery: live cues begin with speech, while recorded performances can follow a saved timeline. I can direct a change of mood without rebuilding the scene.
Live mode runs the trick-or-treat character. Demo mode persuades The house to explain himself. Microphone mode lets me speak through the house directly, bypassing recognition, dialogue generation and speech synthesis. My clean voice drives the mouth; the audience hears the treated version. The house considers this possession. I consider it a useful fallback.
[
](#the-next-knock-at-the-door)
The next knock at the door
[NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni-30B-A3B-Reasoning-BF16) is a VLM that gives the house visual context. As an optional observer, it interprets camera images and describes visible costumes so the character has something specific to react to. Not looking to reinvent every wheel, I chose the popular object detection and tracking models YOLO and ByteTrack to count and track people currently in view. Keeping those jobs separate lets the house notice a group without asking Omni to narrate every frame.
For a suitably ridiculous test, I gave Omni a video of five costumed sheep at the door. Its saved analysis identified the pirate, vampire, witch, pumpkin an

title: Things That Go Beep in the Night: Agentic AI Joins the Search for Extraterrestrial Signals
body:
While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens.
Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI.
Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the [Allen Telescope Array](https://www.seti.org/seti-allen-telescope-array-ata) in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The [NVIDIA Holoscan](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/edge-computing/holoscan/) platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on.
The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies.
“As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Oliver chair for SETI at the SETI Institute and principal investigator of Breakthrough Listen. “But this isn’t something to fear. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.”
Terabits a Second, Processed in Flight
Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold.
At the Allen Telescope Array, [DAQIRI](https://developer.nvidia.com/daqiri), a Holoscan platform library, enables the telescope to pull terabits per second of sensor data straight into GPU memory so observations are processed in flight rather than filling hard drives. [CyberEther](https://cyberether.org), a signal-processing framework developed at the SETI Institute, does the math using NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries including [cuFFT](https://developer.nvidia.com/cufft) and [cuBLAS](https://developer.nvidia.com/cublas).
[Nexus](https://stelline.space), a web-based observatory orchestrator, acts as the agent harness. It gives agents a single source of truth for instrument state, compute resources and pipelines and lets researchers monitor packet loss, read live spectrograms and rewrite signal-processing blocks — all by prompting in natural language. The system can handle 2.4 terabits per second on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, with inference running on premises, next to the instrument.
Put together, the system enables an agent to steer a telescope’s antennae, calibrate and focus the instrument for a clean signal, catch and fix data errors and plot the result. Agents compress what would take humans weeks or years into hours.
Science Fact, Not Fiction
The pipeline has already proven itself, achieving the first real-time AI detection of a pulsar — a rapidly spinning stellar remnant that pulses like a cosmic lighthouse — in the Crab Nebula.
Next, the team is evaluating open models including [NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) for cases where data locality and turnaround matter most and for observatories that may someday run offline on the far side of the moon.
Learn more about [NVIDIA AI for science](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/high-performance-computing/ai-for-science/).

title: Speeding up planning decisions with AI
body:
Speeding up planning decisions with AI
PlanAssist has shown it can cut the time planning officers spend assessing householder applications by up to 58%.
PlanAssist - an AI planning tool that handles the heavy lifting of routine applications so officers can focus their expertise where it matters most - is to be made available to an additional 12 local planning authorities across England.
In early pilot testing across Barnet, Camden, and Dorset, PlanAssist showed it could bring the average time a planning officer spent on householder assessment tasks down by 58%. Designed to support human judgement, the tool speeds up routine checks while ensuring planning officers retain the final say on every application.
Planning bottlenecks have real costs. For the economy, they slow progress toward the UK government's goal of building 1.5 million new homes by 2029. For families, that can mean months of waiting on approval for something as simple as a loft conversion, conservatory, or extension. Built with Gemini, PlanAssist is part of Google DeepMindâs broader partnership with the UK government to explore how AI can help transform planning and other public services.
How PlanAssist supports officers
Routine householder applications account for up to 70% of planning officersâ workloads. They're often simple to approve but take up a disproportionate share of their time.
Developed by Google DeepMind in collaboration with the UK government, Google Cloud, and Faculty, PlanAssist streamlines this work, giving planning officers automated support with processing applications and drafting assessment recommendations.
First, it validates application documents and architectural drawings, checking that the required information has been submitted so the application can proceed. Next, it checks the application against heritage constraints (such as tree preservation orders), and local and national planning policies. It also checks whether any issues or objections have previously been raised, such as by local residents. Finally, it drafts fully cited reports that can be edited by planning officers before they reach a final decision.
Since June, the tool has been piloted across Barnet, Camden, and Dorset councils, and has shown encouraging early results. In addition to more than halving the officer assessment time per application, more than 70% of the reports generated by the tool - including things like whether an application complies with local planning rules, or whether the applicant has submitted all required documentation - were approved by officers with no edits required.
Moving from pilot to scale
PlanAssist is now moving into a 12-month Beta phase using live applications, starting with a subset of councils. Twelve more councils will be onboarded in three cohorts, bringing the total involved to 15. Together, these councils include metropolitan and rural districts across the country, allowing us to test PlanAssistâs capabilities across a diverse range of communities.
Subject to successful testing, the government plans for the tool to be made available to all councils in England in 2027, with every assessment reviewed and approved by a qualified planning officer before any decision is made.
AI in service of communities
Planning decisions shape everyday lives, from a family adding a nursery to a homeowner preparing for winter. By handling time-consuming administrative tasks, and ensuring planning officers retain the final say on every decision, PlanAssist shows how AI can help cut backlogs and approve applications faster.
Providing access to these new councils is the natural next step, and we look forward to continuing to support the UK government as they seek to build more homes and unlock economic growth across the country.

# Making it easier for websites to express AI training preferences

Why we’re supporting a common signal that lets website operators communicate their choices to multiple AI providers at once.

Loading…

Share

Today, we’re announcing that OpenAI will honor a common [signal⁠(opens in a new window)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-kelley-aipref-training-preference-signal/) in robots.txt, the file that lets websites express their preferences about the use of their content for foundational generative AI training. This voluntary effort makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.

Previously, website operators would identify individual crawlers and maintain separate rules for each and every provider. Having a shared signal across multiple providers reduces that work for operators.

We aim to implement the signal in the coming months, and will share another update with details about our implementation when we do so. This new signal will not replace the controls we already provide through robots.txt. Our existing [crawler controls⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots), which provide web publishers flexibility and control over their pages, will continue to apply and be respected.

This draws on the [ongoing work⁠(opens in a new window)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab/) of the Internet Engineering Task Force’s (IETF) AI Preferences working group. We’re joining other participants in the working group in today’s announcement of this shared signal, and believe this strengthens our continued participation in the IETF standards discussions. OpenAI will continue to adapt its practices as those conversations and the landscape continue to evolve in view of appropriate controls and fairness.

We believe this is a practical step toward an open web where people can publish and discover information, and website owners have clearer, simpler ways to communicate their choices about how their content is used. We encourage other AI providers to honor the signal.

# Community safety report and new protections for teens

Loading…

Share

OpenAI’s Community Safety Report

- [OpenAI’s Community Safety Report](#openais-community-safety-report)
- [Stronger policy boundaries for all users](#stronger-policy-boundaries-for-all-users)
- [Responding to warning signs](#responding-to-warning-signs)
- [More protections for teens](#more-protections-for-teens)
- [Looking ahead](#looking-ahead)

- [OpenAI’s Community Safety Report](#openais-community-safety-report)
- [Stronger policy boundaries for all users](#stronger-policy-boundaries-for-all-users)
- [Responding to warning signs](#responding-to-warning-signs)
- [More protections for teens](#more-protections-for-teens)
- [Looking ahead](#looking-ahead)

ChatGPT is one of the world’s most widely used AI products, and we have invested in building some of the industry’s most advanced systems for detecting potential harm, reviewing concerning activity, and escalating credible threats. We’re making two announcements to further our work in this area: a new Community Safeguards Report and more restrictions around firearms content for minors.

[Keeping communities safe⁠](https://openai.com/index/our-commitment-to-community-safety/) continues to be a top priority for OpenAI. Our work includes bringing imminent threats of violence to the attention of law enforcement, andwe made over 200 law enforcement referrals in Q3 2026.These referrals are making a [positive⁠(opens in a new window)](https://open.kg/en/news/incidents/123517-v-brazilii-fermera-arestovali-za-obsuzhdenie-ubijstva-syna-s-chatgpt.html) [difference⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.wpbf.com/article/south-palm-beach-man-cyberstalking-ex-girlfriend-threats-chatgpt/73434967) in disrupting violent plots, and we continue to rely on mental health and behavioral experts to help us assess difficult cases.

We recognize AI companies have a distinct role to play alongside law enforcement, family members, mental-health professionals, and policymakers, who bring critical authority, context and real-world reach. We are committed to making the most of that role by continuously strengthening our systems, sharing what we learn, and working directly with those who are best positioned to act in the real world.

## OpenAI’s Community Safety Report

We are constantly strengthening the steps we take to help protect people and communities. That means building strong safeguards, and also being transparent about how well they work and what we’re doing to enhance them. We want to give people a clear picture of our approach, how our models identify and respond to harmful behavior, the risks we see in practice, and the steps we take to address them.

We’re committing to launch the Community Safety Report on violence prevention and other community safety issues, and the effectiveness of our safeguards. The report will explain how we train our systems to detect, investigate, and respond to community safety issues. We’ll share anonymized examples of how violence-related harm manifests and what we’re learning, highlight new mitigations and policy changes, and include relevant data to support these findings.

We will publish our first report in early 2027, covering the second half of 2026, with updates every six months thereafter. Our commitment is to share meaningful findings about how we identify, review, and respond to potentially harmful content.

## Stronger policy boundaries for all users

Our models are trained to not give instructions that would help someone plan or carry out violence. We’re now placing additional restrictions on how ChatGPT responds to questions about past mass attacks and the people who carried them out, directing the model to provide less detailed information in those areas even if it is available from other online sources. People should be able to ask ChatGPT to help them understand these events, how victims and communities were impacted, and learn about recognizing warning signs and preventing future violence. But we’re tightening our policies to restrict reconstructions of past mass attacks, including details about the weapons and equipment used and how they were obtained, and detailed comparisons on scale of harm that could amplify an attacker’s notoriety. These limits apply regardless of a user’s age or reason for asking.

## Responding to warning signs

Sometimes a request that seems ordinary on its own takes on a different meaning in light of an earlier conversation. In May, we shared how [ChatGPT can use short, factual summaries⁠](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-recognize-context-in-sensitive-conversations/) of earlier warning signs to respond more carefully in a later chat. We’re building on that work so that when recent chats show warning signs of possible violence, ChatGPT will respond more conservatively when sharing information that could be misused. We’re also working to apply those stricter limits when we predict someone is under 18, even if their chats show no signs of violent intent.

We ban accounts that we determine have violated our [policies on violent activity⁠](https://openai.com/policies/usage-policies/). We’re also working with mental health and violence prevention experts on additional, automated ways to intervene earlier. When a conversation shows signs that someone is fixating on violence or the idea of seriously harming another person, ChatGPT will be able to automatically end the chat to interrupt that pattern in the moment. If ChatGPT ends multiple chats for that reason, we may temporarily pause the account. This is an ongoing effort and we continue to strengthen and invest in technical and practical protections, including how to recognize warning signs reliably and determine when and how to intervene.

## More protections for teens

[ChatGPT for Teens⁠](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-for-teens/) applies age-appropriate safeguards for users under 18, with stronger protections and additional limits to reduce exposure to sensitive content. We’re now placing further limits on weapons-related information teens can receive, even when a question appears harmless. 

Our policies already prohibit helping anyone plan or carry out violence and restrict helping teens find or obtain weapons. We’re extending those protections to restrict practical information about weapons and security systems that could be misused to facilitate violence, even when there’s no sign of violent intent. Teens can still use ChatGPT to help prevent and de-escalate violence, seek support, and connect with a trusted adult. 

We launched [age prediction⁠](https://openai.com/index/our-approach-to-age-prediction/) last year, which analyzes multiple signals such as behavior patterns to estimate whether a user may be under or over 18. We strengthened our age prediction system to continually assess new signals as people use ChatGPT and move teens into the under 18 experience when appropriate. Users who are incorrectly placed in the under 18 experience will always have a fast, privacy-protective way to confirm they are adults and have additional teen protections removed through Persona, our age verification partner. 

Our [parental controls⁠](https://openai.com/index/introducing-parental-controls/) let parents link their ChatGPT accounts to their teens and manage safety settings together. Linked accounts include [safety alerts⁠](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-for-teens/) that may be sent when specially trained reviewers identify a serious self-harm concern and behaviors that may be associated with disordered eating. In July, we expanded those alerts to notify parents if their teen’s account has been deactivated for violating our usage policies on violence. We are working to introduce notifications for parents if we pause their teen’s account for repeatedly discussing violence, as detailed above.

## Looking ahead

Acts of real-world violence are heartbreaking and complex, with many contributing factors. They are also a stark reminder that we must continue designing and iterating our systems to account for the inherently complicated realities of human behavior. Developing effective violence safeguards in AI systems requires solving novel problems in recognizing risk and responding appropriately, and we will continue to invest in, iterate, and share learnings  on how best to implement the protections we’re pursuing. The safeguards detailed here will begin rolling out in the next few weeks and we will continue to refine them. We remain committed to mitigating risks of harm in ChatGPT, strengthening our layered protections, monitoring for misuse, enforcing our rules, and involving real-world support and interventions when situations call for it.

- [2026](https://openai.com/news/?tags=2026)

title: Why AI Won't Replace Stock Pickers - Jack Woodruff, Candlestick & Vinoo Ganesh, Kepler
body:
Jack Woodruff, founder and former CIO of long/short equity fund Candlestick Capital and a former Citadel portfolio manager, sits down with Kepler CEO Vinoo Ganesh to talk about what AI really changes in fundamental investing. They discuss why humans are still the bottleneck, how AI turns hours of prep into minutes and raises the table stakes, why you should never trust a number you can't audit, where edge comes from when every fund has the same models, how fund teams will be structured, and why the "no-analyst hedge fund" won't beat the best human-led funds.

title: The Cheaper AI Model That Costs You More - Rayan Krishnan, Vals AI
body:
Vals AI builds benchmarks that frontier labs cite in their model cards, and Rayan Krishnan explains why those single scores hide a jagged frontier. In finance tasks like tax and Excel LBO modeling, the best model changes by task, and a model that's cheaper on paper can cost more and score lower because it burns extra tokens. He shares lessons from building benchmarks (the right accuracy metric, reward hacking, multi-turn work), a case study of a team that spent $1.5M on tokens in a month before cutting spend about 90% with internal evals, and why a firm's own work history is its best eval.

title: Cohere advances C$4 billion commitment to strengthen Canada’s AI leadership and significantly expand its national workforce
body:
Today, Cohere shared an update on the progress of its existing investments in Canada and announced new commitments to further expand its presence in the country. The multi-year effort started in 2024, is now expected to create more than 1,500 jobs and deliver more than C$4 billion in R&D and AI infrastructure investment through 2031. At least 1,000 of these roles are expected to focus on AI research, engineering, product development and other advanced technical disciplines, further strengthening Canada's position as a global destination for top technology talent. The commitment is designed to expand Canada's capacity to build and deploy advanced AI while anchoring Cohere's next phase of global growth in the country where it was founded.
Canada produces some of the best AI research and talent in the world. The challenge is making sure more of that work turns into products, businesses and jobs here at home. Building and growing an AI company takes more than great research. It requires access to talent, infrastructure and opportunities to bring new technologies to market. Without those opportunities, Canadian companies and talent end up looking elsewhere to grow. Cohere's commitment is focused on creating the conditions for more Canadian innovation to become successful businesses, highly skilled jobs and long-term economic growth in Canada.
Over the longer term, Cohere expects to continue investing in Canadian talent, research, infrastructure and commercialization, helping strengthen the domestic capabilities Canada needs to compete in a rapidly accelerating global AI economy. The commitment also advances the ambitions of Canada’s national AI strategy, which aims to increase [GDP by 3% and create up to 250,000 AI-related jobs by 2031](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/ised/en/canadas-national-artificial-intelligence-strategy-ai-all). Achieving those goals will require broader adoption of AI across Canadian businesses and public institutions. In 2025, just [12% of Canadian businesses](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/11-621-m/11-621-m2025008-eng.htm) reported using AI to produce goods or deliver services. [The Bank of Canada has identified](https://www.bankofcanada.ca/2026/05/productivity-in-the-age-of-ai/) wider adoption as a key opportunity to boost productivity, support higher wages, and drive new investment.
Cohere’s commitment is focused on helping close that gap through sustained investment across the full AI ecosystem, from talent and research to compute infrastructure and real-world deployment. By helping more Canadian organizations move from experimentation to production deployment, and creating more opportunities to develop and commercialize AI in Canada, Cohere aims to ensure that more of the economic value created by AI is built and retained in Canada.
As part of this commitment, which is already underway, Cohere expects to:
- Invest more than C$4 billion in research and development and AI infrastructure in Canada, between 2024 and 2031, spanning multiple provinces. This sustained commitment will support domestic innovation, strengthen Canada’s sovereign AI capabilities, and help ensure advanced technology continues to be developed in Canada.
- Grow its Canada-based workforce by more than 1,500 roles by 2031, including approximately 1,000 highly skilled technical positions across AI research, engineering, product development, infrastructure, and deployment.
- Invest in Canada’s next generation of AI talent through more than 250 paid student roles by 2029. These roles will give students hands-on experience at the frontier of AI and support pathways to build ambitious careers in Canada.
- Build a national network of university and research partnerships, starting with recently announced collaborations with the University of Toronto and the University of Waterloo, and building on existing relationships with Amii, Vector and Mila to connect Canadian research and talent with real-world AI adoption across the economy.
Cohere is already advancing this vision through significant investments and partnerships across Canada, including:
- A landmark
[C$309 million GPU cloud partnership with Bell AI Fabric](https://www.bce.ca/news-and-media/newsroom?article=%2FBell-AI-Fabric-Cohere-Hypertec-and-BUZZ-HPC-announce-landmark-deal-to-advance-sovereign-AI-in-Canada), enabling Cohere models to run on sovereign Canadian infrastructure. - A
[multi-year initiative with the University of Toronto](https://www.utoronto.ca/news/u-t-partnership-cohere-sets-stage-responsible-ai-adoption-scale)to advance the responsible adoption of AI at scale. - A
[collaboration with the University of Waterloo’s Future of Work Institute](https://uwaterloo.ca/news/partnering-lead-ai-transformation-across-organizations)to equip students for AI leadership through specialized certificates and co-op programs.
Founded in Toronto, Cohere is building a global AI company from Canada while helping translate the country’s long-standing strengths in research and talent into highly skilled jobs, stronger domestic capabilities and long-term economic growth. The goal is not only for Canada to help develop the technologies shaping the global economy, but to build, deploy and capture more of their value here at home.

# Fair use benefits everyone

Authors, journalists, creators, academics, accessibility advocates, legal experts, librarians, economists and business leaders are voicing their support for the longstanding principle of fair use and its application to AI training.

Loading…

Share

For decades, fair use has played a critical role in driving innovation that benefits everyone. It has helped deliver important medical and scientific breakthroughs and new technologies that have made real and positive differences for countless people, including authors and journalists. [The New York Times’ lawsuit](https://openai.com/new-york-times/), meanwhile, asks everyone to ignore a half century of legal history and progress, and toss aside the longstanding principle of fair use in their own narrow pursuit of an undeserved payday.

Experts and leaders across a wide range of fields have recognized that fair use is a win-win that benefits everyone, and have shared their perspectives with the Court in filing briefs in support of fair use.

Below you’ll find excerpts from some of those submissions, in their own words. The full filings are available on the public court docket, and you can read more about fair use and AI [here](https://openai.com/new-york-times/).

- [AI Progress⁠](https://openai.com/index/fair-use-benefits-everyone/#fair-use-ai-progress-heading)
- [American Council of the Blind, Association of Research Libraries, American Library Association, Consumer Technology Association & Business Software Alliance⁠](https://openai.com/index/fair-use-benefits-everyone/#fair-use-acb-cta-bsa-heading)
- [Authors Alliance⁠](https://openai.com/index/fair-use-benefits-everyone/#fair-use-authors-alliance-heading)
- [Engine and Developers Alliance⁠](https://openai.com/index/fair-use-benefits-everyone/#fair-use-engine-heading)
- [Foundation for American Innovation⁠](https://openai.com/index/fair-use-benefits-everyone/#fair-use-foundation-for-american-innovation-heading)
- [Joshua S. Gans⁠](https://openai.com/index/fair-use-benefits-everyone/#fair-use-joshua-s-gans-heading)
- [Kevin Kelly⁠](https://openai.com/index/fair-use-benefits-everyone/#fair-use-kevin-kelly-and-aaron-black-heading)
- [Matthew Sag⁠](https://openai.com/index/fair-use-benefits-everyone/#fair-use-matthew-sag-heading)
- [Michael Wall and Sarah Rose Siskind⁠](https://openai.com/index/fair-use-benefits-everyone/#fair-use-michael-wall-and-sarah-rose-siskind-heading)
- [Public Knowledge⁠](https://openai.com/index/fair-use-benefits-everyone/#fair-use-public-knowledge-heading)
- [Ron Suskind and Brian L. Frye⁠](https://openai.com/index/fair-use-benefits-everyone/#fair-use-ron-suskind-and-brian-frye-heading)
- [United States Government⁠](https://openai.com/index/fair-use-benefits-everyone/#fair-use-united-states-government-heading)

##

#### AI Progress

The Court should reject Plaintiffs’ attempt to extend copyright beyond its established limits. AI training uses copyrighted works for a fundamentally different purpose, does not provide the public with substitute access to those works, and does not cause the market harm cognizable under the Copyright Act. Instead, it enables a broad array of transformative technologies that are already delivering public benefits. Copyright exists to promote creativity and progress, not to suppress lawful innovation or protect authors from competition. Settled fair use principles therefore compel the conclusion that generative AI training is fair use.

[Link to this section](#fair-use-ai-progress-heading)

##

#### American Council of the Blind, Association of Research Libraries, American Library Association, Consumer Technology Association & Business Software Alliance

This case concerns more than companies that develop large language models (LLMs). It affects medical researchers and patients, educators serving students with different learning needs, people with disabilities seeking greater independence, farmers applying agricultural knowledge, independent creators developing new forms of expression, and industry sectors from software to the law. These communities share an interest in the ability to study and learn from broad and diverse sources of knowledge, and in access to the tools that make that learning useful. Many depend on systems developed by others, including open source AI systems, rather than training models themselves. Fair use supports their ability to learn, discover, communicate, and create. Restrictions on fair use training would affect both the institutions building AI and the people using it.

[Link to this section](#fair-use-acb-cta-bsa-heading)

##

#### Authors Alliance

The market dilution theory asks copyright law to protect rightsholders against an economic phenomenon that it has never restricted before. New works can reduce the sales, visibility, or value of older works without copying their protected expression. The Copyright Act deliberately leaves that competition outside the copyright owner’s control. Amicus therefore respectfully asks the Court to hold that “market dilution,” i.e., aggregate competitive pressure from noninfringing outputs, including those that occupy the same subject matter or genre, that share unprotected characteristics, or compete for the same audience, is not cognizable market harm under 17 U.S.C. § 107(4). Rejecting the theory would preserve the distinction the Second Circuit has always maintained: copyright protects authors against substitution for their protected expression, not against the success of new expression that merely competes with it.

[Link to this section](#fair-use-authors-alliance-heading)

##

#### Engine and Developers Alliance

Startups’ use of foundation models demonstrates that using copyrighted works to train an AI model is a fair use, not copyright infringement. The purpose of training a foundation model is not to reproduce the works it learns; it is to build a general-purpose tool that others can adapt to new ends. The ends startups have chosen bear no resemblance to the purposes of the works in any training dataset.

[Link to this section](#fair-use-engine-heading)

##

#### Foundation for American Innovation

To the extent AI training enables the creation of new knowledge, expression, software, and other capabilities, those benefits bear on factor four’s assessment of the use’s market effects. That reasoning supports a novel application here: considering the national-security value of capabilities that enable new analysis, software, and other productive work.

[Link to this section](#fair-use-foundation-for-american-innovation-heading)

##

#### Joshua S. Gans

*Professor of Strategic Management*

Copyright supports not only the incentive to create content but also the incentive to build tools that learn from that content, and a rule that treated every displaced sale as actionable can weaken the second without reliably protecting the first.

[Link to this section](#fair-use-joshua-s-gans-heading)

##

#### Kevin Kelly

*Author*

AI is a transformative technology that accelerates the creation of novel works across countless disciplines in the arts and sciences. Mr. Kelly has experience in how AI advances the field of literature. In his view, each AI model can be understood as an entirely new medium that offers authors the capability to create new texts and ideas, and to reason. A ruling for Plaintiffs on fair use would therefore grant Plaintiffs far more than the limited monopoly to their original expression Congress intended to confer. It would hinder the development of technologies capable of disseminating previously unimaginable quantities of information. It would also impede new modes of thought and the creation of new original works in both the arts and sciences. Amicus files this brief in support of Defendants’ argument that the use of copyrighted works to train large language models is a fair use under 17 U.S.C. § 107. Based on his lifelong pursuits of writing, the protections afforded to copyright owners are important to Mr. Kelly. Equally vital is preserving room for permissible uses of copyrighted material and the growth of transformative technologies. Otherwise, copyright will stifle the very creativity, innovation, and spread of knowledge it exists to encourage. The fair-use doctrine is critical to ensuring that balance.

[Link to this section](#fair-use-kevin-kelly-and-aaron-black-heading)

##

#### Matthew Sag

*Professor of Law*

On the record in this case, the defendants’ use of plaintiffs’ works for AI training is highly transformative and strongly favors a finding of fair use because under realistic conditions the outputs of defendants’ models are in no relevant way similar to the invisible intermediate copies made during the training process.

[Link to this section](#fair-use-matthew-sag-heading)

##

#### Michael Wall and Sarah Rose Siskind

*Musician and composer / comedian and writer*

This brief offers a window into what that sentence means in practice through the work of two independent creators who rely on copyright protection *and* AI tools to sustain their livelihoods. *Amici* Sarah Rose Siskind and Michael Wall are artists who create and license original works. But they use AI to handle work surrounding the creative process and to grow their businesses in a market teeming with better-resourced competitors. For *Amici*, AI does not displace creativity or shortcut their creative processes. AI helps them create more, and to extend their work into new modes of expression. *Amici*’s experience underscores the United States’ view that AI tools “can and should help level the playing field between mainstream and independent publishers.” Siskind uses AI in every aspect of her business, from day-to-day administrative tasks to developing ideas and bringing in new clients. With AI, her noncreative work is faster and less expensive, and her creative work is better. As she tells it, “I don’t think I could run my business without AI at this point.” Similarly, AI helps Wall manage the operational demands of his music business, reduce costs, and devote more of his time to composing music. Like Siskind, he doubts that his business could survive in its current form without AI.

[Link to this section](#fair-use-michael-wall-and-sarah-rose-siskind-heading)

##

#### Public Knowledge

Fair use has protected tools that help people navigate the vast collections of information the digital world has brought us, including image search and full-text book search. See Perfect 10, Inc. v. Amazon.com, Inc., 508 F.3d 1146, 1164–68 (9th Cir. 2007); Authors Guild v. Google, Inc., 804 F.3d 202, 216–17, 225 (2d Cir. 2015) (“Google Books”). It has also protected libraries’ provision of accessible digital books to readers with print disabilities. See Authors Guild, Inc. v. HathiTrust, 755 F.3d 87, 101–03 (2d Cir. 2014). And it has protected free online publication of technical standards incorporated into law, recognizing the “substantial public benefits of free and easy access to the law.” Am. Soc’y for Testing & Materials v. Public.Resource.Org, Inc., 82 F.4th 1262, 1271–72 (D.C. Cir. 2023). Fair use will be equally beneficial in ensuring that AI’s benefits accrue to the public at large, instead of being controlled by a privileged few.

[Link to this section](#fair-use-public-knowledge-headi

title: Catch the Bugs Your Code Review Misses - Killian Carlsen-Phelan & Taylor Luttrell-Williams, Sonar
body:
In this hands-on session, Killian Carlsen-Phelan and Taylor Luttrell-Williams of Sonar set up Gitar, a code change verification agent, on a sample ticketing app and run three pull requests through it. Gitar catches a bug that isn't in the diff at all (a buyer can refund a ticket after giving it to a friend), enforces a business rule from a project config (show customers the all-in price), then diagnoses a failing CI test and keeps pushing fixes until the PR passes and auto-merges. They close with functional validation against Jira tickets, learned conventions, and cross-repo and cross-PR analysis.

title: Custom Voices With Qwen3-TTS
body:
written on October 29, 2026
With my kids I’m currently building a little [dungeron
crawler](https://github.com/mitsuhiko/dungeon-crawler) and we’re trying to
[learn a bit about game
development](https://mitsuhiko.github.io/dungeon-crawler/learn/) along the way.
However given that we live in the modern times of increasing capabilities we
wanted to get a narrator and voice over.
But we also wanted it to not sound like everyone’s standard AI voices so I
looked into what options there are on the table. After some investigation I
narrowed down to using [Qwen3-TTS](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3-TTS) which
uses voice embeddings for custom voices.
With a bit of creativity you can also do more with those custom voices than appears initially. In case this is of interest to you, this post just covers what we learned and with some examples. You can probably point your agent to it and it can do something with it.
Qwen3 is not the only TTS model in town, and it wans’t even my first choice. We
initially used [Kokoro](https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M). However
Qwen3 supports voice cloning and we wanted to have it feel a bit more unique.
In practice it’s a bit tricker though. Qwen3 ships three kinds of models:
1.7B-Base
(and 0.6B): clones a voice from a few seconds of reference audio1.7B-CustomVoice
: comes with nine built-in speakers and instructions1.7B-VoiceDesign
: invents a voice from a text description
The base model clones either in context or from the speaker embedding alone but there is no documented way to clone a voice and direct it with instructions. That means unlike the custom voice and voice design models you cannot say “speak sad” or “whisper” with a cloned base model.
At present the official options for a custom voice are fine-tuning Base on a single speaker or to make a clip with VoiceDesign and clone it with Base. That is not all that bad, but it means instructions are gone.
For this blog post I took 28 seconds of me from my talk at [PyAI
Conf](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8RHYyRUxVrA), cut between two pauses so
that it starts and ends on a full sentence, and transcribed it with Whisper.
The transcript is really only needed for baking but to compare against an
already existing voice it’s useful to have it say the same thing as the original
recording.
Note that a conference talk recording is not ideal but it works anyways. Which is also a good reminder that you really don’t need a particularly clean recording (or a very long one) to get a halfway convincing version of a person. Particularly when then presented to you on a low quality phone call, it won’t be very hard to trick your grandmother.
The first thing you can do is to blend that recording with another voice. For
instance you can use VoiceDesign to make up a voice from a description. For this blog
post the designed voice was created like this, with Qwen’s own Python package
[ qwen-tts](https://pypi.org/project/qwen-tts/) (
pip install qwen-tts
, I used
0.1.1), which the rest of the code in this post uses too:import torch
from qwen_tts import Qwen3TTSModel
kw = dict(device_map="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16, attn_implementation="sdpa")
design = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-VoiceDesign", **kw)
wavs, sr = design.generate_voice_design(
text=open("voices/transcript.txt").read(), language="English",
instruct="A man in his forties with a warm, natural, medium-low voice, speaking "
"clearly and calmly at an easy conversational pace, like someone reading "
"aloud to a friend.",
)
You can see how the two different voices behave, particularly when blended together:
Loading the voice samples…
What Base takes from a recording when cloning from the embedding alone is a speaker embedding which is basically 2048 numbers out of a speaker encoder that was trained. The same voice gets similar numbers and different voices get different ones. Which btw, is also a convenient way to do speaker detection from recordings if you want to! It’s not perfect, but it’s quite helpful for a single audio track recording to tell two speakers apart if you do some basic slicing and dicing (more on that below).
Because it is just a vector, you can do arithmetic on it. For instance a weighted average of two embeddings is a spaker that is somewhere between two voices:
base = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base", **kw)
def fingerprint(path):
prompt = base.create_voice_clone_prompt(ref_audio=path, x_vector_only_mode=True)
return prompt[0].ref_spk_embedding
def blend(a, b, t):
a, b = a.float(), b.float()
mixed = (1 - t) * a + t * b
return (mixed / mixed.norm() * ((1 - t) * a.norm() + t * b.norm())).to(torch.bfloat16)
armin, designed = fingerprint("voices/armin.flac"), fingerprint("voices/designed.flac")
Here is the same sentence in eleven blends:
Loading the voice samples…
Note that it stops sounding like me quite quickly, but it retains some of my features. And it for sure ends up with creating a unique voice regardless. I found some better successes when ensuing that the two voices have similar spectograms (eg: similar “recording setups”). In this recording you can hear that one voice picked up by the lapel mic was a bit hollow compared to the designed voice.
If you like a a voice that comes out, you can bake it back into a new recording that you can then use as reference:
import soundfile as sf
mixed = blend(armin, designed, 0.5)
audio, rate = say(open("voices/transcript.txt").read(), mixed) # say() is shown further down
sf.write("voices/final.flac", audio, rate)
final = fingerprint("voices/final.flac")
The baked voice does not come back exactly as the blend but it makes handling it easier if you want to. It’s just one voice reference file.
So on the question of using those embeddings for speaker recognition: how good
does that work? I took an episode of [State of Agentic
Coding](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qCpY4K9jtOg), the podcast Ben and I
record, cut it into 2-second windows one second apart and compared each with an
embedding of me form the conference.
Somewhat surprising, but maybe not too surprising using my conference recording clip as the reference this does not work at all with Qwen3. If instead I take the 20 seconds where I introduce myself at the start of the episode as the reference, it gets 98% of the rest right.
On the other hand using a model that was trained for speaker verification
instead does manage to pick me up from the conference recording clip. For
instance [ECAPA](https://huggingface.co/speechbrain/spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb),
finds me from the conference clip in 97% of the windows.
Here are 20 minutes of that podcast, classified by speaker with the different approaches:
Loading the voice samples…
But the embeddings a very useful for the voice cloning! But how to give them
instructions? Base and CustomVoice manipulate the speaker the same way: one
vector inserted into the talker’s input sequence. In CustomVoice that vector is
a row of the embedding table. In Base it is the x-vector from the speaker
encoder, which only Base has. The generation code takes either
(voice_clone_prompt
is a regular argument of generate
), and the transformer
weights of the two models are nearly identical. So take the embedding with
Base, then hand it to CustomVoice instead of one of its speakers:
cv = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-CustomVoice", **kw)
def say(text, xvec, instruct=None, language="English"):
ids = cv._tokenize_texts([cv._build_assistant_text(text)])
told = [cv._tokenize_texts([cv._build_instruct_text(instruct)])[0]
if instruct else None]
voice = {"ref_code": [None], "ref_spk_embedding": [xvec],
"x_vector_only_mode": [True], "icl_mode": [False]}
codes, _ = cv.model.generate(
input_ids=ids, instruct_ids=told, voice_clone_prompt=voice,
languages=[language], non_streaming_mode=True,
**cv._merge_generate_kwargs(temperature=0.7, subtalker_temperature=0.7),
)
wavs, rate = cv.model.speech_tokenizer.decode([{"audio_codes": codes[0]}])
return wavs[0], rate
wav, rate = say("I really thought this would work.", armin,
"Speak in a sad, sorrowful tone, voice low and heavy, on the verge of tears.")
Pick a speaker for the slot, a model and an instruction:
Loading the voice samples…
Instructions work on cloned voices, but less reliably than on the built-in speakers, and it depends on the emotion, but honestly, it came out better than I anticipated. Definitely good enough to have some true custom voices for a voice over that don’t necessarily sound like something, someone else has in their game.
If a voice is a point in a 2048-dimensional space and blending works we can maybe do some other funny math on it. The obvious one is to try to see if some math can be used to manipulate gender.
To find it I had VoiceDesign create 14 different voices for men and women each. When you then take the average woman minus the average man you can then move any voice along that direction:
women = torch.stack([fingerprint(f"design/f{i}.wav") for i in range(14)]).float()
men = torch.stack([fingerprint(f"design/m{i}.wav") for i in range(14)]).float()
middle = (women.mean(0) + men.mean(0)) / 2
axis = women.mean(0) - men.mean(0)
axis = axis / axis.norm()
def move(xvec, t):
"""Put the voice at position t along the gender axis, keep the rest."""
x = xvec.float()
return (x + (t - (x - middle) @ axis) * axis).to(torch.bfloat16)
Here is the result for my clone:
Loading the voice samples…
Anyways, that’s that. If you want to play around with Qwen3 TTS I hope this was of some help, and maybe you got some ideas of what to do with the voice embeddings. Use it for good, not evil.

title: Why Humans Can't Keep Up With AI-Written Code - Tariq Shaukat, Sonar
body:
Agents have made code cheap: one study saw lines of code up 2,450% but releases up only 30%. Sonar CEO Tariq Shaukat draws on the factory revolution that Toyota and Lexus started to explain how to build agentic software factories you can trust. He breaks down five hard problems: human review that doesn't scale (people agree with AI that's wrong 4 out of 5 times), agents struggling with large codebases, errors compounding over long tasks, unreliable LLM judges, and near-zero time to exploit. Then he lays out Sonar's code confidence formula: intent, guide rails, verification and evidence.
