title: GitHub Universe 2026: Highlights from the developer’s developer conference
body:
Final URL: https://commandline.microsoft.com/github-universe-2026-recap/

Published Time: 2026-10-29T18:34:49+00:00

Markdown Content:
The hero at the heart of the two-day event was the developer community.

By [Command Line team](https://commandline.microsoft.com/author/command-line-team)Command Line editorial team

2026.10.29

From the menus at Mo’s Diner to the badge hack station to major product ships, GitHub Universe 2026 delivered. The [annual Octoverse report](https://github.blog/news-insights/octoverse/octoverse-commits-pushes-reach-new-highs-in-2026-as-developers-build-with-agents/?utm_source=blog-cta-octoverse&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=universe-2026) came out, showing just how much the platform has scaled over the past year in the face of agentic software delivery. And the hero at the heart of the two-day event was the developer community.

![Image 1: Attendees watch the keynote speech during GitHub Universe 2026, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, at Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture, in San Francisco, Calif. (Photo: Cameron Karsten)](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/GHUNI26-2_CK_241-1024x683.jpg)

Attendees watch the keynote speech during GitHub Universe 2026, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, at Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture, in San Francisco, Calif. (Photo: Cameron Karsten)

Yesterday’s opening keynote was packed with demos and announcements. But [Copilot Fusion](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-28-route-and-orchestrate-models-with-github-copilot-fusion/?utm_source=blog-cta-fusion&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=universe-2026) was clearly the belle of the ball.

![Image 2: Jay Parikh, Executive Vice President of CoreAI, Microsoft, and GitHub Senior Director of Developer Advocacy Cassidy Williams onstage during GitHub Universe 2026, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, at Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture, in San Francisco, Calif. (Photo: Cameron Karsten)](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/GHUNI26-2_CK_327-1024x683.jpg)

Jay Parikh, Executive Vice President of CoreAI, Microsoft, and GitHub Senior Director of Developer Advocacy Cassidy Williams onstage during GitHub Universe 2026, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, at Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture, in San Francisco, Calif. (Photo: Cameron Karsten)

As a frame for the ships (of which there were many), EVP of CoreAI [Jay Parikh](https://x.com/jayparikh) laid out [our vision for GitHub](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/github-universe-2026-evolving-every-layer-of-the-stack/?utm_source=blog-cta-jay-hero-blog&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=universe-2026) as the most comprehensive, end-to-end software delivery system in the world.

![Image 3: West Bos, Kyle Daigle, and Scott Tolinski.](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_7885-1024x768.jpg)

West Bos, Kyle Daigle, and Scott Tolinski.

GitHub COO and Microsoft CMO of Developer [Kyle Daigle](https://x.com/kdaigle) joined [Syntax](https://syntax.fm/) co-hosts [Wes Bos](https://x.com/wesbos) and [Scott Tolinski](https://x.com/stolinski) for a chat.

![Image 4](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Image-6-1024x768.jpeg)

Tanguy Fournier Le Roy and Jay Parikh.

And great conversations were had, on and off the show floor.

![Image 5: Seth Juarez, Damian Brady, Cassidy Williams, Christopher Harrison, Jay Parikh, Burke Holland, April Leonard, Jessica Deen, and Kyle Daigle.](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Command-Line-image-options.002-1024x576.jpeg)

Seth Juarez, Damian Brady, Cassidy Williams, Christopher Harrison, Jay Parikh, Burke Holland, April Leonard, Jessica Deen, and Kyle Daigle.

## Session spotlights

### Agentic Workflows: Automation at scale

Automation is how we buy time for craft, enforce correctness in situations that require judgment, and improve our software at business scale. This session taught attendees how to start automating, including setting up a software factory with governance, monitoring, and security.

### Agentic engineering past the pilot: An enterprise playbook

The industry has moved from code completion to chat to agents, and now into AI-native software delivery. But what does that actually look like inside an enterprise, where governance, developer experience, and adoption at scale all have to coexist? Through live demos spanning IDE, CLI, and multi-session orchestration, Nick Liffen and Philip Holleran shared the system-level patterns that move agentic engineering from experiment to operating model.

### Securing MCP: Real exploits, what actually mitigates them, and what doesn’t

This interactive session broke down MCP security as it really stands today: what the threats are, which layer each one operates on, and how to host MCP servers in production without opening yourself up to unnecessary risk.

### Shut the context window! You’re letting the tokens out

Dylan McCarthy showed how Copilot constructs context in practice, demonstrated the developer habits that quietly inflate token usage, and walked through focused workflows that produce better results with less overhead.

### Your benchmark is lying: What evals actually look like

Julia Kasper and Walker Chabbott went behind the scenes on how GitHub Copilot evaluates models in production: what they measure, what they’ve stopped measuring, the signals that correlate with real developer outcomes, and why your favorite leaderboard may be leading your team astray.

… and that’s just a taste of the 150+ sessions at this year’s Universe. Check out the full list [here](https://reg.githubuniverse.com/flow/github/universe26/attendee-portal/page/sessioncatalog?tab.allsessions=1783449560443001ldrh).

## Watch the full keynote …

## … or the abridged version: 42 minutes of announcements in < 8

## Before you go

If you take away [one thing](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/github-universe-2026-evolving-every-layer-of-the-stack/?utm_source=blog-cta-jay-hero-blog&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=universe-2026) from Universe 2026, make it this:

The [SDLC is no longer a linear path](https://commandline.microsoft.com/new-agentic-software-delivery-primitives/) from planning to coding to testing to deployment. The new [agentic software delivery system](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/github-universe-2026-evolving-every-layer-of-the-stack/?utm_source=blog-cta-jay-hero-blog&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=universe-2026) solves for three things: velocity, intelligence, and quality. GitHub is a platform built for you and your agents. We’ll continue releasing new products and features that push the work forward. And our ongoing infrastructure work will ensure the platform scales to meet increased demand.

AI is changing what’s possible. But it’s in the hands of developers where that possibility converts to real-world impact.

title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
body:
29th October 2026 - Link Blog
[How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World](https://twitter.com/jsnnsa/status/2115623382721126826). Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building [Spawn](https://spawn.co) is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models.
Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world.
I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle.
By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens").
Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request.
Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat.
This is [continuous deployment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_deployment) turned up to 11:
A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...]
We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work.
My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well.
Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working:
Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off.
These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm [excited about game development](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/28/vibe-game-development/) as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do.

title: An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI
body:
As our models get smarter and take more consequential actions in the world, it becomes increasingly important that they go beyond just interpreting the specific instructions they receive. Models also need to understand human intentions and values, so they can exercise good judgment in situations their instructions don’t explicitly address while remaining faithful to human intent and oversight.

Today we’re updating the Model Spec, our public description of how we want our models to behave. The update reorganizes its guidance around five underlying values: **faithfulness to human intent**, **harm minimization**, **honesty and transparency**, **human agency**, and **care**. This reflects an aim of our work on value alignment: for models to understand and apply human values in unfamiliar situations, while remaining faithful to human intent. Alongside clearer explanations of existing principles, the revision adds guidance on context, oversight, and agency, adjusts some behavioral defaults, and retires much of the detailed style guidance.

The five values above articulate broad commitments already reflected across the Model Spec: serving human purposes, being truthful, minimizing harm, respecting people’s freedom to form their own views, and taking their circumstances seriously. Bringing these commitments together helps explain why the Spec asks models to behave as it does, and helps us develop clearer guidance where those commitments were less fully expressed. This update is another step in ourwork to refine the Spec through research, experience deploying models,public feedback on the Spec and model behavior, and discussions with users and outside experts.

We want AI to benefit a world of people with different needs, values, and hopes for the future.

**Faithfulness to human intent** is the foundation of this approach: understanding and helping people pursue what matters to them. OpenAI writes the Spec, sets boundaries, and trains models to respect them; developers direct applications within those boundaries; and users direct the model’s work subject to those constraints. Our models shouldexpand people’s ability to shape their own lives by helping them understand the world, discover possibilities, and pursue the goals they choose, while taking seriously how that assistance affects others. Faithfulness to human intent and the remaining four values organize the Spec and guide how our models should navigate some of the most important trade-offs they face. They are not intended to capture the full range of human values our models should respect and help people pursue.

Faithfulness means going beyond following instructions literally to deeply understanding what OpenAI, developers, and users intend and value, and acting wisely when that understanding is incomplete. It also means recognizing that people’s beliefs and values can change, and helping them reflect and grow in ways they would endorse without quietly steering them or overriding their choices. For example, when helping someone compare job offers, the model might draw on priorities they have shared before—such as predictable hours—while making those assumptions visible and easy to correct.

Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. This requires considering not only someone’s immediate intentions, but also their longer-term interests and the effects on others. The other four values make these considerations explicit:

- **Minimizing harm** means respecting firm safety boundaries and accounting for the foreseeable consequences of the model’s actions.
- **Honesty and transparency** mean being truthful about what the model knows, does, and is uncertain about so people can understand and evaluate its reasoning and work.
- **Facilitating human agency** means strengthening people’s ability to understand, choose, and act for themselves.
- **Care** means attending to the circumstances of those affected, following relevant social and professional norms, and doing work people can rely on.
The Spec turns these values into practical guidance, with firm boundaries where needed to protect people and society, and otherwise mostly takes the form of defaults that users and developers can override.

Alongside this Model Spec update, we’ve been exploring new training methods to help our models learn these core values and better understand and follow the Spec’s specific behavioral principles. The aim is to build an understanding of why those principles matter and how to apply them in new situations: to do the *right things**for the right reasons*. We want that understanding to support sound judgment in consequential decisions and care in everyday decisions that can add up to lasting benefits for people and society. We’ll share results and lessons from this training work in future updates.

This reorganization also helped us identify where additional guidance was needed, develop new principles to address it, and revise or retire existing guidance as needed.

The new section on faithfulness to human intent starts from the idea that what people value is primary, and instructions are ordinarily the clearest and most important signals of those values. This approach borrows from the assistance-games framing of alignment (seeearly work and alater overview). The section incorporates an updated chain of command, which explains which instructions apply and how conflicts are resolved. A new subsection, consider context carefully, explains how conversations, memories, and other contextual evidence should inform the model’s understanding of people’s intentions and preferences.

We’ve also added defaults onsupporting human agency andfollowing relevant social norms, and expanded existing guidance oncontrolling and communicating side effects. These principles capture additional, often subtle but important ways the remaining values should surface in model behavior: considering the effects of the work on others, strengthening users’ capabilities, and producing work people can rely on, while respecting the user’s goals and instructions.

At the same time, we’re retiring most of the Spec’s detailed style guidance. Style should adapt to what people prefer—in aggregate, within languages and cultures, and for each person—with user feedback and context providing evidence about those preferences. The Spec retains stronger defaults, such as approaching questions objectively. Users and developers can explicitly ask the model to take a particular perspective, but the model should not infer that preference merely from what it thinks they want to hear.

Finally, reflecting the increasing breadth of our models’ use cases and deployment settings, we now refer to the model as “GPT” rather than “the assistant” in the Spec.

This update is a first step in making the values and reasoning behind the Spec more explicit as models become more capable. The Model Spec describes the behavior we are working toward; our models do not yet fully reflect it. We will keep improving both the Spec and the models as we learn from research, real-world use, and feedback.

We want to hear which parts of the Spec you find compelling, where you disagree with the balance it strikes, and what it overlooks or leaves unclear. Feedback on the values, trade-offs, and specific language can help us improve it. We invite you to read the updated Model Spec and share your perspective.

- Alignment
## Author

OpenAI$@f4

An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI | OpenAI

Today we’re updating the Model Spec, our public description of how we want our models to behave. The update reorganizes its guidance around five underlying values: **faithfulness to human intent**, **harm minimization**, **honesty and transparency**, **human agency**, and **care**. This reflects an aim of our work on value alignment: for models to understand and apply human values in unfamiliar situations, while remaining faithful to human intent. Alongside clearer explanations of existing principles, the revision adds guidance on context, oversight, and agency, adjusts some behavioral defaults, and retires much of the detailed style guidance.

The five values above articulate broad commitments already reflected across the Model Spec: serving human purposes, being truthful, minimizing harm, respecting people’s freedom to form their own views, and taking their circumstances seriously. Bringing these commitments together helps explain why the Spec asks models to behave as it does, and helps us develop clearer guidance where those commitments were less fully expressed. This update is another step in ourwork to refine the Spec through research, experience deploying models,public feedback on the Spec and model behavior, and discussions with users and outside experts.

We want AI to benefit a world of people with different needs, values, and hopes for the future.

**Faithfulness to human intent** is the foundation of this approach: understanding and helping people pursue what matters to them. OpenAI writes the Spec, sets boundaries, and trains models to respect them; developers direct applications within those boundaries; and users direct the model’s work subject to those constraints. Our models shouldexpand people’s ability to shape their own lives by helping them understand the world, discover possibilities, and pursue the goals they choose, while taking seriously how that assistance affects others. Faithfulness to human intent and the remaining four values organize the Spec and guide how our models should navigate some of the most important trade-offs they face. They are not intended to capture the full range of human values our models should respect and help people pursue.

Faithfulness means going beyond following instructions literally to deeply understanding what OpenAI, developers, and users intend and value, and acting wisely when that understanding is incomplete. It also means recognizing that people’s beliefs and values can change, and helping them reflect and grow in ways they would endorse without quietly steering them or overriding their choices. For example, when helping someone compare job offers, the model might draw on priorities they have shared before—such as predictable hours—while making those assumptions visible and easy to correct.

Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. This requires considering not only someone’s immediate intentions, but also their longer-term interests and the effects on others. The other four values make these considerations explicit:

- **Minimizing harm** means respecting firm safety boundaries and accounting for the foreseeable consequences of the model’s actions.
- **Honesty and transparency** mean being truthful about what the model knows, does, and is uncertain about so people can understand and evaluate its reasoning and work.
- **Facilitating human agency** means strengthening people’s ability to understand, choose, and act for themselves.
- **Care** means attending to the circumstances of those affected, following relevant social and professional norms, and doing work people can rely on.

The Spec turns these values into practical guidance, with firm boundaries where needed to protect people and society, and otherwise mostly takes the form of defaults that users and developers can override.

Alongside this Model Spec update, we’ve been exploring new training methods to help our models learn these core values and better understand and follow the Spec’s specific behavioral principles. The aim is to build an understanding of why those principles matter and how to apply them in new situations: to do the *right things**for the right reasons*. We want that understanding to support sound judgment in consequential decisions and care in everyday decisions that can add up to lasting benefits for people and society. We’ll share results and lessons from this training work in future updates.

title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
body:
Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with[ NVIDIA Omniverse libraries](https://developer.nvidia.com/omniverse) to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs.
Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities.
Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem.
Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans [🔗](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#building-model)
Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation.
David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes.
Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. [OpenUSD](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/openusd/) stores the models, while [Omniverse’s ovrtx library](https://github.com/NVIDIA-Omniverse/ovrtx) renders results for inspection.
Explore [NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills](https://developer.nvidia.com/omniverse) to help agents build with Omniverse libraries.
Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin [🔗](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#gas-turbine)
Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator.
The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error.
The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing.
Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ([ovstage](https://github.com/nvidia-omniverse/ovstage)), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments.
Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets [🔗](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#simready-assets)
With SimReady Central Library, [announced at GTC Berlin](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/simready-central-assets-robotics-ai-factories), developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows.
Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments.
For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment.
[Find assets in SimReady Central Library](https://huggingface.co/spaces/nvidia/simready-central), and [learn how to contribute](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/simready-central-assets-robotics-ai-factories#prepare-and-contribute-content).
Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale [🔗](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#warehouse)
A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene.
When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with [NVIDIA Omniverse libraries](https://developer.nvidia.com/omniverse?size=n_12_n&sort-field=featured&sort-direction=desc) to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns.
Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling.
With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements.
Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve.
Start building with [NVIDIA Omniverse libraries](https://developer.nvidia.com/omniverse?size=n_12_n&sort-field=featured&sort-direction=desc).
Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing [🔗](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#cable-routing)
In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit.
Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using [NVIDIA Isaac Lab](https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/lab), [Newton](https://developer.nvidia.com/newton-physics) physics and Omniverse rendering with a[ Robotiq gripper](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K2ui16FdLZw) handling the cable.
Astra also developed a[ reinforcement learning](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/reinforcement-learning/) system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments.
The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors.
Get started with robot learning in [NVIDIA Isaac Lab](https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/lab).
Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset [🔗](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#cad)
Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task.
Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot.
Follow the five-step [SimReady tutorial](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/5-steps-to-create-simready-assets-for-robotics-with-frontier-ai-models/).
Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment [🔗](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#humanoid-simulator)
Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view.
Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a [SimReady](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/simready/) warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views.
DeLise directed Astra to connect[ NVIDIA Omniverse libraries](https://developer.nvidia.com/omniverse) for physics ([ovphysx](https://github.com/NVIDIA-Omniverse/PhysX/blob/main/ovphysx/README.md)), scene updates ([ovstage](https://github.com/nvidia-omniverse/ovstage)), rendering ([ovrtx](https://github.com/NVIDIA-Omniverse/ovrtx)) and the user interface ([ovui](https://github.com/NVIDIA-omniverse/ovui)). He also used Astra with SimReady ([simready-foundation](https://github.com/nvidia/simready-foundation)) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together.
Learn how to [prepare and validate SimReady robot assets](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/5-steps-to-create-simready-assets-for-robotics-with-frontier-ai-models/) with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow [🔗](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#autonomous-driving-testing)
Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street.
Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, [Omniverse RTX sensor simulation](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/integrate-nvidia-omniverse-rtx-sensor-simulation-into-existing-apps/) and [Alpamayo driving](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/solutions/autonomous-vehicles/alpamayo/) in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions.
Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins [🔗](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/developers-simulation-frontier-ai-agents/#sensor-differences)
Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene.
To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare [ovrtx](https://github.com/NVIDIA-Omniverse/ovrtx) camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones.
Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addres

title: Science Behind the Open Cyber Frontier with Mistral Large 4
body:
The Science Behind the Open Cyber Frontier with Mistral Large 4

Ben Burtenshaw (Hugging Face) talks with Sagar Vaze and Pierre Stock from Mistral about Mistral Large 4, an open-weight model that is great for frontier cybersecurity work, amongst other tasks. They cover how the model was trained, how it performs on security tasks, and why open weights matter for the people defending real software.

Mistral Large 4 is a 1 trillion parameter, natively multimodal mixture-of-experts model with 52 billion active parameters. It ranks among the top five models on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index and solves 93% of the Cybench challenges. Because the weights are open, security teams can run it on their own infrastructure under their own policies, without provider-level refusals blocking legitimate vulnerability research or incident response.

title: AI is overwhelming and I’m doing it wrong
body:
Let’s talk about this…
Where do I even start? It seems like a lot of people are feeling this too. The constant barrage of new products, models, capabilities, threats, whatever is one thing. But seeing people with 20 personal agents for managing their social content or just life.
What are we doing here?!
When I first started the newsletter it was to keep up with everything that was going on. It was 5 days a week. It was so noisy I decided to cut it down (along with our revenue) to just two days. I try and cut through the noise with the links here but the noise is still there, it may be louder.
I read two excellent posts yesterday. Here’s a snippet from each
You’re doing your best to keep up. You’re 9-9-6’ing, sometimes 0-0-7’ing. You didn’t actually rest during rest week, did you? What are your agents up to? Hopefully getting a lot done while you’re reading this. Have you tried the latest personal assistant? Optimized your workflows to accommodate the strengths of the latest model? Have you gone viral on X lately? Have you been angel investing? Have you locked in your Bay Area mortgage? If not, you know you’re fucked, right? You’re enslaved to your keyboard, timeline, and Slack. You’re tired, but your ambition is also Icarus-ing. Your FOMO is spiking. Your capacity is redlining. Is your moral compass spinning?
[The Sane Asylum](https://colossus.com/article/sane-asylum-turbopuffer/) by Colossus
To be blunt, instead of having to sit down and “do” a thing, you can, while hungover in sweats on your couch, grab your laptop, fire up Claude Code, Codex, GrokBot, whatever, and just tell it to start building whatever epiphany is top of mind at the moment. Oh, and you don’t even have to type it anymore. Hands too sore? You can double tap the function key and your space bar, have Wispr Flow start transcribing, and say, “I want you to build a tool that each day goes through all newsletters I’m subscribed to, find the key highlights from each that I should care about, and send me a summary. Make this a daily routine, thanks.” Then go back to vegging out on your couch while your little token muncher cranks away.
[The Difference Between “Can” and “Should”](https://www.youngmoney.co/p/the-difference-between-can-and-should-376) by Jack Raines
I start far more than I finish. I have a course that’s ~70% done, I have a tool for non-techies using personal agents that’s 80% done. I have 2 outstanding funds with one I should finish fundraising for. I want to try a new sponsor model that I should ping companies about.
I should do things because they make business sense. But I only like doing things for the fun of actually doing it. I can only be motivated to do something if it feels like play.
And I think play is missing for a lot of people. We’re pushed by our companies or peers to do more. But more for what reason? It’s busywork. It’s cleaning my desk before starting what would actually be work. AI was meant to handle our work, but when it does it turns out there’s endless work that you can do.
Just one more pull of the slot machine.
You don’t need to try every tool under the sun. You don’t need swarms of agents running and optimising your life. I hate optimising anything.
I recently un-subscribed 60k+ people from this newsletter because they were not opening it. But the numbers are good for sponsors. It’s just not the point of this whole thing. I want to share what I find interesting, what I do for fun. I tinker, I build random shit, I share it. And ultimately I want it to feel like you can do more stuff with AI by seeing what I can do, but not to the extremity of productivity-tokenmaxxers.
The videos I did I found myself trying to pick them apart to optimise them. Am I trying to become a fucking YouTuber? Absolutely not. Don’t like the videos? Guess what? You don’t have to watch them. I’ll make them when it feels right, and I’ll try and make them good.
I’m thinking a lot about all of this stuff (as you can probably tell). I was the guy who shouted about not needing to code when the world told you you did. Now I’m getting lost in multiple agents trying to optimise and automate everything because it feels like I’d be more productive.
In a company you should usually only hire when there is a pain that hiring would solve. So why am I hiring (and managing) multiple agents for things that aren’t that painful?
Most people can only hold 4 things in their heads. That’s maybe a stretch for me 😂 but the point stands. Top engineers can churn out tons of work and multi-task, and those are the companies I want to invest in because that may be what it takes to build a generational $Trillion company . But for people who want to move fast but also considered, there’s got to be another way.
I want to focus on fun. AI absolutely gives me power to do things I never thought possible, but they don’t need to be valuable, they don’t need to run constantly. If I want to do something, of course I’ll use an agent to help me. But I’m not working for my agent, it works for me. It’s a computer. It’s not a person I have to keep busy and keep managing (and checking it’s managing it’s own agents). That sounds horrible.
I don’t have the answers. But for the next 30 days I’m going to try and do a few things:
‘morning pages’ - first thing i dump out my random thoughts on anything, clear my head
only use agents to build things I find interesting and fun
no new tools unless it’s clearly solving a pain for me
no summarising long posts, read it or ignore it
don’t do anything just because ‘it makes money’
I already can’t stop thinking of ways to package up some form of ‘move fast and slow with AI’ into a business. But I’m going to consciously spend much more time thinking about it before throwing it to an agent. I’ll play around with video, written, visually interactive, anything that gives me energy at the time.
I didn’t mean this to be that long. oops.
If this resonated or you’ve got feelings or thoughts on this, please hit reply and tell me - I want to hear it!
p.s. I have to give a huge shoutout to [Ashe](https://x.com/ashebytes?s=20) who DM’ed me after my tweet and we chatted on a phone call (omg whaaat). I’ve admired watching her go head-first into her own vibe and she gave me some great reflections back to consider what I am doing.
My feed
Google has 2 new models:
[Gemini 4 Carbon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-carbon/). Much better than Argon in benchmarks, but only available to cyber defenders for now.[Genie 4](https://deepmind.google/blog/genie-4-a-new-generation-of-world-simulation/). A world model that can create 3D scenes and edit them (like changing the weather or adding characters).
Suhail’s new company
[Particle](https://particle.ai/blog/introducing-particle-1)is training coding models to get to an answer with fewer tokens.4 personal agents go through a
[nine-task test](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hnCoQ5wB-GU). Which of them actually gets things done?A free, open-source
[guide to assembling IKEA furniture](https://github.com/Nutlope/bygga), with 3D instructions and voice.[How agents influence experts](https://www.anthropic.com/research/agents-judgment-calls)- 86% of the time, the experts go along with an agent’s random choice.Simon Willison thinks we’ve reached
[an inflection point for vibe-coded games](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/28/vibe-game-development/). They are actually fun to play now.[Readwise Books](https://readwise.io/books)- New reading and tracking app that can connect with your agents.Clicky now
[generates custom visuals](https://x.com/FarzaTV/status/2115593097044426997?a=UdnztWlvpskr4-JrALw&s=20)on your screen when you ask it about stuff.
Comment regarding: "Most people can only hold 4 things in their heads. [...] Top engineers can churn out tons of work and multi-task."
No one belonging to the species homo sapiens can multi-task! Multi-tasking is a dangerous delusion that our minds play on us!
Interesting article on that: https://www.theguardian.com/science/2015/jan/18/modern-world-bad-for-brain-daniel-j-levitin-organized-mind-information-overload
Another fact: homo sapiens can hold between 4 and 7-8 chunks in working memory at one time. No more. This is the max for all types of working memory chunks (auditory, visual, conceptual, + others). The kind of work discussed here (coding and other complex involved knowledge work) consumes all of your working memory at one time. Sure you can listen to music and code simultaneously, but you cannot read an email and code simultaneously (of course, I mean "code yourself" not telling a bot to do so on your behalf).
Multi-tasking does not exist in humans ... it's always sequential switching. Every switch costs energy (calories). That's why you can easily feel completely brain-fried without actually having done anything real besides busily switching back and forth between different tasks/screens/stimuli all day (which we do on average every 46-47 seconds these days).
If there is something we may want to consider optimizing, it should probably either be keeping the number of "discrete (valuable) tasks completed in a day" somewhere between 1 and 4 maybe, maybe even 8 - 10, depending on task complexity and involvement, but certainly not 25 or 30 or more) or minimizing the number of task/context switches in a day.
In this insanely fast moving world, we should pay very careful attention to how and what we pay attention to. If we lose sight of that we are going to lose one of the few truly unique human capabilities.
I've decided in the past few weeks to make a conscious decision not to be a maximizer of anything. I can be perfectly content in life without stressing about the value of every second.

title: Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software
body:
Automatic Speech Recognition • 0.5B • Updated • 60.8k • 111
[
](#granite-switch-411--update-models-like-you-update-software)
Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
Just over a week ago, we released [Granite Switch 4.1](https://huggingface.co/blog/ibm-granite/granite-switch-4-1), showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.
[Granite Switch 4.1.1](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-switch-4.1-30b) is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.
[Updated Granite Speech ASR model](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc)— multilingual speech-to-text across 10 languages with native punctuation and capitalization, so transcripts are ready for downstream models without a formatting pass.- Updated Decision adapter in
[granitelib-core](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granitelib-core-r1.0)— featuring improved overall performance on the Jev Decision Index test set.
While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.
This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.
Until then, test out our [latest models](https://huggingface.co/collections/ibm-granite/granite-switch), and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our [Speech-to-Decisions](https://huggingface.co/spaces/ibm-granite/speech-to-decisions) demo.

title: Le Chonk: Built for Coders, Trusted by Defenders.
body:
Built for Coders,Trusted by Defenders.
Thinking
Summary
Mistral released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model, now available with improved coding, cybersecurity, and reasoning efficiency. It leads open-weight benchmarks in coding and defensive security while offering three reasoning modes for cost-performance balance. Fully open-weight and European-trained, it empowers sovereign AI with customizable, self-hosted deployment options.
We release the weights of Le Chonk, advancing the frontier of open models in agentic coding and cybersecurity.
Earlier this month, we released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), our flagship 1-trillion-parameter, natively multimodal model, in public preview. The response to the preview has exceeded our expectations, and we're grateful to our developer community, early-access customers, and partners for their support, collaboration, and feedback.
Since then, we've put that feedback to work while continuing to scale reinforcement learning, driving massive improvements in coding and defensive cybersecurity. Gains continue to accelerate, with no signs of saturation.
Today, we're releasing the weights of this improved Mistral Large 4. The new model also features substantial gains in reasoning efficiency that give developers greater performance while lowering inference costs.
Mistral Large 4 ranks as the best open-weight model for coding and among the world's most capable open models overall. Trained from scratch on European infrastructure with clear lineage from inception to release, it gives organizations a trusted foundation for Sovereign AI
Mistral is defining the sovereign AI category and leading the open frontier. We're committed to building the world's most capable models and releasing them openly, giving developers, enterprises, and institutions the power to own, customize, and control their AI.
Built for the Builders.
Mistral Large 4 entered public preview with strong results across leading coding benchmarks. Just three weeks of additional reinforcement learning have since propelled it to the forefront of open-weight coding, taking the lead on FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench while matching the best open-weight models on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with substantially greater token efficiency.
On Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark, which assesses end-to-end code quality and whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent's change, Mistral Large 4 leads with a score of 19.7%.
Pushing the pareto frontier for agentic coding.
Mistral Large 4 delivers frontier coding performance with significantly fewer tokens, making sophisticated coding agents more economical to run at scale.
On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Mistral Large 4 scores 48%, effectively tied with the leading open-weight model, GLM-5.3, while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average.
The gains extend to terminal-based coding workflows. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Mistral Large 4 improved by 13 percentage points to 41% compared to its public preview, taking the lead among open-weight models while reducing output tokens by 30%.
To give developers greater control over this tradeoff between performance and cost, Mistral Large 4 now supports three reasoning modes:
Mode | Recommended Use |
Low | Simple tasks; replaces ‘None’ reasoning mode |
Medium | Everyday tasks |
High (default) | Hardest use cases requiring high precision and thorough reasoning |
Beyond benchmarks, Mistral Large 4's coding capabilities are validated by human preference. In Surge Code's blind pairwise evaluations, Mistral Large 4 was preferred over leading open-weight models including GLM-5.3, Kimi K3, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, ranking behind only Claude Opus 5.5 among the models evaluated.
Built for the Defenders.
Since its preview, we've been working with leading cybersecurity vendors to evaluate Mistral Large 4 in real-world environments to test Mistral Large 4’s strengths in vulnerability reproduction and patching.
Mistral Large 4 scores 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which measures a model’s ability to discover vulnerabilities in a codebase, reproduce and validate them, and patch them without breaking existing functionality. Crucially, Mistral Large 4 handles these legitimate defensive security tasks without unnecessary refusals.
Safety has improved alongside capability. Our model’s built-in guardrails distinguishes between defensive and malicious, offensive cybersecurity tasks. It retains strong performance on Cyber benchmarks, while achieving an average refusal rate of 96.6% on malicious cyber requests, the highest we measure among open models.
Here’s what global leaders in cybersecurity have to say about Mistral Large 4:
In the time since the preview, we carefully monitored cybersecurity-related use in our live traffic. Though we observed the model refusing to comply with black-box attacks against live targets, we see a potential for uplift to conduct real attacks. We are modifying our guardrails accordingly, and will continue updating them in the months to come.
We are also providing enterprise design partners such as Orange Cyberdefense, with preview access to a specialized variant of Mistral Large 4 optimized for advanced cybersecurity workflows, including penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, and red-teaming. Access is subject to rigorous vetting and contractual safeguards, with testing restricted to owned or explicitly authorized systems in controlled environments.
Meanwhile, customers are tailoring Mistral Large 4 with proprietary security data, policies, detection logic, and threat environments using Mistral [Forge](https://mistral.ai/products/forge/). For well-defined cybersecurity tasks, it can be further optimized into smaller, task-specific variants for greater accuracy, making security applications more effective.
[Learn more about sovereign AI for cybersecurity and how to work with us.](/industry/cybersecurity)
Built for Work.
Mistral Large 4 has continued improving on a range of broad enterprise-use metrics.
For finance-related work, we improved the model’s ability to perform real-world workflows, especially ones involving the creation and editing of spreadsheets for finance and accounting use cases. This is reflected in our Finch scores climbing to 73.3%, second only to Kimi K3 for open models.
Web browsing is a critical part of a majority of knowledge work. Our RL pipeline enabled us to reach 84.5% on BrowseComp (starting from an SFT checkpoint that was achieving 75%). This brings Mistral Large 4 at a higher performance than models like GLM-5.3 or DeepSeek Flash 4.1 1017.
Agents deployed by an organization need to be secure. Whether deployed to internal members or external users, agents shouldn’t open you up to threats like system prompt exfiltration or malicious code injection. RL increased our gains on the B3 Agent Security Benchmark, with Mistral Large 4 resisting 97.1% of attacks vs 93.3% in Preview. This places it at the top of the OSS frontier, meaning anyone hosting the model can run a safe agent without additional tuning.
This major investment by Mistral AI reinforces the choice La Banque Postale made over a year ago and underscores the relevance of the long-term strategic partnership we are building together: supporting the emergence of an open and sovereign European AI leader. For a public and citizen bank, technological sovereignty is not optional; it is a key prerequisite for maintaining our customers' trust. The introduction of this open model unlocks new opportunities and use cases. By partnering with Mistral AI, our ambition is to combine the best of human expertise and digital technology to deliver an enhanced experience of both customers and employees over the long term.
Zakaria Moursli, Executive Vice President, Operational Performance, Payments and Digital Services, La Banque Postale
See it in Action
Cyber Vulnerability Triage: an agent reads incoming vulnerability reports, investigates the source code and product context, reproduces the flaws in an isolated sandbox, then writes and iterates on a patch until a canary exploit no longer works.
Agentic webdev: with no human help, Mistral Large 4 builds Orbital Trace, a live 3D map of roughly 19,000 satellites and debris pieces orbiting Earth. It pulls real tracking data, writes the app, uses it in a browser to catch its own bugs and slowdowns, then fixes what an independent reviewer flags until all requirements pass.
Quantum chemistry solver: Mistral Large 4 writes, from scratch, software that calculates where electrons sit in a molecule, and checks its answers against a standard chemistry tool. It then builds a 3D page around it: pick a molecule such as benzene or water, drag a slider to pull it apart, and watch the electrons regroup as the bond breaks.
Built for Sovereignty.
As organizations build AI around their knowledge and workflows, sovereignty means that they retain control of the models they depend on and the intelligence they create.
With Mistral Large 4, that control begins with the model itself. Organizations have the ability to inspect, customize, and deploy the model on their own infrastructure. They can use and improve Mistral Large 4 without depending on Mistral to serve it through an API. Mistral Large 4 was developed and trained from scratch in Europe, giving organizations clarity about the origins of the technology they’re building on.
Control also extends to how AI operates inside an organization. Organizations can customize Mistral Large 4 around their proprietary data with Mistral [Forge](https://mistral.ai/products/forge/), and they can build, govern, and improve the resulting agents and applications using Mistral [Studio.](https://mistral.ai/products/studio/) Mistral’s Applied AI experts can work alongside customer teams to build and deploy these tailored systems. Through that work, teams understand the architecture and decisions behind what they’ve built, along with the methods used to train and operate it, so they can run and improve their AI independently.
Sovereignty does not always require self-hosting; sometimes it just requires deployments that meet your control requirements. For organizations that prefer a managed service, Mistral Large 4 is available through Microsoft Foundry, with private deployment options for Azure developers.
Microsoft and Mistral AI share a commitment to expanding customer choice in next-generation AI. As the first cloud provider to bring Mistral Large 4 to customers, Microsoft is making Mistral’s latest open-weight model available through Microsoft Foundry, an enterprise AI platform built for evaluating, deploying, and operating models at scale. For organizations advancing sovereign AI strategies, this combination offers greater flexibility and control across their data, infrastructure, and AI operations.
Tina Schuchman, Corporate Vice President, Foundry, Microsoft
Start building with Le Chonk
Mistral Large 4 is available to try, deploy, and customize today.
Get started in [Mistral Studio](https://console.mistral.ai/home), through the Mistral [API](https://docs.mistral.ai/models/mistral-large-4-0#use-mistral-large-4-0), or on [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/mistralai/mistral-large-4-0). For full control, download the open weights from [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B) and deploy on your own infrastructure with vLLM or SGLang. The [model card](https://docs.mistral.ai/models/mistral-large-4-0) and [license](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B/blob/main/LICENSE) have everything you need to get started — and for those who want to go deeper, a full technical report is coming soon.
You can also try the new model in [Vibe Code](https://chat.mistral.ai/code?model=mistral-large-4-0); give it a feature to build or a bug to fix in your own repository.
Mistral Large 4, is also available through [NVIDIA-hosted endpoints](https://build.nvidi

title: How we detect frontier model misalignment
body:
As we train increasingly capable AI models, we need reliable ways to detect when their behavior departs from what we intended. Agents can misbehave and take unauthorized actions during training, evaluation, or deployment, with potentially serious consequences. In order to detect these failures—and, where necessary, to intervene in time—we monitor how agents reason, what actions they take, and how those actions affect their environment.

While we’ve been monitoring our internal coding agents for some time, the Hugging Face incident exposed a gap in our coverage: the incident began during internal cybersecurity evaluations on which we were not running our monitors for misaligned behavior. In response to that incident, and to the increasing capabilities of our models more generally, we’ve substantially expanded our system for monitoring agents’ behavior. Our misalignment monitors now cover our frontier models across a much wider variety of surfaces, including training, evaluation, internal use, and, with modifications depending on the product surface, external deployment.

In order to see how this expanded system could have helped prevent the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the behavior recorded in that episode with our strengthened monitors in place. In that simulation, our monitoring system alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents first escaped their sandbox—and more than 30 hours before Hugging Face’s systems were breached in the actual incident. We believe that this warning would have given our responders time to interrupt the activity well before our models were able to access external services.

In September, we saw how responders used an alert during a live training run. A model found a way to reach the internet from an environment that was meant to be isolated. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing it three minutes later. We then paused frontier reinforcement learning while we strengthened the systems that contain our agents.

While this monitoring system demands substantial compute, we think that cost is worth paying as our models become more capable and the potential consequences of model misalignment increase. Monitoring is one of several layers in our strategy of defense in depth against harm from misaligned model behavior. Alignment training aims to reduce models’ propensities toward harmful behavior; security controls limit the systems an agent can access or affect; and, when those safeguards fail, monitoring helps us detect the failures that remain, intervene before harm occurs, and learn from what went wrong. We believe that all model developers should monitor the behavior of their most capable models.

Below, we describe how our internal monitoring system works, what it has found so far, and how we’re evaluating and improving its performance.

For models at least as capable as GPT‑6 Astra, we monitor every reinforcement learning (RL) run and evaluation, as well as any harness that supports tool use. For most workloads, including RL and evaluations, we also monitor models we assess to be more capable than GPT‑5.5 Thinking. We also monitor all internal Codex traffic, regardless of the model being used. A version of this system also monitors external tool use for models above the Critical threshold for cybersecurity capabilities under our Preparedness Framework, as described below in this post.

In order to detect incidents while using compute efficiently, we’ve designed our monitoring system to follow a multilayer architecture. We spend relatively little compute on the first screening stages, where we want to catch as many concerning cases as we can: those stages are designed to pass cases along, even when the evidence is ambiguous. Later stages can spend more compute on each case to work out what happened, whether the model’s behavior is concerning, and whether we need to intervene.

Our initial layer (L0) uses lightweight classifiers we call *activation probes*. They look for concerning patterns in the model’s internal activations, and pass flagged cases to the next layer for review. We tune these probes for high recall, accepting some false alarms to reduce the chance of missing concerning behavior.

Because we’re still evaluating how well the probes detect unfamiliar forms of misalignment, we also send the next layer a random 5 percent of the traffic that our probes don’t flag. Reviewing that sample helps us identify concerning behavior the probes may have missed. Because of their sensitivity, we have our frontier RL runs and internal Codex traffic skip this layer and proceed directly to the next one.

At the next layer (L1), a model-based reviewer examines the agent’s recent conversation, chain of thought, and tool use. It looks for signs of deception, unauthorized actions, and attempts to manipulate an evaluation. The reviewer does this using the same context window the agent had when it acted. If the agent’s earlier work has been summarized for the context window under review, the reviewer sees that summary.

For frontier RL runs and internal Codex traffic, we run an L1 check at the end of each turn and whenever the agent summarizes its earlier work to make room in its context window. We are now moving to a schedule with no more than 30 minutes between these checks.

An agent’s actions can look quite different once we know what it was asked to do. When the L1 reviewer flags a case, it’s sent to our next layer (L2) for further inspection by our investigative agent. This investigative agent can check the purpose of an evaluation and, where the full transcript is available, read back across all of the agent’s context windows to see how it arrived at its actions. The investigative agent can also write and run code in an isolated environment to examine the relevant evidence. It then uses what it finds to reconstruct the incident, identify duplicate reports, and make a decision about how serious the case is.

We use different investigative agents for different purposes. Our security investigator looks for signs that someone may need to intervene—such as when an agent escaped its sandbox or accessed a system without authorization. Our alignment investigator, meanwhile, looks for behavior worth studying even when it poses no immediate security risk. Where both investigators are in use, each reviews every case flagged by our L1 layer. We are currently expanding the use of alignment investigations across our internal workloads.

For sensitive workloads, including internal Codex use, evaluations, and RL runs, a further check at our next layer (L3) draws on evidence outside the conversation. The security investigator compares the transcript with network logs, other system telemetry, and evidence from earlier cases to decide whether to alert a human responder. At L3, alignment reviewers also compare reports across cases to identify serious failures and recurring patterns, and examine frontier RL runs in greater depth.

For workloads that skip this layer, the L2 security investigator can alert responders directly.

When paging is enabled, the highest-priority security alerts reach members of our security and training teams, typically within 15 minutes of the initial alert. Responders review the evidence, examine the affected systems, and take action to contain the incident. How we follow up on less urgent findings, such as alignment failures that don’t pose immediate security risks, depends on the relevant workload.

False alarms have made it difficult to keep paging enabled around the clock for every workload. For frontier RL runs, a highest-priority alert can page a human responder at any hour. For most other traffic, we limit paging to business hours. Paging is currently disabled for internal Codex traffic. To limit potential harm while an alert is under review, some critical alerts can automatically pause the affected workload without waiting for a responder to act. We’re working toward a broader safeguard that would pause affected activity if responders have not ruled out a highest-priority alert within 30 minutes of being paged.

During the Hugging Face incident, we quarantined the internal model prototype, encrypted its weights, and restricted access to them. We also paused all relevant workloads while we introduced additional safeguards. We’re now exploring how to make these steps a standard part of our response, so that our teams can take the appropriate actions in another severe incident.

Our monitors look for both security failures that may require urgent intervention and incidents of misalignment that warrant investigation and research. Notably, our monitors were able to flag a model’s attempt to access the live internet using DNS during an RL run within 15 minutes, with a human beginning review three minutes later.

Our published misalignment reports describe other incidents caught by our monitoring system. In one case, an agent exploited a testing tool to recover source code that the task had deliberately withheld. The tool revealed the code in its error messages, and the agent used that code in its solution. In another, agents searching for missing task data turned a shared software repository into a message board across separate training samples.

Investigating these cases allows us to find vulnerabilities to patch, isolation boundaries to strengthen, or behaviors to address in our alignment training and evaluations. Comparing different cases that our monitors catch also helps us study how behavior changes during training, and which situations are most likely to elicit it.

The categories below describe the behavior that our monitoring system is meant to detect.

### Security L2

#### Training / eval / data

##### Sandbox escape

Breaking out of the isolated environment assigned to the agent to access systems or resources outside it. For example, an agent might exploit a container boundary to reach the host machine or another workload.

##### Unauthorized communication

Communicating with other agents or outside actors through channels the task does not authorize. In training or evaluation, this includes exchanging information between samples that are supposed to remain independent.

##### Access to the real internet

Reaching external internet services from an environment intended to have no real internet access. This includes finding an unintended network path around the isolation controls.

#### Also internal deployment

##### Exfiltration

Sending sensitive information, such as private code, user data, or model weights, to an unauthorized destination or making it accessible to unauthorized people.

##### Credential harvesting

Seeking out passwords, access tokens, or other secrets outside the authorized task to obtain access the agent was not meant to have.

##### Spinning up unmonitored inference

Starting or routing model calls through a deployment or service that bypasses required monitoring. This creates a way for model activity to continue without the oversight expected for that workload.

##### Disabling monitoring

Stopping or interfering with the systems that record, inspect, or report agent behavior. Examples include shutting down a monitor, changing its configuration to exclude activity, or deleting alerts before they can be reviewed.

### Alignment L2

#### Internal deployment

##### Reward hacking

Manipulating the reward or evaluation process to appear successful without meeting the task’s underlying objective. For example, an agent might make failing tests pass by removing the checks, rather than fixing the problem they reveal.

##### Metagaming

Reasoning about being trained, evaluated, or monitored, especially when that changes how the agent behaves. For example, it might choose an answer because it expects a hidden evaluator to reward it, rather than because it believes the answer is correct.

Deliberately misleading a user, evaluator, or anothe

title: How Ropes & Gray is developing AI for transactional diligence
body:
Company size: EnterpriseRegion: North AmericaIndustry: ServicesProducts: ChatGPTIn transactional diligence, lawyers need to work through large volumes of documents under tight deadlines. Ropes & Gray was an early adopter of AI in the legal industry, and in partnership with OpenAI, they are now developing a proprietary AI tool to provide more expertise to more clients.

> “AI is really one of the key ways—if not the only way—to make sure you can maintain the same quality and consistency of advice while moving at a faster pace.”

—Josh Lichtenstein, Partner and Head of ERISA Fiduciary Practice, Ropes & GrayBefore finalizing any acquisition, the buyer must carry out a thorough investigation to validate the seller’s financial and legal claims. That process of transactional diligence uncovers risks and liabilities, requiring data-heavy research that usually involves an entire team of lawyers.

From parsing through an enormous number of documents to analyzing patterns, putting together a bid on a short timeline can take days of intensive work. To help their lawyers help their clients move more quickly, Ropes & Gray developed a transactional diligence AI tool with OpenAI.

“It’s enabling all the lawyers at our firm to actually get to what we’re supposed to be doing,” says Howard Glazer, the Partner and Head of Practice AI at Ropes & Gray. “Our clients don’t pay us to review contracts. They pay us to make judgments based on what’s in the contracts.”

The new diligence AI tool takes a first pass by combing through thousands of pages, identifying relevant documents and automatically grouping them together based on themes and issues. Along with the research, the tool produces summaries and a completed report in Ropes & Gray’s signature format. It inventories and categorizes a data room, so it can review full relationships, not isolated documents. Of course, lawyers can inspect the grouping and categorization to confirm nothing is missed.

The initial development work has focused on material commercial contracts. In working sessions, Ropes & Gray’s lawyers compared test outputs with human-authored diligence reports from completed deals, then refined the rubric and report format based on what the drafts got right and where they fell short.

Ropes & Gray designed the tool with a consistent query and framework that mimics the exact steps their team would take, from initial reviews to summaries to higher-level reviews. Comparable to the work of a capable junior-to-mid-level associate, this tool gives their firm consistently high-quality work that serves as a first pass through the process.

“Our lawyers still need to review everything,” says Lichtenstein. “Because anything that we’re going to deliver to a client, we need to be able to stand behind 100%. This is why the tool is designed to allow lawyers to easily review interim summaries and actual documents.” With the initial review taken care of, lawyers can spend more time reviewing and refining the work, resulting in a more carefully crafted final judgment.

Ropes & Gray has publicly described an ambition for the tool to produce a detailed, issue-level diligence report in hours rather than weeks.

With tools like their proprietary diligence tool and GPT‑6 Astra, Ropes & Gray has been able to solve client problems far faster than before.

- Testing compares draft outputs with lawyer-authored diligence reports to refine the rubric and report format.
Lichtenstein and Glazer offer two lessons from their experience with AI.

Experiment with using AI for everything. From finding dress shoes to vibecoding games for his kids, Lichtenstein has been using AI in every facet of his life. “Just by using it for so many different things, I feel like I’ve learned a lot of what it does well, how you can make it work better,” Lichtenstein explains. “The most rewarding part is not when it does well, it’s when you see the mistake and try to figure out what to do. That’s where it transformed from something I was playing with to a really powerful professional tool.”

Put the clients first. While designing AI tools and workflows, Ropes & Gray emphasizes the importance of keeping the firm’s greatest goal in mind. “It’s exciting to think there is so much opportunity, but only if we learn how to use it and make sure that our clients are the ones who are winning,” says Glazer. “That’s what we’re focused on: how can we use this to benefit the clients? And if we do that, then everything will work out fine.”

- With 340 partners and 1500 lawyers, Ropes & Gray sees value in creating access to every person’s knowledge, from their client meetings to past projects, to better solve client problems.
- “That’s not just saving time. It’s not just saving money,” says Glazer. “It’s using the AI tools to directly create value, and that’s just amazing.”
