## Building for a profession where time—and trust—are scarce

Founded in Stockholm in 2023, [Legora⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.legora.com/) is building what CEO and co-founder Max Junestrand calls “the agentic operating system for legal work”: bringing AI into the workflows lawyers rely on every day.

The company started with the insight that legal teams are unusually time crunched, meaning some valuable work doesn’t get done. Think of the junior lawyer told to review an impossible number of contracts overnight and only able to focus on a fraction.

Legora can provide those services “on tap”, which is why Junestrand’s ambition is that every piece of legal work in the world should run on his platform. OpenAI has been part of that journey from the beginning: the release of GPT‑3.5 was the moment many of the legal use cases the founding team had been experimenting with became possible. Today, OpenAI is a key model provider for Legora, powering core workflows across its legal AI platform, from agentic legal work to large-scale document review. Legora builds on new OpenAI model capabilities as they become available, translating advances in intelligence into what lawyers can accomplish with its product.

> “***The world needs more legal services and legal intelligence. With Legora, we get that on tap.***”

*—Max Junestrand, CEO and co-founder, Legora*

## An AI-native company building an AI-native product

Legora’s use of AI goes beyond the product it sells, and has expanded its use of ChatGPT Work, Codex and dots across its own teams. OpenAI’s technology is becoming part of both the product Legora builds for its customers as well as shaping how the company itself operates. “It’s incredibly important to me that we stay as AI-native as possible,” confirms Junestrand.

For Jacob Lauritzen, CTO at Legora, coding agents have changed how quickly the engineering team can develop new ideas. Instead of researching one possible solution and committing engineering time before knowing whether it’s the right path, teams can prototype many approaches at once. “We can explore **20 solutions at the same time** and, within days, pick the one we know will be the best.”

The same approach changes how Legora responds when something goes wrong. Previously, diagnosing a product issue could mean several engineers investigating different possible causes over a number of hours. Coding agents can now search millions of lines of logs and pursue many possible explanations simultaneously, sometimes taking Legora from bug report to working fix in **around five minutes**.

Customers, of course, don’t see the engineering efficiency itself. But they do experience the results: problems can be resolved faster, feedback can reach product teams sooner, and new ideas can be tested with customers earlier in the development cycle.

> “***We can go to customers much more quickly with feedback. It enables us to build a better product faster.***”

*—Jacob Lauritzen, CTO, Legora*

## Giving Legora’s own lawyers room to do higher-value work

Legora’s own legal team experiences the same transformation its product is designed to create for customers. General Counsel Emma Kadri Bergström points to the example of NDAs. Her team analysed the agreements they had historically signed and built a playbook that allows Legora to take a first pass at incoming NDAs, highlighting terms that fall outside acceptable parameters.

Before the workflow was introduced, Kadri Bergström estimates that reviewing these “boring documents” consumed around **20% of the legal team’s capacity**. Today, it’s **under 1%**.

That reclaimed time matters because the company itself is scaling rapidly. In the past year, Kadri Bergström says the business has expanded from **three offices to 18**, completed **three**** financing rounds** and made **five acquisitions**. The legal team has had to support that growth while remaining closely connected to the business.

AI has also allowed the team to take on work that might previously have been outsourced or narrowed because of limited capacity. In M&A diligence, for example, agents can begin reviewing contracts and surfacing information across the deal set, with lawyers reviewing and interpreting the output.

> ***“AI doesn’t just make you faster. It also increases quality.”***

—Emma Kadri Bergström, General Counsel, Legora

## From faster review to broader, higher-quality analysis

For Legora’s customers, the opportunity isn’t simply to complete the same work faster. AI has also increased the scope of work that can be taken on.

Alex Fortescue-Webb, Global Head of Legal Engineering, points to due diligence as an example. In a traditional review, time and cost constraints can force teams to concentrate deeply on only the most valuable contracts. Legora’s Tabular Review workflow can analyse thousands of contracts across multiple questions in minutes, allowing lawyers to apply detailed scrutiny much more broadly.

That can alter the quality of the final work. Risks that might previously have sat in contracts outside the manually reviewed subset can now be surfaced for a lawyer to assess.

The results are already measurable. Junestrand cites one Fortune 100 customer that has:

- reduced contract turnaround time by **90%**
- saved **more than $20 million** on external litigation and diligence
- returned **9.5 hours per lawyer each week** for higher-value work

> “***AI has fundamentally changed both the speed at which you can do existing tasks and the breadth of analysis you can apply.***”

*—Alex Fortescue-Webb, Global Head of Legal Engineering, Legora*

Through the [Legora plugin for ChatGPT⁠](https://openai.com/business/plugins/legora/), legal teams can also use Legora’s capabilities within their ChatGPT conversations.

## Results at a glance

- **95%+ reduction** in Legora legal-team time spent reviewing NDAs, from \~20% of team capacity to under 1%.
- **90% faster contract turnaround** for one Fortune 100 Legora customer.
- **$20M+ saved** on external litigation and diligence for the same customer.
- **9.5 hours returned per lawyer, per week** for higher-value work.

## Leadership lessons

- **Lead by using.** When more than 75% of leaders actively use Legora, median usage across the organisation is 3× higher.
- **Start with the problem.** Focus on what people need to accomplish, then determine where AI can improve the workflow.
- **Build a network of champions.** Internal advocates help turn experimentation into sustained adoption.
- **Be ready to rebuild.** As models improve, yesterday’s product assumptions can quickly become outdated.
- **Design for trust.** Build evaluation, testing and transparency into the experience from the start.

## What’s next

For Legora, the next frontier isn’t just making today’s legal workflows faster. It’s expanding the kinds of work AI can take on, while making collaboration between lawyers and AI increasingly natural.

Jacob Lauritzen sees two advances happening in parallel. First, agents will be able to tackle longer-running tasks that require far greater context and autonomy. He imagines due diligence spanning millions of pages running overnight, with the analysis ready for a lawyer to review when they arrive the next morning.

At the same time, increasingly capable models are becoming faster. That opens up a different kind of experience: real-time collaboration where a lawyer and AI can work back and forth on a contract, analysis or piece of advice rather than treating AI as a tool that receives a task and returns an answer.

> ***“When you blend human and AI, that’s when the output comes out best.”***

—Jacob Lauritzen, CTO, Legora

That moving frontier means Legora’s roadmap can’t be static. “Model improvements force me to reconsider the roadmap on a biweekly basis,” says Lauritzen. Engineers, product managers, designers and sales teams all frequently ask him what’s the new thing that’s become possible for customers.

For Bergström, it’s about changing the perception of legal teams. “Every legal department is worried about becoming a bottleneck. That’s when the business stops coming to you,” she says. AI is transforming legal teams from bottleneck to business partner, from the people you avoid to the people you want in the room alongside you.

If Legora succeeds, the outcome won’t simply be lawyers completing today’s workload more efficiently. It will be legal teams able to take on work that capacity once made impossible, with more time for judgement, strategy and the high-value decisions that still require a human.

As Junestrand puts it: “It’s the best time in history to be a lawyer.”

title: Stop Guessing Your vLLM Config: Benchmarking LLMs on Runpod - Chris Vela, Runpod
body:
Most teams spin up a new open model with the default vLLM recipe and hope for the best. Runpod forward-deployed engineer Chris Vela shows how to choose configs from data instead, starting with the use case and concurrency, and demos BenchPod, a benchmarking dashboard built on vLLM that tests configs live without restarts. title: Who Is Making This Request? Agent Auth 101 - Kamil Potrec, Keycard
body:
When an agent sends an invoice using your token, who actually made the request? Kamil Potrec of Keycard breaks down how agents get credentials today (personal tokens, static keys, over-privileged service accounts) and what proper agent auth requires: per-agent identity, delegation, short-lived scoped credentials, federation with legacy systems, policy and audit. He compares SDKs and gateways for keeping credentials out of an agent's reach, including the gateway tradeoffs.

title: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions
body:
We’re highlighting 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups from around the world that we’ve partnered with in an expansion of our [AI for Science program](https://www.anthropic.com/news/ai-for-science-program), which gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects.
We started the AI for Science program in May 2025 with the belief that AI could significantly speed up scientific progress. Our goal is to increase access to AI tools and resources to enable researchers to deepen and expand their own scientific work. (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted [Team plan for scientists](https://claude.com/programs/team-plan-for-scientists) and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics.)
Scientists have told us that they’re working with Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, swiftly analyze complex data, and communicate findings. With scientists at the center of this transformation, the field is setting the questions and developing the research projects that will help us tackle some of humanity’s toughest problems.
Over the past year, we’ve started to expand this work and partner with scientific organizations to build collaborative research projects. For instance, we partnered with HHMI Janelia Research Campus to develop the [Model Hardware Standard](https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-hardware-standard-research-preview) (MHS), a shared specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments. MHS is currently in research preview. We also support the Allen Institute, a leader in creating large open datasets and tools to advance research on the brain, cells, and the immune system. The institute is building teams of AI agents to analyze that data, turning months of manual analysis into hours.
AI for Science began by supporting individual scientists. By partnering with institutions and foundations, we’re now able to reach more researchers across many fields. Many of these projects will also produce public goods that benefit the wider scientific community: open datasets, open-source software, open standards, and shared libraries. We look forward to seeing how AI resources can expand what scientists can attempt and lead to new discoveries.
Science funders and societies
Science funders and societies play an enormous role in finding and funding original, high-impact projects. We’re sharing Claude credits with the following organizations, which will distribute these resources to ambitious researchers aiming to use AI for scientific research:
- The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation. Founded in 1934, it supports original research and education in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and economics.
- The Simons Foundation. This foundation advances the frontiers of research in mathematics and basic sciences through grants and its Flatiron Institute.
- Schmidt Sciences. Founded in 2024 by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, it works to accelerate scientific knowledge and breakthroughs with the most promising, advanced tools to support a thriving planet. The organization prioritizes research in areas poised for impact, including AI and advanced computing, astrophysics, biosciences, climate, and space—and supports researchers in a variety of disciplines through its science systems program.
- Open Source for Science Fund, a program of Renaissance Philanthropy. This is a time-bound philanthropic fund at Renaissance Philanthropy sustaining and evolving the open-source software stack that underpins science.
- The US National Science Foundation. This $9 billion federal agency established by Congress in 1950 promotes the progress of science, advances national health and defense, and funds competitive research and education, accounting for about 25% of federal support for basic research at US colleges and universities.
- CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society. For more than a century, CAS has indexed the world’s published chemistry, and it maintains the CAS REGISTRY®, the standard system for identifying chemical substances.
Institutions
Leading research institutions produce some of the world’s most important scientific advances, data, instruments, and tools. These institutional partners will use Claude credits inside their organizations to enable scientific discovery:
- Space Telescope Science Institute. STScI runs science operations for NASA’s Hubble, James Webb, and Roman space telescopes. Managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA), STScI also holds one of the largest astronomy data archives used by scientists worldwide.
- Wellcome Sanger Institute. One of the world’s leading genomics centers, it generates genomic and functional data at scale, with work that spans human genetics, biodiversity, and drug development.
- The Francis Crick Institute. Based in London, it’s one of Europe’s largest biomedical research institutes, with more than 100 research groups studying the biology behind health and disease.
- Imperial College London, Department of Life Sciences. One of Europe’s largest life science departments, it conducts research ranging from the structure of single molecules to whole ecosystems, with a focus on health, disease, and climate resilience.
- EMBL. The European Molecular Biology Laboratory is Europe’s intergovernmental life science laboratory, with six sites across the continent delivering both research and services across experimental and computational approaches in biology. EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) hosts a number of key open data resources that biologists use every day, such as Ensembl, Protein Data Bank in Europe, and Europe PMC.
- Gladstone Institutes. An independent biomedical research institute in San Francisco, it integrates AI and data science across its work on cardiology, neurology, infectious diseases, cancer, and autoimmune diseases.
Research projects and initiatives
As part of this work, we’re also continuing to support innovative research by providing Claude credits directly to specific research initiatives, focusing on problems with the potential for large public impact. The new projects are:
- FlyWire, Princeton University (neuroscience). It produced the first complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly’s brain and develops open data and tools for connectomics, enabling researchers to discover how neural circuits give rise to perception and behavior.
- LEAP, Columbia University (Earth system). Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics is a National Science Foundation center that combines machine learning with physics to improve how climate models capture clouds, oceans, and land.
- AstroPath, Johns Hopkins University (cancer research). Built by a pathologist and an astrophysicist from the Mark Foundation Center for Advanced Genomics and Imaging and the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, AstroPath uses calibration methods from astronomical surveys to image tumors cell by cell, with measurements consistent across slides and labs.
- gnomAD, Broad Institute (genomics and rare disease). The Genome Aggregation Database pools DNA data from over 800,000 people into an open reference of human genetic variation that researchers and clinical labs around the world use to support rare disease discovery and diagnosis.
- Tau Ceti (mathematics). This open, community-driven project is building a shared autoformalized library of mathematics in Lean, a language that lets computers check every proof.
- Centre for Population Genomics. A joint initiative between Australia’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research and Murdoch Children’s Research Institute, it increases the inclusion of Australia’s multicultural communities in genomic resources and builds tools for rare disease diagnosis.
What’s next
Many of these collaborations are still in their early stages, and we’re eager to see how they can support novel research and scientific discovery. We look forward to sharing the impact of this work and showcasing new ways of working in these scientific fields.
As AI changes how science is done, our AI for Science program will continue to support and collaborate with scientists, institutions, and foundations. We hope to expand these efforts to even more partners around the world.

title: IDC brings Quanta into Claude and adopts Claude across the company
body:
IDC brings Quanta into Claude and adopts Claude across the company
IDC integrated Claude as part of its Quanta platform, and it has rolled Claude out across its own business
IDC Research (IDC), a global leader in technology intelligence for more than 60 years, worked with Anthropic to bring IDC Quanta into Claude, available to IDC customers today. IDC Quanta gives customers access to IDC’s trusted and validated forecasts, market data, research, and more, and now, they can ask questions in Claude to get answers enriched with IDC’s insights in minutes. IDC has also rolled Claude out across the company, where teams use it every day.
Applying market research has traditionally meant reading through long reports to get to the answers a customer needs, such as a vendor shortlist or a competitive brief. Now, an IDC customer describes the market, strategy, or purchase they're working on, and the IDC Quanta MCP connector for Claude returns finished analysis built on IDC's trusted forecasts and data.
What customers can do with IDC Quanta in Claude
IDC Quanta, an AI-powered technology intelligence platform that helps customers do better work, faster, with credible, verified intelligence from IDC’s proprietary data and research. In Claude, IDC Quanta enables customers to benchmark performance, size markets, choose vendors, and shape strategy. It’s as simple as a customer describing the question they're working on, and Claude answering it using IDC's intelligence.
The questions that users ask vary by role, but they tend to look like this:
- Competitive briefs: A corporate strategy lead asks Claude for a competitor brief. Claude returns the competitor’s positioning, market share, product capabilities, and recent acquisitions, cited to IDC's research. A job that used to take a day’s worth of research is complete in minutes.
- Vendor shortlists: A CIO evaluating procurement software asks Claude which vendors are the best fit based on her existing architecture and unique business requirements. Claude returns the top three by IDC's procurement database and MarketScape research as an Excel scorecard, ready for the evaluation team to act on.
- Analysis of their own numbers: A CFO uploads next year's IT budget, and asks how it compares to IDC's forecast. Claude returns where the two differ, and by how much, while updated data stays private to the customer.
IDC Quanta works wherever the customer already uses Claude, including the Claude app on desktop and mobile, Cowork, and the Microsoft Office add-ins. It gives Claude the same data and definitions an IDC analyst works from, so a market share or growth rate matches what IDC would publish, and each answer cites the IDC document or dataset it came from.
How IDC uses Claude internally
IDC has also put Claude to work across the company, where its engineers, product, marketing and sales teams are using it daily to build, plan, and sell. A clear example of the difference it's making is in engineering: IDC's engineers rebuilt the internal data repository its analysts use for research in three weeks instead of an estimated three months, and since they began using Claude Code for testing, bugs in the code they ship have come down significantly.
Engineering was the first team to adopt Claude, and the rest of the company has followed. Here's how they're using it:
- Building and testing software: Product managers use Claude Code to build working prototypes before engineering starts, which has cut the time it takes a feature to reach engineering from months to weeks. Engineers use it to run tests in parallel, and a code review that once filled five days is done in about 30 minutes.
- Planning and strategy: Product teams give Cowork their research and internal files, and it writes the first draft of the plan. Planning sprints that took three weeks now take three days. Writing a new test to check that code works now takes about 20 minutes, down from days.
- Optimizing sales: IDC's sales team runs a tool built with Claude that reads an export from the company's CRM. In minutes, it tells each rep which of their deals have stalled and which are worth chasing.
- Producing marketing content: IDC's content marketing team built an assistant in Claude to draft much of its marketing content. It optimizes the content for search and AI answer engines (SEO/AEO), and checks it against buyer personas and IDC's own research. From there, the team edits, proofs, and publishes the work, publishing content faster than it could on its own
“Assessing the impact of a competitor’s acquisition used to mean a market intelligence professional spending hours pulling multiple reports, synthesizing the findings, and turning them into an executive-ready brief. Now, they can open Claude, ask what that acquisition means for their business, and get a board-ready analysis in minutes, grounded in IDC’s research and more than 15 billion data points,” said Lorenzo Larini, CEO, IDC. “We brought IDC Quanta into Claude because that’s where many of our customers already work, giving them a faster, more intuitive way to put IDC’s trusted data and research to work.”
“IDC has spent 60 years helping leaders make better technology decisions, and now it’s using Claude to rethink how its teams work and how it delivers value to its customers,” said Paul Smith, Chief Commercial Officer, Anthropic.
Getting started
IDC Quanta customers who use Claude can add the IDC Quanta connector from within Claude. Others can contact IDC or[ book a demo](https://idc.com/quanta/book-a-demo). To learn more about Claude for Enterprise, visit anthropic.com/enterprise.

title: Introducing artifacts for legal work
body:
Introducing artifacts for legal work
Claude for Legal now includes ready-to-use artifacts for legal work that teams can adapt with their own data and connectors, and share across the business.
Today, we’re introducing ready-to-use artifacts that legal professionals can adapt to how their teams work and share with colleagues across the business. Since we launched Claude for Legal in May, the most common requests from legal teams have been for simpler setup and easier ways to work with colleagues.
Artifacts are interactive tools, such as trackers and dashboards, that teams can use and share in Claude. Our new legal gallery includes artifacts for specific tasks, such as reviewing a stack of contracts, tracking regulatory changes, and taking in legal requests from the business. Each artifact opens with an example, so legal professionals can see how the work comes together before adding their own data and connectors. Each answer or output has a link to its source.
We are also funding public interest groups building artifacts for access-to-justice work and legal education programs teaching tomorrow’s lawyers to build with Claude, and we are starting a Legal Ambassadors Program so legal professionals can learn from each other.
What’s in the gallery
With these artifacts, a legal professional brings their own documents and sources, Claude completes the first pass, and a lawyer applies their judgment to the results. They cover the work legal teams raised with us most often:
- Cite check compares a legal document with its sources and flags quotes that don’t match, wrong page numbers, and sources that don’t support the claim.
- Jurisdiction survey matrix compares a legal topic, such as data breach notice rules, across states or countries in one table, with links to the underlying law.
- Matter board turns engagement letters, emails, or spreadsheets into one board of open matters, showing the owner, next step, and next deadline.
- Playbook deviation board compares contracts with your company’s standard terms, flags each clause that differs, and sends it to the person who approves exceptions.
- Regulatory horizon scan maps upcoming regulations on a timeline, based on your company’s business and where it operates, and ranks them by impact with links to the sources.
- Tabular review builds a table from a set of contracts, showing the terms you ask about, such as severance or non-competes, with links to the exact language.
Tailored to how teams work and shared with guardrails
Every legal team works differently and artifacts work best when they’re connected to the systems legal teams already use. Legal professionals can ask Claude to tailor artifacts to their team and use connectors to bring in their playbooks or research sources, so nobody has to upload documents manually.
Since we launched Claude for Legal, we’ve added more than 60 legal connectors, including Bloomberg Law, Filevine, Ivo, Legora, and Patlytics. See our [legal directory (opens in new tab)](https://claude.ai/directory/legal) for the complete list.
Artifacts enable collaboration inside and outside the organization. A legal team can work on an artifact with colleagues across the business or with clients and partners, with sharing settings that ensure privacy and support ethical walls between teams.
Opening the gallery to legal tech and law firms
We partnered with legal tech companies and law firms to build artifacts for legal professionals. Each artifact is in the gallery for legal professionals to discover, test, and adapt to their work:
- AI Governance Benchmark built by
[Goodwin (opens in new tab)](https://www.goodwinlaw.com/en)benchmarks a company's approach to AI governance to surface potential gaps. - Harvey Intake built by
[Harvey (opens in new tab)](https://www.harvey.ai/)gives business users one place in Claude to send legal questions and requests, answering routine ones from Legal’s own guidance in Harvey and routing the rest to a lawyer, whose reply comes back in Claude. - Obligations Checker built by
[Foley & Lardner (opens in new tab)](https://www.foley.com/)reviews agreements for the obligations of both parties and helps validate expectations pre-closing and track expectations post-closing. - Subpoena Response Tool built by
[PwC (opens in new tab)](https://www.pwc.com/)turns your team's precedents, standard objections and templates into automated, audit-ready first drafts so lawyers can focus on the complex issues while responding faster.
We are excited to see legal tech companies, law firms, legal aid organizations create and share their own artifacts, and have more artifacts coming from Legora and Orrick.
“At Accenture, Claude is helping us transform the way our legal teams work. We're excited about the opportunity to reimagine legal workflows and unlock new ways for our legal professionals to support our business.”
“Anthropic has invested heavily in building the best models for legal work. We build agents on Claude because it is best in class in our internal benchmarks and we're excited to continue pushing the frontier in legal with Anthropic.”
“Legal sits at the center of every agreement, but too often the work is disconnected from the rest of the business. With Anthropic, we're bringing the power of the Docusign platform directly into Claude, enabling legal teams and cross-functional stakeholders to create, review, and move agreements forward.”
“At Eve, we built PlaintiffBench to measure AI on the work plaintiff attorneys actually do, using real drafts, corrections and edge cases our customers have flagged. Every new model has to prove itself there before it reaches a firm, and Claude Opus 5.5 has made a real leap. For a plaintiff firm juggling hundreds of cases, those hours add up fast.”
“Personal injury cases aren’t built in one step. They’re built over months, through hundreds of connected judgments and tasks across records, notes and emails. Claude is the frontier model we trust to orchestrate that long-running work, so EvenUp can deliver at the standard firms and their clients depend on.”
“Litigation demands absolute precision: retrieving case-defining facts from vast stores of evidentiary materials and deploying purpose-built agents to take follow-on action, whether preparing a witness or drafting a motion. By connecting Filevine and LOIS to Claude, our customers can take that toolkit wherever they work and act directly on their case files.”
“We built the AI Governance Benchmark with Claude so any company can work through the same questions our AI practice uses with clients, see where its approach to AI governance has gaps, and know which areas to address first.”
“Business teams are already bringing their questions to Claude. Harvey meets them where they work, giving Legal the ability to set the rules, see what’s being asked, and step in to manage risk. We’re proud to build with Anthropic to make that possible.”
“The businesses that win act on their agreements as fast as they make decisions. Claude for Legal brings Ironclad's contracting intelligence directly into the platforms business teams already use. Ironclad's integration helps every Claude for Legal user move faster, reduce risk, and stay compliant, with trusted AI built on every agreement, approval, and obligation.”
“With Ivo and Claude, legal teams can turn the contracts they already keep in Ivo into artifacts they can share across their team—like a renewal calendar that tracks every notice date across their portfolio—with no manual uploads. Every answer is backed by the contract language it came from, and Ivo stays the system of record.”
“As legal teams adopt AI across more parts of their business, they need trusted legal intelligence available in those environments. By connecting Legora to Claude, we’re making it easier for mutual customers to get answers to legal questions within their broader enterprise AI workflows, with links back to Legora for source review, citations and deeper legal work.”
“For those of us protecting immigrant rights, the pace of change is dizzying. Moreover, the consequences of falling behind can be devastating. Immigration Papers Reader gives overstretched teams the tools to keep up and help families in turbulent times.”
“AI delivers value in Legal when it’s built into how lawyers actually work. Through our alliance with Anthropic, PwC’s engineers and our Legal Business Solutions team are building Claude-powered skills and integrations that connect directly to the systems legal teams rely on every day, with the security and governance the profession demands. This isn’t experimentation; it’s becoming part of how legal services are delivered.”
“For DC residents facing eviction or the burden of an old criminal record, legal assistance can change lives. Rising for Justice used Claude to develop tools that help attorneys identify rent ledger errors and assess eligibility for record sealing, streamlining case preparation and letting teams focus on clients' needs and goals.”
“On our chemical structure benchmark, Claude Opus 5.5 correctly identifies over 10% more structures than Opus 5 while using less than half the output tokens. In Solve, it powers patent work from drafting to litigation-grade claim charting.”
“Claude continues to power us as the most widely contract review tool in the world—we're approaching 500,000 contracts per month moving through Spellbook and we wouldn't be here without Claude.”
“At The Access Project, we build tools that help legal teams and self-represented litigants navigate record clearance. This artifact lets anyone start the clean slate process: screen for eligibility, obtain the record, understand how state law applies to each case, and find local filing guidance.”
“There is never enough time, and every minute spent on the math is a minute not spent on who the person is beyond the charge. The Criminal Charge Reality Check tool started with one question: how do we make that part faster, so the time goes to the person instead?”
Access to Justice and the Legal Ambassadors Program
The gallery includes nine access-to-justice artifacts, five of which were built by nonprofit and public interest organizations we supported with Claude credits:
- Criminal Charge Reality Check built by
[Zealous (opens in new tab)](https://zealo.us/)takes a criminal charge and shows defense teams the sentencing range, public data on how those cases usually end, and standard playbooks for release. New York only. - Immigration Papers Reader built by
[Mobile Pathways (opens in new tab)](https://www.mobilepathways.org/)turns a client’s immigration paperwork into a plain-language first read of key dates and missing documents. - Rent Ledger Reviewer built by
[Rising for Justice (opens in new tab)](https://www.risingforjustice.org/)helps attorneys find errors in a landlord’s rent ledger when preparing an eviction case. Based on D.C. law. - Record-Sealing Screener built by
[Rising for Justice (opens in new tab)](https://www.risingforjustice.org/)helps attorneys assess whether a client’s criminal record is eligible for sealing. Based on D.C. law. - Record Clearance built by
[The Access Project (opens in new tab)](https://accessprojectca.org/)helps legal aid teams work out whether a client’s record can be cleared under their state’s rules.
This builds on the Oxford Justice Innovators Programme, our 12-month program with the Oxford Institute of Technology and Justice and Microsoft that supports up to 10 innovators expanding access to justice.
We are also launching the Legal Ambassadors Program, a community for legal professionals who build with Claude to share their work and learn from each other. [Join the waitlist (opens in new tab)](https://form.typeform.com/to/GyMebQvL).
Getting started
Legal teams can [browse the gallery (opens in new tab)](https://claude.ai/artifacts?templates=legal) in Claude or start from our [Claude for Legal (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/solutions/legal) page.

title: Smart reports, surveys, and pooled group budgets for Claude Enterprise
body:
Smart reports, surveys, and pooled group budgets for Claude Enterprise
In many organizations, members have identified the unique work that Claude can unlock. The next step is expanding that work to every team.
Smart reports show what that work is, and where that work is happening, in-app surveys capture their feedback about how Claude is enabling them to do new work, and pooled group budgets let admins set one shared budget per team. All three are now generally available for Claude Enterprise.
Smart reports show how your teams work in Claude, and how to spread what’s working
[Smart reports](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/16893491-get-started-with-smart-reports) surface what a team gets done with Claude, and what that work costs. The reports show ambitious work your teams are doing with Claude, and how Claude made it possible. They then show how to turn that work into repeatable workflows, so the rest of your organization can do it too.
Pick a team, a date range, and the products to include. Claude analyzes a sample of the team’s transcripts and groups the work into workstreams. See the spend for each one, the deliverables produced, and the most common points of friction, such as a missing connector or a failed tool call.
Each report has one consolidated list of recommendations, including recurring workflows to turn into skills and rules to add to your code repository. Share any finding as an artifact with the people who can act on it. Reports also answer custom questions about model usage and cost, and admins can save their questions and custom insights as templates to reuse in future reports. If a spend limit is holding someone back, admins with billing permission can raise it from the report.
Owners can let team leads who aren’t admins run reports for their own groups, so the people closest to the work act on the findings. Smart reports help admins understand adoption and inform investment planning, but they aren’t for evaluating individual performance or making employment decisions.
“Smart reports give us greater visibility into how AI is used across the enterprise, helping inform decisions about deployment and governance. Early insights from smart reports are helping us identify effective workflows and emerging skills, providing a foundation for sharing what works more broadly across the organization.”
“I'm very close to how our teams use Claude, and smart reports still surfaced things I didn't know. That matters, because driving enablement at our scale means knowing where teams are thriving and where they need support. It's become a go-to part of my toolkit for those conversations with leaders across DoorDash.”
“Smart reports show us how teams use Claude, from coding Docusign IAM, our AI-native contracting platform, to everyday work. That visibility helps us show leadership real outcomes, fix connector bottlenecks, and scale what's working across teams.”
“We use smart reports across several initiatives. They give our applied AI team a grounded view of how Claude is being used across the company, which helps us prioritize what to do next and drive greater impact.”
“Claude smart reports give us a new level of visibility into how AI is actually being used across our organization. What's especially valuable is the ability to turn those insights into action, helping us identify high-value use cases, shape our enablement strategy, and focus learning where it can have the greatest impact.”
“Each smart report is based on tens of thousands of sessions, surfacing the most common pain points and the recurring workflows worth turning into skills. It’s exactly the visibility we’ve been looking for to get more value out of Claude.”
In-app surveys capture feedback
[In-app surveys](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/16764057-create-surveys-for-your-organization) add the team's own perspective on that work. The default questions focus on value: the most valuable thing someone has done with Claude recently, how Claude changed the time that work took, which use of Claude a teammate should copy, and, if the team lost access tomorrow, what would break or slow down first. Admins can customize or remove questions and choose who receives a survey, when it runs, and where it appears. Members see it as a short card after a reply in the tool they’re already working in.
Responses appear on the survey page as they arrive, and admins can export them to a spreadsheet. In-app surveys can now be enabled for organizations that use customer-managed encryption keys, and for organizations that set one retention period for all data, surveys and their responses are deleted on that schedule.
In-app surveys are treated as your data, so Anthropic accesses them only as necessary to operate the service.
Pooled group budgets put spend where the work happens
[Pooled group budgets](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/17005973-manage-pooled-group-budgets-on-enterprise-plans) give a group one shared monthly budget, so people who use Claude heavily are less likely to hit an individual limit early in the month while others leave budget unspent. Member limits still work as a guardrail against unusually high individual use. Every request counts against both, and a member stops at whichever runs out first. When someone hits a limit, they can request more from inside Claude, and the request goes to admins for review. The setup suggests an amount based on the group's recent usage, and admins with billing permissions receive email alerts at 50%, 75%, 95%, and 100% of a budget.
Getting started
Smart reports, in-app surveys, and pooled group budgets are generally available today for Claude Enterprise. Availability varies by configuration, including for organizations with a HIPAA configuration or customer-managed encryption keys. Visit the [Help Center](https://support.claude.com/en/) for eligibility and detailed setup steps.

title: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3
body:
Text Generation • 8B • Updated • 30.7k • 798
[
](#build-specialized-multimodal-models-with-lfm3)
Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3
[Team Article](/blog)
[LFM3](https://huggingface.co/collections/LiquidAI/lfm3) is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.
LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:
- More capability per parameter: a new tri-hybrid architecture and training recipe allow LFM3-1.7B to outperform LFM2.5-2.6B while using 35% fewer parameters.
- Every modality on one backbone: six 2B-class models (text, vision, audio, omni, and decision) trained from LFM3-1.7B-Base, including our first omni model and video input for our vision model.
- Built for the edge: the text model fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit precision, new in-house vision and audio encoders speed up processing, and the text model’s 256K context window lets agents run on-device.
- Made to be specialized: every model fine-tunes on a single GPU, so you can adapt it to your data, terminology, and deployment environment.
[
](#how-we-built-a-more-expressive-backbone)
How we built a more expressive backbone
LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.
LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:
- Tri-hybrid layer mix: 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention (SWA) layers with a 256-token window, and 6 global attention layers. The convolutions use a kernel size of 7, up from 3 in LFM2.
- Head-wise gated attention: a sigmoid gate scales each head's output, so a head can switch off when it has nothing to add. This can help suppress activation outliers that hurt quantization.
- Partial RoPE: global attention layers rotate only the highest-frequency half of each head, so the other half matches on content regardless of distance. SWA layers keep full RoPE.
- Sandwich norm: each block normalizes both its input and its output to keep activations well-scaled.
The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as [LFM2.5-8B-A1B](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-8B-A1B). The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.
[
](#one-backbone-for-six-models)
One backbone for six models
Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.
| Model | Input | Output | Built on |
|---|---|---|---|
|
[LFM3-VL-2B](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B)[LFM3-Audio-2B](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B)[LFM3-Omni-2B](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-Omni-2B)[d1-2B](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/d1-2B)[d1-omni-2B](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/d1-omni-2B)The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:
- Vision encoder: it combines convolution and attention and uses 3x less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models. Our 164M-parameter encoder matches Qwen3.5-2B's vision encoder in accuracy while requiring 2.2x fewer FLOPs (both measured with the same LFM2.5-230M language backbone). For video, it embeds each pair of sampled frames into one temporal slice, halving the temporal sequence length.
- Audio encoder and LiquidCodec: the audio encoder mixes sliding-window attention and short convolutions and is fully causal, so the model can prefill while you speak, with time to first token as low as 50 ms. LiquidCodec, our new audio tokenizer, turns generated tokens into speech at about 87x real time on a single CPU thread on Apple M4 Max and supports streaming decoding.
[
](#how-to-use-the-lfm3-models)
How to use the LFM3 models
Each model runs in transformers
. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.
[
](#lfm3-17b)
LFM3-1.7B
Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the [LFM3-1.7B model card](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B).
To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers
:
pip install -U transformers
Then load and run the model:
from transformers import pipeline
generator = pipeline(
"text-generation",
model="LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B",
trust_remote_code=True,
)
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What is C. elegans?"}]
output = generator(
messages,
do_sample=True,
temperature=0.1,
top_k=50,
repetition_penalty=1.1,
max_new_tokens=2048,
)
print(output[0]["generated_text"][-1]["content"])
For local agent setup, see the [Agent Harnesses guide](https://docs.liquid.ai/examples/agent-harnesses).
[
](#lfm3-vl-2b)
LFM3-VL-2B
Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the [LFM3-VL-2B model card](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B).
To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:
pip install "transformers>=5.21.0" torch torchvision pillow
Then load and run the model:
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, AutoProcessor
model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B"
model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto", trust_remote_code=True)
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
messages = [
{
"role": "user",
"content": [
{"type": "image", "url": "https://placecats.com/300/200"},
{"type": "text", "text": "Describe this image."},
],
}
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
messages,
add_generation_prompt=True,
tokenize=True,
return_dict=True,
return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)
with torch.inference_mode():
output_ids = model.generate(
**inputs,
do_sample=True,
temperature=0.1,
top_k=50,
repetition_penalty=1.1,
max_new_tokens=16384, # generate() needs an explicit limit; reasoning can be long
)
generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :]
print(processor.batch_decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)[0])
See the [LFM3-VL-2B model card](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B) for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.
[
](#lfm3-audio-2b)
LFM3-Audio-2B
Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the [LFM3-Audio-2B model card](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B).
To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2
with its audio dependencies:
pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch accelerate librosa soundfile
Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:
import torch
import soundfile as sf
from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor
model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B"
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code=True
).eval()
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device).eval()
Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:
conversation = [
{"role": "system", "content": "Respond with interleaved text and audio."},
{"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "audio", "audio": "question.wav"}]},
{"role": "assistant", "content": "<|mixed_start|>"},
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
conversation,
continue_final_message=True,
tokenize=True,
return_dict=True,
return_tensors="pt",
).to(device)
with torch.no_grad():
outputs = model.generate(
**inputs,
max_new_tokens=1024,
audio_temperature=1.0,
audio_top_k=128,
audio_repetition_penalty=1.1,
audio_repetition_window=4096,
return_dict_in_generate=True,
)
text = processor.decode(
outputs.sequences[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:],
skip_special_tokens=True,
)
waveform = codec.decode(
outputs.audio_codes[:1, :, :outputs.audio_lengths[0]]
).audio_values[0] # 24 kHz
print(text)
sf.write("reply.wav", waveform.float().cpu().numpy(), 24_000)
See the [LFM3-Audio-2B model card](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B) for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.
[
](#lfm3-omni-2b)
LFM3-Omni-2B
Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the [LFM3-Omni-2B model card](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM3-Omni-2B).

title: Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?
body:
Viewer • Updated • 3.68k • 238 • 4
[
](#can-we-trust-llms-to-judge-whether-a-research-idea-is-novel)
Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
Today we’re releasing [Old Ideas, Novel Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02022), a new study of how reliably large language models can evaluate the novelty of scientific research ideas. Alongside the paper, we’re publishing a benchmark, data, and code for testing novelty judges, plus an automated pipeline researchers can use to build new evaluation sets.
At Ai2, we’ve been developing AI systems that support different parts of scientific discovery. [DataVoyager](https://allenai.org/blog/asta-datavoyager) helps researchers explore and analyze structured data, [AutoDiscovery](https://allenai.org/blog/autodiscovery) generates and tests hypotheses, and [Theorizer](https://allenai.org/blog/theorizer) synthesizes evidence across large bodies of literature into candidate scientific theories. Together with [Asta](https://allenai.org/asta), these projects point toward systems that can help researchers move from understanding prior work to proposing, testing, and refining new ideas.
But generating research ideas is only part of the challenge of automating scientific discovery. Those ideas also need to contribute something genuinely new, which means these systems need a way to distinguish a novel direction from one that mostly repackages existing work.
That judgment is often handed to another LLM—what we call a novelty judge. Novelty judges assess whether a research idea is new relative to prior work, either on its own or in comparison with another idea. There’s no standard way to build one; research teams choose a model, prompt, evaluation format, reasoning budget, and sometimes a literature-retrieval system. Those choices can materially affect the verdict. Yet these judges are often validated only on human-written papers rather than the AI-generated ideas they are actually meant to evaluate.
Our new benchmark results suggest novelty evaluation itself is far from reliable. Across six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – seemingly small changes to the evaluation setup produce dramatically different judgments of the same ideas. In one experiment, changing just a few words in a prompt shifts a model’s accuracy in identifying which of two ideas is more novel by more than 50 percentage points. Retrieval and additional reasoning do not consistently improve judgments, and two purpose-built novelty evaluation systems perform worse than a simple prompted Claude Opus 4.6 baseline.
If AI is going to play a larger role in scientific discovery, we need more dependable ways to tell whether it is actually proposing something new. Our work provides tools for studying that problem, while showing how much remains unresolved.
[
](#building-a-benchmark-for-novelty-judges)
Building a benchmark for novelty judges
To test how reliably novelty judges can distinguish more novel research ideas from less novel ones, we first needed examples where there was strong evidence about the originality of the underlying scientific contribution.
So we built an automated pipeline around ICLR 2026 peer reviews. Rather than treating paper acceptance as a proxy for novelty, we mined the reviews themselves for passages where reviewers explicitly discussed a contribution’s originality. That distinction is key; a paper can be accepted without being particularly novel as long as it is strong enough in other aspects. Likewise, a rejected paper with an original contribution can have other weaknesses.
We created a high-novelty pool of 154 human-authored research ideas by selecting accepted papers in the top-rated 10% of their ICLR research area whose reviewers positively identified novelty and where no reviewer disputed it. We applied the reverse criteria to build a lower-novelty pool: 145 ideas from rejected papers in the bottom 10% whose reviewers raised originality concerns without any reviewer positively identifying novelty. In a separate check of the review-mining process, an annotator agreed with the extracted novelty-signal polarity in 47 of 50 cases; none of the disagreements would have changed whether a reviewer was counted as praising or disputing the paper’s novelty.
Together, these two pools form our first evaluation setting, Human-Only, which tests whether novelty judges can tell apart human-authored ideas with strong evidence of higher or lower novelty. But in practice, novelty judges are increasingly being used to evaluate AI-generated ideas. So we created a second setting, Human+Generated.
For this pool, we paired the same 154 validated human ideas with 154 ideas produced by a simple LLM generator. We assumed the generated ideas were less novel than their human-authored counterparts; these are weak labels, not verified judgments for every idea. The generator received only a research area and an instruction to propose a novel idea, with no literature search, tools, iteration, or feedback. This gave us a conservative comparison between ideas from a basic generator and contributions from top-10% ICLR papers whose reviewers had explicitly endorsed their originality.
As additional checks, an expert independently reviewed 30 Human+Generated pairs, heavily weighted toward cases our strongest judge got wrong, and we rewrote the human- and AI-generated ideas into a common structure to test whether judges were simply reacting to differences in writing style. The expert preferred the human idea in all 30 pairs and judged none of the generated ideas novel.
Importantly, many of our core findings don’t depend on the labels at all. If two reasonable evaluation setups give opposite answers for the same pair of ideas, that disagreement itself reveals instability.
[
](#small-changes-can-produce-very-different-verdicts)
Small changes can produce very different verdicts
Using our collections of human-authored and AI-generated research ideas, we tested how well six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – could evaluate novelty through both pointwise (i.e., absolute novelty ratings) and pairwise (i.e., comparing two ideas to find the most novel) comparisons. We varied one factor at a time: the prompt, reasoning budget, whether the judge could see related papers, how the ideas were formatted, how many judgments were combined into a final verdict, and – for AI-generated ideas – which model generated them.
The largest shifts in performance came from how we prompted the model to judge novelty.
For example, we showed GPT-5.4 the same Human+Generated pairs – each containing one validated human-authored idea and one AI-generated idea – with two prompts. One prompt told the model that reviewers had found exactly one idea in each pair to be novel and asked it to identify which one; the other simply asked which idea was novel. When we switched to the simpler prompt, accuracy dropped from 93.5% to 40.9% – below chance – and the model changed its verdict on more than half of the same pairs.
By contrast, the same prompt change shifted accuracy by only about seven percentage points on the Human-Only dataset, which pairs human-authored ideas with stronger and weaker evidence of novelty. That suggests a novelty judge can appear relatively stable on human-authored research but behave very differently on AI-generated ideas.
That said, human-authored ideas weren’t immune. We saw substantial shifts on the Human-Only dataset as well; the same change moved Claude Opus 4.6 accuracy by 21 points. The shifts were just less severe than on the AI-generated ideas.
There was also no universally better prompt. For example, when judging ideas individually, dropping an instruction that warned judges not to treat trivial or incremental contributions as novel improved accuracy for some judges while reducing it for others. A prompt that works well for one model may not transfer to another, in other words.
We also tested a common use of novelty judges: comparing ideas from two AI generators. We paired ideas from Claude Opus 4.5 with Claude Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5.4 with GPT-5.1. Across the tested prompt changes, roughly a quarter to a third of verdicts changed on average across six judges. This disagreement can be measured without assuming which generator produces more novel ideas, showing how the choice of judge prompt can affect comparisons between ideation systems.
More search and reasoning didn’t necessarily produce better novelty judgments. We gave GPT-5.6 Sol an extra-high reasoning budget and live, iterative search restricted to arXiv, then compared it with standard-retrieval judges that each saw five pre-retrieved abstracts. (All judges in this comparison ran once per idea on Human+Generated.) The agentic judge scored 0.78 macro-F1 – 11 points behind Claude Opus 4.6 at 0.89, and in roughly the same range as simpler Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.4 setups – while costing roughly 10× more per decision at current API prices. (In this context, macro-F1 measures how well a judge identifies novel and non-novel ideas; higher is better.)
Purpose-built evaluators weren’t more accurate either, despite costing substantially more. On the Human+Generated set, a simple Claude Opus 4.6 prompt using low reasoning and majority voting across three calls achieved 0.854 macro-F1 at a total evaluation cost of $2.59. By comparison, Idea Novelty Checker, a literature-grounded retrieval and reranking pipeline, scored 0.642 at $30.66, while Sakana AI’s AI Scientist, whose novelty evaluator iteratively searches Semantic Scholar, scored 0.772 at $82.05. (Both dedicated evaluators used Claude Opus 4.6, with one call per decision.)
In other words, the simple prompted baseline was both more accurate and considerably cheaper than either purpose-built system.
Taken together, these results suggest that novelty evaluation is particularly brittle on the AI-generated ideas these systems are increasingly being asked to judge.
[
](#toward-more-reliable-evaluation-of-novel-research)
Toward more reliable evaluation of novel research
Our results suggest that LLM-based novelty evaluation remains a major open problem. Judges that appear reliable on human-authored research may behave differently on AI-generated ideas; prompts that help one model can hurt another; and more search or compute does not necessarily produce more consistent judgments.
Future work should test judges on the kinds of ideas they will actually evaluate, measure sensitivity across prompts and models, improve how prior literature is incorporated, and build benchmarks that can evolve as the scientific literature grows and AI systems improve. Our benchmark and reusable data pipeline are a starting point—researchers can apply them to new peer reviews, other scientific communities, and future generations of novelty judges.
Automated ideation depends on more than generating plausible research directions; we also need ways to tell when those ideas are genuinely new. By making the weaknesses of current novelty judges easier to measure, we hope this release helps researchers build more robust ways to evaluate AI-generated research ideas.

title: Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation
body:
Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation
Today, we are announcing Genie 4, our new world model, which unlocks unprecedented realism and improves real-time interactive simulation. Genie 4 is natively multimodal, enabling audio-like music, ambient noises, and interactive dialogue to be simultaneously generated with the world.
The Genie 4 model incorporates and builds on capabilities from the Gemini family: Gemini Omni anchors the simulations in real-world appearance and behavior, while other Gemini models provide the complex reasoning needed to help maintain a simulationâs coherence and continuity.
With this foundation, you can set an event in motion, and Genie 4 simulates what happens next: how the world responds, how it sounds, and how the people in it move, react, and speak.
Understanding and simulating the world is a crucial aspect of building AGI. Genie 4 advances our ability to create safe, infinitely variable simulations that can help with everything from developing training environments for robots and agents to unlocking the creation of new interactive experiences.
We have started rolling Genie 4 out as a research preview for trusted testers â gathering feedback before we release it to consumers and developers, starting with Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Join the waitlist for Genie 4 in Project Genie [here](https://forms.gle/WQnSNEM3omF7Uruu7).
Genie 4 advances four key capabilities
The following are recordings of real-time interactions from Genie 4, where users use standard keyboard controls for navigation and camera control, and text prompts to steer the scene as it evolves.
Shaping world simulation in real-time
With Genie 4, you can use natural language to modify a simulation in real-time â like changing the weather, moving the camera, or introducing a new person or object â and Gemini will contextually adapt your prompt to match the surrounding scene. Between your inputs, Gemini also monitors and steers the scene to keep the world progressing cohesively.
Turn on audio to hear Genie 4 worlds.
Pushing the frontier in realism for physics and human action
Genie 4 introduces a new standard of realism to real-time interactive simulation. Built on an advanced physical understanding of the world, Genie 4 simulates real-world physics scenarios, such as aerodynamics, collisions, and more.
The most dramatic leap is how Genie 4 simulates people, creating characters that move naturally, respond organically to their environments, and can be interactively steered in real-time.
Modeling how the world sounds
Genie 4 is our first real-time world model to generate audio natively. Every world carries the ambient sound of its own setting, from wind in the trees to waves crashing at the beach.
The true frontier, however, is human speech. Genie 4 introduces interactive dialogue that adapts on the fly. Characters converse and react to your inputs or events in the world, all in real-time.
Simulating complex events with Gemini models
Bringing Gemini and Genie 4 together adds a new layer of reasoning to world simulation, allowing us to model complex, multi-step events and test how AI systems navigate different environments before bringing them to the real world.
To achieve this in real-time, Gemini 3.8 Flash serves as a guiding agent in the loop: as Genie 4 generates a world in real-time, Gemini continuously observes the scene, breaks down goals into a sequence of steps, and reviews incoming frames to track the progress and verify that each step succeeded. As the world shifts or the user intervenes, Gemini adapts its plan in the moment, unlocking worlds with reliable causality, procedural behaviors, and multi-step reasoning.
As part of exploring this capability, we have also been experimenting with Gemini 4 Argon and Genie 4 to bring our frontier research together with [Gemini Robotics](https://deepmind.google/models/gemini-robotics/).
In the example below, Argon breaks down a user-instructed task into steps for Genie to render. These steps are interleaved as text captions to Genie 4 as the simulation is rendering. Because Genie 4 can be steered in real-time with text captions using Gemini, this now unlocks the path of adapting the simulation as it progresses towards the completion of that task. This capability becomes a path for simulating a breadth of scenarios in imagined worlds, using Gemini 4 Argon and Genie 4.
Learnings from trusted testers
While Genie 4 is a major research milestone, it remains an early, experimental model. To understand how interactive world models can support real-world workflowsâand where they still need to growâweâve been working with cohorts of trusted testers across creative industries, journalism, education, gaming, and engineering.
Testers highlighted how the leap in photorealism, native audio, and real-time steering allows ideas and concepts to be turned into realistic simulations, unlocking new abilities across disciplines:
- Creative direction: Creatives and technologists are testing Genie 4 as a rapid "draft mode" for pre-visualization and ideation. For example, filmmakers can step into a live simulation of a scene and run multiple "takes" in real-time, adjusting camera angles, lighting, dialogue, and action on the fly.
- Historical scenarios & immersive photographs: Photojournalists are exploring how a single 2D archival photograph can become a grounded simulation of that environment in seconds. Teams are testing how populated, dynamic worlds can help experience historical spaces or visualize how short-term environmental events, like a flash flood or wildfire, unfold.
- Interactive experience concept design: Game developers and creative technologists are testing Genie 4 to go from an initial idea to an explorable prototype in seconds, testing visual styles, material aesthetics, and interactive mechanics through natural language prompts before writing a single line of engine code.
- Simulation: Aside from our robotics research, enterprise partners across industries are evaluating Genie 4 as a tool for rapid "zero-to-one" scenario generation, and identifying gaps to further improve Genie to best fulfill that simulation need.
Future Work: Towards hybrid world models
A promising path for future progress lies in hybrid world models, which combine the logical, structured reasoning of code and language models with the rich, sensory representation of pixel-level simulation.
Bringing Genie and Gemini models closer together is an early step in this direction. Gemini works behind the scenes to map the structure and plan the narrative timeline, while Genie generates the immediate physical realityârendering how the world looks, sounds, and responds, pixel by pixel. Together, these complementary strengths can unlock a new class of world models that are far more coherent, controllable, and grounded than either approach could achieve alone.
Building world models responsibly
Genie 4 marks a new area of frontier research that merges real-time generation and photorealism, introducing a new range of capabilities and dimensions that we want to roll out and explore in a responsible way. Genie 4 includes strict safety guardrails that are consistent with our safety policies across other models. Before launching this preview, we evaluated Genie 4 through internal rigorous safety evaluations to prevent the generation of harmful or malicious content. Also, we have intentionally deployed it first to trusted tester partners to get early feedback, before we release the model more broadly.
To maintain transparency, all video and audio generated by Genie 4 will include SynthID, our imperceptible digital watermarking technology that helps identify AI-generated content across visual and audio modalities.
Understanding current limitations
Genie 4 remains an early, evolving area of research.
While it can maintain coherent environments over short sessions, visual details and object permanence can still shift or drift over timeâespecially as a simulation runs longer, after multiple complex prompt edits, or when navigating throughout the scene. Complex physical interactions, real-time audio accuracy, rendering legible text, spatial accuracy, and long-term consistency are active areas of ongoing research. We are sharing Genie 4 as a preview to learn alongside our community and safely advance the frontier of interactive simulation.
Next steps for Genie 4
Genie 4 has been released as a research preview to trusted testers, and is coming soon to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Join the waitlist for Genie 4 in Project Genie [here](https://forms.gle/WQnSNEM3omF7Uruu7).
Weâre excited for users to step inside, experiment, and build their own interactive worlds soon.

title: How AI Is Changing the Pace of Discovery for Millions Living With Dementia
body:
There are 57 million people worldwide living with dementia today. For the researchers working to help them, the obstacle isn’t a lack of effort — it’s too much data, too few experts to synthesize it and a pace of discovery that can’t keep up with the disease.
The Consortium for Biomedical Research and AI in Neurodegeneration (C-BRAIN), working with NVIDIA, is using AI to change that.
Alzheimer’s disease is one of today’s leading global health challenges, with over 10 million new dementia cases diagnosed each year. Despite a 7x increase in National Institutes of Health funding in the last 15 years — reaching $3.9 billion annually — no treatment has been found to stop, prevent or reverse the disease yet.
The bottlenecks are not enough high impact scientific findings, too much data living in institutional silos and too slow a pace of synthesis to keep up with the research that is published.
C-BRAIN, led by Dr. Randall Bateman and a consortium of 18 member institutions across academic, philanthropic, pharma and research organizations, launched in November 2025 to help scientists make better, faster discoveries by accelerating the research that makes new treatments possible.
“We have a window of opportunity with artificial intelligence to do research fundamentally different than we’ve ever done before, in a way that accelerates discoveries to help patients,” said Bateman, founder and director of C-BRAIN and the Charles F. and Joanne Knight Distinguished Professor of Neurology at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. He described their work as “AI tools built by scientists, for scientists.”
The consortium is building a system that harnesses previously untapped Alzheimer’s research data to support scientists’ work.
Speeding Research From Weeks to Hours
Essential assets in Alzheimer’s research are datasets that have never been publicly accessible to AI tools or human researchers. This includes unpublished findings, negative results and governed proprietary data from member institutions.
“A lot of life sciences data doesn’t make its way into the frontier models,” said Dr. Ade Ojewole, chief technology officer of C-BRAIN. “The consequence of that is we’re leaving a lot of intelligence on the table.”
C-BRAIN refers to this as “dark data,” which slows down Alzheimer’s research.
Some dark data is directly deposited into secure computer systems for AI tools to access. To use this data without compromising patient privacy or institutional governance, C-BRAIN uses a hybrid centralized and federated approach — where AI models learn from data at each institution without that data ever having to leave its walls. This kind of infrastructure is technically demanding to build and scale, which is part of what NVIDIA brings to the collaboration.
C-BRAIN currently runs 64 [NVIDIA data center GPUs](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/) on premises alongside cloud-based nodes on Microsoft Azure, with additional NVIDIA GPU capacity, including [NVIDIA Blackwell systems](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/technologies/blackwell-architecture/), on the horizon as the consortium’s ambitions scale.
To explore how AI and accelerated computing can advance Alzheimer’s research while navigating its technical demands, C-BRAIN is working with NVIDIA to incorporate technologies including the [NVIDIA BioNeMo](https://github.com/NVIDIA-BioNeMo) open developer platform and the MONAI framework for C-BRAIN’s research pipelines.
“The C-BRAIN collaboration with NVIDIA aims to unlock those models in a way that they can deliver something quite impactful and important,” said Bateman.
“A great deal of optimization is going to be needed as we push the boundaries of what today’s spatial omics machine learning architectures can model,” Ojewole said. “NVIDIA software is definitely going to come into play there.”
Researchers at C-BRAIN have already built two tools: OpenScientist — built with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in an effort led by research scientist Justin Reese — and InsightEngine, built with 387 Labs.
OpenScientist is an open source agentic AI co-scientist that takes a scientist’s research question and dataset, then semi-autonomously generates hypotheses, runs analyses and produces verifiable, auditable insights. InsightEngine is an open source research platform that uses agentic AI to test hypotheses against the scientific literature, analyzing user-supplied datasets, exploring a biomedical knowledge graph and checking every claim against evidence to catch hallucinations before researchers commit to costly experiments.
In published case studies, OpenScientist completed analyses in minutes that domain scientists estimated would take weeks to months, at a cost of under $10 per run. At C-BRAIN’s current reach of over 200 research groups, this capability could release substantial research capacity, potentially exceeding one million hours annually at scale.
From Correlation to Cause
Looking ahead, C-BRAIN aims to build a multimodal biological foundation model trained on the full breadth of its data — neuroimaging, multi-omics, fluid biomarkers and longitudinal clinical measures.
By year three, it aims to discover new causal mechanisms of brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease, moving to testable scientific principles using the full scope of available research and data.
Bateman said, “AI that can think and reason has the potential to accelerate discoveries that will lead to powerful and implementable preventions and treatments for the entire population.”

title: What a $900M Bank Error Teaches Us About AI Agents - John Feminella, Two Sigma
body:
In 2020, Citibank accidentally sent about $900 million to Revlon’s lenders instead of an $8 million interest payment, even though the procedure, the warning pop-up and three approvers all did what they were supposed to. John Feminella, who works on AI architecture and engineering at Two Sigma, uses that story to show how to give AI agents real autonomy without locking everything down. He walks through five composable controls: an agent registry, risk-based review, tool access that follows an agent’s declared purpose, shared firm-wide evals, and classifiers that send humans only the approvals that matter. Views are his own, not Two Sigma’s.
