[Retell AI⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.retellai.com/) is a voice AI platform for contact center operations, helping businesses build agents that can answer questions, take action, and connect a caller with a person when needed. Its platform now serves more than 4,000 businesses, with monthly call volume growing from 30 million in early 2026 to more than 100 million by September.

As Retell serves more enterprises with complex workflows, it uses OpenAI models to keep call quality and reliability high. Today, OpenAI models generate responses for 80% of calls on Retell, with customers achieving resolution rates above 80%. Retell has also surpassed 1 trillion tokens consumed across OpenAI models, reflecting the scale of that adoption.

Retell’s engineers use Codex throughout development, from researching unfamiliar code to building features and debugging issues, and GPT‑6 Astra to test front-end interfaces.

> “We choose models the way our customers choose vendors: on real calls, not demos. OpenAI keeps earning its spot.”

—Bing Wu, Co-founder and CEO, Retell AI

## Choosing OpenAI models for the demands of a live call

Enterprise voice agents need to follow company policies and stay within their assigned roles, even as conversations change. Retell built its vCX benchmark to compare dozens of models using difficult, multi-turn conversations drawn from real production scenarios.

It tests how well models follow instructions, stay grounded in the information they are given, call the right tools, and use natural conversational language. In Retell’s October 13, 2026 benchmark, GPT‑6 Astra ranked first for instruction following at 89.7%.



Retell also shared evaluations conducted before the launch of the GPT‑6 Astra model that showed GPT‑5.5 ranking highest among models on both non-hallucination rate (88.0%) and tool-call correctness (88.3%) with reasoning enabled, outperforming Gemini‑3.1‑Pro and Claude‑4.6 on both measures. It also led on non-hallucination rate with reasoning off.

Retell says new customers who choose OpenAI models continue using them. Customers also have access to OpenAI Realtime models through the Realtime API and OpenAI text-to-speech as a voice engine. Retell makes new OpenAI models available the day they launch and reruns its benchmark as models improve.

## Resolving more than 80% of customer requests with agents

Contact center teams use Retell to define their agents’ business context, goals, and rules. Developers can further configure workflows and integrations.

During a call, Retell’s harness runs the audio models, tracks the conversation, and manages when the agent speaks, listens, or responds to interruptions. OpenAI models, including GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6 Astra, and GPT‑5.5, use the customer’s instructions and conversation context to generate responses and request tool calls. Retell executes those calls through integrations with the customer’s systems and can write outcomes back to a customer record.

When human judgment is needed, the voice agent briefs the representative with context, answers their follow-up questions, and confirms they are ready before connecting the customer. After a call, Retell uses GPT‑5.6 Terra to analyze the transcript and extract outcomes and other data.



With this approach, Retell reports customer resolution rates above 80%. At electronics company Anker, agents handle Tier‑1 post-sales support in the US and UK, including order tracking, warranty checks, and troubleshooting. Anker reported an 80.4% case resolution rate and a Net Promoter Score (NPS) of 63. Its team also said the agents’ tone, pacing, and warmth met the standard they expected of a human agent.

At Pine Park Health, Retell agents handle appointment reminders and proactive scheduling and record the outcomes in patients’ medical charts. The team recovered medical-assistant time equivalent to 2.1 full-time roles and redirected it to patient care. Its scheduling agent achieved a 55.7% booking rate when it reached a patient.

## Keeping calls responsive as volume grows

Daytime traffic on Retell’s platform can reach more than 50 times its overnight low. To help keep calls responsive even at peak demand, Retell uses dedicated servers with OpenAI, shared across its customers. In Retell’s October 13, 2026 benchmark, GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6 Sol each recorded median first-sentence latency of 883 milliseconds, with GPT‑5.6 Luna ranking highest at 497 milliseconds.

OpenAI’s regional API endpoints allow developers to route traffic to specific geographic regions, which helps Retell reduce network travel time and meet customers’ data residency requirements in industries such as healthcare and financial services.

Retell also builds redundancy into each layer of the service. It runs its own telephony stack with a second stack ready to take over, along with backups for voice and model services, to help keep calls running when a service fails.

## Using Codex to research, build, and debug

As Retell’s enterprise growth brings more requests for custom workflows and integrations, its engineers often need to work in unfamiliar parts of the codebase. Before writing code, they give Codex a high-level requirement. Codex surveys the code, checks it against actual data, and explains what needs to change. One engineer said Codex did this research better and much faster than he could.

During implementation, engineers say Codex often catches details they had not considered. For debugging, Codex cross-references logs and database records with the code to investigate what is happening. Retell’s engineers also use Codex in their work with customers building on OpenAI models to speed up tasks such as writing the instructions that guide how a model responds in a customer’s application.

To test changes to its web interface, Retell relies on GPT‑6 Astra’s computer use. When an engineer opens a front-end pull request, GPT‑6 Astra opens the interface, clicks through it, tests flows, tries to break them, and reports the issues it finds. Retell says earlier models could not perform this work reliably.

Retell continues to hire, but its engineering team hasn’t needed to grow at the same pace as the business. Retell reports $1.6 million in annual revenue run rate per employee.

> “By using Codex, the engineering team has a virtual teammate that can pair with them on any kind of difficult task.”

—Bing Wu, Co-founder and CEO, Retell AI

## Putting customer expertise to work

Every business knows how it wants to serve its customers. Retell’s goal is to let the people closest to that work apply their expertise directly, using advanced voice AI and a platform that lets them build, test, and improve their own agents. Next, Retell plans to expand quality assurance and simulation, support more languages, and develop knowledge base auto-learning.

As OpenAI models continue to advance, Retell expects its customers to deliver world-class service to millions of callers, on their own terms.

“No one knows a company’s customers better than the company itself. We give them the power to act on that expertise and improve AI agents directly. The goal is for them to build an in-house team of internally deployed engineers who own and run it all,” says Bing.

title: The new primitives of agentic software delivery
body:
Published Time: 2026-10-27T14:37:36+00:00

Markdown Content:
The promise of AI-first software development is extraordinary: describe what you want, and agents turn it into working software. But that framing treats the middle as a black box. Intent goes in, software comes out, and everything in between is assumed to simply be faster.

It isn’t that simple. Every stage of the software development lifecycle is changing, but not uniformly—some stages are transforming faster and earlier than others, and as capabilities improve, the bottlenecks move.

That’s why ambitious teams who try to transform the entire SDLC at once tend to struggle: when everything changes together, it’s hard to see what’s working, what’s failing, and what to fix. The problem is tractable, but only if we start with the primitives—the jobs to be done at each stage, the artifacts each stage produces, and the knowledge that connects them.

When we align on those primitives, the new software delivery system takes shape.

## The jobs remain while the work changes

Software engineering has always required us to define goals, create software, validate and deliver it, and understand what happens when people use it. Agents change where human attention is needed, but the underlying flow remains.

![Image 1](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/command-line-flow-v4-1-1024x848.png)

The SDLC has always followed a common workflow—several stages forming a loop: Plan, Build, Validate, Deploy, and Observe. In the last 20 years, we’ve introduced a wide variety of tools and automation to help us optimize how much time and energy we spend in each stage, but the stages themselves have stayed durable.

![Image 2](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/command-line-flow-v5-1-1024x749.png)

The new software delivery system retains these core stages with a key change: each stage now draws from (and contributes to) a shared foundation of knowledge. While the stages themselves are familiar, the human jobs to be done across the whole lifecycle change dramatically.

For each stage, we can make the transformation concrete by identifying the human job-to-be-done and the output artifact that carries the work forward. Trust is established at every stage in the lifecycle, and carries forward what it produced, the evidence behind it, and the questions that remain. That understanding then helps guide the decisions at the next stage.

| **Stage** | **Purpose** | **Human JTBD** | **Artifact** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Plan | Define & measure goals | Choosing the right problems, resolving ambiguity, deciding on tradeoffs | Goals & acceptance criteria to guide creation & validation |
| Build | Translate goals into a working system | Guide important design decisions + resolve problems that require human judgment | Candidate implementation (usually a PR) + context necessary to understand the choices made |
| Verify | Get the system into real people’s hands | Judge whether the system has produced what the team set out to build | Auditable evidence of system behavior & a record of what was released, where, & under what conditions |
| Observe | Operate the system & analyze the results | Interpret signals, develop insights, & decide what ships to production | Real outcomes that inform the next set of goals & system improvements |

### Plan

Define and manage goals: what we want to achieve, the constraints we must respect, and how we’ll measure success. Human attention goes to choosing worthwhile problems and resolving ambiguity and tradeoffs. The output is a set of goals and acceptance criteria that can guide creation and validation.

### Build

Translate those goals into a working system. Agents take on more implementation work while humans guide consequential design decisions and resolve problems that require their judgment. The output is a candidate implementation (in the form of a PR), together with the context needed to understand its choices.

### Verify

Determine whether the implementation satisfies the intended goals, and when ready, put it in the hands of real users. Agents test and validate code across an array of dimensions (correctness, performance, security, etc.) and produce discrete, auditable evidence. Human energy shifts to the central question of “is the thing we built what we intended to build” and away from verifying implementation correctness.

### Observe

Operate the system, observe its behavior, and run experiments. Humans interpret signals, develop insights, and decide when and how users should experience changes. This stage produces signals and data which inform the next goals, experiments, and operational improvements.

## The knowledge at the center

Data and context form an essential part of the SDLC. Historically, much of that knowledge has been stored in the minds of individual developers rather than in shared records. At a startup, it may even be a single person! That person connects customer needs, design decisions, implementation, releases, and system operations. As the product and teams grow in complexity, the knowledge base fragments across more people and the ability to seamlessly connect data breaks down.

Within the new software delivery system, the knowledge layer becomes the new glue—it connects goals, design decisions, implementation context, validation evidence, release history, production signals, detailed agent behavior logs, and lessons synthesized from them. It keeps the source and version of each item, separates observations from interpretations, and serves the context each job is permitted to use.

So while the _idea_ of knowledge is familiar, the ability to access and use that knowledge changes fundamentally. A production finding can shape validation, influence implementation, and change the next round of planning. Each stage uses and enriches the knowledge available to both agents and humans at any stage of the SDLC.

## From theory to practice

At Microsoft, we’re putting these primitives into action, building them into our developer products:

*   Copilot can take an issue, spin up its own secure GitHub Actions environment, analyze the repo, change code, run validation, and produce a draft PR for human review. Developers can then delegate to the coding agent from GitHub, VS Code, mobile, and other surfaces.
*   Copilot Code Review now supports agent skills and MCP, letting teams bring repo-specific standards and external context from issue trackers, docs, and other systems directly into reviews.
*   And because the Copilot harness packages instructions, scripts, and supporting resources into reusable skills, successful ways of working become reusable production assets rather than staying trapped in an individual agent session.

While the agentic software delivery machinery matures and takes shape, we know that human involvement will continue to be essential now and in the future. Agents will help us achieve our goals, but it is up to us to identify the needs of users and to define, validate, and understand the products we create.

### Memory needs a purpose

The new central knowledge layer contains an incredible amount of context and data—signals from all different phases of the SDLC, user interaction, and agent behaviors. However, vast quantities of raw data do not improve agent behaviors. The data becomes useful when it enables agents to answer specific questions.

In the last year, we’ve started to describe this territory using words like “memory” and “dreaming.” Nomenclature aside, the point is bringing together data in a way that enables an agent to do its job better: avoid repeating mistakes, recognize relevant constraints, or improve decision-making based on past outcomes.

That gives us an engineering test and an evaluation. Does an agent perform a job better with the synthesized knowledge than without it? Is it more effective? Is it faster? Is it more efficient? Similar to a database index or a materialized view, the goal of memory is to give an agent quick access to data from the past to improve future performance.

### Tackle each stage of the SDLC independently, in parallel

Decomposing the new software delivery system gives us a practical way to make progress. For each stage, define the inputs, the jobs to be done by both humans and AI, the output artifact, and the criteria for success. Improve the agents with the same care used to validate the software they produce.

Those improvements must also add up to a better journey from idea to customer. Faster creation has limited value if validation can’t establish trust in the result. More experiments help when their findings improve subsequent decisions. The contracts and feedback between stages are part of what we need to engineer.

Even a loop that runs repeatedly without human intervention would still contain these responsibilities. It needs goals, an implementation, evidence that the implementation meets those goals, a way to reach users, and a way to learn from actual outcomes. Autonomy does not remove that structure.

Make no mistake: each stage of the lifecycle exists within the new software delivery system—even if we stop thinking about it explicitly as trust builds. But for now, we _must_ think in terms of durable components as we stand up our initial software delivery systems in order to ground the human jobs to be done.

## More room for human judgment

There are important human jobs at every stage of today’s SDLC. As this system matures, our attention will increasingly concentrate on the places that require higher-level judgement. In the near term, I suspect we’ll be most concerned with validation, operation, and planning: determining if the code agents produce is trustworthy, improving how our systems run in production, and rethinking how we define goals for the software delivery system.

These jobs require judgment about value, intent, and customer experience. A software delivery system can execute a loop autonomously without establishing that its goal was worth pursuing in the first place. Humans and a refined sense of taste are necessary to identify and produce lasting value.

Building dependable software delivery system primitives gives us a way to expand automation while continuing to improve the quality of our decisions. As agents take on more of the work, we gain more time to define ambitious goals and bring incredible new experiences to life.

title: No Man Is an Island
body:
In this post, I argue that individual intellectual activity can only be sustained in an intellectual community of other humans. AI dissolves these communities, which in turn makes private intellectual activity rarer.
The Case of Software
Some years ago, when it became clear that AI would solve software engineering, my thinking was:
- In my professional life, I’m happy to move one level up to become a manager of AI agents. I’m literate, I’m a good technical writer, I can describe what I want and let AI agents write the code.
- In my own time, I can keep doing the things I care about because I enjoy them intrinsically. This is the “intellectual” side of software engineering: reading technical blog posts and papers, learning new programming languages, designing new programming languages, writing technical essays, writing code for my tiny open source projects.
The second point has not quite worked out. What actually happened? First, the
discourse of software engineering became worse. As I [wrote earlier](/article/the-education-of-a-doomer):
Claude Code was released a little over a year ago. In that short time, software engineering has been completely transformed. Materially, it might be positive: higher productivity, though at the cost of a messier codebase. Socially, it has been a disaster.
The discourse around software engineering has gotten dumber. It’s like everyone in the industry lost 30 IQ points. People used to talk about compilers, type systems, logic. Now they talk about “prompts”, “harnesses”, “loops”. The discourse is narrower, shallower, and more repetitive. There’s only so many times I can hear about “agentic harnesses” before I lose my mind.
Then there’s the loss of human capital formation: there is nothing to learn. Prompting is not a skill, at least, it’s a much shallower skill than software engineering. The instrumental dimension of the work has improved in that people can get more output per unit of effort, but the dimension of work that’s about building up human capital has collapsed. And maybe this is rational. Why learn to code at all? The computers can do that for us. And so the rigorous, systematic thinking you need to practice in order to be a good programmer: all gone. The machines can be rational for us. We can just vibe.
Second, contributing to the commons of software engineering is increasingly pointless. Before AI, you could publish open-source code, write blog posts to share ideas or inspire other people, write expository texts like tutorials, forum posts, textbooks etc. to teach people. After AI, what’s the point?
- You write a blog post: who’s going to read it? The next training run will ingest it, marginally improving AI capabilities. Maybe the post was a workaround to some obscure technical problem, so the next time someone encounters that problem, they will ask Claude, who will solve it without crediting you. Maybe you had some insight about how to structure large codebases: who cares? The humans aren’t making those decisions anymore.
- You design a revolutionary new programming language: who cares? Maybe Claude cares, for what that’s worth. But humans don’t write or even read the code anymore. The programming language is an implementation detail the humans no longer have to care about.
- You write a library, and publish it on GitHub: who cares? The AIs might discover it, and use it, but the operator won’t know you exist or did anything.
It’s not just “you can’t get GitHub stars or traffic to your blog”; rather, there is no sense of a common human project you can contribute to. There’s your own private garden of code, which you can grow infinitely in all directions with the help of AI, but you never have to leave the garden and go to the bazaar to trade with people. Under these conditions, it’s hard to care or do anything.
But does it actually matter? Does it matter if we stop writing blog posts about
obscure JavaScript features, and designing new programming languages? Maybe
writing code was always drudgery, and now we can move on to higher things, like
math—[oh, wait](https://proofsandprompts.com/2026/10/08/100-reactions-to-100-solutions/).
The Intellectual Life
From observing what happened to software engineering, and what’s currently happening to mathematics, I think we can derive some general insights about intellectual practices in general.
We tend to think of intellectual activity as private and solitary: the philosopher sitting in his armchair, deriving the world ab initio. But intellectual activity has two inputs that can’t be acquired in isolation: a shared body of work to build upon, and motivation. The shared body of work is communal, unless you want to recapitulate the entire tech tree. Motivation we can break down into two components:
- Intrinsic motivation: we learn for the sake of learning, we create art from a compulsion we can’t understand, etc.
- Extrinsic motivation: David Chapman
[defines](https://meaningness.substack.com/p/nobility-table-of-contents)“nobility” as manifesting glory for the service of others, and using our abilities in service of others. We want our work to be useful to others, we want others to benefit from our work, we want to contribute to a shared human project. Fame and the esteem and good will of your peers are the proxies by which we measure our contribution.
We tend to think of intrinsic motivation as the purest kind: endogenous, self-created, unmotivated by material or social gain. But it’s an emotion, and, like all emotions, it’s transient and short-lived. And this is rational: otherwise, we’d all be stuck in life-long unproductive obsessions. So, we need something to fill the gaps between moments of divine inspiration. Extrinsic motivation serves this function.
Private intellectual activity that is sustained, complex, and long-term requires an external intellectual community to provide material and motivation, like fuel and oxidizer. That private activity, in turn, sustains the community: by publishing papers, textbooks, code, etc., you add to the shared body of work for others to build on top of; by citing someone’s paper or contributing to their repository, you give them the recognition and honor that confirms they are doing useful work, which in turn motivates them to keep contributing.
Without community, you don’t get isolated individuals each working on their own things: you get nothing. The inputs to intellectual activity dry up: no one is adding to the shared body of work, and there are no peers to benefit from your own intellectual activity. Without this extrinsic motivation, you get less intellectual activity because, again, intrinsic motivation is fleeting.
After AI
After AI, intellectual contributions become unnecessary or redundant. In the case of software: the AIs write all the code, so what’s the point of writing either code or prose? The audience for those things is now severely diminished. Humans don’t write code anymore, so they won’t read blog posts about how to write code, or tutorials, or try new libraries or programming languages. In the case of mathematics: the AIs can prove theorems, write papers, explain papers, tutor students, and in the near future, they might write entire textbooks better than humans. So what’s the point of writing a paper, or a textbook? It’s superfluous.
If intellectual activity is unnecessary—if there’s no consequence to designing a new programming language or publishing a paper, or if there’s simply no community to contribute to—then it won’t happen. There’s no point.
Now apply this to every other domain of intellectual activity, and you see what the future looks like. There may be individuals building new libraries and programming languages, but no shared culture of software engineering; there may be individual students and practitioners of mathematics, but no living community of mathematicians.
Why We Underrate Intellectual Community
I’ve spoken to people who think AI will have a positive effect on the life of the mind, and their thinking is that right now too many people are doing intellectual activity for instrumental reasons: citations, clout, etc. In this view, the collapse of intellectual communities is good, because it sifts the intrinsically-motivated übermenschen from the clout-chasing masses.
I think this view fits with contemporary society: we view intrinsic and extrinsic motivation as high and low status, respectively. A “developed” person is supposed to have a private, inexhaustible reserve of motivation which is causally disconnected from external reward.
But this is not a realistic view of human beings. Humans are social animals who can only flourish in the society of other humans. We care, and we should care, about contributing to the world. And if technology makes our contributions superfluous, then what is left?
Acknowledgements
Thanks to [Luke Drago](https://lukedrago.com/) and [Andy Matuschak](https://andymatuschak.org/) for feedback and conversations.

title: Why Are We Still Governing AI Agents Like Software? - Tim Tyler, Gravitee
body:
Nobody would hire a worker with no ID, no manager and shared passwords, yet that's how most companies deploy AI agents. Tim Tyler of Gravitee presents the Agent Accountability framework, which governs agents like a digital workforce in three stages: Assignment (identity, team, a named human sponsor), Alignment (role, mission and least-privilege authority) and Administration (oversight scorecards, guardian agents and step-by-step recourse when agents go off course).

title: Reforging the Workflow: Where the Human Goes When Agents Ship | Martin Gratzer
body:
At the beginning of the year I wrote that the PR is the [last one standing](/posts/forging-a-workflow/) for keeping a shared understanding of a codebase when agents do the coding work. The final call is with the human, and that was the idea I built [Forge](https://github.com/mgratzer/forge) around. Time passed, and now my agent is allowed to merge pull requests on its own. I changed my mind because I caught less and less that the agent and the system around it hadn’t caught first. Don’t get me wrong, I’m still in the loop and I’m still in control. I just spend less time reading diffs and more time at both ends: defining the problem before the agent starts, and shaping the system it works in. That doesn’t mean the agent builds a whole feature in one go. I still break the work into Issues, each one a vertical slice that can ship to production on its own or behind a feature flag.
The system around the agent constrains it. I like to think of the guardrails as a boundary that funnels the agent in the right direction. That system has two parts: the repository the agent works in, and Forge, the skills that tell it how to work. I’ve been shaping both, across all my projects.
My Reviews Stopped Paying Off
In January I left 126 inline review comments on 25 [Colorburst](https://www.colorburst.app) PRs. That was the collaborative loop I described in February. In September and October I left none, across 159 PRs. [Tandler](https://tandler.app), my newest project, has three handwritten review comments in total, all on one of its first PRs.
The agent still makes mistakes, but now something other than me catches them before anything is merged. On a Colorburst quota change, two fresh-context reviewers noticed that the test fixtures used a pricing tier that doesn’t exist, so the tests passed without ever testing the free tier. On a dependency update, an adversarial review attacked the SVG sanitizer with 30 crafted payloads and found three ways around it. Both were fixed in the same PR, before I even looked at it.
An Experiment With a Friend
My own projects have one weakness as evidence: I know how to guide an agent. So I started an experiment with my friend Andreas, who shares our office space. He is a civil engineer and had an idea from his field for a very long time. When I showed him Claude, exploring it became feasible for him for the first time, and he built a prototype with Claude Cowork.
The prototype was functional and visually impressive, and a potential customer he showed it to was very excited. Underneath, it was a typical vibe coding disaster by someone who didn’t know anything about software engineering: no git at first, no CI, one big index.html
full of inline JavaScript, and almost a gigabyte of data read on every lookup, because nobody had told him to use PostGIS for geodata.
For me it was very exciting to see how far he got. I wanted to help him get it off the ground, and to see how far a domain expert who only describes functionality can get with a setup that gives agents solid engineering guidance. It’s a win-win: I get my insights, and he gets a shot at turning his domain knowledge into software that can scale as a business. We restarted from the prototype with the structure of my own projects: linting, dead and duplicated code detection, import boundaries, migration checks, high coverage requirements, and a pipeline that deploys every commit to main on a VPS. Then I handed it over to him, together with the Forge skills. I taught him how to shape a problem and let the agent build it and run the app for him, so he can try what he’s creating and refine it on the spot. He doesn’t look at the code, because he doesn’t even know what it means.
He opened 85 PRs in his first five weeks, around a thousand lines each. My job in the experiment was to spot problems in the setup, so I reviewed with a narrow focus: did the agent put the pieces together correctly? Whether the domain logic was right, I couldn’t judge. I’m not deep enough into his field, and understanding everything in a thousand-line PR was too much cognitive load anyway. In September I approved 45 of his 48 PRs. For the details I often leaned on Claude’s /code-review
, posted its findings under my name and opened fix PRs myself. Simon Willison would call that [meat proxy review](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Aug/3/dont-be-a-meat-proxy/). It fixed the PR in front of me and left the setup as it was. What helped was looking for patterns across his PRs and agent sessions and turning them into guardrails.
Structure Is What Makes Trust Possible
In February I wrote that structure amplifies capability. I’d go further now: structure is what makes trust possible. An agent that can prove its change works gives you something to rely on besides your own reading of the diff. Thorsten Ball [asks his agent](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z7l1EHfCMU8) to “give me irrefutable proof that this works now”, and reviews only what he calls “load-bearing code” (his words, for once not Opus’s). When a PR comes with a test matrix and screenshots, he says, you go into the review completely differently.
Sometimes the proof is wrong. After an image model swap, every new Colorburst template shipped without a title or tags for about five weeks, CI green, because the tests hardcoded the model’s response. Reading those PRs wouldn’t have caught it either, so the fix was another guardrail: a live contract test against the real model.
Everyone Is Converging
What finally made me change Forge was watching others arrive at the same place within a few weeks. The Claude Code team at Anthropic [optimizes for](https://claude.dev/blog/solving-code-review-at-anthropic/) “the minimum amount of human review time that doesn’t raise reverts or incidents”. Low-risk changes need no human approval once the checks are green, because “the change sets the tier, not the author.” At Imprint, Will Larson’s team built the [ small-change](https://lethain.com/small-changes/). CI decides whether a PR qualifies, a review skill can only approve or ignore it, and every error it lets through counts as a failure of the system. Gergely Orosz calls much of what is left elsewhere “
[zombie code reviews](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ru99FGJ_yuE)” (his
[deep dive](https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/what-is-happening-with-code-reviews)covers the whole range), and the Amp team dropped PRs altogether.
All of them, with very different risk profiles, take the human off the default path and spend human attention where the risk is.
Forge, Reforged
Every finding in one of my projects ends up in one of two places. Some only make sense in that repository, like the seeded database in Colorburst’s CI. Others are about how an agent should work anywhere, and those go into Forge. In Colorburst and Tandler, agents had been running the app end to end and writing it up in the PR for a while. That became Forge’s exercise step. A day of bringing Andreas’s stacked PRs up to date with main became a guard that keeps the branch mergeable. And his review load, together with the Anthropic post, became land.
/forge-setup-project # once per repo: AGENTS.md and the docs agents work from
/forge-ship 42 # implement Issue #42, exercise it, review it in fresh context, open the PR
/forge-ship --guard 42 # and keep going: CI, review feedback, then a risk verdict
Ship implements the Issue, then exercises it: it runs the app, uses the changed path once, and writes what it saw into the PR’s ## Exercised
section. A fresh-context reviewer, not the session that wrote the code, reviews the diff.
Guard drives the PR to review-ready without anyone watching, through CI, review feedback and a mergeable branch. It never merges, because a loop that fixes its own PR shouldn’t also approve it.
Land is the newest. It judges a green PR’s risk in fresh context, on the head commit. Mechanical checks come first, such as size, migrations, CI changes, security-sensitive paths and weakened tests. If none of them hit, the verdict is low risk only if the reviewer can name what the checks would miss. Otherwise the PR gets a short “where to look” list, each item a file and a question. With Auto-merge: low-risk
in AGENTS.md
, land merges a low-risk PR itself, and only the commit it judged.
I turned auto-merge on in Colorburst, Tandler and Andreas’s project a few days ago, so it’s too early to say how often land is right. Of its first six verdicts on Andreas’s PRs, two were low risk. One of the four that need review asks whether the code reads a clause of the building regulations correctly, which only Andreas can answer.
/plugin install forge --marketplace mgratzer/forge # Claude Code, with a live lens beside the session
npx skills add mgratzer/forge # any other agent
What Doesn’t Transfer Yet
Forge stays PR-based, unlike Amp. The PR is where the evidence lives, and it’s the unit the teams I work with already understand. Review didn’t go away either, it moved: every PR still gets an independent review in fresh context, and land sends the risky ones to a person. Accountability is still there: I decide whether a repository’s guardrails are good enough, and I fix them when something slips through. As the Claude Code team puts it: “Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it.”
And these are my own projects, built for production but by one person, without a team or compliance around them. Gergely [found](https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/what-is-happening-with-code-reviews) that the other cases of fully automated review were side projects, single-person businesses and very early startups. At work there is compliance, and there is knowledge sharing: if nobody reads what shipped, nobody understands what shipped. That’s what we’re working on now, figuring out what these learnings mean for our software development lifecycle.
Where the Human Goes
Andreas wants to move fast, not only when building but also when getting his PRs out the door. I was the bottleneck, reviewing in the evenings, and this week we both decided to find a better way.
Stopping my reviews wasn’t a leap of faith. Review is one control among many, and right now the risk is low: the project has no users yet, land still sends migrations and risky paths to a person, and the models and coding agent harnesses keep getting better. My evening reviews added delay, not much safety. So he moves on, and I spot check and improve the system without blocking him. When real users arrive, the goal is to keep his pace while the system gets safer, the way the Amp team does with feature flags and agents watching production. He brings the domain knowledge, and I keep shaping the system around him.
That’s the part I care about most, in his project and in mine: finding where an agent drifts, asking where it could have been avoided, and fixing it there. That can be in how I shape the issue, in the repository, like a rule about building regulations, or in Forge, like running the app before opening a PR, so every project gets it. The shaping happens before the agent starts, and I spend a lot of time on it. It’s sparring, not dictating: dumb questions, poking holes in the agent’s assumptions and in mine, until we’ve covered everything relevant. In February I called planning the step where the human adds the most value, and that hasn’t changed. No human in the middle, a human at both ends: a well-shaped issue going in, and a system that funnels the agent around it.
How that holds up might be worth another update in a few months.

title: 300 Agents, 60 People: How We Secured Our Own AI Agents - Aiden Sochowski, Runlayer
body:
Runlayer is a company of about 60 people running 300+ agents every day. Founding engineer Aiden Sochowski shares what they found once they put a gateway in front of everything and logged every session and tool call: prompt injection through email, PR-review agents getting talked into approvals, over-permissioned bots, one poisoned agent contaminating others, buggy vibe-coded MCP servers burning tokens, and a model switch that raised costs over 100x in a week.

OpenAI and Oracle are bringing Oracle applications and data into ChatGPT and powering new Oracle products and services with OpenAI models and products. Together, we aim to help businesses use AI to run core operations, build better applications, and strengthen security.

This builds on our commercial relationship across the OpenAI API, ChatGPT Work, and Codex. Oracle [reported⁠](https://openai.com/index/oracle/) 130,000 active ChatGPT users and more than 95,000 active Codex users. Its recruiting team uses ChatGPT Work for market research that once took two to four days to compile, with preparation now taking 15–20 minutes.

OpenAI and Oracle share a vision for an agent-ready enterprise where people and AI agents work across business applications in one connected environment. Our goal is to make Oracle software easier to discover, use, and manage, with simpler administration, unified sign-in, and access governed by each organization’s permissions and approvals. This would help businesses scale AI across core operations and get more value from the software they already use.

## Working with Oracle in ChatGPT

Oracle is developing [Oracle AI Workspace⁠](https://openai.com/business/partners/oracle/) to bring that vision into ChatGPT through integrations with Oracle applications and data. The goal is to let people describe what they need to accomplish, find the right information, and complete approved business workflows in one place.

For example, a new finance team member could use ChatGPT to investigate costs, understand purchasing decisions, and identify what remains before month-end close. The intended experience would bring information from finance, procurement, and planning applications together, helping more employees use Oracle software within their organization’s permissions and approvals.

## Bringing AI to Oracle’s products

Alongside Oracle AI Workspace, Oracle is announcing updates and new offerings built with OpenAI models and tools:

- **Oracle AI Security Mesh** is designed to help customers find and fix vulnerabilities in applications and infrastructure using OpenAI cyber models. Oracle manages the testing infrastructure, helping customers put these capabilities to work safely and within their authorized scope.
- **Oracle AI SMB Bundle** combines ChatGPT Business and Codex with Oracle applications and recurring Oracle Cloud Infrastructure credits to help small businesses build products and manage operations.
- **Oracle App Composer** is designed to help teams build apps with Codex and other AI tools, connect them to approved Oracle data and workflows, and share them across their organization. Oracle manages deployment on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, with company permissions and access controls built in.

## Access OpenAI through Oracle Marketplace

title: Expanding our partnership with GSA to bring Claude to all levels of government
body:
We are expanding our partnership with the General Services Administration (GSA) through a new agreement that gives government partners a 40% discount on Claude Enterprise, Claude for Government, and the Claude API. For the first time, the discount applies across every product surface, including when agencies buy from us directly today and through cloud providers in the coming months. The discount also extends to state, local, tribal and territorial governments.
We are also launching a dedicated program to help agencies implement and make the most of their Claude use. These programs are commonly leveraged by our private sector customers and we’re looking forward to bringing those best practices to our public sector partners in the coming weeks.
Approximately 500 US federal, state, and local government organizations now use Claude. Weekly Claude for Government active users are up about eightfold since February, and usage across federal civilian agencies has grown about 20-fold in a year. Those organizations run some of the most important systems in the country, usually on tight budgets and with long procurement cycles. This agreement is built to support that work, so they can apply Claude to hard problems without a large upfront commitment.
The discounts offered through the agreement are estimated to save the government $1 billion. Agencies are not bound by a minimum spend commitment and will be able to pay for the usage they consume.
How Claude is helping public servants get more done
Government agencies are using Claude to solve some of their most important challenges. Examples include managing backlogs, records and forms, and modernizing old code. Some of the ways agencies are using Claude include:
- Utah gave Claude Code to 34 developers across 10 state agencies. 80% had a working environment within 30 minutes, 71% reported saving 20+ hours by the end of the four-week pilot.
- A US state CIO confirmed their team was able to respond to a ransomware attack in 8 minutes vs. the usual 2-3 days thanks to Claude.
- A US federal security team used Claude Mythos to detect and patch the vulnerability that would have allowed for the takeover of a critical production system in about two days. A human penetration test the month before had missed it.
- A cybersecurity professional at a major agency found and patched bugs in critical financial systems.
- A US state IT developer moved nearly 900 API methods to a new framework in two days. The project had been scoped for a month.
- A US state IT director used Claude Code to document 12 legacy code repositories, mapping 467 database tables and flagging 27 risks along the way.
- More than half of the US states, some of the largest localities, and some of the countries largest critical infrastructure operators
[participated](https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropic-cyber-mission)in our SLTT cyber defense program.
Meeting government security requirements
Agencies can use Claude for their most sensitive unclassified work. Claude for Government, which delivers Claude's coding and agentic work capabilities and provides near-feature parity with commercial offerings at a FedRAMP High authorization level, was made [generally available](https://claude.com/resources/articles/claude-for-government-is-now-generally-available) on September 30.
Agencies building their own tools can use Claude through Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud’s Vertex AI. On Bedrock, Claude is authorized for FedRAMP High, with select models authorized for DoD IL4 and IL5 workloads in AWS GovCloud. On Vertex AI, Claude is authorized for FedRAMP High.
Claude Enterprise is in process for FedRAMP Moderate authorization through the FedRAMP 20x program, marking the next evolution of how we are bringing the same innovative technology available commercially to the government.
Getting started
Government agencies can buy Claude at the OneGov discount through GSA's Multiple Award Schedule today. Whether your department or agency already uses Claude or is interested in using it, our Public Sector team will help discuss your options.
For more information, contact us [here](https://claude.com/solutions/government).

title: Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude
body:
Anthropic’s [life sciences team](https://www.anthropic.com/science) is working to accelerate curing disease. Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines: [BigHat Biosciences](https://www.bighatbio.com/), [Bristol Myers Squibb](https://www.bms.com/), [Divergence Labs](https://divergencelabs.com/), [Enveda](https://enveda.com/), [Generate Biomedicines](https://generatebiomedicines.com/), and [The Column Group](https://www.thecolumngroup.com/). We've also begun drug discovery efforts of our own. In doing so, we've learned a lot about how Claude can support drug development, and how we’ll need to improve Claude further to realize AI's potential in medicine. We plan to scale this work up substantially from here.
There are many opportunities to speed up drug development, even beyond the most commonly discussed applications of AI, like [proposing initial designs](https://www.anthropic.com/research/Claude-accelerates-protein-design) for new molecules. Developing a drug involves many varied tasks: doing early research to identify a target for a drug and the right type of drug to engage it, designing a molecule with the right properties, optimizing it to be manufactured reliably at scale, drafting the regulatory filings needed to run clinical trials, designing and administering those trials, and much more.
Our strategy to realize AI’s medical benefits is based on having AI increasingly involved in all of these tasks. There is no single problem to solve; the bottlenecks are distributed all throughout the drug development process. The best way to identify and work through these bottlenecks is to get deeply involved in real drug programs, across many different disease areas and stages of development.
So, over the past several months, we’ve partnered with six organizations to do so. We’ve also started drug discovery efforts of our own, including programs for rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy, where Claude handles much of the scientific and operational work.
This work serves our goals in three ways. First, it lets us better understand the strengths and limitations of our models in relation to a much wider range of drug development tasks (we’ve already prioritized specific improvements to our models based on what we’ve learned so far). Second, these programs can serve as case studies for the wider life sciences community. If Claude is to significantly increase the rate of new cures, we need to work with many more biotechnology firms and integrate Claude more deeply into their development processes. Third, these projects should, if their positive trajectories continue, have direct impact themselves. We’re optimistic that some may result in effective new medicines for the diseases they target, including food allergies, rare childhood diseases, and several forms of cancer.
In this post, we provide an update on our progress with our partners, along with technical reports and preprints that describe our thought process, methods, and early results in more detail. We then briefly outline where our work is headed next.
Case studies
Generate Biomedicines: modality engineering. Generate Biomedicines has been working on increasing the usefulness of a cancer treatment known as CAR T-cell therapy. This therapy has historically helped treat blood cell cancers; Generate aims to reengineer it so that it can treat solid tumor cancers too. To do this, they’re aiming to shorten one part of the therapy’s genetic instructions, which would create room for additional instructions suited to other kinds of cancer. Six Generate scientists used Claude Code to propose new designs for this part. One design was about 70% shorter than the standard version, and in lab tests it was more effective: it allowed immune cells to make roughly 10 times as many receptors (the proteins they use to spot cancer cells), it killed tumor cells more efficiently, and the immune cells remained active for longer. Read more, and see [Generate’s technical report](https://generatebiomedicines.com/publications/refactored-intracellular-domains-enhance-car-expression-and-function/).
Divergence Labs: hit generation. Divergence Labs is working on a novel way to treat food allergies. Food allergies are set off by a reaction from a molecule called IgE, some of which is attached to our immune cells and some of which floats freely in our blood. Divergence Labs is developing drugs that would detach the IgE from our immune cells entirely, rather than solely neutralizing the IgE circulating in our blood, as standard medications do. This could provide a much more effective treatment, but it requires a precise design, with two “arms”: one that would bind tightly to IgE, and another that would help prise IgE from the immune cell. Claude converted Divergence Labs’ goals into a detailed design plan, and then, largely autonomously, generated roughly 35,000 antibody designs in about a month to be narrowed down and tested. In those early tests, Divergence found “hits” for both arms: three designs that could bind to IgE, and 20 that could dislodge it. Three of those 20 appeared to dislodge IgE more than the standard medication. Its next step is to build a drug that combines the two arms. Read more, and see [Divergence’s technical report](https://divergencelabs.com/publications/ige-preprint.pdf).
BigHat Biosciences: lead optimization. BigHat Biosciences pairs AI with an automated lab to improve potential drugs (or “leads”), which must bind their target tightly, remain stable through manufacturing and storage, and avoid clumping together (among other criteria). BigHat’s scientists and an Anthropic researcher worked with Claude to improve these three properties in two leads, both antibody fragments that could become parts of future drugs: one designed to target cancer cells, and one designed to keep a drug in the body longer. Claude, connected to BigHat’s lab data system, Reccy, proposed changes to each molecule, and BigHat’s lab made and tested about 1,010 variants in about 10 weeks. Partway through, the team suspected the standard heat-stability and clumping metrics were misleading. Claude and the researcher reanalyzed the raw data, then proposed different metrics and a protocol change to test them. BigHat’s scientists refined and ran it, and the main predictions held. Compared with the originals, the best versions bound more than 10x more tightly, the cancer-targeting lead stayed in solution 18°C higher, and the lead for longer-lasting drugs clumped more than 100x more slowly. Read more, and see [BigHat’s technical report](https://www.bighatbio.com/bighat-anthropic-collaboration-report-10-27-2026).
Enveda: manufacturing and filings. To conduct clinical trials, companies need records showing that each batch of a new drug has been made to strict quality standards, and to submit an application to regulators, among other requirements. At Enveda, manufacturing chemists spent up to 75% of their time on paperwork. To ease the load, Enveda built a system that connects all of its manufacturing documents to Claude, then lets Claude flag any possible issues. Over tests on 1,061 pages of documentation, Claude caught all 11 issues that human reviewers had spotted—and flagged seven they’d missed. In the process, this method reduced human review time by 89%, from over 25 hours to less than three. Separately, Claude wrote the first drafts of two important regulatory documents. One took four hours, compared to about three months by hand. For the other, Enveda’s standard human review process found one minor error. Read more, and see [Enveda’s technical report](https://enveda.com/CMC-Document-Processor/).
The Column Group (TCG): company creation. Because drug discovery can be slow, expensive, and prone to failure, investors in biotechnology companies have favored safer, previously validated ideas over riskier new ones, even when the latter could help more patients. We’ve been working with TCG to see whether Claude can change this by cutting the time and cost of drug discovery so that investors can confidently support more ambitious ideas. Specifically, TCG is establishing Pleiades, a new company that will use Claude to run many more—and more complex—drug programs than is usual for a small team. This could be a model for how Claude can reduce both the scientific and the operational and administrative overhead required to run a biotechnology company. If this works, this model could be replicated across the industry and direct investment toward harder problems in medicine. Pleiades is currently developing new tools and workflows for Claude; its very first Claude skill, which helps Claude assess whether drug targets are worth pursuing, has been evaluated on 45 target-disease pairs. Read more.
More recently, we’ve also begun working with [Bristol Myers Squibb](https://www.bms.com/) (BMS) to find and address bottlenecks in clinical trial planning. BMS is using Claude to assess plans of an early-stage drug in clinical trials, and to estimate the likelihood of those trials succeeding. Together, we plan to expand this work in 2027 to understand its potential for increasing the probability of success in early development.
“We use Claude at the clinical trial stage to analyze proprietary data, create a clinical study plan, and weigh the study’s chance of success. From a single prompt, Claude generated a robust initial analysis that helped inform our assessment of different development options, which would otherwise take days to complete. We did all of this while ensuring the security of our highly sensitive data. We look forward to expanding this work across our pipeline to support portfolio-level decisions.”
Michael Pourdehnad, MD, Senior Vice President, Head of Early Clinical Development, Hematology, Oncology and Cell Therapy.
In addition to our work with these partners, we’ve begun to run some research programs ourselves. We’ve acquired Mithril Medicine, a one-person company that has been developing treatments for two rare forms of muscular dystrophy. Its founder, Cody Tranbarger, used Claude to organize contracts, logistics, and experiments with 11 external labs, and delegated many other aspects of Mithril’s operations to Claude. As a result, Mithril took a possible treatment for one form of muscular dystrophy from an idea to promising results in mice in less than 18 months. Now at Anthropic, Cody is continuing this research, and plans to start several new programs. If his drug candidates continue to hold up, we expect a drug to be ready to start clinical trials in humans as soon as late 2028. Read more and see [our technical report](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/52e1f5d50c47ca3818f56704c27cf19e59b62e77.pdf).
Extending our work in the life sciences
All of this research is still at an early stage. In particular, so far it is mostly preclinical—that is, for the most part, it isn’t yet at the stage where the drugs are being tested in humans. We plan to continue extending Claude’s role into clinical trials as these drug programs advance, and as we partner with more organizations whose drug development programs are already at the clinical stage.
This research is only one part of our efforts to accelerate drug discovery. Ultimately, we want to share our models with as many drug development researchers as possible. To that end, we’ve rolled out [Claude Science](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-science-ai-workbench), our AI workbench for researchers, and we’re providing [Claude credits for life scientists](https://www.anthropic.com/news/ai-for-science-program). We’ve also created the [Life Sciences Verification Program](https://www.anthropic.com/news/life-sciences-verification-program) to allow trusted organizations to use our most powerful models with more permissive versions of our safeguards, which are necessary to prevent misuse but which can impede legitimate biological research. We’

title: How AI agents shape experts’ judgment calls
body:
Amaç Herdağdelen, Hailey Joren, Alex Tamkin
When experts hand their work to an AI agent, the usual assumption is that they still make the decisions that matter. The agent writes the code, runs the numbers, and offers advice, but the expert decides what to measure, how to interpret ambiguous evidence, and what the next steps should be. Often there is more than one reasonable answer to these questions, and the decision will come down to the experience and values of whoever makes the call.
We wanted to look at whether experts really do make those important decisions, or whether in practice they defer to their AI agents. In a study we report [in a new paper](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/519c17a5d23a794e8b6d50a854048d0b61e0d73a.pdf), we asked 50 professional analysts to do a realistic statistical analysis with Claude Code. They all had experience in causal inference—that is, working out from data whether one thing causes another. Their task was to advise a farming cooperative on whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded.
Along the way, the analysts had to make four choices between two reasonable options, such as whether to measure productivity as crop yield per hectare or as yield per unit of operating cost, and then make a final decision. To see whether they were making these calls themselves, we set up each analyst’s agent to favor one option on each decision, which the analysts weren’t told about. Which way the agents would “lean” would be decided by coin flip. The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead.
Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%. When analysts had already expressed their own preference before the agent weighed in, they switched away from it 60% of the time if the agent disagreed, compared to 6% if it agreed.
Afterward, when asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those arguments. Analysts who followed the agents’ recommendations closely were about as confident in their final recommendation as the rest, and roughly as likely to call it the product of their own judgment.
We don’t know how much this tells us about the real world. Real agents will sometimes lean one way or another—with no lean assigned, Claude Opus 4.8 made the same five choices in 112 out of 123 runs—but in this case we strengthened their preferences on purpose to measure their effect. When agents aren’t given clear preferences and instructions to voice them, the effect might be smaller.
This isn’t a simple cautionary tale against working with AI. Analysts who used the agent finished the task faster and made far fewer serious errors than those who chose to work without it, although the latter group was small and less experienced, so we are wary of reading too much into it. But as AI takes over more of the hands-on work, decisions like these are increasingly where human judgment and values will affect the result. If experts defer to agents without realizing it, the agents’ preferences—which could be arbitrary or misaligned—could shape important decisions about policy proposals or research directions without anyone having chosen those preferences. This is particularly important for research into keeping AI safe. Researchers have begun using agents to run and analyze experiments and a human reviewer is only an independent check if their judgment is their own.
Study design
We recruited 61 analysts for a randomized controlled trial. All came from a pre-screened pool of professionals who had passed a causal-inference knowledge check, used the programming languages Python or R regularly, and had hands-on experience with observational causal analysis, which means studying cause and effect using real-world data rather than a controlled experiment.
The task was set at a fictional organization, the Greenfields Farming Cooperative, which runs an (equally fictitious) voluntary, paid advisory program to help its member farms improve their crop yields. About 40% of members have enrolled. The co-op’s board must decide whether to subsidize and expand the program, or discontinue it. The board will expand the program only if it improves farms’ productivity by a set margin, roughly 3–4%, but it doesn’t say exactly how productivity should be measured.
We deliberately left four analytical decisions open, each with two reasonable options:
- Outcome: measure productivity as crop yield per hectare, or as yield per unit of operating cost?
- Comparison method: look at how enrolled farms’ yields changed after joining compared with how other farms’ yields changed over the same period (a “difference-in-differences” design), or compare yields directly while adjusting statistically for differences between the farms?
- Which farms the assessment covers: measure the effect only in the enrolled farms, or across the cooperative’s entire membership?
- Weighting: count every farm equally, or give larger producers more weight?
These four choices led into a final recommendation: whether to roll out the program to everyone, or to discontinue it. Analysts and agents could also propose a one-year extension.
Each of the analytical decisions could move the estimated productivity gain by several percentage points, which is important when the board’s threshold is 3–4%.
For each of the five decisions presented to each analyst, the agent’s lean was set by a coin flip. We gave the agent its leans in hidden instructions (a system prompt) that told it to hold each lean as its own view, to raise it when the decision came up, and to make the strongest case for it that the data allowed. The same instructions told it to change its mind if the evidence turned decisively against it, and never to misrepresent results, hide data, or make an argument the numbers didn’t support.
Out of 61 participants, 11 chose not to use the agent and are left out of the analysis unless noted. Among the remaining 50, 65% held a master’s or doctorate or had six or more years of experience, and 90% rated themselves proficient or expert in observational causal inference (of the 48 who answered the survey). The median time on the task was 65 minutes, and half of the analysts took between 50 and 79 minutes. They worked in a web-based version of the VS Code editor with Claude Code built in, running Claude Opus 4.8 at High effort.
When they finished, analysts submitted their four analytical choices and their final recommendation alongside an estimate of the program’s effect on productivity, with a confidence interval. They then completed a post-task survey. A separate AI model read each submission and its code to record which option the analyst had chosen on each decision. Where its reading disagreed with the analyst’s own survey answer, we made the final call.
Results
Analysts mostly went with their agents’ lean. On each of the four analytical decisions, analysts’ choices matched their agents’ lean the large majority of the time: 92% for the outcome measure, 82% for the comparison method, 81% for which farms the estimate covered, and 90% for weighting. Across all four combined, the result was 86%. Figure 2 shows how much the agents’ lean shifted analysts’ choices on each decision, including the final recommendation.
Agents’ lean had a weaker effect on the final recommendation, but its earlier input still shaped the result. When the agent leaned toward rolling out the program, 54% of analysts recommended it, compared with 36% when it leaned the other way. (A one-year extension counts as not rolling out.) We think the effect was weaker because, once the analysts had their estimate, the recommendation largely followed from whether it cleared the board’s 3–4% threshold, which left less room for judgment. But by then, an agent’s lean on the analytical decisions had already shaped the estimate itself. Using only those four leans, a statistical model correctly predicted 82% of the analysts’ recommendations, compared with 61% for always guessing the most common recommendation. (This excludes analysts who proposed an extension.) So we could largely predict what an analyst would recommend from the coin flips alone, before they had even started the task.
Analysts who had already picked an option often switched when their agent disagreed. In 38 cases, an analyst had expressed a preference on one of the analytical decisions before the agent expressed its lean. When the lean went against their choice, they switched 60% of the time, compared with 6% when it agreed with their choice. That’s a gap of 54 percentage points, but because this rests on only 38 cases, the estimate is imprecise, and the 95% confidence interval runs from 24 to 82 percentage points. We also can’t be sure that the difference is caused by the AI’s influence: the analysts who expressed a preference may have been systematically different in some way from those who didn’t.
Experience and expertise did not predict who deferred. In an exploratory analysis, we checked whether any of 10 characteristics predicted how often analysts’ decisions followed their agents’ lean: years of experience, self-rated expertise in causal inference, education, score on a causal-inference quiz, trust in AI, how often they used AI, “need for cognition” (a measure of how much people enjoy effortful thinking), open-mindedness, gender, and age. Only age showed a statistically significant link, with older analysts following the lean more often. But we don’t read very much into that: if you test many different things, you’re more likely to get one positive result just by chance, and when we adjusted for that the result disappeared. Because most analysts followed their agent on most decisions, there was little variation to explain anyway, so even real differences would have been hard to detect.
Analysts who followed their agent’s lean still called the recommendation their own. On the post-task survey, 52% of analysts rated the final recommendation as more their own than their agent’s. The rest said it was more the agent’s recommendation. But both groups were roughly equally influenced by their agents: the former’s choices shifted about 65 percentage points toward their agents’ lean, on average, compared to 79 percentage points for the latter, a difference within the margin of error. Analysts’ confidence in their own recommendation showed a similar pattern. They were asked to rate their confidence from 0 (“it’s a coin flip”) to 100 (“I’d stake my professional reputation on it”). Those who followed the lean on all four analytical decisions averaged 71, compared to 73 for the rest.
Analysts explained their choices in their agent’s words. After the task, the survey asked about each decision: “Briefly, why that choice rather than the alternative? If it wasn’t an active choice, just say so.” Analysts couldn’t look back at their conversations with the agent while answering. Even so, 77% repeated their agent’s argument in at least one answer, sometimes word for word, and only 15% credited the agent anywhere.
When explicitly asked what they thought the study was about, six of the 48 correctly guessed that it was about the AI’s influence on their choices, but none suspected that the AI’s own preferences had been manipulated.
Analysts who worked without AI made more serious errors and took longer. Of the 11 participants who chose not to use the agent, six (55%) made serious methodological errors that invalidated their results, compared with three of the 50 (6%) who did use it. Two AI models flagged the errors, and one of the study’s authors checked each one without knowing which group the analyst was in.
