## Select the type of decision your application needs

Using the Decisions API is simple: developers define a question and its allowed answers, then provide context as text, images, or native JSON. The API returns one of three supported answer types—a probability, choice, or score—that applications can use to determine what happens next. The variety of answer types allows Decisions to be applicable across a wide variety of use cases.  
  
Decisions API supports three answer types:

| Type | Use it to | Main result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| predicate | Estimate the probability that a condition is true, such as whether a product has visible damage. | probability: an estimate from 0 to 1 that the condition is true. |
| choice | Select one of your predefined options, such as whether an agent should continue, retry, or ask for clarification. | choice: one of your supplied values. The response also includes probabilities and confidence. |
| score | Rate an input against ordered levels in a rubric, such as the severity of damage. | score: the probability-weighted average of the level indices. |

## Build real-time voice experiences with the Decisions API and GPT‑Live

With [GPT‑Live](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-live-1-in-the-api/), you can bring natural, expressive conversation to your voice applications, with smooth interruption handling that keeps conversations flowing. Decisions API now [integrates natively with GPT‑Live⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/decisions-voice), helping applications make fast, focused decisions during live conversations. A customer support agent can decide whether to ask a clarifying question, route a request, or escalate an issue. An avatar can adjust its facial expressions as a user speaks to it, and based on the user’s words, respond with a wink or a smile to create a more interactive experience.

The example below uses transcript updates to select an avatar’s expression. Add this configuration to `session.triggers` in an existing GPT‑Live session.

#### JSON

```` ```
1{2  "type": "decisions",3  "event_type": "session.input_transcript.delta",4  "decisions": {5    "questions": [{6      "type": "choice",7      "name": "reaction",8      "instructions": "Choose an appropriate reaction for the avatar based on the user's latest message.",9      "choices": [10        { "value": "neutral" },11        { "value": "happy" },12        { "value": "sad" },13        { "value": "concerned" }14      ]15    }]16  }17}
``` ````

Live emits a `decision.event`; the application reads the selected `reaction` and animates the character accordingly. [Learn more about connecting voice to Decisions API. ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/decisions-voice)

## Build and evaluate your first decision

Decisions API is generally available today with GPT‑6 Luna through the dedicated Decisions endpoint. See the [pricing and availability guide⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/decisions#pricing-and-availability) for current rates and caching details.

Start with one recurring decision your application makes often. Define the question, the possible answers, and the context needed to distinguish them. Test it on examples that reflect real usage, in the [Decisions Playground⁠(opens in a new window)](https://platform.openai.com/decisions) with your own text or images, or follow the [developer guide⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/decisions) to make your first request.

Decisions API costs $0.10 per million input tokens. Cached input costs $0.01 per million tokens. For 30-minute and 12-hour cached writes, [read our pricing guide.⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing?utm_source=chatgpt.com) You only pay for input tokens: there are no output-token charges. Regional processing is available in the US and EU, and [Zero Data Retention⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data) is available to eligible customers. title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
body:
22nd October 2026 - Link Blog
[Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation](https://www.anthropic.com/news/donating-agent-skills-to-the-agentic-ai-foundation). News today from Anthropic:
We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation,
[which we co-founded]with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
I'm pleased to note I called this one [last December](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Dec/19/agent-skills/), when Anthropic first declared skills to be an "open standard":
I wouldn't be surprised to see this end up

title: OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet
body:
Image Feature Extraction • Updated • 157 • 10
[
](#olmoearth-v13-state-of-the-art-embeddings-for-the-whole-planet)
OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
🤗 [Models](https://huggingface.co/allenai/OlmoEarth-v1_3-Base/) | 📄 [Tech Report](https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth-v1-3) | 📊 [Data](https://source.coop/olmoearth/olmoearth-v1-3-embeddings) | 💻 [Code](https://github.com/allenai/olmoearth_pretrain) | 🌎 [Embeddings Explorer](https://olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings) | 🗺️ [Interactive story](https://narrative.allen.ai/olmoearth-embeddings)
Today, we’re releasing [OlmoEarth v1.3](https://huggingface.co/allenai/OlmoEarth-v1_3-Base/), a state-of-the-art satellite embedding model. Alongside OlmoEarth v1.3, we’re sharing precomputed, annual embeddings for the whole planet (10m, 64- and 128-dimensions), plus a new browser-based tool to explore and customize maps based on those embeddings — the [OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer](https://olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings). This means anyone can put OlmoEarth v1.3 to work right away, from tracking change over time to finding similar places—no sign-in, and no advanced technical knowledge required.
Until now, the primary way to use OlmoEarth was fine-tuning in OlmoEarth Studio: training a model for each task and running it over satellite imagery to make a map. That requires GPU access and the ability to download and store the [imagery](https://allenai.org/blog/olmoearth-infrastructure). Embedding models compress satellite data into ready-to-use features that can be reused cheaply for many tasks.
With OlmoEarth v1.3, we’re excited to give users more ways to explore and engage with planetary artifacts in whatever way suits them best.
[
](#compute-once-reuse-everywhere)
Compute once, reuse everywhere
An embedding represents what the model learned from millions of images. OlmoEarth v1.3 reads a year of radar (Sentinel-1) and multispectral (Sentinel-2 and Landsat) satellite time series and produces one 128-dimensional vector for every 10-meter pixel on Earth; the first 64 dimensions also work on their own as a smaller embedding.
Foundation models and global embeddings are expensive to produce, and to make sure everyone is able to access the benefits, we’ve computed these embeddings for the entire planet and shared them with the community on [Source Cooperative](https://source.coop/olmoearth/olmoearth-v1-3-embeddings). From there, a crop map, a land-cover map, or a change analysis becomes a lightweight modeling problem: train a small classifier on top and run it locally.
How OlmoEarth v1.3 makes an embedding: a vision transformer reads the satellite data, an Attention Pooler pools it into one vector per patch of land, and a linear layer reduces it to 128 numbers.
[
](#state-of-the-art-embeddings)
State-of-the-art embeddings
We evaluated OlmoEarth v1.3's embeddings against AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) and Tessera v2 across 27 evaluations, covering six continents and many different tasks. OlmoEarth’s 128-dimensional embeddings score highest on 20 of 27 evals and rank highest overall. The 64-dimensional version, at half the size, still leads on 18 of 27 evals. As part of this evaluation, we introduce [PLANTEUR, a new crop-type benchmark for tropical farming](https://allenai.org/blog/planteur), and the embeddings generalize best to places a classifier has never seen (PLANTEUR technical report is available [here](https://allenai.org/papers/planteur)). Everything behind them is fully open: the model weights, the pretraining data, and the pretraining code.
In practice, this means a small classifier trained on the OlmoEarth embeddings is enough to map what’s on the ground: think classifying smallholder crops in Kenya, detecting brick kilns west of Dhaka, assessing fire damage in Indonesia, and tracking gold mining in the Peruvian Amazon.
Compared to previous generations of OlmoEarth models, OlmoEarth v1.3 was also our cheapest model to train. It took 53% of the computing time of our last version (v1.2) and 18% of our first (v1), with 50% and 22% of the carbon emissions. And it also remains a strong fine-tuning model, matching v1.2's performance across research and partner labels. Our latest model builds on the same foundation as earlier OlmoEarth versions, tuned so the embeddings stay lightweight without giving up accuracy across tasks, and that efficiency work carries forward into the versions ahead.
Full results and methodology are in our [technical report](https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth-v1-3).
If you wanted to reproduce it, pre-training OlmoEarth v1.3 Base would cost roughly $2,720 of rented H100 time for the final run. The weights, data, and code are all open.
[
](#one-place-nine-years)
One place, nine years
How much each pixel’s embedding changed between 2017 and 2020 (left) and 2020 and 2025 (right). Magenta is the largest change. Left: mining spreading southeast, the big patch at lower right. Right: that corner has gone quiet; the change now sits in the older mining zone to the west, part regrowth, part renewed digging. Explore it yourself in the [OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer.](https://olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings#map=11.38/-12.9486/-69.9637&s=zdY7bCoJAFEX_ZT0fh3GycTy_Ij5MJnaxm4Ug4r9HJfRSb5vFXrAmBtQJd5R8uBX2gHBCqXfx3DYIW9RnwhhRK4yb970eUK5x3yMca9QLFzQVIjrRo2VZJrk11qdrSdKVsc77SsrEFya4LPxhzoQ8hBf7ur_Y4lbVJ7xv6gdCt8x4bruGeX4C)
In Peru's Madre de Dios region, illegal gold mining around La Pampa peaked in 2017 and 2018, clearing more than 1,200 hectares of forest in the buffer zone of the Tambopata National Reserve, [according to Amazon Conservation's MAAP monitoring program](https://www.maapprogram.org/lapampa_opermercury/). In February 2019, Peru's Operation Mercurio shut most of it down. The question ever since has been, did it stay down?
The embeddings help answer that. Compare each pixel's vector across years, no model training required, and the 2017 to 2020 pair lights up where the mining was spreading to the southeast. Run the same comparison from 2020 to 2025, and the signal shifts. The crackdown is visible in the embeddings.
The more interesting part is what the second map still shows. It is not dark. According to [MAAP](https://www.maapprogram.org/gold-mining-peru/), pockets in the northwest kept operating, and the old mining zone keeps changing as the land recovers. The embeddings register that too. The reprieve was brief, and the pressure is building again. In August 2026, the [Associated Press](https://apnews.com/article/illegal-mining-peru-military-operation-amazon-gold-mercury-navy-728d312a5687ecc6a1e6c6d6798965fe) reported, Peru sent navy patrols back into the reserve after prosecutors found mining had crossed into Tambopata itself.
Our [interactive story](https://narrative.allen.ai/olmoearth-embeddings) opens on this stretch of Madre de Dios, and walks through several other examples from there.
[
](#the-olmoearth-embeddings-explorer)
The OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer
The [OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer](https://storage.googleapis.com/ai2-olmoearth-embeddings-us-central1/explorer-global/index.html#s=zdY9BDoIwFETvMutv09_SAP8qTRe1EjRBRDAkSLi7sbhwobvJS-Ylb8UMYcIEQTvdu-EBwhWCdI5924BwgrCpCAni2VhVszN0MLWyheVAeEJYq5IJS4RownLMxjRDMMTLCMItkwhZMUK8z6LSOZtFhbEukGdTKK0r_susdjv7-v5i-RvCHjU26Z3UfWbs267Btr0A) is an interactive analysis tool built from the embeddings themselves, rendered as a false-color map of the planet. Pan anywhere, flip between years to see how landscapes have changed, and pull up the underlying Sentinel-2 imagery to check the map against the real thing. Then start asking questions: click a place to find others that look similar, or drop a few labeled points and train a small classifier on the spot, then export the result as a GeoTIFF. No account, no setup required.
For many teams, testing an idea against OlmoEarth has meant a fine-tuning run, on the order of hours. In the explorer, a first pass takes seconds. You can analyze entire regions from a handful of labels, no GPU needed. When a task calls for fine-tuning, the embeddings can help you decide whether it deserves the compute, and where the model falls short.
The archive behind the Explorer holds embeddings at 10-meter resolution, roughly 150 TB per year, covering land and adjacent coastal waters. At launch, 2025, 2024, and 2023 are global, and 2017 to 2022 cover select countries, with more coverage on the way. You can retrieve the embeddings in the full 128-dimensional version or the lighter 64-dimensional version. Every embedding also comes with a record of where it came from. For each 20-kilometer tile and year, open provenance tables list the Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, and Landsat scenes the model read, with links to the public catalogs that host them, so you can trace any pixel back to the imagery behind it.
[
](#get-started)
Get started
This release includes the OlmoEarth v1.3 Base model, the precomputed global embeddings, the OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer, and the technical report. If your work needs a specific time window, OlmoEarth Studio runs the same model over the dates, modalities, and resolution that you choose, and a [tutorial](https://github.com/allenai/rslearn/blob/master/docs/examples/OlmoEarthEmbeddings.md) shows how to generate embeddings on your own compute. These tools work together: explore in the Embeddings Explorer, fine-tune in Studio when a task calls for it, and take your map from there. Everything is published under the OlmoEarth Artifact License, the same open license as v1 and v1.2.
Pull the embeddings for a place you care about, put your question to them, and show us what you find.

title: NVIDIA Unveils Minerva to Bring End-to-End Observability for AI Factories
body:
Launched today, [NVIDIA Minerva](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/networking/products/software/minerva/) is an AIOps platform built to help teams find problems earlier and keep AI factories productive. It brings together telemetry from infrastructure and AI workloads, then applies purpose-built AI models to turn that data into timely, actionable insight.
AI factories are among the most complex operations in the world, with vast numbers of GPUs working across high-speed networks to train models and serve AI applications. At that scale, a single degraded component can slow an entire job. The warning signs may be easy to miss, such as a GPU running hotter than its peers or an NVMe drive losing performance under load.
The platform focuses on AI factory yield, a measure of the useful work infrastructure produces through GPU hours, goodput, cluster uptime and token production.
Delivering a Dynamic View of an AI Factory
Traditional monitoring tools often divide the data center into separate views. Networking, compute, site reliability and machine learning teams each see a different part of the operation. Minerva connects those signals across NVIDIA GPUs, networking, storage, schedulers and workloads.
With these signals, Minerva builds a dynamic knowledge graph that logically maps the infrastructure — GPUs, SuperNICs, switches and cables — and the jobs running on it. This context helps operators trace a slow training job to the component affecting it, even across a factory with hundreds of thousands of GPUs.
It analyzes billions of data points per hour using supervised and unsupervised machine learning. It learns normal behavior, detects previously unseen anomalies, predicts emerging failures and correlates related events based on the factory’s topology. Instead of sending every symptom to an operator, it can group an event storm into a focused incident with a likely root cause.
Minerva comes with a native AI assistant and connects to external agentic AI tools. This adds a natural-language interface grounded in live telemetry. Operators can investigate cluster health and receive recommended remediation through conversation. Teams can keep a person in the loop to manually implement fixes or connect Minerva to automation through infrastructure application programming interfaces and external systems.
Results That Maximize AI Factory Yield
The ability to correlate workload and infrastructure issues along with its agentic AI capabilities help simplify AI factory operations. Instead of dealing with a blizzard of alerts, Minerva aggregates related problems into a single actionable item. This allows AIOps teams to move from reactive to proactive maintenance. And all of this helps AI factories maximize GPU uptime.
Minerva delivers value for the key metrics AI factories focus on:
- Longer time between interruptions: Minerva spots trouble before it happens, so jobs run longer without incident.
- Faster time to repair: When an incident does happen, Minerva pinpoints the problem, leading to a significantly quicker resolution.
- Greater insight: Modern AI infrastructure generates a flood of data; Minerva filters it out, leaving only the handful of alerts that actually matter.
IREN is among the NVIDIA partners using Minerva to optimize its AI factories.
“As we scale our AI factories, the key to providing the best service for our customers is maximizing the productivity of our GPUs,” said Denis Skrinnikoff, chief technology officer of IREN. “NVIDIA Minerva gives our operations team one view across the network, the GPUs and the jobs running on them, so we focus more on proactive maintenance rather than troubleshooting. That visibility strengthens our operating model for the infrastructure we’re building next.”
Joining IREN, Aolani, [Bitdeer AI](https://www.bitdeer.ai/en/blog/nvidia-minerva/), IBM, Jio, Lambda, Quake AI and Tesla plan to deploy Minerva.
In addition to Dell Technologies, [Lenovo ](https://news.lenovo.com/europes-ai-moment-gtc-berlin-26)and [Supermicro ](https://learn-more.supermicro.com/data-center-stories/supermicro-nvidia-minerva-supercloud-ai-factory)will offer Minerva as part of their AI factory operations portfolios.
Learn more about [NVIDIA Minerva](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/networking/products/software/minerva/).
See [notice](https://www.nvidia.com/en-eu/about-nvidia/terms-of-service/) regarding software product information.

title: Beyond tree cover: mapping the world’s forest types
body:
Beyond tree cover: mapping the worldâs forest types
A new 10-meter resolution map shows which of the world's forests are natural, planted, or farmed, and how they are changing over time
Protecting the planet's forests starts with a simple question: what type of forest are we looking at? From space, an old-growth rainforest, a eucalyptus plantation, and an oil palm estate can look like the same patch of green. But they hold very different amounts of carbon and biodiversity. Telling them apart, and knowing how each patch has changed over time, shows us where conservation is working and where natural forests are being converted into plantations and farms.
Today, Google DeepMind and Google Research, together with the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA), are releasing[ Forest Typology (ForTy) 2020](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-08299-5), a global map that categorizes every 10-by-10-meter patch of land on Earth into six distinct forest and land-use types, a key baseline for the EU's deforestation regulation. Alongside it, we're sharing an early time series that tracks how these forests changed each year from 2017 to 2025, including where natural forests were replaced by plantations or farms. For the first time, users can see at 10-meter detail worldwide, year by year, not just where forest was lost, but what replaced it: a timber plantation, a tree-crop farm or other land.
Why "tree cover" isn't enough
All forests store carbon and, together, forests are home to most of the world's land-based plant and animal species. But a forestâs ecological value also depends on its history: a primary forest that has never been cleared holds far more carbon and biodiversity than a single-species timber plantation that is harvested every decade or two.
Most global maps only indicate whether trees are present. That's a challenge for those trying to protect natural forests. The European Union's regulation on deforestation-free products (EUDR), for example, requires that products like coffee, cocoa or palm oil do not originate from land that was forest in 2020 and has since been converted to agriculture. Similarly, wood products, such as furniture, must also be free of forest degradation: they can't come from primary forests that have since been converted into plantation or planted forests, or from naturally regenerating forests that have since been converted into plantation forests. As a result, companies and regulators need to know not just where trees are, but what kind of forest they form (primary or regrowing, planted or plantation, forest or farm) and what replaces that forest after a harvest.
Last year, we jointly released [Natural Forests of the World 2020](https://research.google/blog/separating-natural-forests-from-other-tree-cover-with-ai-for-deforestation-free-supply-chains/), a 10-meter resolution global map that separated natural forests from all other tree cover. It offered a starting point to help companies and regulators implement the EU Deforestation Regulation, and to support commodity producers in meeting their commitments not to convert natural forest. That map answered one question for every patch of land: was it natural forest in 2020 or not? ForTy goes further, showing what kind of forest is there, from primary forest to timber plantation to tree crops, and, with the new time series, how that changes each year.
How ForTy classifies the world's forests
Specifically, ForTy sorts land into six categories based on definitions from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO):
- Primary forest: native forest with no visible signs of human disturbance.
- Naturally regenerating forest: forest that grew back on its own, for example after logging or fire.
- Planted forest: forest that people planted or seeded, and managed over long cycles.
- Plantation forest: fast-growing, intensively managed tree farms, often of one species.
- Tree crops and agroforestry: farms that grow things other than wood, like oil palm, rubber, cocoa, or fruit.
- Other land: everything else, from grassland and cropland to cities and water.
Training our ForTy model was challenging because these categories depend in part on how land is used, not just how it looks. To teach our model the difference, we built a large-scale collection of forest-type examples with about 1.7 million labeled locations drawn from expert surveys, national and regional datasets, and targeted reviews of places where the model struggled. The model uses a custom architecture designed for the challenges of remote sensing data, and takes as a key input [AlphaEarth Foundations embeddings](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/GOOGLE_SATELLITE_EMBEDDING_V1_ANNUAL), data-compact summaries of years of satellite observations for each 10-meter pixel, so it can spot subtle clues like planting patterns, growth cycles and harvest rhythms.
Putting the map to the test
A map is only useful if people can trust it. So, with IIASA and WRI, we validated ForTy against more than 9,000 randomly chosen sites around the world. At each site, two trained experts studied high-resolution imagery and years of satellite records to determine which type of land was really there. ForTy picked the right forest type 90% of the time, and told forest apart from non-forest land 95% of the time, outperforming other global forest maps.
Beyond accuracy, we know that global conservation is not one-size-fits-all. Instead of giving a yes-or-no label for a specific patch of land, ForTy provides a probability score for each class, enabling users to adapt the classification to regional contexts and application-specific precision trade-offs. For example, a company assessing deforestation risk under EUDR might set a strict threshold, only accepting pixels the model is highly certain about to avoid regulatory risks. Meanwhile, a researcher estimating total forest extent might use the full spectrum of probabilities to get a fuller picture of the potential landscape.
From a single snapshot in time to a story of change
A map of a single year is a useful baseline, but forests change. Our [new early-release time series](https://nature-trace.projects.earthengine.app/view/forest-typology) applies a similar approach to every year from 2017 to 2025. It shows not only where forests disappear and where they grow back, but also what kind of change happened: a natural forest turned into a timber plantation, for example, or abandoned land slowly regenerating into forest.
This differentiation matters because some of the most important changes are hard to see from space. When a natural forest is logged and replanted as a plantation, the land soon looks green again, so standard tree-cover maps might not pick up the change. ForTy's time series makes these hidden changes visible, both losses and gains.
What's next
The Forest Typology 2020 map [described in Scientific Data] and the new time series are now freely available on Google Earth Engine under an open license. We hope governments, companies, conservation groups and scientists will use them to help build deforestation-free supply chains, direct forest finance where itâs needed, and protect the natural forests that matter most. Over the coming months, we'll keep improving the time series with our partners and users, and we'd love to hear how you use it. ForTy is part of our [portfolio](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/publisher/nature-trace) of research on [AI for Nature](https://deepmind.google/blog/mapping-modeling-and-understanding-nature-with-ai/), which includes mapping the drivers of forest loss, forecasting deforestation risk, modelling global species distributions, and monitoring biodiversity in the field. FortTy is also the latest addition to [Google Earth AI](https://ai.google/earth-ai/), Googleâs collection of geospatial models and datasets designed to help tackle the planet's most critical environmental challenges.
Acknowledgements
This work was co-developed by Google DeepMind and Google Research, with the World Resources Institute and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis. We'd like to thank our co-authors Anton Raichuk, Peter Potapov, Myroslava Lesiv, Matthew Overlan, MÃ©lanie Rey, Ravindran Rajakumar, Michelangelo Conserva, Radost Stanimirova, Michelle Sims, Sarah Carter, Elizabeth Goldman, Yuchang Jiang, Linus Scheibenreif, Ivelina Georgieva, Maria Shchepashchenko, Steffen Fritz, Nicholas Clinton, Dan Morris and Drew Purves, as well as the trusted testers who helped improved the map.

title: Cloud Deployment Incoming: ‘Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’ Arrives on GeForce NOW
body:
Lock in and load out this GFN Thursday. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 arrives on [GeForce NOW](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/?ncid=pa-srch-goog-673352&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24109411186&gbraid=0AAAAAD4XAoFI7HGI1e1ouyUf4Z1vqL6Yj&gclid=Cj0KCQjw5vLVBhCiARIsAD56SFLLXG-prLkw0jX3AoX_rJn-CLfJKlNygVblhTr8HBpxVWSPe9WUkusaAvP1EALw_wcB) at launch, bringing a new campaign, multiplayer action and DMZ, high-stakes extraction mode to [supported devices](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/system-reqs/#windows-pc). The campaign also gets an enhanced look: GeForce RTX 5080-class performance arrives for Ultimate members, bringing support for ray-tracing features in the cloud.
There’s a new way to join the cloud, too: Existing supported Fire TV Stick users can now purchase one-month Performance or Ultimate memberships directly through Amazon, making it easier to sign up and start streaming on the big screen.
Plus, Square Enix’s FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE brings cinematic pixel art and strategic battles to the cloud, and The Elder Scrolls Online’s Echoes of Skyrim Season adds the entire Greymoor Chapter free for all ESO Standard Edition owners.
It’s all part of six games joining the [GeForce NOW library](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/games/) this week.

The library includes thousands of ready-to-play games, including many of the world’s most-played titles and more than 100 free-to-play games. No downloads, installs, patches or updates stand between a new game and playtime. An Amazon Fire TV Stick, the GeForce NOW app and an Ultimate membership are all it takes to level up the living room with GeForce RTX 5080-powered gaming.
A Pixel-Perfect Fantasy
Classic roots. A new adventure.
Square Enix’s FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE launches today on GeForce NOW, bringing the series’ classic roots into a cinematic pixel-art world.
Travel with companions bound by fate and uncover the truth behind a force threatening to bring everything to ruin. Strengthen the party with Visions of beloved FINAL FANTASY characters, each bringing unique skills and abilities to battle. Dynamic camera angles and pixelized 3D models give familiar fantasy a fresh perspective.
Exploit enemy weaknesses to stagger foes, break their defenses and seize extra turns before finishing the bonus phase with powerful Resonance attacks. Airships, crystals, espers and moogles bring familiar series favorites to a world filled with secrets to discover.
GeForce NOW handles the game’s downloads and storage in the cloud, leaving more space on supported devices for everyday essentials. Save the inventory management for potions and Phoenix Downs.

title: Automate CSV to Parquet with Hugging Face Buckets, Webhooks & Jobs
body:
Files keep landing in your Hugging Face Storage Bucket. Here is how to process each one automatically, without downloading anything.

In this live-coding video we set up a webhook on a bucket that triggers a Hugging Face Job whenever a new file arrives. The Job runs the `optimize-parquet.py` uv script, converts the new CSV to optimized Parquet, and writes it to a second bucket. We upload a 10,000-row slice of the NYC taxi dataset, and the triggered Job finishes in about 8 seconds. For data engineers already using Buckets who want to automate what happens next.

Topics covered:
- Hugging Face Storage Buckets with the hf CLI
- Running a uv script as a Hugging Face Job
- Webhooks that trigger Jobs on bucket changes
- Converting CSV to Parquet automatically
- Checking Job status, logs and output

title: 1,368 AI Failures and What They Teach About Evals — Vishal Srivastava & Tanmay Sah, New York Life
body:
Vishal Srivastava and Tanmay Sah studied 1,368 incidents from a public AI incident database to ask what real failures say about how AI systems should be tested. They sort failures across three areas (technical strength, deployment controls and business impact) and 13 sub-areas that cover about 98% of incidents. Weak deployment controls, such as human review and monitoring, are the most closely tied to harm. They show how to rank use cases by how much is at stake, why the evaluator itself needs checking, and a build-break-fix loop that tries to prove a system wrong instead of right, applied to a real airline chatbot that gave a customer the wrong refund policy.

title: How to Test AI Agents When No Benchmark Exists — Nathanael Weill, Air Canada
body:
Nathanael Weill leads a team building AI agents at Air Canada, where tasks are so specific there's no public benchmark and domain experts have little time to grade results. His fix is to write the answer first: start from a known answer, generate the input from it, and check whether the agent finds its way back. He shows how that took a past RAG project from one expert-graded test a week to dozens of automated tests a day, then applies it to a supplier-contract review agent with five ways to build a test set: past decisions, planted rule violations, removed clauses, changes that shouldn't matter, and contract templates with filled-in blanks. He also explains why he avoids LLM judges whenever code can check the answer.

title: Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models
body:
Time Series Forecasting • Updated • 255 • 7
[
](#ensemble-forecasting-with-ibm-granite-time-series-models)
Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
Four open Granite models, one extensible forecasting interface, and less guesswork about which model to use.
Pre-trained time-series models can forecast without training on your dataset, but you still have to choose one. A model that handles smooth industrial signals well may struggle with noisy retail demand or a long seasonal horizon, and the best choice depends on the series and the task.
Granite Timeseries Ensemble reduces that choice to a sensible default. One recipe combines four complementary Granite architectures and returns median and quantile forecasts, with no retraining and no fitted ensemble weights. Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling), compare the adaptive Inter Quartile Range (IQR) Ensemble, and extend the same interface with compatible forecasters. The ensemble recipe and its default Granite members are permissively licensed.
The idea will be familiar from weather forecasting. [Ensemble forecasts](https://www.ecmwf.int/en/about/media-centre/focus/2017/fact-sheet-ensemble-weather-forecasting) explore a range of possible outcomes, and systems such as the [North American Multi-Model Ensemble](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/NMME/NMME_description.html) combine different models for seasonal prediction. Time-series forecasting benefits in a similar way: complementary models offer different views of what comes next, and an ensemble merges those views into one forecast.
[
](#try-granite-timeseries-ensemble)
Try Granite Timeseries Ensemble
Install Granite TSFM and load the recommended four-model recipe directly from Hugging Face:
pip install "granite-tsfm>=0.3.11"
import pandas as pd
from tsfm_public.models.ensemble.modeling_ensemble import QuantileEnsembleForecaster
df = pd.read_csv(
"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset/main/ETT-small/ETTh1.csv",
parse_dates=["date"],
)
ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained(
"ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1",
)
result = ensemble(
df.tail(1024),
timestamp_column="date",
target_columns=["OT"],
context_length=1024,
prediction_length=24,
)
print(result.prediction_outputs) # point forecast
print(result.quantile_outputs) # quantiles
The recipe stores the ensemble configuration rather than merged model weights. It downloads the four member checkpoints at runtime, so allow extra time for the first run. For the full configuration, member checkpoints, evaluation details, and limitations, see the [model card](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1).
result.prediction_outputs
contains the point forecast, while result.quantile_outputs
contains the quantile predictions which by default range from 0.1 to 0.9. Applications can use the point value as a central prediction and selected quantiles to express forecast ranges. For example, the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles define a central forecast interval with nominal 80% coverage.
[
](#the-ensemble-members)
The ensemble members
The default recipe combines four pre-trained Granite models with different architectures:
| Model | Architecture |
|---|---|
|
[Granite PatchTST-FM-r2](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-patchtst-fm-r2)[Granite FlowState-r1.1](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-flowstate-r1)[Granite TTM-r3](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ttm-r3)For background, see the [PatchTST-FM-r1 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06909),
[PatchTST-FM-r2 architecture overview](https://huggingface.co/blog/ibm-research/ibm-releases-sota-granite-time-series),
[FlowState paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05287), and
[Tiny Time Mixers paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03955).
These architectures capture trends, seasonality, and local variation in different ways, so their errors need not coincide. A [50-year review of forecast
combinations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.04216) describes how combining forecasts can reduce the risk of picking the wrong single model, while stressing that member quality and diversity still matter.
[
](#two-ways-to-combine-the-forecasts)
Two ways to combine the forecasts
Each member returns quantile forecasts. The two main recipes use different rules to turn those forecasts into one predictive distribution and its median.
[
](#probabilistic-ensemble-the-recommended-default)
Probabilistic Ensemble: the recommended default
The Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling) gives each member equal influence, pools their quantile forecasts in probability space, and extracts the requested quantiles from the combined values. Because the weights are fixed, there is no fitting step and no weighting hyperparameters to tune for a new series.
The [forecast combination puzzle](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1468-0084.2008.00541.x)
offers useful motivation: in point forecasting, simple equal-weight combinations
have often held up well against methods with estimated weights. This recipe applies the same equal-influence idea to probabilistic forecasts. It is the default loaded in the example above.
[
](#iqr-ensemble-an-adaptive-alternative)
IQR Ensemble: an adaptive alternative
The IQR Ensemble weights members according to their forecast spread, giving narrower intervals greater influence. It approximates each member’s interquartile range from the closest available quantiles around the 25th and 75th percentiles. Weights vary by sample, target, and horizon step, and like the Probabilistic Ensemble, nothing is fitted from historical forecast errors. Isotonic regression keeps the combined quantiles from crossing.
A narrower interval does not necessarily mean a more accurate or better-calibrated forecast, and IQR weighting can favor an overconfident member. If you want to experiment, the recipe exposes a temperature setting (higher values move the weights toward uniform) and an optional cap on any single member's weight.
Load the evaluated IQR recipe by changing only the subfolder:
ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained(
"ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1",
subfolder="recipes/granite-iqr",
)
[
](#which-method-should-i-use)
Which method should I use?
| Your goal | Start with | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A simple default | Probabilistic Ensemble | Equal influence, no fitted weights |
| Adaptive weighting based on forecast spread | IQR Ensemble | Influence varies with each member's predicted spread |
Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble. If forecast spread looks informative for your application, compare the IQR Ensemble against it on representative data, since accuracy and calibration depend on the series and the horizon.
[
](#does-the-ensemble-improve-on-its-members)
Does the ensemble improve on its members?
We evaluated both recipes on 97 GIFT-Eval dataset configurations. The models forecast without fine-tuning, and test targets were not used to select or fit the aggregation method. Here we compare the official ensemble submission results with the four constituent models, using published leaderboard scores and ranks captured on 20 October 2026.
GIFT-Eval reports MASE for point forecasts and CRPS/MWQL (the benchmark's
mean_weighted_sum_quantile_loss
metric) for probabilistic forecasts. Scores
are normalized to Seasonal Naive and geometrically averaged across configurations.
Lower is better.
| Forecast | MASE ↓ | MASE Rank ↓ | CRPS / MWQL ↓ | CRPS Rank ↓ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Granite Ensemble R1 — Prob | 0.683★ | 47.175★ | 0.471 | 50.948 |
| Granite Ensemble R1 — IQR | 0.684 | 48.773 | 0.471 | 47.619★ |
| Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 | 0.685 | 51.371 | 0.467★ | 48.918 |
| Granite FlowState-r1.1 | 0.701 | 66.474 | 0.490 | 69.485 |
| Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 | 0.717 | 74.794 | 0.488 | 68.134 |
| Granite TTM-r3 | 0.724 | 83.062 | 0.520 | 88.959 |
★ Best value among the forecasts shown. Lower is better.
Rank columns average per-configuration ranks against the full GIFT-Eval reference leaderboard, not just these six forecasts, so rank values can shift as entries are added to the leaderboard.
Both ensembles outperform all four individual members on aggregate MASE and average MASE Rank. The Probabilistic Ensemble achieves the lowest MASE among these six forecasts: 0.683 compared with 0.685 for PatchTST-FM-r2. Lower average MASE Rank indicates stronger relative point-forecast performance across GIFT-Eval’s diverse dataset configurations. Together, these results support the ensemble as a practical starting point, without requiring developers to select the strongest individual architecture in advance. The MASE margin over the best single member is small, so the main benefit is robustness: you get comparable or better aggregate accuracy without knowing in advance which architecture will suit your data.
PatchTST-FM-r2 retains the lowest aggregate CRPS/MWQL score. The IQR Ensemble achieves the lowest average CRPS Rank among these six forecasts, while the Probabilistic Ensemble ranks behind PatchTST-FM-r2 on that measure. Aggregate error and average rank therefore favor different choices.
In the 20 October 2026 comparison, the ensemble approach ranks 3rd among eligible systems on MASE Rank and CRPS Rank. The figure below shows both recipes alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Some systems, including entries excluded as fine-tuned or non-permissively licensed, score better than either recipe, so the value of the ensemble is not that it tops the leaderboard. It is that a single default delivers strong, consistent results across many series without requiring you to choose a member.
Figure: GIFT-Eval average-rank standings on 20 October 2026, showing both Granite ensembles alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Eligible systems have replication code and no declared test-data leakage; fine-tuned entries and systems with known non-permissive licenses or member dependencies are excluded. Rank values are taken directly from the published overall leaderboard snapshot; filtering changes which systems are displayed, not their rank values.
[
](#extend-the-recipe-to-other-forecasters)
Extend the recipe to other forecasters
The default recipe uses four Granite models, but the common Forecaster
interface also accepts compatible external models. You can change the member mix or the aggregation method and keep the same downstream forecast format, with no merging or retraining of member checkpoints. That makes it easier to fit the ensemble into an existing forecasting stack, and to add forecasters suited to your domain as your needs evolve.
The repository also includes expanded recipes that add IBM Research checkpoints. These carry separate license terms, including non-commercial and research-use restrictions, so review each member's model card before using them.
For any new combination, check forecast compatibility, accuracy, calibration, latency, and licensing.
[
](#evaluate-the-recipe-for-your-application)
Evaluate the recipe for your application
GIFT-Eval is a broad benchmark, but aggregate gains don’t mean every series benefits, and average ranks don’t establish calibration. The way to find out how the recipes behave for your application is to backtest them on representative data:
- Match your use case. Use historical forecast windows that reflect the data available at each forecast origin, the horizon you need, and the series you expect to serve.
- Compare like with like. Run the Probabilistic Ensemble, the IQR Ensemble, and a strong individual member (such as PatchTST-FM-r2) on the same windows.
- Look beyond point error. Assess quantile loss alongside MASE, and check the empirical coverage of the 0.1 to 0.9 interval against its nominal 80%.
- Measure the cost. Record runtime and memory use to judge whether the benefit of combining four models justifies it for your workload.

title: Why AI Writing Still Reads Like Slop — Louis-François Bouchard, Towards AI
body:
Louis-François Bouchard of Towards AI breaks down what makes AI writing feel like slop: overused words, vague generalities, saying nothing, repetition, hallucination and a voice that sounds like everyone at once. He then shows how his team built a benchmark to measure whether a model can write a video script in his own voice: 10 scripts, 5 drafts per model, 4 LLM judges, nine scoring metrics and 1,000 human A/B checks. He shares what it cost, why judges favor their own model family, and practical tips for writing with AI: very long prompts full of examples, one review pass from a strong model, many cheap drafts merged together, and always a human edit.

# What FDE means at OpenAI

What we do, how we work, and how we solve enterprise’s toughest problems to deliver real impact.  
  
By: Colin Jarvis, Head of Forward Deployed Engineering at OpenAI

[Learn more](https://openai.com/business/forward-deployed-engineering/) [Watch the livestream(opens in a new window)](https://forum.openai.com/public/events/work-at-the-frontier-forward-deployed-engineering-at-openai-vmimj73oz5)
