title: Building agents: When to fold subagents into your main agent loop
body:
Building agents: When to fold subagents into your main agent loop
When building agents in Claude Platform, using fewer subagents in favor of progressively disclosed context and tools can improve quality while reducing cost and latency. Here’s when and how to migrate.
If you’ve built an agent in Claude Platform that includes multiple subagents, see which may make sense to fold into the main agent loop using our [migration kit](https://github.com/anthropics/single-agent-loop-kit). It runs a guided workflow to identify your patterns, evaluate alternatives, and verify the best approach. It includes a demo that you can try on a mock system before running on your agent.
Subagents – agents with their own context window, tools, and instructions, orchestrated by a coordinator – are a core component of agent design. They are effective at verification, parallel work, and modular permissioning. We use them in many of our own agents that we build using Claude Platform, for example our [multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system).
However, recently the Applied AI team has found a pattern of enterprise agent deployments that have benefited from folding routers, planners, and domain subagents into the main agent loop. In [our comparisons across several enterprise deployments](https://claude.com/blog/the-anatomy-of-effective-commerce-agents#:~:text=In%20our%20comparisons%20across%20several%20enterprise%20deployments,latency%20per%20task), a single agent with skills frequently outperformed both the one-prompt-for-everything design and the subagent design on quality, and often at a lower cost and latency per task.
For example, one company found the dozen of specialist subagents within its customer-facing agent made a consistent on-brand experience difficult to maintain and added latency that hurt the user experience.
We also often see proposed agent designs that follow a familiar progression: an intent classifier, a fixed multi-step reasoning pipeline, user-segment buckets, separate recommendation branches, and a multi-agent orchestrator on top.
In these cases feedback is often that most of this structure was doing work the model no longer needed done for it, and that one clear system prompt, 4-5 thin data tools, and firm output guardrails would cover most of the use case.
To be clear, subagents still have their place, including at the research frontier. Use them when:
- A single agent loop hits measurable performance degradation from context bloat, or
- Multiple tasks need to be tackled in parallel with fresh context windows that can be discarded once the task is done, or
- A single agent struggles to select appropriate tools or there are conflicting instructions in the system prompt.
But too often we see enterprises give each team or problem type its own subagent, with the agent architecture becoming a copy of their org chart (Conway’s law at work).
This post explains when to consider folding subagents into your main agent loop with best practices we’ve learned from building agents in large organizations.
Agent building failure modes for large organizations
Companies often want to build an agent that unites multiple products and capabilities into a single customer interface.
Typically, each capability is owned by a separate team, so companies start by letting each individual team build their own agent, then a central platform team builds an orchestrator on top. This can take on several structures including orchestrator-subagent or a single agent with specific agents exposed as MCP tools.
This looks like the simplest solution but introduces immediate complexity around:
- Context management: You need to decide what context is exchanged between agents and often lose details in the back and forth.
- Subagent sprawl: Every team ships its own subagent, so companies end up with hundreds of overlapping subagents with no enforced standards and no specific owner.
- The Frankenprompt: Every team adds a sentence to the system prompt, resulting in conflicting rules and no consistent voice.
- Unvetted, overly localized evals: Everyone adds their own evals that are overly optimized for their subtask. No one owns or maintains the whole set, and leadership makes decisions based on watered-down, overly localized scores.
- Latency: Multi-agent architectural complexity adds latency. One customer that evaluated their multi-agent harness against a single agent loop saw a roughly 2x faster runtime with the latter.
Using an agent loop with progressive disclosure
The orchestrator-subagent design described above is a reasonable approach to coordinating specialists built across teams, but often a more effective approach can be progressively disclosing context via skills and progressively disclosing tools via tool search. In other words, the agent sees short descriptions of the skills and tools, which are fully loaded only when needed.
There are three reasons why this approach can make sense:
- Shared context produces better answers: for longer-running agents, we want the context from several different tasks to sit in the main context window. An agent that has seen the result of each earlier step can connect them, which leads to richer outputs and better insights than a set of summaries handed back by subagents. It also means
[fewer context windows and fewer lossy handoffs](https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them). - Progressive disclosure prevents context bloat: this technique allows teams to build single agents that can accomplish a wide variety of tasks without requiring all of the context to be immediately loaded into one long system prompt. This removes the main reason teams previously split work across subagents. In fact, we
[reduced Claude Code’s system prompt for more advanced models by over 80%](https://claude.dev/blog/the-new-rules-of-context-engineering-for-claude-5-generation-models/)which included cuts related to progressively disclosing skills and tools. - Models are more capable: starting with Opus 4.5, models became capable of managing far more in a single loop than most teams expected. You cannot turn off thinking on Opus 5.5, and Fable 5.1, and recent models increasingly narrate their progress and check their work as they go, which makes some harness elements redundant. Each new model lets you move more of the decision-making out of the harness and into the model itself. A simpler loop is also easier to move to the next model; in migrations we have helped customers with, rigid multi-agent structures were often what stopped the new model from doing more of the work.
The single agent loop design requires discipline: a carefully managed system prompt, skill and tool descriptions that trigger at the right times, and deliberate handling of context windows, memory, and note-taking. This article goes deeper into migration and design considerations in subsequent sections.
One central team should own end-to-end quality and the system prompt, vetting every new tool and eval before it ships. Keeping that central team small helps iteration move quickly and lowers coordination cost across a large org.
If you go the multi-agent route, start with the simplest pattern (generator-verifier, orchestrator-subagent, or other) that could work. Decompose boundaries effectively by dividing by context: give each subagent a piece of work that needs little from the rest of the system and have it hand back a compact result (good candidates are independent research paths, separate components with clean interfaces, or black-box verification). When agents are split by problem type, they engage in a "telephone game," passing information back and forth with each handoff degrading fidelity.
How to fold subagents into the main agent loop
Many teams already have an orchestrator and a set of specialist agents in production. The following is the single loop design we'd suggest working toward:
- One model and one context window running an open-ended tool loop, with limits (turn and cost budgets, write gates) set in the harness.
- Each turn, the model emits a batch of tool calls. The harness runs them in parallel and returns raw results to the same model, which decides the next step: another batch, a question to the user, or an answer.
- The loop stops when the model answers or hits a
[budget](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/task-budgets). A goal or verifier check can optionally run after the answer. - The model writes its plan in context on the first turn and revises it as results arrive. This is the main change from the orchestrator and specialist agents setup: the model that writes the plan is also the one carrying it out, so it can change the plan mid-turn.
- Context still gets loaded, and is managed by the agent itself:
- A code step that rewrites the plan from a catalog of rules is no longer needed, since the model decides each step.
- Ordering and domain procedure move into skills.
- Hard limits (validation, approval gates) and anything else that comes up mid-conversation (e.g. memory lookup) move into the tools.
- Code can still be used to load anything cheap and almost always relevant (e.g. an entity resolution step), and to handle any mechanical parts (payload construction, stream parsing, resuming a clarification) inside tools the loop calls.
This single loop design also helps with the end state many teams are working toward (an agent that understands a user's high-level goals and acts on their behalf), since it keeps everything the agent has learned in one context.
The suggestions below are how a team could get from a multi-agent system to a single agent loop in stages, and how several teams can keep contributing to that agent along the way.
Task-completion evals
The first step is to create an eval set that can help you determine whether you should fold a subagent into the main agent loop. The eval structure we’ve seen work is one shared end-to-end set owned by a central team with smaller eval sets shipped with each skill by the team that owns it. Even a set of 10 golden examples is enough to start.
Grading the agent's final message against a rubric is a good starting point for tracking answer quality. While you still have an orchestrator, you should also track routing accuracy (did it pick the right subagent?). Once a subagent is folded in, check instead whether the agent loaded the right skill or called the right tool. Working toward task-completion evals over time is helpful as this matters most when comparing architectures.
This can be complex in environments where internal systems are difficult to replay and user engagement is difficult to simulate. One approach that has worked for us internally is to record timestamps on important events, so they can be replayed later to run as targeted evals.
Reducing subagents over time
Evolving toward a single agent loop involves folding the subagents into tools and skills. This can be done by merging domain subagents, calling them as tools, or replacing them with skills and tools.
Combining domain agents
Build a small end-to-end eval before the first merge. Then fold in by shared context starting with subagents that have the most use.
[Merge specialists](https://claude.com/blog/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them) that chain on each other's output, touch the same data, or are often called together. For example, if a significant share of production traffic is one specialist followed by a second, that is a tightly coupled pair, which makes it a candidate to merge into one domain agent.
Subagents called as tools
When one of the three conditions above applies and you keep a subagent, it can be effective to have the main agent call subagents as tools so it can continue holding the conversation with the user.
We’d only recommend a full handoff, where the subagent takes over the conversation, when it needs to talk to the user directly. Everything else can be a

title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
body:
Keane Lucas, Aengus Lynch, Luna Tong, Luke Champine, Zygi Straznickas, Dino Distefano, Harshikaa Agrawal
Evyatar Ben Asher, Ava Howell, Sami Jawhar, Chris Rohlf, Nickolai Zeldovich
Nicholas Carlini, Rajashree Agrawal, Jason Gross
Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily [find](https://hacks.mozilla.org/2026/05/behind-the-scenes-hardening-firefox/) and [exploit](https://www.anthropic.com/research/exploit-evals). The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with [Theorem](https://theorem.dev/), however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level. While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite [trillions of test runs](https://opensource.googleblog.com/2016/12/announcing-oss-fuzz-continuous-fuzzing.html). As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development.
Introduction
Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are [increasingly adept](https://hacks.mozilla.org/2026/05/behind-the-scenes-hardening-firefox/) at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had [over 1,000 vulnerabilities](https://lwn.net/Articles/1097401/) disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of [chaining seemingly benign bugs](https://www.anthropic.com/research/exploit-evals) into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild.
Ideally, such techniques could find and patch all bugs, and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. Formal verification is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules.
However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but 20 person-years [to formally verify it](https://sel4.systems/Research/pdfs/comprehensive-formal-verification-os-microkernel.pdf). Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as [Airbus’s avionics code](https://www.astree.ens.fr/papers/astree_airbus_sas2007.pdf).
But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can never crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V[1](#footnote-1) CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing all possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end.
We’re publishing a [subset of these proofs](https://github.com/theorem-labs/oss-verify-proofs) so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the [RISC-V and OS semantics](https://github.com/theorem-labs/rocq-linux-process-semantics). [Theorem](https://theorem.dev/), our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same pipeline for [other open-source projects](https://theorem.dev/oss-verify/), and is publishing a [Claude skill](https://github.com/theorem-labs/oss-verify/blob/main/.claude/skills/add-project/SKILL.md) to help developers get started with verifying their own code.
Formal verification is a broad field with many methodologies. Below, we also describe our initial explorations using other formal verification methods to accelerate other security or software development tasks, such as assessing the security of the zlib compression algorithm, proving behavioral equivalence of a Python interpreter written in Rust, and rooting out long-standing bugs in critical software.
The road ahead for formal verification is promising. The cost of writing proofs is falling as models become more intelligent. Moreover, as more code is formalized and methods of achieving security guarantees become more standardized, the ability to reuse or modify proofs across codebases will amortize the cost. We encourage all developers to explore formal verification with LLMs—especially those who previously tried it with less capable models and found it didn’t work.
In the rest of this post, we cover our formal verification experiments in more detail.
Turning tests into proofs
To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the specification (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a [PNG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PNG) decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following [RFC 2083](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2083/)) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale.
To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test suite always passes,” using a general model of what it means to execute any RISC-V-compiled binary on Linux. Historically, proving such specs was intractable, given the inherent complexity of writing a proof that can encompass and make an argument over all possible behaviors and interactions of tens of thousands of assembly instructions over any input (and the fact that proofs tend to be extremely large as a result). This is where today’s LLMs come in: churning through millions of lines of code in pursuit of a well-defined goal is a task that LLMs are extremely well suited for.
For this project, we started with fuzz tests. In these tests, developers write an entry point[2](#footnote-2) into their code that takes inputs, such that any input that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about. Then the fuzzer, a testing engine, generates enormous numbers of semirandom and mutated inputs at the entry point to try to find a bug (visualized in Figure 1). The longer a fuzzer runs, the more bugs it can find. But this is inherently a brute-force process, with no guarantee of exercising every possible code path, regardless of how many inputs you try.
To find all the bugs that would’ve been surfaced by a fuzz test, we turned the fuzz test into a spec defined over the compiled RISC-V instructions. The spec says that the fuzz test won’t crash for any input less than 64 MB.[3](#footnote-3) If Claude can prove this spec, the fuzz test on RISC-V becomes superfluous: fuzzing that entry point will never find any bugs.
We did this for hundreds of projects in Google’s [OSS-Fuzz](https://github.com/google/oss-fuzz) initiative, which provides continuous fuzz testing for qualifying open-source projects. OSS-Fuzz contains thousands of developer-authored entry points that look for broken code properties by crashing (for example, on a failed assertion). OSS-Fuzz automatically instruments C and C++ programs with AddressSanitizer[4](#footnote-4) (ASan), causing them to crash whenever memory is accessed improperly (which is a [leading cause of software vulnerabilities](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/cisa-nsa-fbi-and-international-cybersecurity-authorities-publish-guide-case-memory-safe-roadmaps)). Broad-spectrum specifications like memory safety apply to almost all software.
Over the span of a few weeks, Claude successfully patched the bugs it found and then proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries. These proofs operate on the compiled RISC-V instructions (i.e., executable binaries), and they comprise about 180 million lines of Rocq, with a typical proof running to about 600,000 lines to provide security guarantees on binaries with a median length of 18,000 RISC-V instructions. These proofs are built by translating the RISC-V assembly code to a mathematical model using Theorem’s RISC-V instruction and Linux process semantics. This means these proofs currently assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS. Expanding the scope of these proofs is well within reach, as it would involve standardizing semantics for more assembly architectures and other operating system processes. See [an expert’s take](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/files/4zrzovbb/website/6867eadf760258fa8b42a504600cd3c036d16358.pdf) on the proofs Claude wrote.
While this is an enormous volume of proof code, virtually none of it needs to be manually reviewed. The Rocq proof checker ensures that the spec is correctly satisfied by the proof. As a result, the only artifacts that a developer needs to trust are:
- The formal models of RISC-V and of Linux processes;
- The exact theorem statements that were proved;
- The Rocq proof checker itself.
[5](#footnote-5)
This doesn’t mean these libraries contain no bugs. Instead, it means that any remaining bugs either are to be found within the artifacts listed above or are outside the scope of Claude’s proof. Hardening those still-possibly-buggy trusted components (Rocq, RISC-V, and Linux semantics) is not insignificant, but it’s a far more tractable task than debugging every line of code the scaled-out proofs cover—especially as this approach can secure an arbitrary number of projects without increasing the size of the trusted components.
We welcome independent verification of our proofs and encourage refinement of our approach. To that end, we are publishing the trusted components (above) made for this project that are not already public; Claude’s complete Rocq proofs for fuzz tests that did not require patching; and specifications for other fuzz tests we were not able to prove.
Finding and fixing bugs
Above, we showed that you can turn many open-source libraries’ developer-written tests (fuzz tests) into specs that Claude can prove will always pass, sometimes after patching the remaining bugs it found. For this reason, the process of attempting to prove these specs discovered hundreds of bugs.

title: Can AI understand culture?
body:
Consider this age-old riddle: “What kind of house do you enter blind and leave seeing?” While English speakers may instantly recognize the answer as “a school,” AI models can struggle with the same riddle if asked in another language. A Cohere Labs [open science project](https://cohere.com/research/papers/culturalriddles-2026-10-22) revealed the complex nature of interpretation, and the results were surprising.
The word "riddle" comes from the Old English "rædan" which means "to interpret" or "to advise,” suggesting that riddles are about interpretation and insight rather than just guessing. Riddles thrive on ambiguity but have specific solutions. Just as humans get better at riddles through practice and feedback, AI improves its abilities through machine learning.
“We could not believe our eyes… It is not ‘just’ research anymore, it IS a movement.”
- Boczka Károly
Hungarian diplomat Boczka Károly was actively exploring opportunities in AI research. When he decided to build tricky, Hungarian trivia-style riddles to test if AI models recognized cultural clues, he received stunning results. The models’ answers sounded right, but they weren't right. The models were missing culturally specific facts, and in certain instances, were hallucinating. In an open-science community discussion around culture in AI hosted by Cohere Labs, Boczka shared his findings with Julia Kreutzer. Kreutzer, the Staff Research Scientist at Cohere Labs, saw immediate potential to test the gap between AI fluency and cultural knowledge. Together, they globally scaled a project to test the fluency, logic, and reasoning within models trained mostly on English data and the blind spots behind each answer.
Participation in the project did not require expertise beyond identification with a culture and a commitment to writing and evaluating riddles, which opened the door for research participants of any age and background. An open call on social media and within the [Cohere Labs existing research communities](https://cohere.com/research/open-science) invited people to join the project with no entry criteria, deliberately removing barriers that typically restrict participation. The community gathered on Discord and built its own benchmarks across cultural segments like sports, history, and politics, with each question designed as a riddle.
Mr. Boczka's idea quickly grew into an international initiative. “We could not believe our eyes,” he says. “We had more than 100 contributors from more than 50 countries. It is not “just” research anymore, it IS a movement.” He continues, “Our collective was so dedicated, independent, and cooperative that the whole project grew like a well-planted plant.” Two contributing members within that well-rooted community were 16-year-old American Henry Gagnier and Canadian retired schoolteacher Jane Smith.
While most teenagers might be hesitant to join a global research team of this magnitude, Henry Gagnier’s infectious enthusiasm outweighed any preconceived notion of what a “typical” research team member should be. “I'd say that AI research is for everybody. There are so many different aspects of AI research. We needed people from many different cultures, and it's not ‘AI skills’ that are helpful for building this benchmark, it is real cultural knowledge.” When asked if he was intimidated or surprised by the group, he says, “What surprised me most was their inclusivity and openness, because I was always kind of intimidated as a high school student, joining this project and saying I want to be a lead for this team. But everyone was so nice. It was an amazing experience.”
This project, while grounded in cultural and semantic nuance, provided him with more insight into research and a possible future within it. “It gave me a nice sneak peek into what actual researchers are doing,” Gagnier says. “I want to continue research in this field. I'm doing some projects to further my knowledge in this field now, so I think this project is a good educational experience, and it's definitely changed my outlook on where I want to go in the future.”
As a retired teacher, Jane Smith took what she calls a “teacher approach” to her research. “When I would evaluate kids if they got something wrong, I always tried to back think it, like okay, ‘Where did it go wrong?’ ‘What led to this completely wrong answer?’ There must have been something that led them there, and so I found myself doing that a lot of the time with the evaluating.” She also tried to anthropomorphize her process by incorporating things like tigers or crabs within her riddles to gamify the logic as a powerful teaching tool.
Each solved riddle or generated puzzle became a data point that refined the project’s understanding of language and logic. What made the riddles project particularly meaningful was that it wasn’t just about entertainment, but it demonstrated interpretive capabilities that define both riddles and AI.
AI’s struggle with cultural riddles across different languages and contexts is potentially one of the most significant challenges in developing models. “I was kind of surprised because it wasn't just a lack of cultural understanding,” Gagnier says. “These models don't know this language at all, and I think Buginese is a fairly frequently spoken language. I'm surprised that these models still had virtually zero knowledge of the language, and that translated to zero knowledge of the culture as well with how we were evaluating it.”
The project underlines that intelligence isn't just about [solving puzzles](https://culturalriddles.ai/), but about understanding the human experience and languages behind them. The etymology of "rædan" (to interpret) takes on new depth when we consider that interpretation must be culturally grounded to be meaningful.
Mrs. Smith reveals a widely shared societal concern regarding AI cultural model accuracy. “I was surprised at how few times the models answered, "’I don't know’. But instead, it gives these quite authoritative sounding [answers] which would lead one to think, ‘Oh, this thing knows what it's talking about’.”
What the team found unsettling were finite conclusions from models that sounded unwaveringly confident despite wrong answers. Recognizing this blind spot, Mrs. Smith says, “The scary part to me is that it sounds so authoritative and people are looking for authoritative answers.” She adds, “I don't think it's AI that's going to kill us. It’s our lack of critical thinking that's going to kill us.”
In an age where some worry that the human elements of daily life are quickly disappearing, the riddles research pushes for a rethink surrounding any resolution that lacks a human touch. In her wisdom, Mrs. Smith poses what may seem like an amusing play on words, but what just might be the decisive outlook on an AI cultural conundrum: “To err is AI. To critically think is human.”
There is an interesting space between human cognition and AI’s thinking. Cohere Labs is working on better contextual understanding by delving into [confidence in today’s models](https://cohere.com/blog/rethinking-confidence-in-reasoning-models). The riddles demonstrate that as AI grows more confident in its answers, we must remember that critical thinking keeps us human.

title: Inside Cohere Model Vault: Building a verifiable confidential AI inference
body:
In our product launch, we introduced [Confidential Computing on Cohere Model Vault](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1BvbHFNbT-GjlvSG7UMaaahsM4OX3A4YtZPp_330XT0g/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.vv3sfmm4rp2q), now in public beta with NVIDIA GPUs on Microsoft Azure.
This article goes deeper into how the system works.
The goal is not simply to encrypt inference. It is to reduce the infrastructure that customers must trust with plaintext data and give them cryptographic evidence they can verify before sensitive information is released.
That requires more than a confidential virtual machine. A confidential inference system has to protect the computation itself, the path that carries sensitive requests to it, and the mechanism customers use to decide whether the destination can be trusted.
Model Vault brings those pieces together around a dedicated model deployment.
From confidential hardware to confidential inference
Confidential computing protects data in use, while an application or model is actively processing it.
At the foundation are two properties:
- Isolation, which uses hardware-enforced controls to protect workload memory from infrastructure outside the confidential environment.
- Attestation, which produces cryptographically signed evidence about the environment so another party can evaluate it before releasing sensitive data.
Together, these properties change the traditional infrastructure trust model. Privileged access to the underlying host no longer automatically implies access to the workload running inside the confidential environment.
For AI inference, however, the boundary cannot end at the CPU.
A substantial portion of model computation runs on accelerators. If the CPU were protected while the accelerator remained outside the confidential boundary, sensitive model state and intermediate computation could become exposed at the point where inference moves to the GPU.
Confidential Computing on NVIDIA GPUs protects GPU memory from infrastructure outside the protected environment and encrypts communication between the CPU and GPU. This allows the confidential boundary to span the confidential virtual machine with the accelerator performing inference.
Inside a confidential Model Vault
No single component makes an inference request confidential.
Model Vault combines several controls around a dedicated model deployment, each addressing a different part of the trust problem.
Confidential CPU and GPU execution
The model-serving stack runs inside a confidential virtual machine.
The operating system, drivers, inference server, and their memory are protected from the host environment through hardware-backed isolation. The workload is also constrained by policy so that only approved software can run inside the environment and operators do not have an interactive path into the workload.
The NVIDIA Confidential Computing extends protection to the accelerator and encrypts traffic between the CPU and GPU.
This matters because the security boundary needs to cover the systems actually performing the inference, not only the CPU coordinating it.
Microsoft Azure provides the underlying confidential computing infrastructure. Model Vault builds the managed model-serving, encrypted request, attestation, and customer-verification layers around that foundation.
The result is that customers do not need to assemble, integrate, and operate these controls independently.
Encrypting the request itself
Protecting the compute environment solves only part of the problem.
Sensitive data also has to reach that environment.
TLS protects network connections, but connection-level encryption alone does not guarantee that every intermediary involved in operating a service remains outside the plaintext path.
Model Vault therefore protects the application payload itself.
It uses Oblivious HTTP, or OHTTP, to encrypt sensitive request contents to a public key associated with the attested confidential environment. The encrypted message can then pass through intermediary infrastructure as ciphertext.
Only the OHTTP gateway inside the confidential environment has access to the corresponding private key and can decrypt the protected request. The response is protected on the return path in the same way.
This creates an important separation between operating the service and accessing the contents of the request.
Intermediary infrastructure can still perform functions required by a managed platform, such as routing traffic, without needing access to the sensitive application payload.
Applications continue to use the Model Vault API and familiar request formats. The additional protection is implemented in the client and infrastructure layers rather than requiring customers to redesign their application payloads.
Remote attestation: proving what will process the request
Isolation prevents infrastructure outside the confidential boundary from directly reading protected workload memory.
But isolation alone still leaves an important question:
How does the customer know that the destination is actually running the hardware and software configuration it expects?
Remote attestation addresses that question.
The confidential environment produces cryptographically signed evidence describing the environment that is running. This includes measurements and security-relevant properties associated with the hardware, firmware, operating environment, and application software.
That evidence is then evaluated against an approved policy.
This separation between evidence and policy is fundamental.
Attestation evidence answers:
What environment is actually running?
The policy answers:
Is this an environment I am willing to trust with my data?
A verifier can require that specific properties match approved values before a protected request is released.
Those requirements can include the expected software measurements and security state of the confidential environment, including whether the GPU is operating in the expected confidential mode.
The customer therefore does not need to rely solely on Cohere's assertion that a particular environment is trustworthy. Verification is performed before sensitive data is released.
Attestation as an enforcement mechanism
Attestation matters most when it changes what the system does.
In Model Vault, verification is part of the decision about whether protected data is released at all.
Before sending a protected request, the client evaluates the destination against the approved policy.
If an expected property is missing or incorrect, for example because a software measurement has changed or the GPU is not operating in the required confidential mode, verification fails and the client refuses to send the protected payload.
The sensitive request therefore remains inside the customer's environment rather than being sent to a destination that did not satisfy verification.
This turns attestation from an audit artifact into an active security control.
Attestation evidence is renewed frequently. Each time it is refreshed, the client verifies the new measurements and security state against the approved policy before continuing to send protected requests.
This is the practical meaning of verify before you trust.
The trust boundary and threat model
Confidential computing reduces the amount of infrastructure that must be trusted with plaintext data.
It does not eliminate trust entirely.
Understanding the remaining trust boundary is therefore as important as understanding the protections themselves.
What remains trusted
Several components remain part of the trusted computing base, including:
- the underlying confidential computing hardware
- firmware
- measured software running inside the confidential environment
- the reference measurements used to define an approved configuration
- the attestation infrastructure used to evaluate and sign evidence
The important difference is that this trust can be made more explicit and measurable.
Hardware produces evidence about the environment, while customer-controlled verification checks that evidence against approved values before protected data is released.
The system therefore replaces some forms of broad, implicit infrastructure trust with a smaller set of components whose state can be measured and evaluated.
What is protected
Within its threat model, Confidential Computing on Model Vault protects prompts, documents, responses, and model execution while they are being processed.
Intermediaries outside the confidential environment, including the host operating system, hypervisor, infrastructure administrators, cloud provider, and Cohere operators, are prevented from reading protected workload memory.
Because sensitive application payloads are encrypted end-to-end to the confidential environment, their contents also remain protected while crossing intermediary infrastructure.
The protection therefore spans both:
- the path carrying sensitive request contents to the confidential environment
- the environment performing the inference
That distinction matters. A confidential execution environment alone would not prevent plaintext exposure elsewhere in the request path.
What remains outside the protection boundary
A useful threat model also needs to state what it does not protect.
Confidential computing does not claim to prevent every possible attack.
Physical and side-channel attacks
Some physical and side-channel attacks remain outside the protection boundary. For example, an attacker may be able to infer information indirectly from timing or other shared hardware behavior, even without directly reading protected memory.
Availability
An operator that cannot read a protected workload may still be able to stop it, delay it, or prevent it from running.
Confidential computing therefore does not prevent denial-of-service attacks or provide availability guarantees by itself.
Application-level vulnerabilities
Software running inside the confidential environment still needs to be secure.
Prompt injection, insecure tool use, authorization errors, application vulnerabilities, and other software-level risks are not solved simply by placing the application inside confidential computing hardware.
Observable metadata
The contents of protected application payloads are encrypted, but some information remains visible outside that payload.
This can include:
- request timing
- message size
- traffic volume
- routing information
In the current architecture, information required for authentication and routing, including the API credential and model identifier, also remains outside the OHTTP-protected application payload.
That distinction is intentional and important when reasoning about what the system hides and what it does not.
What confidential computing is not
Confidential computing is one security control within a broader architecture.
It is not:
- A replacement for application security. Software inside the confidential boundary still needs to be designed, reviewed, and secured correctly.
- A data-residency mechanism. Confidential computing governs access to data during computation. It does not determine the jurisdiction in which that computation occurs.
- A replacement for compliance or contractual controls. DPAs, access controls, certifications, security reviews, and legal obligations remain necessary.
- Homomorphic encryption. The model still operates on plaintext inside the protected environment. Confidential computing protects that environment rather than computing directly over encrypted values.
Attestation also provides assurance only when signed evidence is actually validated against an appropriate policy.
Evidence describes what is running.
Policy determines whether that environment should be trusted.
Confidential computing does not eliminate trust. It makes trust smaller, explicit, measurable, and verifiable.
Built in the open
Verification becomes more meaningful when customers and security researchers can understand what they are verifying.

title: Introducing Confidential Computing on Cohere Model Vault
body:
Today, we are announcing the public beta of Confidential Computing on Cohere Model Vault, bringing hardware-backed protection and independently verifiable security to managed enterprise AI.
Model Vault gives enterprises dedicated, fully managed model inference. With Confidential Computing, we are extending that experience to some of an organization's most sensitive workloads and data, including financial information, clinical records, privileged documents, proprietary source code, and intellectual property.
The goal is simple: enterprises should be able to use the capabilities and operational simplicity of managed AI without giving the infrastructure that operates it access to their sensitive plaintext data.
Protecting data in use
Encryption traditionally protects data in two places: while it is stored and while it travels across a network.
Confidential Computing on Model Vault is designed to protect the third state: data in use.
Inference runs within a hardware-backed confidential environment spanning the CPU and GPU. Hardware-enforced isolation protects workload memory from everything outside the confidential boundary, including privileged infrastructure software and operators. With NVIDIA Confidential Computing, GPU memory is protected and traffic between the CPU and GPU is encrypted as the model performs inference.
This enables enterprises to bring more sensitive workloads to AI while reducing the number of parties and systems they need to trust with their data.
Verify before you trust
Protection alone is not enough. Enterprises also need a way to know that those protections are actually in place.
That is why remote attestation is a core part of Confidential Computing on Model Vault.
Before sensitive data is sent, customer-side software verifies cryptographically signed evidence about the environment that will process it, including its hardware, firmware, and software configuration. That evidence is checked against an approved security policy.
If the environment does not satisfy the policy, the client refuses to send the request.
This changes the trust model from "trust us" to "verify it yourself."
“Enterprises should not have to choose between the simplicity of managed AI and control over their most sensitive information. With Model Vault and Confidential Computing, customers can verify the environment that will process their data before they send it. With hardware attestation, customers not only have cryptographic proof that workloads are running in a secure, confidential computing environment, they also can verify that their data is protected from unauthorized access, even from Cohere.”
- Phil Blunsom, CTO at Cohere
End-to-end protection for sensitive request contents
Confidential Computing protects what happens inside the compute environment. Model Vault also protects sensitive request contents on their way there.
Rather than relying only on connection-level encryption, Model Vault encrypts application payloads end-to-end to the attested confidential environment. The encrypted request can pass through intermediary infrastructure without exposing its contents, and only the confidential environment can decrypt it. Responses are protected on the return path as well.
This preserves the operational advantages of a managed AI platform without exposing the plaintext contents of customer requests to intermediary infrastructure.
Customers continue to use the Model Vault API and familiar request formats. The additional protection is built into the client and infrastructure layers rather than requiring applications to redesign their payloads.
Built with Microsoft Azure and NVIDIA
The public beta is powered by NVIDIA H100 GPUs on Microsoft Azure.
Microsoft Azure provides the underlying confidential computing infrastructure.and NVIDIA Confidential Computing extends those capabilities to the NVIDIA H100 GPUs. Cohere brings these technologies together through Model Vault's managed model serving, encrypted request path, remote attestation, and customer-side verification.
The result is a managed AI platform that combines the operational simplicity of cloud AI with stronger technical control over access to sensitive data during inference.
“Enterprises need confidence that their most sensitive AI workloads are protected by more than contractual promises. Our work with Cohere on Model Vault demonstrates how confidential computing can combine the simplicity of managed AI with independently verifiable technical controls.”
- Vikas Bhatia, Head of Product, Azure Confidential Computing at Microsoft
“Confidential Computing opens new possibilities for enterprises that need to run AI on highly sensitive data. NVIDIA Confidential Computing on NVIDIA GPUs provides hardware-backed protections that help platforms like Cohere Model Vault bring confidential AI inference to enterprise workloads.”
- John Fanelli, vice president, Enterprise Software at NVIDIA
Unlocking AI for sensitive enterprise workloads
For many organizations, the question is no longer whether AI can perform a task. The question is whether the data required for that task can safely be used with AI at all.
Confidential Computing on Model Vault is designed to protect workloads where security, contractual, or regulatory requirements may have kept valuable data outside managed AI platforms, including:
- Fraud investigations in financial services
- Privileged document search and due diligence in legal services
- Sensitive public-sector information
- Patent and research material
- Proprietary engineering design documents (EDD), Interface design documents (IDD) and architecture materials
- Search and analysis across proprietary source code
These are the kinds of workloads where reducing privileged infrastructure access and giving customers independently verifiable evidence can make previously restricted AI use cases practical.
Confidential computing does not eliminate all risk, nor does it replace application security, compliance, contractual controls, or data-residency requirements. It provides a hardware-enforced and verifiable protection boundary around data and computation while inference is taking place.
Available now in public beta
Confidential Computing on Cohere Model Vault is now available in public beta, powered by NVIDIA H100 GPUs on Microsoft Azure.
Customers can create and manage encrypted vaults through Model Vault and integrate them using the same Cohere APIs, with customer-side verification and end-to-end encryption protecting sensitive request contents before they leave the customer's environment.
For a deeper look at the confidential compute architecture, encrypted request path, remote attestation, trust boundary, and threat model, read [Inside Cohere Model Vault: Building Verifiable Confidential AI Inference](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1x6HKQHN3WFKhIf80Ca5KfaaCz_juyQg_EFk524f-Ons/edit?tab=t.0).
Get started at [vault.cohere.com](http://vault.cohere.com)

# Uber brings ChatGPT Work to all employees with OpenAI

Uber announced the company-wide rollout of [ChatGPT Work](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-for-your-most-ambitious-work/), an agent that helps employees take on a wide range of tasks within ChatGPT Enterprise, starting today. The rollout will make ChatGPT Work available to more than 30,000 employees across Uber’s global workforce.

Expanding from an initial pilot of 1,000 employees, the rollout will give teams across Uber access to an agentic platform designed to take on complex, multi-step tasks and deliver finished work. The expansion makes ChatGPT Work Uber’s first company-wide deployment of an agentic platform tailored for knowledge work.

ChatGPT Work connects with tools companies like Uber use on a daily basis, including Google Drive, Gmail, Google Calendar, and Slack, enabling workers to research information, prepare meeting briefs, create presentations, analyze data and complete workflows across applications.

ChatGPT Work also gives Uber access to OpenAI’s portfolio of frontier models. Uber will benefit from models like [GPT‑6.1 Sol⁠](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-1-sol/) which will be deployed as the default capability within ChatGPT Work, balancing frontier performance and cost efficiency. Uber teams will also be supported by OpenAI multimodal capabilities, including voice and image generation, giving them the flexibility to choose the right models and tools for different needs.

The rollout will be supported by Uber’s internal AI skills library, approved integrations and dedicated employee training, helping teams across functions including operations, finance, marketing and product put the technology to work. Uber’s developers and software engineering teams will also continue using Codex to accelerate software development and streamline coding workflows.

> “Uber has always been a company of builders, and every day, millions of people around the world rely on what we create. As AI transforms how we work, we want to give everyone the tools to innovate, solve problems and help shape Uber’s future. Rolling out ChatGPT Work across the company is an exciting step toward that ambition, and I can’t wait to see what our teams build with it.”

Over the past few months, we’ve worked with customers and partners to align safety policies across services that provide our models. We’re also updating our Usage Policies to make those requirements clearer and easier for developers to follow.

Models such as GPT‑6 Astra expand what developers and businesses can build. As those capabilities grow, we’re working to keep safeguards effective and consistently applied across the services that offer our models.

## Responsibility starts with us

Before deploying a model, we evaluate its capabilities and risks, train it to follow safety requirements, and test whether its safeguards hold up when people deliberately try to bypass them. As we describe in our [approach to safety and alignment](https://openai.com/safety/how-we-think-about-safety-alignment/), we combine safeguards designed to reinforce one another.

After deployment, we monitor for potential abuse and investigate concerns. To [mitigate cyber misuse](https://openai.com/index/strengthening-cyber-resilience/), for example, we train models to refuse harmful requests and use systems that look for suspicious patterns across interactions to decide how to respond. Trusted access programs provide another layer of protection and set eligibility requirements and conditions for access to our most powerful capabilities.

Some safeguards are built into the model and others depend on the systems and people around it. Both need to be effective whether people access our models directly or through a partner.

## Consistent standards across services

Developers and businesses should be able to choose where they access our models, with consistent safeguards across those services. We developed policies to align our safeguards across providers and are working with each of our partners to ensure their implementation meets or exceeds our safety standards. These policies apply whether people access our models directly through OpenAI, partners that host them, or through reseller partners.

These policies require partners that provide access to OpenAI models to maintain safeguards consistent with our own, investigate potential violations, and take appropriate action when concerns are identified. That includes coordinating on enforcement so that restrictions remain effective across services providing access to our models.

Putting this into practice means accounting for how different services work and how customers use them. Our work with customers and partners on [Private Safety Processing](https://openai.com/index/offering-zero-data-retention-for-frontier-models/) is one example of how we can develop effective safeguards while giving customers greater choice and control over their sensitive data.

## Clear policies and predictable enforcement

We’re also updating our [Usage Policies](https://openai.com/policies/usage-policies/), effective November 20, 2026, to clarify the rules for safe model development and sensitive uses of AI. The updated Usage Policies build on that work by requiring services that provide direct access to our models such as model routers or AI gateways to get our review and approval before offering that access.

We’ll keep explaining what’s allowed, what’s restricted, and how customers and partners can ask questions or resolve compliance concerns.

As our models become more capable, we’ll keep improving how we detect, investigate, and respond to misuse. Customers can face misuse through their end users, compromised accounts, or leaked API keys and we work with them to understand and address those problems.

We’re also working with customers to introduce SafetyIDs, which customers can provide to help us distinguish between individual end users in an investigation without OpenAI learning those users’ identities. With SafetyIDs, we can respond to potential misuse more precisely while reducing disruption to others.

We base enforcement decisions on documented conduct and risk, apply our rules consistently, and respond in proportion to the circumstances. When we restrict access, we revisit those restrictions if meaningful changes in conduct, commitments, or safeguards address the concerns behind our decision.

We want more people to benefit from AI. Clear rules and consistent safeguards should make it easier for developers and businesses to build, compete, and choose the services that work best for them.

title: Does Code Quality Still Matter? It Depends on This — Max Kanat-Alexander, Capital One
body:
Every senior engineer's answer is "it depends." Max Kanat-Alexander says what it actually depends on. Code quality always existed for two things: understanding a system and safely changing it. AI is making a new kind of software common: disposable software, with low consequences, few dependents and near-zero cost to replace or maintain. For that software, quality doesn't matter. For durable software it matters more than ever. He also shows how to make systems more disposable and how to make rigor cheap through standards, in-workflow tooling, easy testing and maximum strictness.

title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security
body:
21st October 2026 - Link Blog
[Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security](https://thephp.foundation/blog/2026/10/21/todays-php-security-release-and-how-were-strengthening-php-security/) ([via](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50182987)) If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process.
This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong:
On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and
[published it at 19:30 UTC]. It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...]As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st.
[This article](https://www.wiz.io/blog/php2shell-php-rce) from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure:
- August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol.
- August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal.
- August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress.
- August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team.
- September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix.
- October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available.
- October 21, 2026: Public disclosure.

title: NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required
body:
[
](#nvidia-kumo-relational-outperforms-supervised-machine-learning-on-relational-data-no-training-required)
NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required
[Enterprise + Article](/blog)
[
](#tldr)
TL;DR
NVIDIA Kumo Relational is a pre-trained relational foundation model that makes predictions directly on enterprise databases. Given a predictive query, it gathers up to 10,000 historical examples as context and predicts outcomes such as churn, demand, or fraud in a single forward pass. It needs no task-specific training, no feature engineering, and no flattening of tables. Kumo Relational is the first few-shot foundation model to outperform supervised machine learning on common relational benchmarks. Across 41 tasks on 15 databases, it beats supervised relational deep learning models and expert-engineered gradient-boosted tree pipelines, and on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark it surpasses AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR). It scales to databases with 500B+ rows and works for humans and agents alike, through NVIDIA's open-source, GPU-native structured-data-models library or as an NVIDIA NIM.
- Paper:
[https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596) - Documentation:
[https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview](https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview)
[
](#the-shift-to-structured-data-foundation-models)
The Shift to Structured Data Foundation Models
Foundation models have already rewritten the playbook for language and vision. Not long ago, production NLP meant a dedicated model per task, each fed by its own pipeline of tokenization, lemmatization, and n-grams. LLMs made that stack largely obsolete for three reasons: they were more accurate than the best task-specific models, far simpler to put into production, and flexible enough to open a new era of agentic applications.
The same shift is now underway for structured data. Relational databases power the world's most critical business decisions, yet predictive modeling on them still requires weeks of feature engineering, task-specific training, and tuned pipelines. Structured data foundation models change that for the same three reasons:
Better accuracy today: As drop-in replacements, these models already beat many production pipelines, especially XGBoost. On RelBench V1 classification tasks, Kumo Relational outperforms gradient-boosted trees on expert-engineered features by nearly 4 AUROC points on average. On SAP SALT, it beats XGBoost on engineered features by 7 MRR points out of the box and by 13 MRR points after fine-tuning. These results make a compelling case for replacing production XGBoost pipelines with Kumo Relational.
Simplicity and agility: One pre-trained model replaces separate pipelines for individual tasks. A new prediction becomes a query instead of a project, so ML teams can finally take on use cases that traditional ML made too laborious to build at every level of the organization.
Agents that can predict: LLMs let agents read, write, and reason. Structured data foundation models let them anticipate what happens next, such as which customer will churn, and act on it. Kumo Relational is already built to be called by agents, and its Predictive Query Language (PQL) gives them a simple interface for asking predictive questions.
Today, we are introducing Kumo Relational ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596), [documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview)), a pre-trained foundation model that brings this paradigm to relational data. Connect a database, describe what to predict, and get predictions in a single forward pass. No training required.
[
](#how-kumo-relational-works)
How Kumo Relational Works
Most foundation models for structured data operate on a single flat table. Real-world data lives in relational databases instead: users connected to orders connected to products, all evolving over time. Flattening these relationships into one row through manual aggregation (e.g., "average order value in the last 30 days") loses fine-grained structural signals and takes significant human effort.
Kumo Relational is a Relational Foundation Model that operates directly on the database, respecting its tables, foreign keys, and timestamps. It is pre-trained once on synthetic relational data that reflects real-world datasets and adapts to each new task through in-context learning, reading up to 10,000 context examples at inference time. Each example pairs a local subgraph around an entity at a point in time with its ground-truth target (e.g., "this user churned" or "this item sold 142 units").
![Overview of the NVIDIA Kumo Relational system: (a) database integration, (b) a prompting interface that turns natural language into a predictive query, and (c) automatic context generation feeding the NVIDIA Kumo Relational model, which scales horizontally across tenants.]
Figure 1. Overview of the Kumo Relational system. Connect a database, specify a predictive query, and Kumo Relational handles the rest, from context generation to model inference.
To make a prediction, Kumo Relational has to do three things: (1) understand the values within each table, (2) relate records across tables, and (3) relate context examples with known targets to the entity being predicted. Here is how it works:
![Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input with task, users, orders and items tables; (b) column and row attention within tables with injected context targets; (c) graph attention and cross-sample attention across tables.]
Figure 2. Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input, (b) reasoning within tables, (c) reasoning across tables.
Automatic Context Generation: Tasks are written in the [Predictive Query Language (PQL)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09572), a declarative interface where you state what to predict rather than how. For temporal tasks, Kumo Relational replays historical database states: it samples entity-centric subgraphs up to an anchor timestamp and computes each target from events after that timestamp, while serving the model only the data from before it. This prevents data leakage.
Reasoning Within Tables: A lightweight network processes each table independently, alternating column attention (relating values within a column) and row attention (relating features within a row). The model learns which columns and rows matter for the current prediction and filters out noise before it propagates.
Reasoning Across Tables: A larger network distributes the row embeddings across the relational structure via graph attention over primary-key/foreign-key relationships, interleaved with cross-sample attention across context examples. This is where relational reasoning happens, such as linking a user's profile to their transaction history. Because this stage works on row embeddings rather than on every cell in every table, the design avoids quadratic cost and scales to large contexts and deeper subgraphs.
[
](#how-kumo-relational-was-built)
How Kumo Relational Was Built
Kumo Relational is pre-trained on entirely synthetic relational data simulated to reflect real-world relational databases with diverse predictive queries. Pre-training proceeds in stages, from single tables to increasingly complex relational structures.
The diverse relational databases needed for pre-training are rarely public, so synthetic data fills the gap. Kumo Relational's generator builds on the approach of [PluRel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04029) (Kothapalli et al., ICML 2026), which extends single-table data generators to full relational databases. Members of the Kumo team helped develop PluRel and co-authored the original paper. PluRel generates each database in three stages: a schema, foreign-key links between rows that cluster as they do in real data, and column values from Structural Causal Models with temporal trends and cross-table dependencies. Generation is lightweight, so pre-training data is effectively unlimited, and the PluRel paper shows that pre-training loss follows a power law as synthetic databases are added, with gains that carry over to real databases.
Through this pre-training, the model learns to filter, correlate, and aggregate information across tables instead of relying on fixed aggregations. When maximum accuracy matters, Kumo Relational can also be fine-tuned on a specific dataset and task.
[
](#performance)
Performance
In this paper, we evaluated Kumo Relational on 41 benchmarks across 15 relational databases from RelBench V1 and V2, SAP SALT, and 4DBInfer, spanning e-commerce, medical, enterprise, social, and academic domains. None of these datasets were seen in pre-training. Kumo Relational outperforms the strongest supervised models in both classification and regression, including relational deep learning models and expert-engineered tabular ensembles. On the [RelArena-α](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16319) leaderboard, which compares relational models and systems on RelBench V1, it also sits on the accuracy-efficiency Pareto front out of the box:
![Scatter plot of the RelArena-α leaderboard: relative accuracy as Elo across tasks (y-axis) versus median inference time per 1,000 samples (x-axis, log scale). Kumo Relational sits on the Pareto front at about 17 seconds and Elo 1,842. The highest-scoring entry, rt-plurel, reaches Elo 1,878 at about 7,300 seconds, roughly 430 times slower. Every other foundation model, feature-engineering system, and supervised model scores lower and runs slower than Kumo Relational.]
Figure 3. RelArena-α leaderboard: Elo across tasks versus median inference time per 1,000 samples (log scale). Kumo Relational is about 430× faster than the highest-scoring entry at similar accuracy.
The paper also reports that on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark, Kumo Relational surpasses large AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR) and recent tabular foundation models by about 25%, and fine-tuning extends its lead over AutoGluon to 16%. It also holds up under hard conditions: it performs well with as little as 0.2% of the training data as context, stays stable when up to 75% of foreign-key links are removed, and barely degrades when many noisy columns are added.
[
](#limitations)
Limitations
Kumo Relational performs best on data with meaningful relationships and temporal dynamics, such as user behavior over time. On tasks with very large training sets, task-specific supervised models may still edge out in-context predictions, which used at most 10,000 context examples in our benchmarks. Fine-tuning of the foundation model is designed for exactly this case. Predictive signals must also be reachable within a limited number of hops, so start with a focused query over a few relevant tables and expand the graph as needed.
[
](#demo)
Demo
Kumo Relational runs in-context learning natively over databases: in memory, through database and warehouse connectors, or through a custom graph engine that handles 500B+ rows via memory-mapped I/O at up to 5 GB/s. It is available in NVIDIA's newly released, GPU-native structured-data-models library, the same open-source library that powers our sister model, [Kumo Tabular](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/kumo-tabular). The library downloads the weights from the Hugging Face Hub on first use, so you can load the model in a GPU-backed notebook and predict directly from it. The code below passes context examples, prediction entities, and their related tables to the model:
# pip install structured-data-models
import sdm
model = sdm.models.KumoRelational(device="cuda")
pred = model(
# In-context training table (fkeys/timestamps/targets):
x_context=...,
y_context=...,
# Prediction examples (fkeys/timestamps):
x_query=...,
# Multi-table information for context/prediction entities:
related_context_tables=...,
related_query_tables=...,
)
See the library's [relational examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models/tree/main/examples/relational) for co
