title: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications
body:
[
](#how-specializing-the-vocabulary-of-slms-can-cut-inference-cost-by-77-in-real-applications)
How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications
[Team Article](/blog)
Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.
The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.
One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.
The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.
We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.
[
](#a-vocabulary-built-for-everyone)
A Vocabulary Built for Everyone
The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.
For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.
The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.
The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.
[
](#reading-is-cheap-writing-is-expensive)
Reading Is Cheap, Writing Is Expensive
The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.
To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.
This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.
Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.
The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.
And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.
[
](#why-existing-solutions-fell-short)
Why Existing Solutions Fell Short
Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's [in-place tokenizer expansion](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/tokenizer-expansion) (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.
They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.
They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.
[
](#how-we-solved-it)
How We Solved It
VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.
First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.
Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.
To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.
Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.
An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.
A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.
That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.
[
](#what-changed-in-the-grader)
What Changed in the Grader
To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.
The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.
Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.
The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.
[
](#beyond-the-grader)
Beyond the Grader
To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.
VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fiftee

# How AT&T is rethinking in-house legal work with OpenAI

AT&T is building on LegalEdge to explore new ways to support its legal team.

[Contact sales](https://openai.com/contact-sales/)



Company size: Enterprise

Region: Global

Industry: Technology

Loading…

Share

AT&T’s in-house legal department has hundreds of lawyers and legal professionals around the world. Before they can advise the business, they need to assemble facts, documents, and relevant past work, often drawing on expertise held across different teams. For David McAtee, AT&T’s Senior Executive Vice President and General Counsel, making that experience easier to access is central to how the department’s work can improve.

AT&T is working with OpenAI to build that next phase. “Our partnership with OpenAI is going to allow us to build that plumbing that powers the knowledge layer throughout the company and that all of us will draw into,” McAtee says.

The collaboration builds on LegalEdge, AT&T’s team of attorneys, legal professionals, technologists, and project managers focused on applying AI to major legal matters. The next step is to connect more of the company’s accumulated expertise to the work arriving on a lawyer’s desk.

Requests arrive from across the business, and legal teams need to respond quickly without overlooking risks. Before they can advise, they have to understand the issue, gather the relevant context and decide what needs attention first. That makes intake a critical part of protecting the business. Bill Ryan, AT&T’s Chief Compliance Officer, describes one planned initiative as an intake system with “a front door where we have natural language intake.” The system would classify and prioritize requests, connect them with relevant precedent, research, and past work, and give the responsible legal professional historical context and recommended first steps.

That would give lawyers a more informed starting point, with less time spent gathering the material they need to assess a matter. Ryan sees the opportunity in helping the department bring its judgment to more of the business’s needs.

“What most excites me about the future is expanding our ability to provide legal judgment at greater scale,” he says.

For McAtee, the principle guiding that work remains clear: “The decision making will always remain with the lawyers.” The partnership’s goal is to put better information within reach so those lawyers can spend more time applying their expertise.

title: Before the ambulance arrives: How AI is helping the NHS rethink patient care
body:
When someone in the UK dials 999 for an ambulance, their focus is understandably on when help will arrive. Less visible is the planning, training, analysis and coordination that happen long before a paramedic reaches the patient.

“We all think about the ambulance when it’s on scene, but there’s so much that happens before that goes on before an ambulance crew even arrives with a patient,” says James Goulding, chief clinical information officer at [Yorkshire Ambulance Service (YAS) NHS Trust.](https://www.yas.nhs.uk/) YAS is one of 200 plus trusts, or organizational units, of the UK’s National Health Service.

That preparation includes planning services, recruiting and training staff, analyzing population health data and understanding the experiences of patients who do not speak English fluently.

![Image 1](https://news.microsoft.com/source/emea/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Microsoft-365-Copilot-Wakefield-YAS-Joanne-Crawford-3_1x1.jpg)

## “So much goes into making sure that when that paramedic arrives in front of a patient,that we’ve done all of this work to make it really easy for them to make good decisions for patients,”Goulding says.

James Goulding,chief clinical information officer at Yorkshire Ambulance Service.Photo by Joanne Crawford for Microsoft.

Following an earlier trial involving 30,000 employees, [NHS England](https://www.nhs.uk/) announced plans in June 2026 to make [Microsoft Copilot](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/copilot) available to as many as 505,000 clinicians and support staff. Participants in the trial reported saving an average [of 43 minutes per working day](https://www.england.nhs.uk/2026/06/500000-nhs-staff-to-get-new-artificial-intelligence-tools-to-help-free-up-more-time-for-patients/) — which adds up to about five weeks of time per person a year.

Dr. Alec Price-Forbes, national chief clinical information officer for NHS England, says that the NHS is still in many ways an analog system. “It’s critically important that we use the opportunity that we have in front of us to truly reimagine the NHS,” he says, “to reduce cognitive load and administrative burden for healthcare professionals, make sure they get a better experience and then are in the position to give the best quality care.”

AI and digital tools such as Microsoft Copilot can help sustain the NHS by reducing administrative burden, releasing clinical capacity and enabling more productive, connected and person-centered models of care.

## Helping NHS teams manage information

![Image 2](https://news.microsoft.com/source/emea/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MSFT_nhs_thumbnail.jpg)

Tom Smith sees that work from several angles. As an area operations manager for Yorkshire Ambulance Service, he oversees operational managers and frontline teams, plans staffing and specialist resources, and responds personally to significant incidents as a tactical commander. The service received [about 1.25 million calls](https://www.yas.nhs.uk/media/5905/final-yas-annual-report-2025-26-unsigned-24-september-2026.pdf) to its 999 number in the 2025-26 fiscal year.

“It’s everything and anything,” he says. “No day is the same.”

Smith also has to read and produce many reports. Microsoft Copilot does not make decisions for him, he says. Instead, it organizes information into a format he can review and interrogate using his operational expertise.

![Image 3](https://news.microsoft.com/source/emea/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Microsoft-CoPilot-YAS-Esme-Mai-12_1x1.jpg)

## “What it does is just give me all the information in a helpful format,which is easy to understand,”Smith says.“It does a lot of my admin tasks for me that would previously have been really time consuming.Then I can just review what it’s done.”

Tom Smith,area operations manager for Yorkshire Ambulance Service.Photo by Esme Mai for Microsoft.

For Smith, who is dyslexic, that support extends beyond saving time. Writing an email can take longer when he begins to overthink the wording or spelling, he says. The ability to structure a draft, summarize a long report and ask follow-up questions helps “level the playing field” for him.

His experience comes as NHS England expands access to generative AI tools across the health service in England.

The NHS has put clear, strict safeguards around its use of Microsoft Copilot: it is only for administrative tasks, not clinical work, says Price-Forbes. The NHS is supporting its digital transformation with standards for clinical safety, information governance, cybersecurity, interoperability and real-world evaluation, with transparency and human oversight considered essential to maintaining the confidence of staff and the public.

Like healthcare systems in many countries, the NHS serves an aging population, and many patients have multiple chronic illnesses.

Price-Forbes says, “It means that we’ve got the opportunity to redesign because we just cannot continue with the old analog model of healthcare delivery. And this is a challenge across the globe. So we now need to redesign care around people and technology, digital and data, and AI is going to be the only way to create those new service models of care.”

“Artificial intelligence can transform the NHS — improving care, giving time back to staff and delivering greater value — but only if we turn ambition into trusted action at scale,” he says. “Proven tools, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, must move rapidly beyond isolated pilots and into everyday workflows wherever evidence shows they improve outcomes, productivity or staff experience.”

![Image 4](https://news.microsoft.com/source/emea/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Microsoft-365-Copilot-Wakefield-YAS-Joanne-Crawford-95.jpg)

## “Done well,AI will not replace the human heart of the NHS;it will protect it—strengthening decisions,restoring time for care and helping create a safer,more personal and sustainable health service.The world has changed.We’ve got to create a digital front door for the NHS.”

Dr.Alec Price-Forbes,national chief clinical information officer for NHS England.Photo by Joanne Crawford for Microsoft.

He says that this transformation goes beyond technology; it requires that work be redesigned so that AI can help clinicians amplify their expertise while relieving them of unnecessary burdens.

This will free “clinicians to focus on judgment, validation and human connection.”

He also says that trust is essential for success.

“Patients and staff must know when AI is being used, how it shapes decisions and where human oversight applies, with unambiguous accountability for consequential choices,” he says.

The challenge now is to use digital capability to redesign pathways, improve flow, support clinical decision-making and release capacity back into care, Price-Forbes says. That means moving at pace, but with discipline.

“Done well, AI will not replace the human heart of the NHS; it will protect it — strengthening decisions, restoring time for care and helping create a safer, more personal and sustainable health service. The world has changed. We’ve got to create a digital front door for the NHS.”

![Image 5](https://news.microsoft.com/source/emea/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Microsoft-365-Copilot-Wakefield-YAS-Joanne-Crawford-87.jpg)

## Copilot“gives us that ability to join dots that we wouldn’t see ourselves without a laborious several hours’worth of trawling through data reports and trying to look at common themes.”

Samantha Robinson,chief digital information officer at Yorkshire Ambulance Service.Photo by Joanne Crawford for Microsoft.

Samantha Robinson, chief digital information officer at Yorkshire Ambulance Service, is responsible for helping information move between frontline teams, local operations and the wider NHS.

Copilot “gives us that ability to join dots that we wouldn’t see ourselves without a laborious several hours’ worth of trawling through data reports and trying to look at common themes,” she says.

The NHS’s information flows in all directions, Robinson says. She may need to turn operational information from across the ambulance service into a briefing for senior NHS leaders. At other times, she must translate national guidance into clear, practical instructions for different teams. Copilot can help produce a first draft, which Robinson and her colleagues review and adapt for the intended audience.

“We have a huge amount of data and information that we need to get out to our staff, frontline crew and contact center about how the NHS is performing,” Robinson says. Copilot helps turn that material into “really digestible information and in a way everyone can understand.”

That information matters when staff are considering how to connect patients with the most appropriate care. Not every patient attended by an ambulance needs to be taken to an emergency department. Depending on their condition, some people may be treated safely at home or referred to another service.

Yorkshire Ambulance Service is introducing a program with community teams, including a transfer-of-care hub that arranges for home care and referral pathways for patients who need non-urgent types of treatment. The aim is to support patients in the most appropriate setting while reducing avoidable pressure on emergency departments.

“We’re trying to get our conveyance to the emergency department down to 50%,” Smith says. Progress is being made; Copilot has helped Yorkshire Ambulance Service to collate the data and understand where opportunities could be, which has supported an improvement from 60% to 56% conveyance today.

“How Copilot has helped me with that is really understanding the data, being able to share that data to different forums, to use it as a big of a sounding board as well,” he says. “Like, ‘if we did this, what do you think the impact would be?’”

As a result, team members have better information to inform decisions about patient pathways.

“The big bit is getting the best patient outcome,” Smith says. “That’s what we’re really trying to drive.”

## Read more

Catherine Bolgar writes about AI and innovation at Microsoft, from advances in quantum computing to how AI is helping ordinary people. Previously, Catherine wrote about technology and business for a number of publications, and she was an editor at the Wall Street Journal in New York and Brussels. She taught high school math in Kenya, where she learned Swahili. She currently lives in France. You can contact Catherine on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/catherine-bolgar-2a47321/ "https://www.linkedin.com/in/catherine-bolgar-2a47321/").

title: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.
body:
Viewer • Updated • 1
[
](#profiling-torchneuron-part-1-system-level-profiling-on-aws-trainium)
Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.
This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and [TorchNeuron](https://github.com/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx), its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile
, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with [Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI)](https://awsdocs-neuron.readthedocs-hosted.com/en/latest/nki/index.html) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:
- How to configure
torch.profiler
with the Neuron backend and capture a clean trace. - How to read the
key_averages()
table to identify which operations consume Neuron device time and compare their Self CPU time. - How to follow one operation through Neuron Explorer, from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution on a NeuronCore.
- How these signals change across three implementations of the same operation.
[
](#neuron-as-a-pytorch-backend)
Neuron as a PyTorch Backend
Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how [Neuron](https://awsdocs-neuron.readthedocs-hosted.com/en/latest/index.html) integrates with PyTorch.
The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1
extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda
. The torch_neuronx
package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see [Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/advanced/privateuseone.html).
[
](#set-up-the-profiler)
Set Up the Profiler
You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:
NeuronConfig
controls which Neuron data streams and NeuronCores to capture and where to write the output. You pass it totorch.profiler.profile
asexperimental_config
.NeuronProfiler
takes aNeuronConfig
and provides anexport_trace
callback. The callback writes the framework trace,trace.json
, alongside the Neuron system traces.
nc = NeuronConfig(
modes=[ProfileMode.DEVICE, ProfileMode.RUNTIME],
profile_output_dir=OUTPUT_DIR,
capture_enabled_for_nc='0',
correlate_device_time=True,
)
exporter = NeuronProfiler(nc)
The modes
parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc
parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True
propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages()
table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode
values, see the NeuronConfig [Profile Modes documentation](http://awsdocs-neuron.readthedocs-hosted.com/en/latest/tools/neuron-explorer/how-to-profile-workload.html#neuronconfig-profile-modes).
[
](#tooling-neuron-explorer)
Tooling: Neuron Explorer
Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages()
reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.
After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff
and .ntff
files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff
and .ntff
files individually. See [Step 5: Upload your profile](https://awsdocs-neuron.readthedocs-hosted.com/en/latest/tools/neuron-explorer/get-started.html#step-5-upload-your-profile) for the UI and command-line instructions.
[
](#profile-rmsnorm)
Profile RMSNorm
For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.
You profile three implementations of the same operation:
- Naive RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations: multiply, mean, add, reciprocal square root, and multiply.
torch.rms_norm()
, the PyTorch built-in lowered to a single fused Neuron kernel.- Naive RMSNorm with
torch.compile
, using the same operations as the first implementation.
The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.
All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx
[examples directory](https://github.com/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx/tree/main/examples/hf_profiling_blog_pt1).
[
](#profile-1-naive-pytorch-operations)
Profile 1: Naive PyTorch Operations
Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.
device = torch.device('neuron')
x = torch.randn(4, 512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)
weight = torch.ones(512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)
def rms_norm_fn(t):
x_sq = t * t # square
mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True) # mean of squares
rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6) # 1 / sqrt(mean_sq + eps)
return t * rms * weight # normalize + scale
Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:
- Include
ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1
to collect activity from the Neuron device. - Pass
NeuronConfig
asexperimental_config
to enable the Neuron-specific Kineto features.
The schedule uses wait=2
, warmup=1
, and active=1
across four prof.step()
calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.
Call torch.neuron.synchronize()
inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.
with torch.profiler.profile(
activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1],
experimental_config=nc,
record_shapes=False,
on_trace_ready=exporter.export_trace,
schedule=torch.profiler.schedule(wait=2, warmup=1, active=1),
) as prof:
for step in range(4):
with torch.no_grad():
_ = rms_norm_fn(x)
torch.neuron.synchronize()
prof.step()
After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages()
table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total
to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages()
output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.
print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="self_privateuse1_time_total", row_limit=4))
The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.
The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul
has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.
| Name | # Calls | Self CPU | Self NEURON | % NEURON |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| aten::mul | 3 | 60.9 μs | 1,164.5 μs | 49.5% |
| aten::add | 1 | 26.6 μs | 434.6 μs | 18.5% |
| aten::rsqrt | 1 | 15.6 μs | 415.0 μs | 17.6% |
| aten::mean | 1 | 21.1 μs | 340.8 μs | 14.5% |
Self NEURON total: 2.355 ms
Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul
runs for x * x
, x * rms
, and the final multiplication by weight
. aten::mean
reduces the last dimension. aten::add
adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt
computes the reciprocal square root.
Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.
[
](#read-the-trace-in-explorer)
Read the Trace in Explorer
In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule
, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running
.
The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:
| Lane | Label suffix | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| Framework dispatch | framework/TID:<id> |
Operator dispatch events (PrivateUse1 runtime), grouped by thread ID. |
| Framework device | framework/Stream:<n> |
Device interaction events (PrivateUse1 driver), grouped by stream number. |
| Neuron Runtime | neuron_rt/NC:<n> |
Neuron Runtime API calls, grouped by logical NeuronCore. |
| Neuron Hardware | neuron_hw/NC<n>:<id> |
Hardware execution events, grouped by physical NeuronCore. |
In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor
from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.
The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.
[
](#profile-2-torchrms_norm)
Profile 2: torch.rms_norm
Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm
function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:
def rms_norm_fn(t):
return torch.rms_norm(t, [512], weight)
The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.
| Name | # Calls | Self CPU | Self NEURON | % NEURON |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| aten::_fused_rms_norm | 1 | 47.6 μs | 403.3 μs | 100% |
Self NEURON total: 403.3 μs
The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.
[
](#compare-the-lowering-path)
Compare the Lowering Path
In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.
[
](#profile-3-naive-pytorch-with-torchcompile)
Profile 3: Naive PyTorch with torch.compile
For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile
.
With @torch.compile(backend="neuron")
, TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.
@torch.compile(backend='neuron', fullgraph=True)
def naive_compiled(t):
x_sq = t * t
mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6)
return t * rms * weight
The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.
| Name | # Calls | Self CPU | Self NEURON | % NEURON |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Torch-Compiled Region: 0/0 | 1 | 98.4 μs | 375.5 μs | 100% |
Self NEURON total: 375.5 μs
The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.
The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is

title: Granite Speech 5.0: Transcribe, Translate, and Attribute more Accurately and Faster
body:
Automatic Speech Recognition • 2B • Updated • 34.8k • 99
[
](#granite-speech-50-transcribe-translate-and-attribute-more-accurately-and-faster)
Granite Speech 5.0: Transcribe, Translate, and Attribute more Accurately and Faster
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
We're excited to share three updates to IBM's Granite Speech collection: a new speech-language model, [granite-speech-5.0-2b](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-5.0-2b), and revised versions of two models the community already uses, [granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc) and [granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus). Together they cover the full range of enterprise speech work: transcription and translation with high accuracy, extremely fast transcription at the edge, and recordings where who spoke, and when, matter as much as what was said.
| Model | Status | What's new | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
granite-speech-5.0-2b |
New | More accurate, noise- and reverb-robust automatic speech recognition (ASR), language-ID prompting, 2,000-term keyword biasing, better long-form translation | High-accuracy multilingual transcription and translation |
granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc |
Updated | Multilingual, native punctuation and capitalization, and more robust to noise and reverb | High-throughput and on-device transcription |
granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus |
Updated | Improved speaker attribution, timestamps, keyword biasing, and long-speech performance | Meetings, calls, and other multi-speaker recordings |
[
](#granite-speech-50-2b-more-accurate-more-robust-more-control)
Granite Speech 5.0 2B: more accurate, more robust, more control
granite-speech-5.0-2b
is the successor to granite-speech-4.1-2b
at the same parameter count. It transcribes English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, and translates to and from English in those languages, plus English to Italian and Mandarin. It was trained on 390,000 hours of public audio, plus synthetic data built for Japanese ASR, keyword biasing, and translation.
What's new compared with 4.1 2B Speech:
- More accurate, more robust English ASR: Higher accuracy on English short-form benchmarks, and better handling of noise, reverberation, and distant-microphone speech.
- Language ID prompting: Name the input language in the prompt to steer multilingual transcription.
- Better long-form and conversational translation: Translation holds up for longer with more natural speech, not just short read sentences.
- Keyword lists up to 2,000 terms: Bias transcription and translation toward product names, people, and acronyms, in every supported language.
- Punctuation and capitalization on request: Ask for formatted output in the prompt; capitalization F1 ranges from 89.7 to 99.5 across our test sets.
The model ships under Apache 2.0 with support in Transformers, vLLM, llama.cpp, and mlx-audio for Apple Silicon.
Chart 1: granite-speech-5.0-2b ranks #2 among top open-weight ASR models on average English WER (5.06%). Lower is better. Results are official, as of 21 October 2026, and averaged over the Open ASR Leaderboard’s public English short-form test sets.
[
](#granite-speech-50-turbo-ctc-now-multilingual-more-robust-and-even-faster)
Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC: now multilingual, more robust, and even faster
When we [introduced Turbo CTC in August](https://huggingface.co/blog/ibm-granite/granite-speech-5-0-470m-turboctc), it was an English-only, 470M-parameter encoder built for speed. This revision keeps that footprint and adds the three things users asked for most:
- Multilingual transcription: English, Japanese, Spanish, German, French, Italian, and Portuguese.
- Native punctuation and capitalization: Transcripts come out ready to read, with no separate punctuation or truecasing step.
- More robust in difficult acoustics: Training that explicitly targets reverberant audio makes Turbo CTC more robust in echoey rooms and far-field recordings.
It's also faster. By compiling a single Conformer block and reusing its graph across the stack, we cut warmup time and pushed Turbo CTC to 19,870 RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard, up from roughly 12,600 RTFx at launch: about 1.6x faster, at the same accuracy level.
Chart 2: Average WER vs. RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard (English short-form, 9 public test sets, as of October 2026). Lower WER and higher RTFx are better; RTFx is on a log scale.
[
](#granite-speech-41-2b-plus-better-at-who-said-what-and-when)
Granite Speech 4.1 2B Plus: better at who said what, and when
The updated granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus
is tuned for the recordings enterprises actually have: meetings, support calls, and interviews with several speakers running long. It keeps the 4.1 name because the architecture, prompt format, and API are unchanged, so it's a drop-in replacement for the current model with improved weights. This revision improves four areas:
- Speaker attribution: More accurate labeling of who is speaking. Word diarization error rate (WDER) drops 7%, and speaker-attributed WER (cpWER) drops 7% overall.
- Timestamps: Average timestamp shift (AAS) is cut by more than half, yielding tighter timing in captions, search, and review.
- Long-speech performance: WER on long-form test sets drops 24%.
- Keyword biasing: Errors on biased keywords fall 45% with 20-term keyword lists.
| Capability | Metric | Previous release | Updated model |
|---|---|---|---|
| Timestamps, all speech | AAS (average timestamp shift) | 210.86 | 98.54 |
| Timestamps, short speech | AAS (average timestamp shift) | 29.27 | 26.20 |
| Keyword biasing | Biased-word WER, 20-term lists | 11.79 | 6.48 |
| Long-form speech | WER, long-form test sets | 13.53 | 10.22 |
| Speaker attribution | WDER | 4.40 | 4.10 |
| Speaker-attributed transcripts | cpWER | 30.50 | 28.48 |
Table 1: All metrics are error rates, so lower is better. For more detailed results, see the [model card](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus).
[
](#get-started)
Get started
Not sure which model to pick? Start here:
- Need high transcription accuracy, translation, or keyword biasing? Use
[granite-speech-5.0-2b](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-5.0-2b). - Need raw speed or on-device transcription? Use
[granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc), and try it in the browser with our[WebGPU streaming demo](/blog/ibm-granite/DEMO_URL). - Working with meetings or multi-speaker calls? Use
[granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus).
These models are all released under an Apache 2.0 license with native support in Transformers. Full evaluation results, architecture details, training data, and usage examples are on each model card. We recommend pairing them with [Granite Guardian](https://huggingface.co/collections/ibm-granite/granite-guardian) for production deployments that need additional risk detection.
Give them a try and let us know what you think!

title: LIVE STREAM: Training Agents IRL Seminar
body:
​An open-source AI community event on reinforcement learning for agentic systems, hosted by GitHub and Hugging Face.

​Join the open-source community at GitHub in San Francisco for an evening with researchers and builders exploring how AI agents are trained and evaluated.

​We will look beyond single-turn RL to multi-step, environment-driven training: reward design, rollouts, benchmarks, and the practical gap between training gains and real-world agent behavior.

​What to expect Short, 10-minute talks with Q&A, followed by a closing panel on what works in RL for agents, where the bottlenecks are, and what the open-source ecosystem needs next.

ML practitioners, agent builders, and RL researchers.

# ChatGPT Ads expands to 26 new countries as over 100,000 advertisers have used the platform

From local businesses to global brands, more advertisers can now reach people as they explore, compare and decide what to buy in ChatGPT.

[Start advertising in ChatGPT(opens in a new window)](https://ads.openai.com/)

Loading…

Share

Supporting more businesses around the world

- [Supporting more businesses around the world](#supporting-more-businesses-around-the-world)
- [Reach people as they explore their options](#reach-people-as-they-explore-their-options)
- [Guided by our ads principles](#guided-by-our-ads-principles)
- [What’s next](#whats-next)

- [Supporting more businesses around the world](#supporting-more-businesses-around-the-world)
- [Reach people as they explore their options](#reach-people-as-they-explore-their-options)
- [Guided by our ads principles](#guided-by-our-ads-principles)
- [What’s next](#whats-next)

More than 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT each week to explore ideas, compare options and make decisions. Ads can help people discover products and services that fit their needs, including options they might not have found otherwise.

Since we launched ads just over eight months ago, over 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns on ChatGPT. Today, we’re expanding ChatGPT Ads to 26 additional countries, extending availability to 89 countries worldwide. This launch builds on our recent expansions across [Europe](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-ads-expands-across-europe/) and [Southeast Asia and Taiwan](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-ads-expands-southeast-asia-taiwan/).

Advertising helps support free and low-cost access to ChatGPT for people around the world. Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. Ads will appear only on the Free and Go plans. Plus, Pro, and Enterprise subscriptions will remain ad-free.

## Supporting more businesses around the world

Following our launches in Mexico and Brazil, we’re bringing ChatGPT Ads to 14 more Latin American countries, including Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru. We’re also launching in more markets across Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia, including Nigeria, South Africa, Serbia, Ukraine, Cambodia, Bangladesh, and Pakistan.

Advertisers can access ChatGPT Ads in these countries through technology partners or self-service access through [Ads Manager⁠(opens in a new window)](https://ads.openai.com/).

## Reach people as they explore their options

In ChatGPT, people can explain what they’re looking for, ask follow-up questions, and refine their options through conversation. Someone training for their first marathon might start by exploring meal ideas for race week, then narrow their options based on their dietary preferences and how much time they have to cook. An ad relevant to that conversation could introduce them to a grocery delivery service they hadn’t considered.

For local businesses, regional brands, and international companies, ChatGPT Ads gives businesses a way to introduce their products during these moments of consideration, when people are still evaluating their options and deciding what’s right for them.

> “At L’Oreal our culture is to ‘seize what is starting.’ Today, as billions of consumers use AI models to discover and explore beauty, our mission remains centered on delivering meaningful value and building deeper connections. Testing early with OpenAI enables us to pioneer helpful experiences and journeys, from discovery, to evaluation, to agentic commerce, ensuring L’Oréal remains the most trusted, expert answer wherever beauty conversations take place.”

*Asmita Dubey, L’Oréal Group CDMO*

## Guided by our ads principles

Protecting the trust people place in ChatGPT is foundational to our approach to advertising.

Guided by OpenAI’s [ads principles](https://openai.com/index/our-approach-to-advertising-and-expanding-access/), we keep conversations private from advertisers and do not sell customer data. Ads in ChatGPT are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT’s answers, and advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides.

Our goal is to make ads useful to people as they pursue their goals and make decisions—and effective for the businesses that advertise with us.

## What’s next

Our focus remains expanding access to AI while staying true to our principles.

With ChatGPT Ads now available in 89 countries, our next phase of growth will include the development of additional formats, objectives, buying options, and measurement capabilities. We are also continuing to explore new ways for businesses to interact with consumers in more native ways in ChatGPT.

As more people turn to ChatGPT to explore needs, evaluate options, and make decisions, we see an opportunity to help them discover products and services—and to help businesses of every size grow and thrive.

Businesses interested in advertising on ChatGPT can learn more at [ ads.openai.com⁠(opens in a new window)](https://ads.openai.com/).

](#highlights-tldr)
Highlights (TL;DR)
NVIDIA Kumo Forecast (formerly known as NV-Tesseract Forecasting) is a multi-variate time-series forecasting model that combines a pretrained Transformer backbone with Domain-Aware Representation and Retrieval (DARR), a context-enhanced forecasting mode that blends direct model predictions with patterns retrieved from historical data. This includes interpretability of the results. Built on the MOMENT-1-large backbone, Kumo Forecast uses an approximately 340-million-parameter base encoder plus a trainable forecasting head.
The library provides a DataFrame-first API, configurable forecast horizons, optional historical context for retrieval, and an interpretability framework that produces horizon-specific explanations without modifying the underlying forecaster.
Kumo-Forecast is available under [Apache 2.0 license](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0).
Model code: [NVIDIA/Kumo-TS](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Kumo-TS)
Model weights: [nvidia/Kumo-Forecast](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Kumo-Forecast)
[
](#the-shift-to-context-enhanced-time-series-forecasting)
The Shift to Context-Enhanced Time-Series Forecasting
A forecasting system can draw on two different sources of information: representations learned during pretraining and historical observations available for the current application. Kumo-Forecast brings these together through a pretrained forecasting model and an optional retrieval pathway over historical context.
In its direct forecasting path, Kumo-Forecast uses a MOMENT-based Transformer and a trained forecasting head to predict future values. In Domain Aware Representation and Retrieval (DARR) mode, it also retrieves related patterns from historical data using a nearest-neighbor approach and combines that information with the direct forecast.
This creates a distinction between the model’s input window and its retrieval context. The input window supplies recent observations for the forecast; a separate historical DataFrame can supply additional context for pattern retrieval. Developers can adjust how strongly the final prediction relies on each pathway through the library’s configuration options.
Further information on DARR mode can be found in this published paper, [Memory-Augmented Forecasting: Scalability and Generalization Across Temporal Domains](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11402442)
[
](#how-kumo-forecast-works)
How Kumo Forecast Works
Kumo-Forecast combines four main components: a pretrained temporal encoder, a trainable forecasting head, historical-pattern retrieval mechanism and an interpretability framework.
Pretrained Temporal Representations: The model uses the MOMENT-1-large Transformer encoder as its backbone. The architecture keeps encoder and embedder weights frozen while training the forecasting head, separating the pretrained representation model from the task-specific prediction layer.
Direct Forecasting: The forecasting head maps the model’s representations to future values for the requested horizon. For horizons beyond the model’s native capability, there is support for autoregressive extension. This distinguishes a directly generated forecast from a longer forecast that extends predictions recursively.
Domain-Aware Representation and Retrieval: DARR augments direct forecasting with k-nearest-neighbor retrieval from historical context data. This process combines direct forecasts with historical-pattern retrieval, while the SDK accepts the historical context through a separate context_df argument.
Interpretability: Kumo-Forecasting also includes a model-agnostic interpretability framework. When enabled, it produces an explanation bundle containing lag and feature attributions per forecast horizon, semantic-flow diagnostics, trajectory-stability diagnostics, and optional embedding Integrated Gradients.These outputs accompany the forecast rather than requiring a different forecasting architecture.
Further details on interpretability can be found in this paper, [NVExplain: Explaining Time Series Forecasting with Latent Trajectory Analysis and Structure-Preserving Surrogates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25080)
[
](#limitations)
Limitations
Data must be numeric, temporal data. Supported input sequence lengths include 256, 512, 1024, and 2048 observations. Inputs consist of a timestamp column and one or more numeric value columns, represented as a pandas DataFrame or a CSV/JSON input. When leveraging DARR mode, the dimensions of the context must be similar to the context of the input.
[
](#demo-predictive-maintenance)
Demo: Predictive Maintenance
The [Factory Operations (FOX) Blueprint](https://developer.nvidia.com/factory-operations-blueprint-early-access) includes Early Access to the Predictive Maintenance module which leverages Kumo Anomaly and Kumo Forecast. It analyzes real-time data to predict future anomalies.
[
](#demo-platform-integration)
Demo: Platform Integration
Please click on the image below to access the session from GTC San Jose 2026
[
](#start-building-with-kumo-forecast)
Start Building with Kumo Forecast
For an application-specific evaluation, compare the direct and retrieval-enhanced configurations on the same held-out forecasting windows. Validate forecast quality across the intended horizons and operating conditions, consistent with NVIDIA’s requirement for use-case-specific testing
Model code: [NVIDIA/Kumo-TS](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Kumo-TS)
Model weights: [nvidia/Kumo-Forecast](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Kumo-Forecast)
The Kumo-TS repository additionally provides an example for fine-tuning Kumo-Forecast on a user-supplied CSV. Developers therefore have both a pretrained inference workflow and a documented starting point for adapting the model to their own data.

title: Mistral Advances AI for Engineering with NVIDIA
body:
Thinking
Summary
Mistral and NVIDIA are collaborating to revolutionize engineering workflows by integrating Mistral’s AI models with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and physics modeling tools, enabling faster simulations and closed-loop AI-driven design. The partnership will introduce public benchmarks and open datasets to standardize evaluations for physics and agentic AI in computer-aided engineering, while leveraging NVIDIA’s Omniverse for 3D simulation and asset creation. Building on their existing work, including the development of Mistral Large 4, the initiative aims to push the boundaries of AI-powered engineering across industries like aerospace, automotive, and semiconductors.
Mistral is collaborating with NVIDIA to develop a new generation of AI-native engineering workflows powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing. Combining [Mistral Large 4](https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-large-4/), with Mistral’s data generation, and physics modeling pipelines, accelerated by [NVIDIA CUDA-X](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/technologies/cuda-x/) libraries and [NVIDIA Warp](https://developer.nvidia.com/warp-python), the initiative aims to accelerate engineering simulation and enable closed-loop workflows that connect simulation, AI model development and engineering design. Mistral and NVIDIA will also work together to integrate Mistral's models with [NVIDIA Omniverse](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/omniverse/) libraries for GPU-accelerated 3D scene generation and SimReady asset creation.
A central focus of the collaboration is the development of public benchmarks and open datasets for evaluating physics models. These benchmarks will give researchers, developers and industrial teams a shared foundation to compare model accuracy and performance and build and validate automated CAD-to-simulation workflows.
"For too long, the pace of engineering has been set by the pace of simulation. With Mistral's open-weight models and [physics AI](https://mistral.ai/news/introducing-physics-ai-at-mistral/) capabilities, combined with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing stack, we’re giving engineers faster simulation cycles, as well as open benchmarks rigorous enough to validate agents on real CAE and EDA work.” Neil Ashton, VP of Computational Engineering, Mistral
Beyond physics AI, Mistral and NVIDIA will also work together to develop dedicated evaluations and benchmarks for agentic AI in computer-aided engineering (CAE) and electronic design automation (EDA) to accelerate the application of [AI for engineering](https://mistral.ai/industry/manufacturing/) within aerospace, automotive and semiconductor use-cases. These benchmarks will assess agents’ ability to use engineering tools, complete multistep workflows and produce technically correct results, while measuring execution time and computational cost.
Through this work, Mistral and NVIDIA will help define standards for agentic and physics AI evaluations in engineering, establishing consistent, reproducible methods for assessing capabilities and tracking progress. Powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing, libraries and tools, Mistral will redefine AI for engineering, transforming how engineers design, simulate and build the next generation of products.
“The next wave of engineering breakthroughs will come from exploring ideas that were once too complex or time-consuming to test,” said Tim Costa, vice president and general manager of industrial and computational engineering at NVIDIA. “By combining Mistral’s advanced open models and deep expertise in physics AI with NVIDIA accelerated computing and libraries, we’re helping engineers push the boundaries of design—with shared industry benchmarks to build confidence in what AI can do.”
Building on the ongoing NVIDIA and Mistral partnership
The industrial engineering collaboration builds on an ongoing partnership between NVIDIA and Mistral spanning open model development, domain-specific AI and the infrastructure needed to bring these capabilities into production.
The companies previously co-developed [Mistral NeMo](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/power-text-generation-applications-with-mistral-nemo-12b-running-on-a-single-gpu/) and are now [working together](https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-ai-and-nvidia-partner-to-accelerate-open-frontier-models/) through the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition to develop a frontier base model that will continue to advance the open weight frontier. This shared foundation will enable developers and enterprises worldwide to specialize AI for their industries, languages and regions, supported by contributions of data, evaluations and domain expertise from coalition members.
Mistral recently introduced the public preview of [Mistral Large 4](https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-large-4/), known as Le Chonk, its largest and most capable frontier model to date. With approximately 1 trillion total parameters and 49 billion active parameters, the multimodal model was trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral-operated data centers in Europe. It advances capabilities across coding, agentic workflows and multimodal understanding, with weights planned for release at the end of October.
Alongside model development, Mistral and NVIDIA are expanding the infrastructure that powers AI training, customization and inference. Mistral is bringing additional NVIDIA-powered AI infrastructure online in support of Mistral’s compute roadmap targeting 1 GW of capacity by 2030.
This expansion strengthens Europe’s role in developing and delivering AI for the world. By connecting European infrastructure and research with open models, specialized engineering capabilities and customer applications, Mistral and NVIDIA are helping enterprises build AI around their own expertise and scale it to serve markets worldwide.

title: Announcing SimReady Central: An Open Library of Simulation-Ready 3D Assets for Robotics and AI Factories
body:
🔎 13
SimReady Central USD Search
Search SimReady assets and retrieve building component data
Published
October 21, 2026
Building robotics simulations and high-fidelity [AI factory digital twins](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/use-cases/ai-factory-digital-twins/) takes more than 3D models. Developers often need to add properties such as collision geometry, mass, and friction. [SimReady](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/simready/) assets are 3D models that come prepared with the properties required for simulation workflows, reducing that manual work.
[SimReady Central Library](https://huggingface.co/spaces/nvidia/simready-central) brings together more than 2,000 simulation-ready (SimReady) [OpenUSD](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/openusd/) assets on Hugging Face, giving developers a free, ungated starting point for [physical AI](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/generative-physical-ai/) training environments and AI factory digital twins. The library includes a variety of infrastructure and equipment assets from robot arms and grippers to warehouse equipment, racks, and cooling infrastructure. Developers can check which capabilities each asset supports, then combine assets from different suppliers into a scene.
Equipment manufacturers (OEMs) can now prepare and validate assets against SimReady requirements and use SimReady Central Library to reach developers and allow their end customers to test and simulate scenarios faster and accelerate decision making. This enables industries to build simulations around their products while managing their own Hugging Face datasets.
We’ll cover what makes an asset SimReady and how OEMs contribute to SimReady Central Library, then show how developers can use those assets to build a [robotic pick-and-place scenario](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/5-steps-to-create-simready-assets-for-robotics-with-frontier-ai-models/) and [compare AI factory layouts](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/developing-an-ai-factory-digital-twin-with-an-agent-assisted-workflow/).
SimReady assets are OpenUSD assets prepared with the properties required for simulation workflows. A detailed 3D model, such as CAD, is a useful starting point. Simulation requires additional information about how that object should be interpreted and used.
For a robot manipulation task, that might include the object’s mass, collision geometry, and friction properties. For AI factory workflows, it might include equipment geometry and the electrical or thermal metadata required by the application.
[OpenUSD](https://openusd.org/release/intro.html) is an open, extensible framework for describing and composing 3D scenes. Using those scenes to train and evaluate autonomous machines also requires information about physical behavior, collisions, and sensor interactions.
[SimReady Foundation](https://github.com/NVIDIA/simready-foundation) provides specifications, profiles, and validation tools that make these requirements explicit. A profile defines the logical grouping of features and capabilities an asset needs for a particular use case.
Figure 1. SimReady Foundation defines asset representation requirements for specific simulation use cases, while developer libraries help prepare and validate OpenUSD assets against those requirements.
Depending on the asset and profile, those features can include:
| Asset structural elements | What it enables |
|---|---|
| Collision geometry and physical properties | Contact and physics simulation in a supported runtime. |
| Joint structure and limits | Articulated robot and equipment movement. |
| Semantic labels | Object identification and annotated synthetic data. |
| Materials and sensor attributes | Rendering and supporting sensor simulation. |
For the requirements associated with each simulation use case, see the [SimReady Foundation requirements and profiles](https://nvidia.github.io/simready-foundation/latest/). Developers should select assets from SimReady Central whose profiles match their workflow needs and compose them into an OpenUSD scene.
OEMs can turn their CAD equipment models into SimReady assets for developers building simulations around their products. SimReady Central Library makes those assets discoverable on Hugging Face, helping manufacturers reach teams building robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins.
For AI factory OEMs like [Vertiv](https://www.vertiv.com/en-us/), the library provides a path to distribute assets such as warehouse equipment racks, server racks, cooling equipment, and supporting infrastructure for AI factory digital twins. Developers and frontier agents can incorporate these assets into [AI factory digital twins](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/use-cases/ai-factory-digital-twins/) reusing the geometry and properties specified by their SimReady profiles.
For robotics OEMs like [Comau](https://www.comau.com/en/), [FANUC](https://www.fanuc.com/), [Franka Robotics](https://franka.de/), [Robotiq](https://blog.robotiq.com/robotiq-releases-new-2f-85-gripper-isaac-sim-assets-on-newton), [Standard Bots](https://standardbots.com/), and [Universal Robots](https://www.universal-robots.com/), the library makes robot arms and grippers discoverable by teams building training and evaluation environments. Developers can combine these assets with industrial equipment to build warehouse and factory scenarios.
For simulation asset providers like [Palatial](https://palatial.cloud/updates/open-simulation-asset-library) the library features the [NVIDIA Robotics 1K Dataset](https://library.palatial.cloud/?collection=nvidia-research) released in collaboration with NVIDIA Robotics, alongside complex articulated assets generated from text, images, scans, datasheets, and CAD. Developers can build assets and scenes for robot training and evaluation.
For OEMs like [LG Electronics (LGE)](https://www.lg.com/global/) that develop robots for the home alongside the appliances they work with, the library provides a path to share assets such as refrigerators and dishwashers. Developers can use assets informed by LGE’s experience in both appliances and robotics to build household simulation environments for robot training, evaluation, and synthetic data generation.
For AI-assisted CAD providers like [ForgeCAD](https://forgecad.io/), the library makes articulated robotics props with high-quality textures available, which developers can use to build environments for robot perception and manipulation training, as well as synthetic data generation.
To contribute, OEMs can use the [SimReady Central submission skill](https://github.com/NVIDIA-Omniverse/simready-central/blob/main/.agents/skills/submit-simready-assets/SKILL.md) to validate assets against the relevant SimReady profiles, package them, and submit them for inclusion in the library.
Figure 2. OEMs prepare and validate OpenUSD assets against SimReady profiles and then submit the asset to SimReady Central. Developers and AI agents discover assets in the library and use them to build simulation environments.
SimReady Central gives robotics and industrial developers a reusable starting point for robot workcells, industrial environments, and AI factory digital twins. Developers and AI agents can find assets in SimReady Central that meet the profiles required by their workflows and compose them into OpenUSD environments.
Developers can use SimReady assets to populate training environments with objects and obstacles, then vary their placement to evaluate robot behaviors. These environments can support projects such as [Microduck](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/microduck-isaac-lab-sim-to-real), an open-source robot from Hugging Face and Pollen Robotics.
Figure 3. Asset datasets connect through SimReady Central on Hugging Face, using its USD search service to support Isaac workflows, SimReady Central library search, and AI agent workflows.
NVIDIA USD Search powers natural-language search in SimReady Central Library, helping developers and AI agents find assets across participating datasets. Hugging Face has also integrated USD Search into their platform search with indexed USD properties and simulation metadata, helping agents discover SimReady assets suited to their physical AI simulation tasks.
AI-assisted authoring adds another way to build with those assets. Developers can use frontier models like OpenAI’s [GPT-6 Astra](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-astra) combined with asset search and scene-authoring tools to build environments using SimReady Central Library. Given task requirements and spatial constraints, Astra can help find suitable assets, write code to assemble a scene, and create scenario variations.
OEMs can also use Astra to help prepare and refine OpenUSD assets against SimReady Foundation requirements before validating and submitting them to the library.
For example, a developer building a robotic pick-and-place scenario could start with this prompt:
Using SimReady assets from SimReady Central on Hugging Face, create a basic warehouse pick-and-place scenario in Isaac Sim using PhysX.
Use the nvidia-simready-central.hf.space to find a FANUC robotic arm, a compatible Robotiq gripper, and suitable warehouse assets. Generate the Python code to assemble the scene and configure the pick-and-place task. Render a .mov preview so I can review the results.
Include the scripts, asset versions, and runtime versions so I can reproduce the scenario.
In this workflow, we expect Astra to do the following:
- Query the SimReady Search API to find relevant assets distributed on Hugging Face
- Reference/Payload them into an OpenUSD stage
- Generate Python code to assemble the workcell
- Configure the Pick-and-place task
- Render a preview for user review
Figure 4. A robotic pick-and-place workcell assembled from SimReady assets illustrates how AI-assisted scene authoring can turn developer requirements into a simulation scenario for review and refinement in Isaac Sim.
The same approach can support an ISV (independent software vendor) building an AI factory digital twin. The task shifts from robot interactions to equipment placement: arranging racks, cooling equipment, and supporting infrastructure within specified spatial constraints.
Using SimReady assets from SimReady Central on Hugging Face, create two alternative AI factory layouts with racks and cooling equipment.
Use the supplied equipment dimensions and aisle-clearance requirements. Check for equipment overlaps and clearance violations, and report any issues.
Save each layout as an OpenUSD scene. Include the scene-building scripts, asset versions, and runtime versions so I can reproduce and compare the results.
In this workflow, Astra would assemble the selected SimReady assets into two OpenUSD layouts, followed up by generating scripts to check equipment overlaps and aisle clearances against the supplied requirements. Developers could then inspect the layouts in their simulation application, compare equipment placement and access paths, and review any flagged issues before refining the preferred configuration.
Figure 5. An AI factory layout assembled from SimReady assets illustrates how AI-assisted scene authoring supports equipment placement, aisle-clearance checks, and layout refinement in OpenUSD.
In either example, developers can extend their environments in a few ways:
- Reuse the environment: Keep layout and task-specific changes in separate OpenUSD layers so the same source assets can support multiple experiments.
- Vary the scenarios: Introduce additional assets from the library and vary object placements, equipment configurations, or surrounding infrastructure to evaluate different conditions.
- Build application-specific tests: For robotics, configure training and evaluation tasks in Isaac Lab. For AI factories, connect the scene to the equipment data and simulation tools needed for analyses such as power distribution or cooling performance.
- Carry validated layouts into operations: For AI facto

title: Bringing the Spark to Europe: Local Intelligence Powers Next Wave of Agents

At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA is showcasing its full lineup of local AI hardware. [RTX Spark](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/rtx-spark/), which [launched last week](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-rtx-spark-pcs-available-today-a-new-beginning-for-windows-pcs), powers personal agents on Windows PCs; [DGX Spark](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark/) supports developers building and scaling applications on Linux; and [DGX Station](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-station/) serves enterprise teams running frontier workloads on Linux, with a Windows version arriving in December.
Announcements include:
- Underdog Desktop Agent now available for RTX Spark
