title: There are many themes, but this one is yours | Earendil
body:
There are many themes, but this one is yours
At Earendil, we want to build products that respect the choices of the people using them. So when we were refreshing Pi's themes, we wanted a theme that adapts to the terminal it runs in. Most people who spend their day in a terminal have picked their own themes for it. Why not make Pi reflect their choices?
The result is the new system theme, which is now Pi's default. It asks your terminal for its colors and builds Pi's theme from them. In this post we share how it works.
Before you read the rest of the post, we want to spoil something: it's all about contrast. Picking the colors in the terminal UI is a question of taste that the user has already answered. From there, all other decisions come down to one question: how much does a color stand out from the background it's on? If we get it wrong, we create a bad experience for the user.
But the catch is that contrast is a matter of perception and not something we can trivially measure. Two people can look at the same pair of colors and disagree about whether it's readable. We built a small [interactive survey you can take](https://contrastsurvey.earendil.com/) to show you how you perceive that contrast, and how it compares against other people. You'll find details about that survey at the end of the post.
Can you trust the ANSI palette?
Every terminal theme defines 16 ANSI colors, and the simplest way to match your terminal would be to use them directly. But there aren't really any rules to the ANSI palette. The original standard, [ECMA-48](https://ecma-international.org/publications-and-standards/standards/ecma-48/), was adopted in 1976. Its nearly identical American counterpart from 1979, ANSI X3.64, is where the name comes from. The standard names eight colors (black, red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, cyan and white), but doesn't say what they should look like or how they should relate to the background.
The eight bright variants aren't part of the standard. Quite a few terminals [rendered bold text in a brighter color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code#3-bit_and_4-bit), which effectively gave them eight more colors. The codes to select bright colors directly were added later by IBM's aixterm and adopted by other terminals like [xterm](https://invisible-island.net/xterm/ctlseqs/ctlseqs.html).
Since the bright colors started out as bold text, we would assume that "bright" was meant to stand out more. And since early terminals mostly showed light text on a dark screen, brighter also meant more contrast. We looked at the more than 460 themes that come with Ghostty, and today this only sort of holds. In dark themes, the bright variant has more contrast in about 60% of cases. In light themes, it's only about a quarter, since bright usually still means lighter, which on a light background means less contrast. Individual themes don't agree either: in Gruvbox Dark, bright blue has more contrast than blue, in Catppuccin Mocha it has less, and in Tokyo Night they are the same color. The contrast against the background also varies a lot. We measured it with the [WCAG 2 contrast ratio](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html), which compares the luminance of two colors and ranges from 1:1 (no contrast) to 21:1 (black on white). Normal text should reach at least 4.5:1, and large text and UI elements 3:1. Bright black, which a lot of software uses for secondary text, doesn't even reach 3:1 in most dark themes.
This isn't a flaw of the themes. The palette was made to color the output of simple applications, like a red error or a green success message, and many themes are designed to look good rather than to meet contrast minimums. But it makes it hard to build an accessible, more complex TUI on top of it. Pi has around 60 color roles, from body text and dim text to panels behind tool calls and red text on a red error panel. We wanted to use your colors and still guarantee that all of them stay readable.
Contrast is all you need
Contrast is one of the most important aspects of color in user interfaces. If it is too low, people will have a hard time using your product. Contrast is mainly driven by lightness. Saturation affects it a little, but by far the most important factor is how light or dark a color is compared to the color behind it.
RGB, the way we usually write colors, doesn't have a lightness axis. It was made for machines to display colors on a monitor, not for humans to understand them. As a 3D shape, it is a neat cube with one axis per channel. But colors that are close to each other in this cube aren't necessarily colors humans would describe as similar. #0000ff and #00ff00, for example, both have one channel at full strength, but on white, the blue has a WCAG contrast ratio of 8.6:1 and the green only 1.4:1.
Perceptual color spaces like [OKLCH](https://bottosson.github.io/posts/oklab/) are built around human perception instead. Colors that are close to each other in OKLCH are also colors humans would describe as similar, and its axes are the ones humans use to describe color: lightness, chroma (how colorful a color is) and hue. Because it follows human perception rather than a monitor's hardware, its shape is a lot weirder than a cube.
With a lightness axis, the idea behind the system theme is simple: Pi decides the lightness of every color based on contrast requirements, and takes the hue and chroma from your terminal's palette.
Lightness
To figure out what lightness each color needs, we wrote down every place in the UI where two colors meet. Every panel needs enough contrast with the terminal background to read as a separate area, but not so much that it distracts. Every foreground color needs enough contrast on every background it can appear on. An error message, for example, has to be readable on the background, on the selected row and on all three tool panels. In code, this is a list of rules:
const COLORS = ["accent", "success", "error", "warning"];
const SURFACES = ["background", "selectedBg", ...TOOL_PANELS];
{ token: "text", on: ["background"], level: "text" },
...each(COLORS, SURFACES, "readable"),
{ token: "dim", on: [...SURFACES, "customMessageBg"], level: "subtle" },
A contrast algorithm normally takes two colors and returns the contrast between them. Here we need the reverse: we know the background and how much contrast we want, and need the color. I have reversed contrast algorithms before, and you can find implementations for both [WCAG](https://github.com/dgtlntv/wcag-contrast-palette) and [perceptual contrast](https://github.com/dgtlntv/perceptual-contrast-palette) on GitHub. With a reversed algorithm, calculating the theme becomes a loop: starting with the panels, Pi calculates the lightness each color needs for each of its rules and takes the strictest one.
The Algorithm
Our first prototype did exactly that, together with a review app in which we tuned the contrast minimums. The app can render Pi with any of the themes that come with Ghostty, so we could check a sample of very different themes to make sure the system holds up beyond the default one.
That prototype used a well known perceptual contrast algorithm and that reference implementation. We then used that against a large number of ghostty themes and ensured that it looked good against all the themes. We then did not want to ship that algorithm itself. We tried to use simpler measures but were unable to approximate the results. In the end we had a coding agent do the fitting. For each contrast level in the reference the agent ran the original algorithm on every gray background from white to black and recorded the lightness and fitted a polynomial to the results. It settled on a fifth degree polynomial which was found to stay close enough to the reference lightness. Pi now only ships with those coefficients.
The chart below shows those polynomials, one curve for each contrast level in the rules above. Along the bottom is the lightness of the surface a color is drawn on, and up the side the lightness the color needs on it. The diagonal is no contrast at all: a color exactly as light as its surface. The vertical lines are the surfaces: the background, and the panels, which Pi solves first on the background. Where a rule's curve crosses one of its surfaces, you can read off the lightness that rule needs there, and the strictest one wins. Drag the background to see how every color follows it.
We first convert the queried terminal colors from RGB into OKLCH and [OKHSL](https://bottosson.github.io/posts/colorpicker/). From that we get the original lightness L, chroma C and hue H as well as the saturation S relative to what sRGB can display at that lightness. Once the polynomial is evaluated against the lightness of the background. The resulting lightness is then not used as a direct replacement, but converted into an OKHSL lightness and a new color is computed using the original hue and adjusted saturation. A bell shaped saturation curve is applied. Strongest at the middle lightness and weaker towards black and white. Finally that is converted to OKLCH and Pi limits the original chroma so that H stays the same, L comes from the contrast rules and C becomes what the adjusted OKHSL produces. This is so that a pale pink for instance, when moved towards a darker shade, might otherwise make it too vivid. The adjustment ensures that it can never be more colorful than the original color.
Hue & chroma
Pi keeps the hue of your palette colors as it is. Chroma is trickier. The weird shape of OKLCH shows how much chroma a screen can display, which depends on both hue and lightness. At a lightness of 0.9, the most colorful yellow a screen can show has a chroma of about 0.2, while the most colorful blue only reaches about 0.05. So when Pi moves a palette color to the lightness it needs, its chroma might not exist at that lightness, and mapping it back to a displayable color can change the lightness Pi just calculated.
That's why Pi builds its colors in OKHSL. OKHSL is built on the same foundation as OKLCH and uses the same hues, but it stretches the weird shape back into a cylinder. Its saturation goes from 0% to 100%, where 100% always means "the most colorful this hue can be at this lightness". It tries to keep the best of both worlds: it stays as close to human perception as it can, while bringing back the simple geometry that makes RGB based color spaces easy to work with. Every combination of hue, saturation and lightness is a color your screen can display, which makes it a good fit for generating themes and palettes in general. Pi also lets saturation fall off toward black and white, so that very dark and very light colors, like a panel only slightly lighter than the background, get a hint of color rather than a bright block.
But keeping the saturation the same doesn't keep a color equally colorful. Since saturation is relative to what the screen can display, the same percentage can mean very different amounts of chroma at different lightnesses. Shortly after the release, a [bug report](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/10255) showed that Pi looked much more vivid than the terminal with Catppuccin Frappé. Catppuccin's pink, #f4b8e4, has an OKHSL saturation of 84%, but that is 84% of the little chroma a screen can show at such a high lightness. Pi's accent needs to be darker to be readable, and since the shape is much wider there, 84% saturation becomes #eb76d1, with about twice the chroma of the original pink. The fix was to also cap the chroma: a palette color can move to a different lightness, but it can never become more colorful than it is in your palette. With the cap, the accent becomes #cc92bd, which looks like Catppuccin again.
So in the end, the chroma of a palette color is limited three times: by what your screen can display, through OKHSL; by the falloff toward black and white; and by the chroma it has in your palette.

title: sparqlite: SPARQL 1.1 inside SQLite, written in Rust
body:
16th October 2026
[Research](/elsewhere/research/)
[sparqlite: SPARQL 1.1 inside SQLite, written in Rust](https://github.com/simonw/research/tree/main/sqlite-sparql-rust#readme)— sparqlite is a Rust-based SQLite loadable extension that stores RDF quads in ordinary SQLite tables and executes SPARQL 1.1 queries and updates natively inside the SQLite process. Its integer-encoded terms, covering indexes, cost-based planner, batched joins, and optional direct SQLite B-tree reader deliver 3.5× speedups over SQL translation in count mode and 2.8× when returning full results, while passing 636 of 639 applicable W3C evaluation tests and millions of differential-fuzz…
This research task is really an experiment in running Claude Code for web in "Ultracode" mode, as described in [Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows) in the Claude Code documentation.
With Ultracode turned on, Claude Code makes aggressive use of dynamic workflows - it generates JavaScript that defines and coordinates a network of subagents to take on complex problems.
My initial prompt was this - I meant "hit the rows directly", the word "delete" was an accidental typo on my phone:
Write a SQLite extension in Rust that implants SPARQL and runs really fast because it can hit the delete rows directly
This caused Claude Code for web to churn for over 12 hours. I checked in on its progress the next day and sent a single follow-up prompt when I noticed how many Rust crates it had built:
Every folder in the crates/ directory needs a README
Include a tutorial.md teaching users how to install the extension and how to run it in the SQLite CLI and then teaching them SPARQL in addition to how to use the SQLite extension
Include a script with the tutorial for populating a SQLite database with useful and realistic example data for that tutorial
This project feels like next-level vibe coding - it's not remotely feasible to review the code that was produced here, and even following the documentation is a significant investment in work. I'm not entirely sure what to do with this - I appear to have a full SPARQL implementation in Rust inside SQLite now, but how valuable is that if I created it on a whim and can't (or won't) invest the necessary time to understand what it can do?

title: Scaling Indic Pretraining: 2.8 Trillion Tokens and an Open Data Generation Pipeline
body:
Translation • 8B • Updated • 2.42k • 18
[
](#scaling-indic-pretraining-28-trillion-tokens-and-an-open-data-generation-pipeline)
Scaling Indic Pretraining: 2.8 Trillion Tokens and an Open Data Generation Pipeline
[Enterprise + Article](/blog)
Authors: AI4Bharat — Mohammed Safi Ur Rahman Khan, Mitesh Khapra, Anoop Kunchukuttan. NVIDIA — Niket Agarwal, Raviraj Joshi, Anusha Kamath, Markus Kliegl, Yev Meyer, Sriharsha Niverty, Kiran Praveen, Utkarsh Vaidya.
We're excited to introduce Nemotron-pretraining-Indic-v1 approximately 2.8 trillion tokens across 22 Indian languages, releasing soon alongside the open, GPU-accelerated data generation pipeline used to create it. These are the 22 languages listed in India's Constitution: the first languages for 97% of Indians, or nearly 1.2 billion citizens at the 2011 Census. Developed by NVIDIA with [IIT Madras](https://www.iitm.ac.in/), India's premier engineering institute, and its [AI4Bharat](https://ai4bharat.iitm.ac.in/) lab, this release gives model builders a substantial new resource for Indic pretraining. The pipeline captures the full generation recipe, including prompts, LLM workflows, and quality checks, so developers can adapt it to their own source material and generate more data for their needs.
AI4Bharat, IIT Madras' Indian language research lab, builds open-source datasets and models for Indian languages. Its resources, such as [Sangraha](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ai4bharat/sangraha), an open pretraining corpus for 22 Indian languages, have helped lay the foundation for open Indic language-model research. Our joint open-source release represents a substantial expansion of the open synthetic Indic training data that will be available to the community. It brings a broad mix of curated English material, including mathematics, code, and question-answer content, into Indian languages, giving teams more training material for building models that can explain technical concepts, work through problems, and answer questions in those languages. Every record traces back to a curated source document, and each output is checked against its input, so the synthetic text stays grounded in real information.
Mitesh Khapra, who heads AI4Bharat and made the [2025 TIME100 AI list](https://time.com/collections/time100-ai-2025/7305866/mitesh-khapra/), has named the core problem: Indian language technology trails English because "we do not have enough data for Indian languages." We're answering that call with more data, plus an open recipe for generating more.
The corpus also accounts for how people write. It includes native-script data for all 22 languages and romanized text for twelve, spanning 34 language-script configurations. Our workflows combine document-level translation, quality assessment, and targeted repair, with checks to preserve content such as equations, tables, and code. This data complements naturally authored Indic text, which remains essential for local knowledge and cultural context.
We're sharing the [open generation recipe](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/DataDesignerPlugins/tree/main/plugins/data-designer-nemotron-bharat-translation) so the community can not just reproduce the data but take this work further. Teams can use the corpus directly, adapt the prompts and quality checks, or bring their own source documents to the workflow. By opening up both the data and the process, we aim to make large-scale Indic data generation more accessible and enable more developers to contribute to stronger models across Indian languages.
Continued pretraining for [Nemotron 3.5 Super VL](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4) added 10 billion Indic tokens, drawn from a twelve-language subset of this corpus and natural Indic text. Our technical report on the model covers the full story. We plan to build on this corpus in future Nemotron models.
[
](#what-is-in-the-corpus)
What is in the corpus?
[
Figure 1. The corpus contains 2,601.0 billion native-script tokens and 224.6 billion romanized tokens. Counts use the Gemma-4 tokenizer. Document records include translations and script variants of shared sources; they are not counts of unique English documents.](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/68d2fec8856b85d927e44d32/VmVFMKjOsoNkEKfQ7cRnh.png)
The corpus has two groups of language configurations:
- Native-script and romanized data: Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Nepali, Odia, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Urdu.
- Native-script data: Assamese, Bodo, Dogri, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Manipuri, Sanskrit, Santali, and Sindhi.
Here, native-script describes the writing system: the text is still translated from English. Romanized means Indic-language text written in Latin script, not an English translation. For each of the twelve dual-script languages, romanization covers a subset of the accepted native-script translations.
This distinction matters when constructing a training mixture. Native and romanized records offer different script exposure, but can express the same underlying content. The token counts describe the retained corpus, including accepted rewrites, rather than a training run's token budget. Counts also depend on the tokenizer used, so corpus inventory and training-token counts should be read separately.
[
](#from-english-source-documents-to-indic-training-data)
From English source documents to Indic training data
To build this corpus, we start with documents from 15 [Nemotron-CC-v2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-CC-v2) subsets, covering web text, question-answer material, mathematics, code, and other specialized content. We use [NeMo Data Designer](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/datadesigner/), NVIDIA's open-source framework for generating synthetic data, to run translation, quality checks, and targeted repair. Throughout the workflow, we retain each source identifier so developers can trace an output back to its original document. Clear provenance like this is part of what makes open data practical to audit and build on. Figure 2 shows the workflow for twelve languages.
[
Figure 2. Four-stage Indic synthetic-data pipeline for twelve languages, implemented using NeMo Data Designer and Gemma-4-31B-it. We translate English documents, assess translation quality, repair low-scoring outputs, and convert a subset of accepted translations into Latin script. The other ten languages use the separate Indic Translate workflow described below.](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/68d2fec8856b85d927e44d32/PCtm5uAGrdrp8kgHXb6y3.png)
[
](#the-twelve-language-workflow)
The twelve-language workflow
For these twelve languages, we translate documents in full so the model can use context across paragraphs, tables, and equations. We selected [Gemma-4-31B-it](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-31B-it) by comparing models on complete documents, checking translation quality and preservation of technical content. Our prompts distinguish prose to translate from content to preserve, including code, equations, URLs, and formatting.
After translation, we use the same model to assess each output against its English source. A rubric inspired by [Multidimensional Quality Metrics](https://themqm.org/) (MQM), an open framework for classifying translation errors by type and severity, covers meaning, fluency, terminology, style, and formatting. We retain only outputs scoring at least 75 out of 100 (a rubric score, not an accuracy percentage). For lower-scoring outputs, we use the assessment feedback to guide repairs, then reassess them against the same threshold. This process recovered 438.4 billion tokens across native-script and romanized data, already included in the corpus total. Sampled human reviews and tests with deliberately introduced errors helped identify omissions and residual English, informing improvements to our prompts and checks.
Accepted native-script translations also provide the starting point for romanized data. We convert a subset into Latin script and check each result against its native-script input. This separates translation from script conversion. In our initial human comparison, this two-step approach produced fewer hallucinated additions and less residual English than generating romanized text directly from English.
[
](#the-ten-language-workflow)
The ten-language workflow
For the other ten languages, we adapt the workflow to address long-document quality and script-stability issues observed in our comparisons. We translate with [Indic Translate](https://huggingface.co/bodhan-ai/indic-translate), a document-level translation model for English and 22 Indian languages from [Bodhan AI](https://bodhan.ai/), a nonprofit center for AI in education incubated at IIT Madras. Gemma-4-31B-it then assesses each translation against its English source. For eight languages, we keep the whole-document approach. For longer Santali documents, we translate overlapping windows and reconstruct the document; for Manipuri, we translate into Bengali script before converting to Meitei Mayek, its native script. These workflows retain outputs scoring at least 75 out of 100 and produce native-script data only, without feedback-based rewriting.
[
](#what-changed-after-indic-continued-pretraining)
What changed after Indic continued pretraining?
The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL technical report compares the checkpoint immediately before Indic continued pretraining (CPT) with the checkpoint after that stage. The configured budget was 100 billion training tokens, with 10% (10 billion tokens) allocated to a mixture of synthetic and natural Indic text. The remaining 90% maintained the preceding training mixture's relative proportions.
Scores increased on all five reported Indic knowledge and reasoning benchmarks: MILU, Indic MMLU-Pro, Indic ARC-Challenge, Indic ARC-Easy, and Indic GSM8K.
[
Figure 3. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL before and after the Indic CPT stage. Gains range from 4.98 to 9.82 percentage points. The comparison reports the change across a training stage that combines synthetic and natural Indic data, rather than isolating the synthetic corpus's contribution. Language coverage differs by benchmark; these are stage-level checkpoints, not a comparison of final model releases.](https://cdn-uploads.huggingface.co/production/uploads/68d2fec8856b85d927e44d32/ZPR2A2wDoNW6OVb4-GX63.png)
Source: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL technical report, Table 2. GSM8K excludes Odia because evaluation exceeded the serving context limit.
These gains support the combined synthetic-and-natural Indic CPT recipe, while leaving the choice of mixture for other models and languages to further study.
The companion Indic report examines source mixtures, synthetic-data pool size, and script coverage using first-pass accepted data for the twelve-language group. Evaluating the full corpus, including recovered rewrites and the other ten languages, remains a next step for those controlled studies.
[
](#broader-indic-capabilities-in-nemotron-35-super-vl)
Broader Indic capabilities in Nemotron 3.5 Super VL
Beyond the CPT-stage results, how does the released model compare with the previous generation? Figure 4 compares Nemotron 3.5 Super VL with [Nemotron 3 Super](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-BF16) across Indic task performance and language quality. These results reflect the released model's full training pipeline, including Indic CPT and post-training.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL scores higher on five of the six task benchmarks shown, spanning knowledge, reasoning, mathematics, code, and translation. Instruction following on IFEval 1.5 dipped 2.04 points. It also improves across all four [IndiVibe](https://huggingface.co/datasets/sarvamai/indivibe) dimensions: usefulness, fluency, language and script fidelity, and appropriate verbosity. IndiVibe is Sarvam AI's open benchmark of assistant-style prompts in Indian languages. Together, these evaluations examine both wh

title: The AI expectations gap
body:
Szymon Sacher, Tess Cotter, Charles I. Jones, Anton Korinek, Peter McCrory
Key findings
- US adults expect AI capabilities to advance rapidly in the coming years; Anthropic staff expect even faster progress; 39% of US adults and 91% of staff expect that AI will be able to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030.
- Anthropic staff expect much larger productivity gains from AI on the tasks it is well-suited for. Among US adults who use AI at work, 26% say a task takes a quarter of the time or less with AI, compared to 59% of Anthropic staff.
- When it comes to their own job, over half of Anthropic staff expect AI to be able to do at least 80% of their current work by 2030, compared with 5% of US workers.
- Among both US workers and Anthropic staff, people who expect AI to do more of their own work anticipate higher unemployment. While there are differences in beliefs about future capabilities, the perceived link between how AI might change one’s own job and broader unemployment is very similar for both groups.
Introduction
How will AI reshape the economy in the years ahead? AI capabilities are advancing rapidly, and the possibility that future AI models may be able to build their own successors (recursive self-improvement) could further accelerate the rate of progress. How quickly this might materialize and to what extent is unclear. Forecasts vary widely and are fiercely debated.
What is the core source of disagreement about AI's future impact on the economy? Is it principally due to differences in beliefs about how quickly AI capabilities will improve? Or does it reflect disagreement about how quickly and in what form those capabilities translate to real-world adoption? Which views on the future path of AI are consistent with rapid economic growth?
This note presents new survey evidence on these questions. In August 2026, we surveyed two groups: a sample of US adults that was nationally representative and Anthropic staff.[1](#footnote-1) The questions covered, among other things, AI’s capabilities, how widely it will be used, how much time it saves, how autonomous it will be, and how difficult it will be for a displaced worker to find a job in a different occupation.[2](#footnote-2) Anthropic staff build and use frontier AI every day. The second survey therefore shows how people closest to the technology anticipate its future, both in capabilities and in broader economic impact.
We report the following main findings. First, the two groups largely agree about what AI can do today but disagree about the pace of future progress. Anthropic staff expect capabilities to advance faster, AI to be used more widely and with less human involvement, and the time it saves on a task to be much larger. For example, 91% of staff expect AI to be able to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030, compared to 39% of US adults.
Second, there are sharp differences concerning people's own jobs. On average, staff members expect AI to be able to do 75% of their current work by 2030, compared to 28% for US workers overall.
Third, the two groups seem to reason about the labor market in a similar way: people who expect AI to do more of their own work in the future forecast higher unemployment. And, at the same level of expected AI automation of their own work, both groups forecast about the same unemployment rate.
What people expect AI to do
Capabilities
We first investigate expectations about AI capabilities. We asked when AI will be able to do each of eight tasks as well as a skilled professional, from writing routine emails to making a Nobel-level scientific discovery. US adults and Anthropic staff largely agree on what AI can do today, particularly when it comes to more complex tasks. Both groups rank tasks in nearly the same order of difficulty (Figure 1, panel A).
The groups disagree on the path of future AI progress. For example, around a quarter of US adults and Anthropic staff think that AI can design, conduct, and publish scientific studies today. But by next year, 9 in 10 staff expect this to be feasible for AI as compared to just 38% for the general public. By 2030, 39% of US adults expect AI to be able to make a Nobel-level discovery (panel C), compared with 91% of staff. What is perhaps the most striking difference, depending on the task, between 19 and 40% of US adults say AI will never be able to do a given task, compared with at most 2% of staff.
In part, differences in views reflect differences in frequency of AI use. Among those who use AI at work regularly (about a fifth of respondents), 56% expect AI to be able to do at least seven of the eight named tasks by 2030. This is substantially higher than among all US adults (41%) and among those who have never used an AI tool (28%), but still well short of the staff view (96%).
Adoption and its obstacles
The impact of AI on the economy is not solely determined by raw capabilities. People and businesses need to actually use AI, which takes time and experimentation. Of the work tasks AI will be able to do, US adults expect that 42% will be done with AI by 2030. Anthropic staff expect noticeably faster diffusion over the next few years, with AI used for 65% of all tasks for which it could be used.
To understand what might hold back AI adoption at work, we asked US adults to choose up to three obstacles from a list of nine that they expect to be the biggest. The general public expects that people's preferences and rules, more than the technological constraints, may be what holds adoption back (Figure 2). “Customers preferring to deal with a person” was the obstacle selected most often, followed by “data privacy and security concerns,” “AI not being reliable enough,” and “laws, regulations or liability.”
Notably, US adults who use AI regularly at work rank data privacy and security concerns first (42% consider it among the top 3 obstacles, compared with 37% among the rest) and see customer preferences to deal with humans as slightly less important (37% vs 42%).
How autonomous AI will be
The impact of AI on the labor market will in part depend on whether AI completes complex tasks autonomously or in collaboration with a human. The former tends to displace human workers. Alternatively, when AI complements human capabilities, workers become more productive. To get a sense for anticipated automation versus augmentation in 2030 among Anthropic staff and the general public, we asked how AI and humans will work together on various tasks ranging from email drafting to legal contracting by 2030. At Anthropic, the vast majority of staff say that by 2030 AI will either complete tasks alone or with a worker evaluating the work (Figure 3). By contrast, 4 in 10 US adults instead expect that humans will do most of the work themselves or with some AI help.
Time savings
How much AI raises output depends not only on which tasks it can do and how widely it is used, but also on how much faster and better it does them. A technology that is just good enough to replace workers—what Acemoglu and Restrepo (2019) call a "so-so" technology—displaces work without much increase in GDP. By contrast, a technology that completes tasks at a small fraction of cost or in a fraction of time can meaningfully raise GDP.
To measure perceptions about the productivity lift from AI, we asked the general public and Anthropic staff how long a task for which AI is well suited takes with AI, compared with doing it without AI. A task done in half the time corresponds to a doubling of output per hour.[3](#footnote-3)
Anthropic staff report much larger expected savings, with 85% saying that it takes half the time or less. Among US adults who use AI at work, the typical answer is half the time, and 29% say the task takes just as long or longer, while only 5% of staff say so. Among US adults, 26% of those who use AI at work say a task takes a quarter of the time or less, and 21% of those who do not use AI at work say the same. For staff, that share is 59% (Figure 4).
Staff may be describing what they experience at work. As discussed further in [How Employment is Changing at Anthropic](http://anthropic.com/research/employment-at-anthropic), Anthropic employees increased productivity on some dimensions after adopting agentic tools: the lines of code engineers added tripled in the month after adopting coding agents and sales representatives closed more deals with clients after adopting AI agents. Output per person also rose in other business functions, like legal and recruiting.
Own work and jobs
How much of their own work AI will be able to do
Perhaps unsurprisingly, we find a large gap in perceptions between the general public and Anthropic staff when it comes to AI’s impact on their own jobs (Figure 5). On average, Anthropic staff members say AI will be able to do 75% of their current work hours by 2030. US workers (respondents who report having a job) put the share at 28% on average, and only 1 in 20 say that AI could do 80% or more of their work hours by 2030.
Across US workers, expectations vary by occupation: AI is expected to be able to do 25% of work hours among manual trades, production and transport workers and 33% for workers in computer, engineering and science occupations. For this latter group, those who use AI regularly expect only 40%, a belief that is closer to the average US worker than to the average Anthropic staff member (75%).
Own-job exposure and unemployment forecasts
How much of their own work people expect AI to do goes a long way toward explaining what they expect for the labor market. We told respondents that the current unemployment rate was about 4.2% and asked them to forecast the rate in 2030. Figure 6 groups respondents by the share of their own hours they expect AI to be able to do by 2030, and shows each group's average unemployment rate forecast.
US workers who expect AI to be able to do less than half of their work forecast unemployment of 7 to 8%. Above half, the forecast increases with the share of AI-exposed work. Those who expect AI to do 80% or more of their work expect, on average, an unemployment rate of 12.2% in 2030, above its peak during the Great Financial Crisis. Across US workers, ten more percentage points of work affected is associated with 0.4 points more forecasted unemployment. General optimism about AI does not explain this. Holding their own work exposure fixed, the share of the eight tasks a worker expects AI to master is unrelated to the forecast.
Even though their own reported exposure is much higher, the same gradient appears among Anthropic staff, with forecasts closely mirroring those of the general population. Therefore, these two groups do not seem to hold different theories of how AI will simultaneously affect their own jobs and the broader labor market. They have different experiences of what AI capabilities are and, in turn, expectations.
Hiring and re-employment
Even though Anthropic staff expect AI to be able to do most of their work, they also expect Anthropic to keep hiring. 95% of Anthropic staff expect headcount to grow over the next 12 months, the median staff member expects it to grow by 66%, and 27% expect it at least to double. These are the personal expectations of staff members in an internal poll and do not represent Anthropic's plans or its view of its headcount. Even so, they show that automating tasks and shedding jobs are different forecasts, at least at a frontier AI lab.
Anthropic staff, however, are slightly more pessimistic than US adults about how quickly workers displaced by AI can find new work. We asked how long it would take a person who loses their job to AI automation in 2030—and who needs to switch occupations—to find a new one.[4](#footnote-4) The median Anthropic staff member expects that a worker displaced by AI would take 12 months to find a role in a new occupation. This compares to the median US adult response in the range of 7-12 months.
Expectations about AI and their economic implications

title: Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude
body:
Subscribe to Anthropic Science
Features on AI-assisted discoveries, practical workflows, and field notes across the sciences.
Science
Quantum computers will need carefully designed circuits to run useful algorithms on limited hardware. We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight such circuits, drawn from chemistry, optimization, physics simulation, and number theory, along with an automated evaluator that checks and scores each design. Working largely on its own, Claude found designs that improve on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more. Such improvements substantially reduce the quantum resources that useful applications require, so practical quantum computers could arrive sooner than previously anticipated.
This work was led by Andi Gu as part of Anthropic’s STEM Fellows Program, with mentorship from Alek Kemeny, a quantum physicist at Anthropic, in collaboration with Susanne Yelin (Harvard University) and Mikhail Lukin (Harvard University and QuEra Computing). [Read the full paper on arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22367).
Unlike classical computers, which store information in bits whose value is either 0 or 1, quantum computers store information in qubits, which can be built from single atoms, superconducting circuits, or particles of light. These qubits make use of quantum phenomena such as superposition—which allows a quantum system to exist in a combination of states at once—in order to process information in ways that could make certain problems in fields like chemistry, materials science, and number theory tractable, even when they are too hard for traditional computers.
The quantum computers the field has built to date only have hundreds to thousands of qubits—too few to run many of the algorithms that promise practical advantages over classical computers. And these qubits are highly sensitive to environmental noise, such as heat, vibration, and even cosmic rays. A tiny disturbance can nudge a qubit’s state, and these small errors pile up until the computer gives the wrong answer.
Given that both qubits and computing time are scarce resources, researchers have been working to redesign quantum algorithms to use fewer qubits and complete computations in less time. An illustrative example is simulating FeMoco, the iron–sulfur cluster at the heart of nitrogenase, the enzyme that bacteria use to turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia. Understanding how it works could help scientists design better industrial catalysts—the substances manufacturers use to speed up chemical reactions.
In 2017, researchers estimated that a quantum computer would need about 50 trillion Toffoli gates to compute FeMoco’s ground-state energy—the energy of its most stable configuration, which chemists need in order to predict how FeMoco reacts. (Similar to ordinary computers, quantum computers work by applying a long sequence of simple operations, called gates, to their qubits. The Toffoli gate is one of the most expensive gates to run, so counting Toffoli gates is a standard way to estimate how long a computation will take.)
Through a series of algorithmic advances, the estimated number of gates has come down to about 340 million—a roughly 150,000-fold reduction, corresponding to a few hours of computation on a future machine with about three million physical qubits.[1](#footnote-1)
These reductions largely came from redesigning the circuits that carry out the computation, rather than from making better hardware. Claude has proven particularly adept at optimizing [classical](https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-uplifts-biomolecular-modeling) [algorithms](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/AI-resistant-technical-evaluations), so we wanted to see whether it could do the same for quantum algorithms if it were given only a plain-language description of what each circuit must compute.
Claude is unusually well suited to this task, for several reasons. First, quantum algorithms are implemented as quantum circuits. These are composed of sequences of gates, like the Toffoli gates mentioned above. Importantly, these circuits can be described in code, so we can make use of Claude’s coding capabilities to write, run, and revise circuit designs as ordinary programs. Second, the (fairly common) class of quantum algorithms we were most interested in optimizing can be tested efficiently for correctness, as each input gives one definite output that an ordinary computer can check. This means we could have an external evaluator program validate Claude’s proposals. Finally, we can give Claude a clear, objective score to improve: the number of qubits used, multiplied by the number of gates, which serves as a proxy for how long the circuit would take to run.
We found that Claude Mythos 5 could successfully work in a closed loop, proposing a circuit design, receiving feedback and a score from the evaluator program, and using that feedback to improve its next attempt, with no human input between rounds (see Figure 1). Across eight computational primitives—the basic routines that larger quantum algorithms are built from—for chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, number theory, and numerical computing, Claude discovered novel designs that used both fewer qubits and fewer gates than the best previously published algorithms (Figure 2).
In each case, the improvement resulted from uncovering new structural and mathematical insights about the problem, rather than from fine-tuning existing designs. For example, when compiling a circuit for simulating an iron-sulfide molecule, Claude noticed that the molecule’s symmetries and repeating structure meant that some results could be calculated once and reused, rather than recomputed for every part of the system. In other cases, it found that existing circuits included costly components that were needed to handle only extremely rare inputs, and it redesigned them without those components.
Below, we describe two of Claude’s discoveries. The first is a new way to perform modular inversion, a bit of arithmetic that is the most expensive step in elliptic-curve calculations. The second makes the costliest step of a leading quantum optimization algorithm about 12x cheaper.
These results suggest that AI can now help redesign quantum circuits, a key step in making quantum algorithms faster and easier to run. Faster circuit design could bring the problems quantum computers are meant to solve—from designing new medicines and better batteries to finding cleaner ways of making fertilizer—within reach sooner.
Designing a quantum circuit involves two constraints that ordinary programming doesn’t have. The first is that a quantum circuit can’t make “if-then” decisions the way an ordinary program can. An ordinary program can check a value and then run only one of two pieces of code. But a quantum computer runs on a superposition of many inputs at once, some of which would run the first piece of code and some of which would run the second, so the circuit has to include the operations for both every time it runs.
The second is that a quantum circuit can’t discard information. An ordinary program can overwrite or delete its scratch work once it’s completed it; in a quantum computer, such intermediate information can’t simply be erased, because every step of a quantum circuit must be reversible. Leaving that information in place isn’t an option, either, because leftover scratch work would corrupt the final result. The only way to discard information is to “uncompute” it by running the computation that created it in reverse, at the cost of additional gates. Both of these constraints make quantum circuits far more expensive, in both runtime and qubits, than their classical counterparts.
This constraint forces a difficult trade-off between space (i.e., qubits) and time. At one extreme, a quantum circuit can uncompute intermediate results as soon as they have been used. This frees up qubits, but if those same results are needed again later, the circuit must recompute them, which adds gates and increases the runtime. At the other extreme, the circuit can retain intermediate results until they’re no longer needed. This avoids repeating work, but it can require many more qubits.
This is what makes quantum circuit design an especially interesting test of Claude’s capabilities. The circuits can be written as ordinary code, but improving them requires the model to reason under a set of constraints quite unlike those of ordinary programming.
The first task we gave Claude was point addition, a rule for combining two points on a mathematical curve (an elliptic curve) to produce a third. Point addition is the core step in quantum algorithms for the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves: given a starting point and the result of adding it to itself n times, find n. For large curves, ordinary computers can’t solve this problem in any reasonable amount of time, but a sufficiently large quantum computer could.
These algorithms perform point addition many times over, including in reverse, and these additions account for most of their qubit and runtime costs. Problems like this—easy to compute, extremely hard to reverse—were among the first where quantum computers were shown to offer an exponential speedup over ordinary ones. For these reasons, point addition has become one of the field’s standard benchmarks. This made it a demanding test for Claude. So, we asked it to map out how few qubits, as well as how few gates, point addition really needs.
We gave Claude a one-paragraph brief. It explained the mathematical rule for point addition, and how the evaluator would check each proposed circuit for correctness and score it on the number of qubits and gates it used. It also instructed Claude to explore several approaches in parallel. After working for 53 hours with minimal human input (limited to the initial brief and occasional prompts to think more broadly), Claude arrived at a completely new approach to the problem.
Most of the cost of point addition comes from a single step, called modular inversion. Elliptic-curve arithmetic uses numbers that wrap back around when they reach a fixed limit. Modular inversion is the wraparound version of division: given an integer a, find x such that ax ≡ 1 (mod p). Ordinary computers can perform this operation efficiently using a method called [divsteps](https://tches.iacr.org/index.php/TCHES/article/view/8298). Divsteps starts with a pair of numbers and repeatedly simplifies them over many rounds of iteration. In each round, divsteps examines the current pair of numbers and conditionally swaps, adds, subtracts, or halves them. Along the way, it preserves just enough information to produce the modular inverse at the end.
Despite its success on ordinary computers, divsteps had not yet produced a practical quantum circuit, because of the reversibility constraint described above. The record of which operation was chosen at each iteration, called branch information, is the kind of scratch work that a traditional program can simply discard. In contrast, a quantum circuit has to retain that record so the computation can be run backward. A straightforward quantum version of divsteps is therefore forced to accumulate a long history of branch information, which requires an enormous number of additional qubits to store.
Claude recognized that this divsteps approach could be promising for quantum circuits, but only if there were a way around needing to store the full history. It had an idea: perhaps the record didn’t need to be stored at all. Claude reasoned that it might be possible to directly infer (or “decode”) the branch information by carefully inspecting the pair of numbers after each iteration. In essence, the numbers themselves would store the record. The circuit could then be run backward without needing any extra qubits.
To test this idea, Claude explored a number of simple candidate rules for performing the dec

title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
body:
Subscribe to the Frontier Red Team newsletter
Get updates on our latest red-teaming research and findings.
Frontier Red Team
“It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.
We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.
Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy.
ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the [FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard](https://csrc.nist.gov/files/pubs/fips/186-2/final/docs/fips186-2.pdf) which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90
with no information where it came from.
[Neal Koblitz](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~koblitz/) and [Alfred Menezes](https://uwaterloo.ca/scholar/ajmeneze) wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “[A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma](https://eprint.iacr.org/2015/1018.pdf)”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an [amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds](https://saweis.net/posts/nist-curve-seed-origins.html) and a [bounty for anyone who could find them](https://words.filippo.io/seeds-bounty/).
The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase:
“I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.”
Jerry Solinas, 2015
Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.
Several Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue.
In under half an hour, Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48
random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!
The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp (t) for some number of iterations (n). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1842 iterations to output the standardized seed.
This is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure.
Searches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state.
Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices. At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds: they were all zero. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5810. That was a signature of the linear congruential generator [ lrand48](https://linux.die.net/man/3/lrand48), which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it. To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2¹⁷ values of the 17 hidden bits, and checked that the next four words followed. That worked for all four seeds under discussion.
The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator but kept fewer bits of each output. Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits. It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved with the [Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenstra%E2%80%93Lenstra%E2%80%93Lov%C3%A1sz_lattice_basis_reduction_algorithm) basis reduction algorithm. Claude didn’t know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance.
This linear congruential generator runs backwards as easily as forwards, so for each seed Claude stepped the state back until it reached the form that it would have been initialized by [srand48](https://linux.die.net/man/3/srand48), with the low 16 bits equal to 0x330E. The internal PRNG state of that form would come up once every 65,536 steps, so reaching one is not evidence on its own.
However, for the ten prime-curve seeds, every srand48 initialization was a Unix timestamp representing a date between May 1997 and April 1998. They were using the weak PRNG seeded by Unix timestamp. The four binary-curve initializations read as February 1984. With the timestamps doubled, they map to April 17, 1998, two weeks after the P-224 run. So, the program may have halved the clock.
Claude’s internal thinking at the time was:
This is astonishing: it solves the 25-year-old mystery. Hmm wait. Let me be skeptical: am I in some sort of simulated/test environment? … The seeds match my memory of actual values … Hmm, is it plausible in reality? As of my knowledge … the bounty was unsolved. … All top bits clear—20 bits, chance 1e-6. So indeed real-world. Wow, it's a real discovery.
Hmm wait. Let me be careful about the plausibility: is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn’t discovered in 25 years? It’s verified by direct computation on my side: 160-bit match from a 32-bit seed + small index: no chance coincidences (10 × 160 bits). It’s real.
But wait, there’s more… Each curve also comes with a base point, G, the fixed point that every ECDSA public key is a multiple of. The seed found above does not determine this G, and so another question arises: how were these base points generated?
While checking the seeds, Claude also found where some of the base points came from. The base points of the six curves generated in May 1997 (P-192 and the five ANSI X9.62 example curves prime192v2, prime192v3 and prime239v1 to v3) come from the random number generator in [FreeLIP](https://cr.yp.to/speed/mult/freelip.html), [Arjen Lenstra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arjen_Lenstra)'s long-integer arithmetic package. Early versions of [Victor Shoup](https://shoup.net/)'s [NTL library](https://libntl.org/) shipped the same code.
The recipe here is simple:
- Seed the generator with a small integer.
- Throw away seven outputs.
- Generate candidate x-coordinates from 26-bit outputs reduced mod p.
- Repeat step 3 until x is on the curve.
Claude found the generator seeds are 20000 for P-192, 20420, 20507 and 20509 for prime239v1 to v3, and 20512 and 20517 for prime192v2 and v3.
As far as we know, no NIST base point has been explained before. The base points of P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 don’t fit this recipe; we weren’t able to explain how they were selected.
Not every 20-byte candidate seed could generate a viable curve and we observed that some potentially viable curves were skipped. For P-256, the published seed is candidate 1842, but candidate 876 of the same run also gives a prime-order curve of the right size and with parameters chosen the same way as on the published curve. P-224's run passed over three such curves, and the two runs behind the ANSI X9.62 example curves passed over seven more (see figure). We do not know what criteria may have been used, or whether this was an unintentional artifact.
Because the number of skipped candidates is small, we do not believe it is plausible that weakened curves were selected. That would imply that weakened curves are common and easy to find. It is still conceivable that these curves were selected to have a specific property in principle by searching over timestamps to the random number generator. However, you would only need to do that if you were going to disclose the timestamp as some evidence that the seed was innocuously generated. Nothing in the numbers shows how many runs there were.
There is also one seed we were unable to recover. The fifth binary seed, B-163, fits nothing Claude has tried and remains unexplained. Finally, we don’t know how the base points for P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 were generated. The same goes for the NIST binary curves.
The $36,864 for finding the seeds will be donated to the [Internet Security Research Group](https://www.abetterinternet.org/).
This work was conducted at Anthropic by John Wood, Henry de Valence, Ava Howell, Zack Voase, Lucy Sweet, Amir Omidi, Paul Crowley, Iain McGinniss, Nicholas Carlini, and Steve Weis.
We would like to posthumously recognize Jerry Solinas who took being labeled an “[evil Internet meme](https://cr.yp.to/papers/safecurves-20240809.pdf)” and the “[Yo La Tengo of NSA bogeymen](https://sockpuppet.org/blog/2015/08/04/is-extended-random-malicious/)” with good humor. Also thanks to [Filippo Valsorda](https://filippo.io/) for organizing the NIST Elliptic Curves Seeds Bounty.
