title: Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint
body:
Automatic Speech Recognition • 0.5B • Updated • 59.1k • 80
[
](#granite-switch-41-chat-decisions-and-speech-from-one-endpoint)
Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
[Granite Switch](https://github.com/generative-computing/granite-switch)project enables a modular approach to model development. Now Granite Switch 4.1 models, armed with a Decision adapter and the fastest ASR model on the OpenASR leaderboard, can move efficiently between natural-language responses, general and specialized decisions, and speech-to-text tasks—all from one hosted endpoint.
Specifically, [Granite-Switch-4.1-8B](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-switch-4.1-8b) and [-30B](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-switch-4.1-30b) models are configured to include:
- A new
[Decision aLoRA](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granitelib-core-r1.0/blob/main/decision/README.md)for general-purpose decision-making (e.g. v1/systemone), - A specialized
[Guardian aLoRA](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granitelib-guardian-r1.0/blob/main/guardian-core/README.md)that, on average, outperforms Jev 1.13, Microsoft-Decision-1, GPT-Luna-Decisions, and Clef-Flash on safety-related decision tasks, and [Granite-Speech-5.0-Turbo-CTC](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc), the fastest ASR model on the[OpenASR Leaderboard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/hf-audio/open_asr_leaderboard), embedded for use in transcription tasks.
All three of these technologies (along with the underlying base model) are composed into one model, taking up approximately the same amount of VRAM on a GPU as the base model would by itself. That means more capabilities with fewer GPUs.
And because the Switch adapters were built as cache-efficient [Activated LoRAs](https://research.ibm.com/blog/inference-friendly-aloras-lora), the KV cache created from a base model generation can be reused for any subsequent adapter-based decisions. Combined with our team's [recent vLLM contributions](https://github.com/generative-computing/granite-switch/blob/main/docs/SWITCH_KERNELS.md) to speed up low rank adapter inferencing, as well as a co-located ASR encoder, Granite Switch 4.1 models can switch between a chat request and a decision request and a spoken request, with blazing fast speeds.
Check out our [Speech-to-Decisions HF space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/ibm-granite/speech-to-decisions) where granite-switch-4.1-8b transcribes audio, generates summaries, screens for harmful content, and tests 15 other user-defined flags—all running on a single endpoint in real time.
[
](#granite-libraries-the-og-decision-models)
Granite Libraries: The OG Decision Models
Decision models aren’t new. Our previous release of [Granite Libraries](https://huggingface.co/collections/ibm-granite/granite-libraries) features a repository of specialized “decision model” adapters and other specialized task adapters that can be composed into custom Granite Switch models. And while Jev and other closed decision models focus on generality, we’ve found that many of our specialized granitelib adapters can outperform generalists on specialized classification tasks.
[Compare granitelib adapters](https://huggingface.co/spaces/ibm-granite/granitelib-evals) with generalist decision models when evaluated on specialized classification tasks.
Because adapters share the base model's KV cache, adding specialists alongside a generalist decision adapter costs almost nothing. You get broad coverage from the generalist and higher accuracy from specialists on the tasks you care about.
In a “Race” between Granite-Switch-4.1-30B (frozen base Granite + 4 specialized aLoRAs) and Jev-27B (frozen base Qwen model + 1 generic decision LoRA), Granite-Switch-4.1-30B was able to complete a real world, 5-step RAG workflow much faster than its competitor.
[
](#compose-and-extend-your-own-granite-switch-model)
Compose and Extend Your Own Granite Switch Model
Granite-Switch-4.1-8B and -30B are released with “batteries included”. They are Granite Switch models that we compiled with a predefined set of helpful adapters. But you don’t need to use our version. Anyone can [compose their own Granite Switch model](https://generative-computing.github.io/granite-switch/adapter_catalog.html), mixing and matching adapters from Granite Libraries to best meet their needs.
Moving forward, we see tremendous opportunity for the community to compose and extend Granite Switch models with custom and third party adapters. We plan to release an Adapter SDK for training adapters in [Mellea](https://docs.mellea.ai/advanced/lora-and-alora-adapters), along side other tutorials and Granite Switch support. These adapters could be specialized classification adapters to augment decision-based workflows or adapters for specialized language tasks. You could even use custom adapters to teach a 3B parameter version of Granite to play the classic game Doom.
Similarly to Jev, our custom 3B parameter Granite Switch model made split second decisions to navigate the Doom game, but was able to do so at 60 - 100 decisions / second, compared to Jev’s reported 10 decisions / second.[1](#footnote-1) Unlike Jev, this Granite Switch model can also narrate and respond to your questions while it is playing.
[
](#resources-for-getting-started)
Resources for Getting Started
[Granite Switch 4.1 Model Cards](https://huggingface.co/collections/ibm-granite/granite-switch)[Speech-to-Decisions Demo](https://huggingface.co/spaces/ibm-granite/speech-to-decisions)[Granite Switch GitHub Repo](https://github.com/generative-computing/granite-switch)[Original Granite Switch and Granite Libraries Release Blog](https://research.ibm.com/blog/granite-libraries-project-switch)- Create your own aLoRA v LoRA race on
[Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/generative-computing/granite-switch/blob/main/tutorials/notebooks/alora_vs_lora_race.ipynb).
Footnotes
[1 ][https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev)

Introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan, offering eligible labs sponsored access to GPT‑Rosalind and tools for life sciences discovery.

We’re introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan to help more academic scientists access [GPT‑Rosalind⁠](https://openai.com/rosalind/), our dedicated life sciences model, which combines frontier reasoning with [Rosalind workbench⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/blog/rosalind-workbench) that enables specialized tool orchestration across medicinal chemistry, genomics, wet-lab assistance, and other scientific applications. Eligible labs can receive up to 30 Business Standard seats at no cost for up to 12 months, with access to GPT‑Rosalind subject to trusted-access approval.

Academic research creates knowledge that entire fields build on. Work that begins with a fundamental question about biology can eventually change how we diagnose disease, develop medicines, or grow food. But those advances depend on scientists having the resources to explore ideas, test them, and share what they learn.

Accelerating scientific discovery is central to OpenAI’s mission of ensuring that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. With this plan, we’re investing in the scientists doing that foundational work—helping more labs combine their expertise and judgment with AI tools built for life sciences research.

## Supporting the research behind future breakthroughs

Many of the advances we rely on today grew out of years of basic research.

The Human Genome Project helped launch modern genomics, transforming medicine, diagnostics, and biotechnology.

Curiosity-driven work on bacterial immune systems led to CRISPR-Cas9, which revolutionized genome editing and is now advancing research in cancer, inherited disease, agriculture, and biotechnology. Decades of university research on mRNA also laid the groundwork for COVID-19 vaccines and a new generation of vaccines and therapies.

Academic research has always laid the groundwork for advances in medicine and biotechnology. By helping more scientists combine their scientific expertise and judgment with the advanced specialized reasoning of GPT‑Rosalind, we hope to support discoveries whose benefits reach far beyond the lab.

## How academic labs are using GPT‑Rosalind

OpenAI is committed to enabling academic researchers to pursue their scientific ambitions. Distinguished academic labs are already exploring how GPT‑Rosalind can support work ranging from protein design to understanding neurodegeneration. These examples show where researchers are applying the model within their scientific workflows.

Zhao LabBourdenx labLaboratory for Evolutionary Design

*Zhao Lab, UCSF*

> “I use GPT models throughout my research, from exploring the literature to refining experiments and computational approaches. They help me iterate on ideas much faster and explore more possibilities than ever before. I feel more efficient as a researcher, with more room to explore and think creatively.”

*Dr. Mathieu Bourdenx, Bourdenx Lab*

> “Rosalind will not only help us improve our current discovery and design tasks, but also apply them at larger scales than previously possible while still providing useful insights to biological researchers.”

*Dr. Brian Hie, Stanford University and Arc Institute*

## What the plan includes

With the new Rosalind Academic Plan, academic researchers can bring GPT‑Rosalind and Rosalind Workbench to their lab with greater flexibility and harness frontier model intelligence for scientific research.

Eligible labs receive:

- Up to 30 Business Standard seats at $0 per user per month for up to 12 months.
- Access to all commercially available frontier OpenAI models, subject to plan usage limits.
- Access to GPT‑Rosalind following trusted-access approval.

Research data shared through the Rosalind Academic Plan is not used to train our models by default.



## Build for life sciences research

GPT‑Rosalind is a specialized life sciences model designed to support deeper reasoning on complex biological questions. Through trusted access, approved researchers can use it to investigate sensitive scientific questions within safeguards designed for legitimate research.

Areas of research include:



### Drug and protein design

Designing candidate drugs, therapeutic proteins, peptides, and enzymes, and optimizing their molecular interactions, selectivity, stability, and suitability for development.



### Disease detection and monitoring

Identifying molecular signatures of disease and developing liquid biopsies and other minimally invasive diagnostics to detect disease earlier, monitor progression, and assess treatment response.



### Vaccines and immune responses

Designing and evaluating antibodies and vaccines against emerging viral variants, investigating host–pathogen interactions, and studying the strength and durability of protective immune responses.



### Genetic and RNA therapies

Developing approaches to correcting genetic defects and modulating gene expression, designing RNA therapeutics, and investigating how to deliver treatments safely and effectively to intended tissues.



### Agriculture and animal health

Investigating crop resilience, plant disease, and animal health, and applying genetic, nutritional, and biological insights to improve food production and veterinary care.



### Ecology and conservation

Studying biodiversity, adaptation, species interactions, and environmental exposures to understand ecosystem change and inform conservation, bioremediation, and responses to climate change.



### Antimicrobial resistance

Studying how microorganisms resist antibiotics, antivirals, and antifungals, and developing new treatments for resistant infections, biofilms, and persistent disease.

01 / 07

Card 1 of 7: Drug and protein design

## Apply on behalf of your lab

The Rosalind Academic Plan is currently available to academic labs at U.S. universities. PIs and lab leads at universities without an OpenAI Enterprise agreement can apply on behalf of their labs through our trusted access process. Labs at universities with an existing agreement must apply through their university’s Enterprise access process.

Once approved, PIs and lab leads can activate free access to GPT‑Rosalind for up to 30 named members, alongside the other OpenAI frontier models included in the plan. API access is not included at this time. Verified PIs and lab leads manage member permissions and are responsible for their lab’s approved use.

Choose the application path for your lab or organization.

[Request GPT-Rosalind access(opens in a new window)](https://chatgpt.com/rosalind/application)

GPT‑Rosalind access is subject to approval.

Learn more about eligibility, application requirements, and getting started in our [**help center guide**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://help.openai.com/articles/20001602).

## Responsible access for scientific research

Before activating access, we:

- Verify the institution’s legitimacy and the PI or lab lead’s identity
- Review the lead’s professional background, institutional appointment, and authority to oversee lab access
- Assess the lab’s institutional affiliation, research activities, and intended use
- Establish clear responsibilities for the lab lead and a designated institutional safety contact

Safeguards continue after activation through monitoring and enforcement. For registered high-sensitivity use cases, our safety checks account for the approved research context. When questions arise, we may follow up with researchers to clarify the work and confirm authorization. This approach is designed to detect potential misuse while accounting for legitimate research context and reducing unnecessary interruptions to authorized work.

## Specialized intelligence for complex scientific questions

Therapeutic peptidesDiagnosticsVaccinesAnimal healthConservationResistant infections

## Get started

We’re starting with academic labs as part of a broader effort to put useful AI tools in the hands of more scientists. By lowering the cost of access, we hope to give more researchers room to pursue ideas whose benefits could reach far beyond their own labs—from a clearer understanding of disease to better treatments and more resilient food systems.

Those advances will come from scientists asking important questions and doing the work to answer them. We want to help more of them do that work.

If you’re affiliated with an academic lab, learn more about the Rosalind Academic Plan and [check whether you’re eligible⁠(opens in a new window)](https://chatgpt.com/rosalind/lab/application).

title: Accelerating the search for antimicrobial peptides with Google Antigravity
body:
Accelerating the search for antimicrobial peptides with Google Antigravity
New antibiotics are urgently needed to help with rising levels of antimicrobial resistance, but searching for new therapeutics is often a slow, labor-intensive process. With Google Antigravity, our agentic development platform, this process can now be made easier.
Google Antigravity provides an agentic science workbench that empowers biologists to discover, structurally evaluate, and prioritize promising targets quickly, compressing what used to be a fragmented search over multiple databases into a single session. It also helps researchers scan through millions of previously uncharacterized proteins in the UniProt database using ProtNLM, a model that predicts biological function from amino acid sequences.
This technical walkthrough shows how biologists used Google Antigravity to uncover a novel antimicrobial peptide candidate which has predicted activity against the pathogens involved in respiratory tract infections. The lead identified here is now undergoing wet-lab validation.
Finding new antimicrobial peptides
Rising [antimicrobial resistance](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/health-matters-antimicrobial-resistance/health-matters-antimicrobial-resistance) is one of the most pressing global health crises of our time and could result in an estimated 10 million annual deaths globally by 2050. To prevent this, we urgently need to discover novel therapeutics. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), particularly bacteriocins, offer a promising alternative to traditional antibiotics because they have naturally evolved to target fundamental vulnerabilities in competing bacteria, from cell envelopes to essential intracellular machinery, making it difficult for pathogens to develop resistance.
The exponential growth of genomic and metagenomic sequencing has populated global databases with billions of natural amino acid sequences. This pool of natural data has already produced globally used bacteriocins like Nisin, alongside recent genome-mined breakthroughs such as Darobactin, Dynobactin, and Lariocidin.
Many, however, remain locked within the unannotated "dark matter" of protein databases, with their function uncharacterized because they arenât similar to known proteins. For example, the world's leading public resource of protein sequence and functional information, [UniProt](https://www.uniprot.org/), holds millions of sequences with unknown functionality, transferred directly from genome sequencing projects.
To bridge this gap, Google developed [ProtNLM (Protein Natural Language Model)](https://www.uniprot.org/help/ProtNLM), a deep learning model trained to directly read the underlying evolutionary âgrammarâ of amino acid sequences. This allows the model to predict biological function directly from raw protein sequences, enriching millions of previously unnamed UniProt entries with high-confidence functional labels.
Collaborative intelligence
Scientific discovery is rarely a single step process; finding viable candidate proteins requires human intuition and iteration to incorporate new empirical evidence. Working in Antigravity, the researcher and AI agent begin by setting a focused biological goal: find and computationally validate novel AMPs in Streptococcus pseudopneumoniae. During an interactive, multi-turn session the researcher steers the scientific strategy, deciding which questions to ask and what evidence to collect, while the agent handles the heavy lifting of cross-database orchestration, structural analysis, and literature synthesis.
The candidate we uncover in this walkthrough represents a biologically plausible lead backed by structural and genomic evidence but it still requires wet lab validation. What makes this meaningful is how dramatically it lowers the barrier to everyday biological workflows, turning days of fragmented database triage into a single collaborative session. While this session focused on a narrow amino acid window in Streptococcus pseudopneumoniae, researchers can take the conversation in any direction, such as layering in new filtering criteria, exploring different sequence lengths, or targeting other priority pathogens. By broadening the search from human commensals to environmental microbes and beyond, scientists can guide the agent across UniProt to discover novel AMP candidates at scale.
A shared 3D canvas for interactive collaboration
A protein's 3D structure can help us understand its biological function. Examining a candidateâs predicted fold in space is key. To provide this end-to-end workflow in a single workspace, we are introducing the Biomolecular Structure Viewer, a 3D visualization tool embedded directly into Antigravity.
The researcher and agent work together over a shared visual state. As the agent retrieves structures from AlphaFold Database or the scientistâs own predictions, it can dynamically drive the viewer. For instance, it can highlight key functional regions to visually explain its hypotheses. Crucially, this awareness flows both ways: actions like highlighting specific residues or pinning notes directly onto a binding pocket are synchronised back to the agent. A researcher can simply mark a region of interest in 3D space and ask, for example, "How might this Î²-strand affect Lipid II binding?", allowing the agent to immediately reason over the exact structural context the scientist is looking at.
Accelerating Scientific Discovery
Historically, uncovering insights like those in the workflow demonstrated above required fragmented and specialised software: writing custom scripts to query databases, manually exporting files to 3D modelling programs, managing disconnected genomic tools and working with multiple experts to design the wet lab assays. Because wet-lab validation remains resource-intensive, narrowing the search space to only the highest-confidence leads upfront is critical. Using Google Antigravity allows researchers to navigate the vast biological search space efficiently while leveraging accurate protein function predictions from a domain-specific model.
Google Antigravity executes this end-to-end scientific reasoning in one place. This allows scientists to spend more time evaluating high-quality hypotheses, running experiments in the lab and solving research challenges.
Acknowledgements
We would like to acknowledge the contributions of the following team members: Maria Gabriela Cardoso, Victoria Johnston, Lexi Walker, Gena Hong, James King, Richard Green, Filip Radlinski, Artem Sobolev, Michael V. LeVine, Ruijie K. Zhang, Zachary Wu, Luca Schulz, Amy Danson, Tristan Oliver Kwan, Ryan Krueger, Oleg Kovalevskiy, Doug Fritz, Yunhan Xu, Sebastian Nowozin

title: Missed a lecture? This AI agent at Bar-Ilan University helps students catch up
body:
AI

15 October 2026 · Written By Lim Ai Leen

When Yarden Shay missed some classes in her first semester at Bar-Ilan University (BIU) last year, she struggled to get up to speed. The lectures were on legal responsibility, just one of 22 modules in the first year of her undergraduate degree in criminology and psychology.

Plugging that knowledge gap with borrowed notes while staying on top of six to eight hours of fresh lectures daily was an ordeal, she recalls.

“It’s like a gap that is growing through time,” says Shay.

“So, you’re already falling behind, and you’re getting new information that isn’t connecting, because you don’t have the previous information. The stress is everywhere.” That stress is less an issue for her today.

Yarden Shay, an undergraduate at Bar-Ilan University (BIU) who is studying for a degree in criminology and psychology. Photo by Yarden Lev for Microsoft.

In February, BIU piloted an AI agent on its Moodle learning platform that helps students search and summarize course materials using natural language queries, turning these vast resources into learning support. Powered by Azure AI Services and developed by KPMG and OpenApp using Microsoft Copilot Studio, the agent is grounded exclusively in course materials uploaded by BIU’s teaching staff, including recorded lectures, transcripts, presentations and articles. Students can ask the agent to zero in on a topic mentioned in a lecture, create summaries and even test them using the quiz feature.

The pilot covered 71 courses and about 2,400 students at BIU, one of Israel’s leading public research universities with over 20,000 students in Ramat Gan, near Tel Aviv. Available in Hebrew, Arabic and English, the agent will be rolled out to another 100 courses in the first semester of the 2026/27 academic year, which began in October.

The agent operates in the university’s secure Microsoft Azure environment.

Using AI for active study

For Shay, having all that information organized and uploaded in one place means she no longer spends hours tracking down her course mates for missing notes. But the AI agent — represented by a blue robotic owl — is not just a means of catching up. She now uses it as a study aid.

“The AI tool takes notes of everything, including the lectures. And I prefer reading the notes because I can’t ask questions during the lecture, and this way I feel like my brain is working,” she says. “I need active study, and that’s what the AI tool is doing. Because it gives you everything you need to know and a way of testing yourself about what you’ve learned.”

Photo by Ron Rahamim for Microsoft.

Shay gets the learning agent to test her, using both the multiple-choice format as well as open-ended questions. It tells her when she’s got an answer right or wrong and why. She now spends about three hours a day studying after lectures, compared with five to six hours previously.

Having the AI tool as her study companion, she says, has made her feel more self-reliant and improved her student experience. And she can now share her own notes, created with the AI agent’s help.

“A few students asked me for my summaries, and it felt so good that they had helped me, and I can now help them,” she says.

AI as teacher’s assistant, not replacement

Eliyahu Biton, a practicing lawyer and lecturer at BIU since 2017, helped test the AI agent before it went live. His priority, he says, was getting the agent to perform well enough to be his teaching assistant. This meant overhauling and updating materials for the online healthcare law and ethics courses he runs for medical imaging students every year.

Eliyahu Biton, a lecturer at BIU, left, and student Yarden Shay. Photo by Ron Rahamim for Microsoft.

“If you want the bot to be grounded in the material, you need to explain it because you want it to teach what you want to teach,” he says. “So, I needed to rephrase the course materials and get detailed papers for it. If I want it to be my assistant, I need to teach it. So, I teach the bot what to learn, what to answer the students.”

Oversight of the course materials is essential to ensure they can be relied on by the students as learning aids. This included feeding the AI agent transcripts of all his video lectures and expanding the bullet points on his slides with research papers and recommended reading. Then he painstakingly tested the agent’s responses until he was satisfied with their accuracy.

So far, he has observed positive changes in his students since the AI learning tool was introduced. He says he fields fewer routine and administrative questions, and students are less nervous about examinations.

“They are more relaxed about exams now,” he says. “Before, I would just upload old exam questions for them to revise. Now I ask them to ask the bot to generate an exam for them. So, they come to the exam more relaxed because they can generate more questions and do their own exams.”

At the finals in August, the average score among his 50 or so students was three percentage points higher than in previous years — an outcome he concedes could also be due to a better-than-average cohort.

As part of the course, Biton continues to hold 90-minute sessions with his students four to six times a year, where he picks a topic from the course for a deeper discussion. He notes, however, that his role is transforming from pure teaching to mentoring now that the learning agent makes it easier to find course information.

“Knowledge is no longer the problem,” he says, referring to how quickly AI can retrieve that information. “But what I can do better than a chatbot is to mentor, to guide the student on how to learn and how to approach challenges in the real world.”

For Shay, the AI agent is an add-on, not a replacement for her teachers.

“It’s something that you build on, and then you get a better understanding of the course,” she says. “So it’s something that goes with the lecturer, not instead of the lecturer.”

Top Image: BIU is one of Israel’s leading public research universities. It introduced the learning agent in 71 courses and plans to expand it to another 100 courses. Photo by Ron Rahamim for Microsoft.

title: Open From Data Center to Desktop: NVIDIA Expands Nemotron Family With Highest Efficiency Super VL and Bolt Models
body:
NVIDIA today released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open 120-billion-parameter model that delivers the fastest task completion and highest accuracy for specialized always-on agents.
Joining it are two new edge models: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, optimized to balance intelligence and speed per GB for local agentic workloads, and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, optimized for intelligence per GB for fast conversational agents.
Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming Oct. 23.
The three [open models](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/open-models/) together cover the full range of agent deployments, from large enterprise servers down to edge devices and local hardware.
Any organization that wants to run agents on NVIDIA infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier, without having to choose between capability and deployability.
Super VL and Bolt join the Nemotron family alongside [Lightning](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/nemotron-lightning-switchyard-rtx-dgx/) and Ultra.
Lightning, released in August, handles high-throughput workloads; Ultra handles the hardest reasoning tasks; and Bolt brings intelligence to the edge.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL: Frontier Accuracy at One-Fifth the Size
Super VL, built in collaboration with the [Nemotron Coalition](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-launches-nemotron-coalition-of-leading-global-ai-labs-to-advance-open-frontier-models), delivers leading accuracy on multimodal agentic tasks — instruction following, tool use, multistep business workflows, and visual understanding — comparable with NVIDIA’s largest reasoning model at roughly one-fifth the parameter count.
As the fastest open agentic model in its class — 5x faster than the next best — it helps enterprise agents complete high-volume tasks faster across workflows that span days or weeks.
Unlike closed frontier models, organizations can post-train Super VL on their own data, deploy it on their own infrastructure and oversee what they build.
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt: Agentic Intelligence at the Edge
Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is designed to run everyday agentic tasks locally on NVIDIA RTX/DGX Spark, using a native 2-bit quantization to fit in 24GB of memory and run alongside other applications.
Relative to other models with a similar memory footprint, it provides a good balance of intelligence and speed: smart enough to get most jobs done, yet much faster than the smartest models.
With Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, users can delegate their projects to popular local agent harnesses — from researching the web to writing to debugging code — all without sending those workloads to the cloud. It is the #1 open model in its class on [PinchBench](https://pinchbench.com/?slm=true), and the #2 open model for [BrowseComp](https://leaderboard.steel.dev/leaderboards/browsecomp/?weights=open&sizes=tiny%2Csmall%2Cmedium).
Bolt E4B 4GB is built for physical and conversational agents on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. It combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power fast local voice assistants, interactive characters and embedded interfaces.
Adoption of Custom Super Intelligence
Dozens of organizations across industries are post-training Super VL on their own data, tools, policies and workflows to push accuracy higher on the specialized tasks that define their agent deployments.
Super VL is being post-trained and customized by organizations across industries. [Scale AI](https://scale.com/blog/scale-partners-with-nvidia) post-trained the model for Skydance’s vendor credit finance agent and for EY’s M&A due diligence agent. AfterQuery customized the model for Hebbia for credit agreement analysis. [AI21](https://www.ai21.com/blog/ai21-post-trains-nvidia-nemotron-35-super-vl/) and [Alice](http://alice.io/blog/nemotron-ai21) post-trained the model for cybersecurity attack resilience. Mercor post-trained the model on APEX-SWE coding benchmark, for coding agents that plan, write and debug code. [ModelScope](https://modelscope.ai/collections/nv-community/Nemotron-35-Super-VL) enables developers to fine-tune the model through its [ms-swift ](https://github.com/modelscope/ms-swift)framework for specialized multimodal applications.
Additional organizations customizing Nemotron 3.5 Super VL include Ramp for financial document intelligence; Dream, sovereign AI-powered cybersecurity research and vulnerability analysis; Lila Sciences for scientific discovery and search, and [R1](http://www.r1rcm.com/resources/long-context-medical-reasoning-to-reduce-denials-post-training-nvidia-nemotron-3-5-super) for medical claims analysis and revenue cycle management. TrainLoop post-trained the model with dermatology data from Nolla, which just became the first company approved for AI to write initial patient prescriptions.
Software platform companies integrating Nemotron 3.5 Super VL include:
- Atlassian, for tasks like agentic search across apps such as Jira and Confluence.
- CrowdStrike, which is customizing the model for agentic blue teaming in enterprise security.
- Dassault Systèmes, powering engineering design and simulation.
- Perplexity, for search and agentic tasks in Perplexity Search and Computer.
[Salesforce](https://www.salesforce.com/news/press-releases/2026/09/15/koa-reasoning-model/), which is customizing Nemotron to power AI agents that digitize and automate complex government workflows in secure customer environments through Missionforce Operations.- Synopsys software for semiconductor design verification interoperates with the model.
What Nemotron 3.5 Super VL Actually Sees
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL’s [vision language](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/vision-language-models/) strengths are targeted at what agents encounter in practice: optical character recognition, tables, charts and structured information in visual documents.
It processes a web page, extracts text, reads graphs and charts, and returns insights from what it finds. The same applies to PDFs and other documents agents commonly work with.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL understands images, webpages and PDFs and acts on that understanding. Combining text and visual understanding in one model means agents don’t need to route tasks between separate systems — context carries through as work moves from document to data to decision.
Open for Maximum Control, Security, and Privacy
Openness and customizability reinforce each other. The model ships with open weights, open datasets and training recipes.
Control runs in two directions. Organizations can run the model wherever their security and data-residency requirements dictate. They also choose to adopt a model they can adapt, rather than one subject to a provider’s restrictions.
In insurance, for example, a customized agent can scan claims for fraud markers on repeat. In financial services, an agent can review credit scores and flag activity against an organization’s own lending criteria. The model stays on premises. The data stays private.
Customization is supported through NVIDIA NeMo, Python-based pipelines and open datasets.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL was trained on about 26 trillion tokens across [pretraining](https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/nemotron-pre-training-datasets) and continued pretraining, then post-trained with roughly 3.8 million samples and reinforcement learning across dozens of environments.
NVIDIA is also releasing open datasets on Hugging Face spanning [agentic tool use](https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/nemotron-post-training-v3), finance, instruction following, long context, fairness and vision-language understanding, along with the reinforcement learning environments in NeMo Gym.
[NVIDIA NIM](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/products/nim-microservices/) packages the model as a production-ready microservice with performance-optimized, validated configurations and enterprise-grade support, refreshed every two weeks with security patches and performance improvements.
And with the model running on NVIDIA Dynamo, organizations can serve up to 8x more users with 85% lower latency.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is available now on Hugging Face, Open Router, [ModelScope community](https://modelscope.ai/collections/nv-community/Nemotron-35-Super-VL) and as NVIDIA NIM.
Runs on DGX Spark, DGX Station, and RTX
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL runs across NVIDIA’s full hardware stack: on [DGX Spark](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark/), [DGX Station](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-station/), RTX PRO and RTX systems for local intelligence at the desktop, on [NVIDIA Jetson](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/autonomous-machines/embedded-systems/) at the edge, and across data center and cloud environments.
[Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-24GB/) is available now on Hugging Face, with support for llama.cpp, [Ollama](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B-24GB-GGUF), [LM Studio](https://lmstudio.ai/models/nvidia/nemotron-3.5-bolt-74b-a9b), [Unsloth](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/nemotron-3.5-bolt), and [vLLM](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B-24GB). Built for [NVIDIA RTX Spark laptops](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/rtx-spark/) arriving Oct. 16, it also runs on [GeForce RTX PCs](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-on-rtx/), [DGX Spark](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark/), [DGX Station](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-station/) and [RTX PRO workstations](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/).
Download the [open weights](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4), explore customization resources with NVIDIA NeMo, or read the [technical blog](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-nemotron-3-5-super-vl-powers-specialized-agents-with-multimodal-reasoning/) for the full architecture breakdown.
Stay up to date on agents, NVIDIA[ Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) and more by subscribing to[ NVIDIA news](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/executive-insights/generative-ai-tools/?modal=stay-inf),[ joining the community](https://developer.nvidia.com/community), and following NVIDIA AI on[ LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/showcase/nvidia-ai/posts/?feedView=all),[ Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/nvidiaai/?hl=en),[ X](https://x.com/NVIDIAAIDev) and[ Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/NVIDIAAI).
Explore[ self-paced video tutorials and livestreams](https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PL5B692fm6--vdRKB14FImVi7MTJ77zjn4&feature=shared).

title: What will the next generation of developers do when AI writes the code?
body:
Published Time: 2026-10-15T15:00:22+00:00

Markdown Content:
Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon University are betting that the junior developers we train today will be the senior engineers of tomorrow.

By [Mark Russinovich](http://commandline.microsoft.com/author/mark-russinovich)CTO, Deputy CISO, and Technical Fellow, Microsoft Azure and [Scott Hanselman](http://commandline.microsoft.com/author/scott-hanselman)VP, Member of Technical Staff, Microsoft

2026.10.15

When AI can produce code in seconds, what is the job of a software engineer? For someone graduating with a computer science degree, what is the future of your daily work if it’s not coding? And when AI is designing the architecture, writing the code, and fixing the problems, how does a software engineer learn software engineering?

Microsoft and [Carnegie Mellon University](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/news/2026/microsoft-cmu-praise) are betting that the career of a software developer is here to stay—and that the junior developers we train today will be the senior engineers of tomorrow.

That’s why we launched PRAISE: an internal preceptorship program that pairs junior engineers early in their careers with senior engineering preceptors. PRAISE stands for Preceptorship for AI-accelerated Software Engineering.

We borrow the preceptorship concept from nursing, where new nurses are paired with experienced nurses to build real-world experience and confidence. The goal isn’t to keep newcomers coding as though AI never arrived. It is to help them develop the understanding, confidence, and accountability to build in the new ways we’re all learning in real-time.

The partnership links practical engineering experience with academic instruction, rather than asking either academic institutions or companies to solely carry the responsibility of training the next generation of engineers.

## Does a CS degree matter anymore? Yes, it does

People asking if software engineering degrees still matter when AI can code—and any human can use prompts to build an app—are asking the wrong question. Would these same people ship AI code in a finished product sight unseen (please, we implore you, say no)?

Of course we need junior software engineers. Senior engineers ensure the technology we ship works safely and effectively, and today’s junior engineers will be tomorrow’s senior engineers.

Coding with AI is only one part of the evolving software development lifecycle. More of our time is now spent on design and architecture than coding every line. But that doesn’t change the need for us to understand what the underlying code does, even if we’re not writing all of it by hand. After all, when a car breaks down, it takes someone who knows what’s going on under the hood to get it back on the road.

With PRAISE, preceptors coach their preceptees to use AI tools thoughtfully, while building strong systems thinking, taste, and judgement. Just as we evolved and abstracted certain elements of software engineering by using compilers, engineers are now adapting to using AI where it provides efficiency in the overall process of creating a product.

AI changes the work; it does not remove human responsibility for outcomes. Preparing the next generation of engineers means giving them access to both AI tools and experienced guides, so they can grow from producing code to deciding what deserves to be built in the first place.

## How the preceptor and preceptee model works

What does the PRAISE model look like in the workplace? Similarly to the nursing model of preceptorship, the key is creating space for junior engineers to workshop questions and problems with senior engineers. Senior engineers need to understand that their junior team members might not always have the confidence to contribute to projects at the speed and scale possible after years in the industry. Building that confidence and rapport with their preceptor gives junior engineers room to learn by doing—not simply watching someone else solve problems.

The preceptor also shares their insights, explains their taste and approach to solving a problem, and provides tips with examples. They can also advise the preceptees on where to focus based on their skills and knowledge.

We teach junior engineers to test assumptions and discuss unfamiliar changes with their colleagues. Mentorship helps turn the process of producing a solution into deliberate learning.

That judgement for when to use AI should be viewed as ongoing education, which is why we’re partnering with Carnegie Mellon University on curriculum as part of the PRAISE program. The intent is to set students up for success in the workplace and accelerate preceptees with formal curricula to complement the guidance from the preceptor on how to build and deliver with confidence.

The courses give them early experiences in how to deploy production-ready solutions. Preceptees will take classes and participate in small group discussions to bridge theoretical concepts of computer science to real-world software engineering practices and their work at Microsoft. The curriculum at Carnegie Mellon University augments the on-the-job learning that engineers get at Microsoft from their teams and preceptors, adding formal classroom education to their training.

“It used to be that early-career software engineers would do a lot of tasks that would build up their expertise,” said Michael Hilton, Teaching Professor & Associate Department Head for Education in the Software and Societal Systems Department at Carnegie Mellon University’s Kenneth C. Griffin School of Computer Science. “Combining forces between academics and practitioners allows us to bring our expertise together and create solutions that draw on computer science research while standing up to the daily realities of software development.”

We’re excited to work with Carnegie Mellon University to train the next generation of software engineers, helping to maintain a healthy talent pipeline for the future workforce.

title: Give your agent a goal, and let it be creative
body:
Learn how to use verification and continuous improvement to make your AI agents better over time. In this video, I walk through building a custom video editor and using a scorecard system to track performance metrics, then having agents autonomously work to improve them day after day.

title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
body:
15th October 2026 - Link Blog
[Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO](https://www.ft.com/content/11632d03-358c-454b-af95-d06d4072932b?syn-25a6b1a6=1). The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from "[people with knowledge of the matter](https://simonwillison.net/2023/Nov/22/deciphering-clues/#hints-to-look-out-for)".
Key things I learned from the article:
- Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn"
- Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn
- Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn
- In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power"
- Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11%
This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine):
The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones.
When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending.
Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter.
Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter!
Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" ([previously](https://simonwillison.net/2026/May/29/anthropic/)) in these communications to their investors.
